The meal was served on a wood plank with side salad and balsamic dressing. The sourdough bread was lightly toasted/grilled, and the chicken, cheese, aioli and lettuce held together well, and tasted great.  The side salad was mostly green with romaine, escarole, carrot slivers and vinegar. It was okay.  Overall, it was a solid, tasty lunch.  With the root beer and tip it came to $22 per person, which is rich for my blood for a midweek lunch. 

Still, it was worthwhile to get inside Vault and appreciate how attractive it was in a dark wood, cloudy, kind of way. On this rainy afternoon, it exuded a quiet historic tone that was relaxing. It definitely calls for a return call, when there is time to enjoy their brewer's craft, and deconstruct one of their pizzas or other tapas.

Santangelo's Cafe is a down to earth example of creative adaptive reuse of old urban factories, this one in Norristown, PA. It is a tiny place with entry around the back of the large red brick structure, requiring attention to signs on the street directing where it is hidden. Plenty of parking back there. 

This family run breakfast, brunch & lunch joint has been going for 15 years, and the siblings certainly know how to work together. They are friendly and justly proud of what they do in the community. I sat at the six stool counter overlooking the small kitchen. Although a curtain separates customer view from flying spatula, the sounds of breakfast making are easily heard and entertaining. 

Coffee was decent, and my ask for milk over Mini Moos, graciously met. Unfortunately, it took too long to get a refill, as the curtain blocked the staff view of customers, and the floor person was obliviously attached to her phone. Yet, the short stack french toast was very good. Nice egg, vanilla and cinnamon mix for dipping, and good caramelization. 

Overall, Santangelo's is a strong find on the post industrial streets of Norristown. A little polish on customer service would elevate this earnest cafe to a higher level to match the quality of its menu.

Thai Orchid of Blue Bell is a beautifully appointed Siamese restaurant on DeKalb Pike in the wonderfully named town of Blue Bell, PA. It is one of those places where the environment is so rich in southeast Asian colors, textures and artistry, that it is possible to eat the atmosphere. From woodcuts to tapestry the space is relaxed and mellow enough to have you believing you've stepped into a palace in Chiangmai. 

I was there for late lunch after a meeting in Norristown. The shop sits in a strip center, the last door on the far right. Don't be put off by that or you'll miss all the magic. There was only one other customer dining when I arrived and was taken to a table on a raised platform that held most of the tables. The menu was full of Thai delights, and lunch combo specials that included soup, appetizer and main entree, for around $10 and change. That seemed the way to go to sample a few things and get more bang for the buck. I went with the Thai Ravioli Soup (wonton), Veggie Roll and Drunken Noodles. 

Believe me, it was a huge amount of food. The soup was vegetable based broth with fancy goldfish wonton filled with ground shrimp and chicken. It had a mild sesame oil flavor and tasted fresh and pleasing. The roll was deep fried with a filling of mixed vegetables, glass noodles and a small dish of sweet & sour dipping sauce. It was good, but a tad over fried.

 The drunken noodle was a large plate full of medium width noodles (not jumbo), loaded with chunky onions, bell peppers, green beans, fresh basil, thin sliced beef and moderately hot Thai spices. I asked for it to be very chilified, but it was still pretty tame. It seems that regardless of what you ask for on the heat scale, it is interpreted as only moderately spicy. How you actually get the "Very spicy yet Bearable," fire level is beyond me. Here, it cost them a star for failing to honor my clear direction. 

Aside from the width of the noodles and the lack of burn, this was a very satisfying meal, and enough to keep me sated for the rest of the day. The decor and food together make Thai Orchid of Blue Bell a worthy stop for quality exotic cuisine. It would be even better if they paid closer attention to what was being requested.

You have to really want to get to Mood Indian Restaurant because the approach is a challenge.

 When 95 South was jammed south of Girard, I was able to jump off, zigzag my way to Spring Garden, make a left on N.4th, and start looking for my destination.  There it was, but at first view it seemed to be behind bars.  Fences and security everywhere.  Reminded of prison gates.  Quickly realized all that parking was for residents, and the street meters were the only nearby option.  At 12 minutes for .25 on a Saturday night, I fished out all my quarters and fed the hungry metal mouth. Then located the narrow opening in the fence and the walkway leading to the resto.  I hoped I had all the necessary credentials to get through customs. 

The boss was squeegeeing his front windows as I walked up to the door.  I was impressed that he had not delegated the work, but took pride in his shop's appearance, knowing that first impressions are so important.  Stepping inside after confirming I had arrived with Ali, I was taken by the crispness of the white linen tablecloths and red napkins.  The space had high industrial ceilings, giving an open sensation.  I was shown to the table and sat down to await the arrival of my friends.  I was alone there at 6 pm; thinking that Indians/Pakistanis prefer late dinners.  I liked the vibe as I perused the menu and took in the details.  

After V & M arrived, we ordered several dishes to get a cross section of the kitchen fare.  Samosa Chaat, Chicken Malabar for apps; Salmon Tandoori, Chicken Makhani, Baingan Bharta(Eggplant), a Bread Basket mix, and Basmati Rice as entrees.   Mango Lassi for me, and Sweet Lassi for M.   All were good to excellent. Most memorable were the Chicken Malabar which was grilled and breaded with Coconut, the Samosa Chaat, which had all the ingredients of a Samosa, but reformulated into an open dish full of Potato, Peas, various crunchy chips and spices. Additionally, the Baingan Bharta was very well done with a complementary heat/sweet texture, and the Makhani was tender in a Tomato base curry that was requested hot spiced and delivered fully.  The Salmon Tandoori was the most colorful dish (see photo), but the fish was a tad dry and the veggies and spices so overpoweringly good, that the mild taste of the Salmon was somewhat hidden by its pushy roommates. 

All in all, a very good meal in a pleasant environment.  By the time we left around 8, the room was full, along with our stomachs.  We ended up taking a large portion home with us.  

I will definitely return once they let me out on parole.

Samarkand is an ancient city in Uzbekistan in western Asia.  It sits astride the Silk Road that Marco Polo travelled on his journeys to the East.  It remains a beautiful and mysterious place with many old walls, narrow streets and amazing markets.  As a centuries old melting pot, it has created its own cultural reality; among the most interesting of which is food.  Taking from cuisine as far away as India, China and the Middle East, their kitchens at once remind you of each of those unique tastes, and at the same time something quite original.  

A visit to Samarkand Restaurant is a much easier way to experience this exotic taste, than to make the overland caravan to this still isolated treasure.  Right in Bucks County the flavor and texture of Uzbeki dishes are available in a house with archways and desert murals that with a little imagination brings you right there. True, this is just the northern outpost of an ever expanding community of Soviet emigres who have settled in Northeast Philly, of which Uzbeks are but a part. Still, some would argue they are the most colorful and delicious. Leave that discussion for others while you take a trip to a terrific meal. 

Our approach was to tapas the appetizers, including mushroom and white corn soup, samsa, cheburek and kutab, followed by lamb and salmon shish kebob.  We shared everything. Service was friendly and attractive in Russian accent. 

Each element was very good to outstanding. Their use of dough to make all the apps was fascinating, as each was different and flavorful, depending on whether baked, deep fried or skillet heated. The lamb and salmon managed to be moist and well grilled at the same time. Excellent hands in the kitchen. 

We finished lunch with their crepe dessert, stuffed with mildly sweet and sour cream, and drizzled with Nutella. It caused a nostalgia wave as sensory images of my grandmother's cheese blintzes danced in my head. Loved them! 

Few of us have broad exposure to Uzbek cuisine, but I intend to spend more time exploring it, as it is quite unusual, fun and delicious.

If you are a Spaetzle lover, Barbara's Hungarian Restaurant is your Nirvana.  Ask for a side of the East European doughy pasta, and it will arrive covering the entire plate. To its credit, it is pretty good, especially with the sour cream mixed into it.  

The rest of our meals were not up to its signature dish.  We ordered the Mushroom Stew and Breaded Chicken Cutlet (Schnitzel).  The Mushrooms were canned, and the sauce the same weak reddish liquid that was at the bottom of the chicken dish.  Little imagination. Less taste.
 
Canned mushrooms? Really? 

The Chicken Breast was large, thick and nicely breaded.  It was juicy, and would have been the winner but for the saltiness of the coating.  It was obvious no one had bothered to taste the ingredients and preparations in the kitchen.  

Both dishes came with Spaetzle overload.  The Mushroom Stew was really canned shrooms and spaetzle, with nothing else to make it a "stew."  The chicken lay naked on another thick bed of the same thing.  Nary a garnish or side dish to break the monotony.  It must have been obvious, because we were offered a Cucumber Salad by Barbara when she saw how forlorn our meals appeared.  That salad was the best part of the meal, although it would have been nice to know we were being charged $5 for that small bowl with sweet vinegar and thin sliced cukes.  

Maybe, they were having a bad night, but based on our experience I wouldn't consider going back.  There are far better East European restaurants in the area where the cuisine really shines.

This Steve's Prince of Steaks is on Comly Road, just off northbound Roosevelt Boulevard, Somerton, PA, in the far Northeast of the city. If possible, it is even smaller than my regular Steve's on Rt. 1 in Langhorne. There are two windows within. One for ordering your sandwich, for which they have posted a long list of rules to follow to get what you want, and the other only for fries and drinks. Like the rest, the burden is on you to know what you're doing, or face the consternation of the staff and your fellow steak lovers. Not an enviable place to be.

I ordered two "cheesesteaks wit provolone," meaning I wanted two sandwiches with fried onions and provolone cheese. I like the Wiz, too, but preferred the extra mellowness offered by the hard white variation. It set me back $25+. Not unexpected, but I'd be lying if I didn't do a double clutch before paying the dude taking my business. 

Normally, we would eat right along the walls at the Langhorne joint, but this shop was smaller and without short shelves and stools. We took them home to consume. These guys are fast and efficient, and it was fun to watch them work through the greasy glass window that separates kitchen from customers. It would have been a thoroughly enjoyable moment, but for Mr. Priss shouting not to take photos (after the last one). 

Oh, me. Oh, my! Have to protect those state secrets. 

At home, we added our own banana pepper rings to bring up the burn; the pickle bar being removed as a casualty of COVID. It was love at first bite. Great cross section of taste and texture as we incisored through the excellent torpedo roll, cheese and ribeye. My wife and I shared one sandwich, and left the other for her still growing son (6'3"). 

I have no dog in the fight between the chopped vs. solid slice approach to this Philly delicacy. I like them both ways, as long as the beef used is high quality. Steve's is among my faves, but with every pizza shop making their own version, we are really living in Cheesesteak Heaven around here. The worst one in the Philadelphia region is better than anything anywhere else.

Just attended a private party in one of Piccolo Trattoria's side rooms in their Newtown store. It went very well. 

We were about 20 people celebrating a successful election season in town. The victorious candidates, their families and the campaign team came together with our own wine and beer, and a pre-selected menu of three entree choices (chicken francaise, eggplant parmesan and grilled tilapia) side salad, penne vodka, bread and tomato based dipping sauce. We had two servers assigned to us who did a great job of keeping everything moving. 

I split the chicken and eggplant with someone, and both were excellent. The egg/lemon/white wine reduction was tart and played well with the pan sauteed tender bird and was ample enough to allow sipping up with the fresh homemade bread. The eggplant was likewise thin sliced and pan fried before going into the oven to meld with the tomato sauce and mozzarella. Delicious. 

With a few glasses of Cabernet Sauvignon, a final sweet bite of chocolate chip mini cannolli and friendly conversation about gearing up for a more successful 2020 presidential election, we were on our way out the door in two hours. 

Hope we weren't too boisterous. We will need the other diners to support our people next year.

MyThai Kitchen recently opened on Brownsville Road, Trevose, PA. It is in an old tiny strip with a narrow parking field right in front. Easy enough to get in, but a bit challenging when departing. Don't let that deter you, because once inside you enter a simple dining room with about a half dozen wood topped tables, and honest to goodness Thai dishes prepared with love and attention by folks who came naturally by their skills - they lived them from birth. No Thai pretenders here.

I was there for a late lunch, arriving just short of 3:00 to an empty house. I was greeted warmly by two women, one the chef and the other working the front room. They thanked me for coming, directed me to a table in the front corner and handed me their small double sided menu. I was in time for the lunch special. I ordered a small bowl of tom yum soup, drunken noodles with beef and an iced tea. I asked them to bring the heat. 

The soup was strongly spiced with lemongrass and loaded with veggies, including fresh mushrooms. The first spoonful took my breath away, but I adjusted to the spicy boil and enjoyed it the rest of the way. I asked for high flames and that was what I got. I was pleased they did not make any "cultural adjustment" for a presumed western pallette. The noodles were broad and mixed with peppers and other multicolored vegetables. Thin slices of grilled beef finished the plate, along with an excellent opulent brown sauce. Loved all of it. The 10% grand opening discount was another nice touch (without asking).

Service was attentive and attractive from the orange apron woman. She stopped by often to see how I was doing and to answer my questions. On my way out I asked to take a photo to memorialize my visit. My wish was granted. 

Take a look and tell me you wouldn't return as soon as possible for more authentic Thai cuisine!

Red Lion Diner in Horsham gives the impression of having had better days. The decor is somewhat worn with torn vinyl seats and dirty wall to walls. The menu attempts to cover the traditional bases, but only in a limited way by offering expected categories with only a few options in each. For example, their breakfast menu fits on half a page of a four sided laminate, rather than running on forever with combinations of possibilities. 

My morning choices were a cup of Chicken Pastina Soup, which was quite good loaded with well cooked veggies, strips of chicken and tiny pastina pasta. Second, came a Sausage, Egg and Cheese on Kaiser, which while filling with two sausage patties, 2 eggs and lots of white gooey, came packaged in the sorriest looking ragged roll I've seen in years. Guess the budget didn't allow for decent bread provisions. It was crushed, dry and lifeless, and took most of the joy out of the substance of the meal. 

Service was fine, bit not exemplary, and managed to pick one of my nits - Asked for milk for my coffee, but got those mini moos, with unwanted and non-nutritious fat and empty calories. 

The soup was definitely the star of this show, leading to the reasonable conclusion that Red Lion was oriented toward lunch, much more than breakfast.

Solstice, the nouveau cuisine restaurant recently opened in the Village @ Newtown Shopping Center, bring something attractive and creative to the fairly standard kitchens that are crowding into town recently. Its space is open and bright, with high ceilings and the feel of a summer home at the beach on a sunny summer day. Walking in for our reservation immediately shifted my attitude from just another dinner, to the possibility of something transformative. It was that beautiful and unexpected. 

The staff was equal to the environment, and took great care of us from seating to, "Thanks for coming. Hope to see you again soon." Likewise, the menu offerings were seasonal, with many vegetarian oriented appetizers and entrees. The summer listings were a cross between colorful blends of meat and leaf, pasta and creative takes on traditional dishes. We went with Lobster Risotto, Filet (medium well), Braised Waygu Short Rib & Mashed, and Sweet Corn Ricotta Gnocchi. I also sampled the Cantelope Gazpacho to broaden our exposure to their kitchen. 

The result was less than perfection, but strong enough to appreciate what the chef was trying to do to separate Solstice from the ragtag assortment of other houses in the neighborhood. Special merit to the Gazpacho, which was just a delicious cold soup on an extremely hot day. In fact, it was the best thing brought to our table. 

The Risotto was visually stunning with the yellow rice base and orange lobster, but not the most tasty rendition available for these ingredients. Liked it. Didn't love it. The Filet was mild pink throughout as described by our server, yet somewhat thinner than anticipated and less flavorful than hoped. Admittedly, my stepson may have been influenced by the same cut he ordered last week at Rocco's, which knocked his socks off. This slab was certainly less overwhelming, but still decent. It just suffered by comparison. 

The Short Rib was perfectly cooked and was again a stunning visual presentation. The sauce could have used more zip, as it had the texture/flavor of American roast beef, rather than accentuating the Waygu or the many Asian or citrus spices that could have made this dish sing. In the same way, the Gnocchi was tender and mixed very well with the veggies and shaved cheese, but had a excess of water at the bottom of the deep plate and was a bit salty. As you can tell, everything was good to excellent, but each left something to be desired. 

There will be a next time, but our approach will be to treat Solstice as a tapas house. We will order several appetizers, rather than entrees, and enjoy tasting many more of their creative dishes. The Gazpacho was the best we tried, and the hummus and other small plates seemed to have potential as we scanned the other tables for reactions to the food. I suspect, without knowing, that this may be the way to go.

Wild Ginger III in the Logan Square Shopping Center, New Hope, has a great name and suggests a deep excursion into the jungles of Southeast Asia. The layout of the restaurant reinforced that sensibility with huge tropical fish tanks and beautiful blue, green and indigo neon lit walls and ceiling. 

It is an auspicious beginning for a new guest, although the fishy smell permeating the room from both the tanks and sushi bar do detract from the gestalt somewhat. Unfortunately, that is not where the disappointment ends. 

I was there for the Thai and Chinese offerings of its fusion menu. Tom Kar (lemongrass/coconut milk soup), Pad Kee Mao and Szechuan Beef were my choices. I planned to eat the first two in house and take the third home for later consumption by the family working until later that evening. I like spicy dishes unadulterated forward the western pallette, so I asked for the hottest rendition available. I wasn't kidding, but the kitchen didn't believe me. 

The soup had plenty of fresh veggies and sweet coconut juice, but lacked the kick of lemongrass. It wasn't in the pot!  Rather than red chili infused broad drunken noodles in a super heated brown sauce, what I got was actually sweet to my tongue, without a hint of the desired fire. I had to send it back to be reworked. It returned, the same noodles, but with some chili sauce or ground Szechuan red peppers or paste mixed in. It wasn't integrated, but I spun it for a moment and it was acceptable. Shame, because the noodles, veggies and chicken were all tender and done well. 

At home we dug into the Szechuan Beef over rice. Again, it looked great and properly wokked, but without a sign of red chili pepper. It was hot as requested, but the burn came from chili powder or paste thrown into the sauce that attached itself to the meat far more that the broccoli, onions and green peppers. Not bad, but clearly prepared by a kitchen lacking the right ingredients to actually produce a Szechuan dish correctly. 

Disappointing.

Wild Ginger is a misnomer. "Mild Ginger," is closer to the truth. Another case of Asian confusion, not fusion.

Be Well Bakery & Cafe does it right.

Not only is the house cozy and spacious, the java very good and the bakery products excellent, but it is all wrapped into a business philosophy that promotes community, creativity, healthy living and complete genuineness. 

All very noble, right? But, let's get back to their house goodies for a second. I was tempted by their lemon tart in the display case. I love lemon bars, so I figured, why not? It was awesome! Creamy tart/sweet lemon filling, thin, flakey crust, plump, cool blueberries sitting on top. An orgy in my mouth. 

There are a lot of good bakeries and coffee houses these days; not as many in combination. Be Well is certainly one of the best of the genre in the region. 

All this in a beautiful part of Montgomery County, just down the road from Bryn Athyn Cathedral and Historic District. Worthwhile drive with Be Well as the final destination.

Decent chicken salad sandwich, but the place is really dirty. Sat at a small table downstairs in their basement shop. The cracks in the red paint were black with grime and lack of strong cleanser for too long. Same for the floor and back shelves and undercounted storage space. 

Need to do better and care more, even if never inspected by L & I.

The name on the Spring Menu breakfast was: "I Can't Believe They're Vegan Pancakes." 

Well, now I know that was just a bit of clever marketing, because after eating the nearly tasteless, dry, syrup sponges, I now fully believe they WERE vegan, and in a word, "boring."  My high hopes were dashed by reality. 

But, I forgive Turning Point for misleading me, because everything else about their new facility in the Village @ Newtown Shopping Center, is first class. The room is sun filled, bright and airy, with high fanned ceilings, white walls, and copious amounts of glass, letting customers be part of any sunny day outside while they sup within. A definite country cottage vibe throughout. Service is uber friendly without being unctuous, and the $2.50 house brewed java comes with a insulted pitcher of coffee, mug, and small glass carafe of milk (upon request). More than enough for me. 

I enjoyed sitting at the bar and watching the coffee operation in front of me, and the dining room activity through the backbar mirrors. The rest of the menu was appealing for both morning and afternoon meals, even if the prices reflected the cost of Newtown's newly discovered sophistication (falling into the category of be careful what you wish for). 

Turning Point, like its sibling nearby, Harvest, is the new order of things around here. Along with all the other restaurants already there, and those being planned (Chipotle, Iron Hill, Starbucks, Melt Shop, etc.), they will either become a sought after destination for fast casual dining, or a place to be avoided because of inadequate parking, and too much sameness. There is already talk of the center becoming a food court. 

It definitely feels like a gold rush around here, and it remains to be seen how deep and wide the rich vein goes. It will thrive for a while, but whether it becomes a permanent part of life or a ghost town, depends on changing tastes, the local economy and how well conceived the plans were at the start.

If mid-20th Century stainless steel railroad car diners are your thing, then Daddypops on York Road in Hatboro, PA, is a "must see" stop on your diner tour.  It sits on the main street in town, all shiny and bright over all these years. The granite counter is split by the kitchen entrance, with a half dozen spinners on each side, and creatively anchored at each elbow by an old barber's chair.  The outer wall is all booths and large windows. The joint oozes Americana charm. 

The menu consists of one sheet, with breakfast on one side, and lunch on the other. Best to plan early meals, as the hours are only from 6:00 AM to 2:00 PM. I sat at the far left counter where I could see the entire dining area.  The two women working the floor were friendly, but respectful - no one called me, "Honey." They were efficient, and ever ready with a hot coffee pour. I sipped my java while awaiting the arrival of my french toast. 

The three bisected thick slices of brioche were served on an oval plate that barely contained its load.  Side dish full of butter cups and Kraft syrup was close at hand for proper doctoring.  I could see that the bread had bathed in the egg/vanilla mix long enough to soak through to the core. The surface was nicely caramelized with enough crispy edges to provide the texture I like.  Allowing time for the butter to melt and run, and the syrup to absorb, I was quickly ready to dive in.  

It was very good.  

No dry spots.  No eggy extrusions. No scorch marks. Nothing fancy at this traditional meal hall. Just perfectly finished egg toast fry that was a pleasure to consume. Old fashioned, just like the house it was made in.

Beautifully converted Lamberville, NJ mansion that offers three squares a day in a quiet, dignified house with plenty of space between the tables for intimate conversation surrounding very good victuals. All very late 19th Century. 

I was there for midweek breakfast and walked in to a mostly empty restaurant.  There is an attractive marble counter with stools, but it was loaded with desserts and didn't seem the place designed to really eat. So, I walked to the next dining room, where there was one other table occupied, but so far across the room that I felt totally alone taking a smaller deuce along the opposite wall facing a window.  

Each table in this room was rough cut from a larger tree trunk and finished with smooth top, but the edges left rough. Beautiful. I'd love one for home. 

The menu is fairly small for the morning meal, and pricing is oriented toward higher end cafes, rather than more reasonable primarily breakfast joints. Still, my turkey sausage, fried egg and cheddar on an unusually attractive and tasty roll, reflected the gourmand focus.  Execution was superlative.  My server incorporated my choice for "lightly runny" eggs with aplomb. That is exactly what I got. Coffee from Counter Culture. Not sure why they don't use java from local roasters better than this North Carolina outfit given the trend toward local sourcing. Still, it was solid Joe, refilled gracefully as needed. 

Nothing run of the mill about Café Galleria. If you're into morning romantic interludes, this is the place.

COVID-19 TAKEOUT REVIEW

Out on York Road just before it enters Montgomery County from Bucks, sits Rey Azteca (King of the Aztecs), a decent Casa Mexicana located in what looks to have been formerly a Pizza Hut. Adequate parking and nicely remodeled interior with those colorful carved chair backs and murals depicting the bright life made famous in all the pastel paintings sold on the streets of almost every small villa in Mexico.  Looking for a place to pick up a good meal, I picked this one because of strong reviews and relative proximity. 

Bottom line - It lost something in-between house and store, as many carry-outs do. Sitting in aluminum containers and covered to keep in all the moisture, it was no longer as fresh and crisp as they would have been if eaten right there. 

The Steak Fajitas were plentiful, but overcooked and too chewy when eaten at our kitchen table. Far too well-done and dried out. The side salad, guac and crema tasted good, but couldn't revive what was already deceased. Luckily, the Los Coco's Special (two beef/chicken quesadillas with red rice) was much better, especially with salsa roja generously applied over top. Very satisfied. 

Neither dish came with the promised side tortillas. 

The Chip & Salsa was a hefty bag of corn crunchies and fresh tomato, jalapeno, cilantro in a large plastic bowl. They were a strong compliment. 

No doubt this meal would have been better if we had spoken with a server about how to finish the steak (medium), and done without the grillman scorch them to well done. It's hard to get it right when the only dialogue is over the phone, and all you see is a packed up brown paper sack with your name on it upon arrival. The dining room, though closed, looked inviting.

I am a little confused by this new chicken shack on Race Street in Philly Chinatown. 

Yes. It is cool the way it is an up the stairs second story shop. Its utilitarian set up with basic tables and chairs with little comfort shouts that this is a fast food joint that doesn't invite hanging around, although the wings are prepped as ordered and take 20 minutes to come out of the fryer. I am okay with all that. Yet, although called, "bbq chicken," all lower case, in fact there is no BBQ chicken there. It is all Korean-type double fried chicken wings and cold drinks, bubble teas, smoothies, etc. The wall menu has about 50 drink options, yet just 7 flavor finishes for their wings. Bird choices are wings, boneless wings or chicken sandwich. If I didn't know better, I'd think this was really another over saturated bubble tea house offering wings on the side (By comparison, Vivi around the corner is all about interesting drinks, and offers deep fried wings as a nosh, for a lot less money.).

Go figure.

What about the wings? Well, they were crispy enough, and the soy garlic and secret spicy sauces were pretty good. As others have said, the secret in the spicy was that it was more sweet than hot, although there was some warmth behind the sugar. I liked the soy garlic better, but as I slowed down after the initial rush to dive into them, I began to taste the underlying oil they were cooked in. Not so nice. 

Soho has nothing to worry about from understated lower case 'bbq chicken'. It needs to decide what it really is and let everyone know.

Mayfair Diner on Frankford Avenue in Northeast Philly, is a classic stainless steel railroad car diner.  The front dining area has been well preserved, so if you are into these iconic food circuses, Mayfair is one you should consider for your collection. 

We stopped in after a concert Saturday night.  The lights were on, and a few tables were occupied. Our server was efficient and gave us time to decide what we wanted as first timers. We ultimately ordered a patty melt, Buffalo chicken cheesesteak and hot Buffalo wings.  Everything came with a boatload of fries.  

My rye burger was pretty good, with lots of sautéed onions on top of a half pounder encased in good rye bread.  The fries were okay, but not as crisp as I like. The cheesesteak was abundant with chopped chicken, onions, peppers and gravy boat of melted cheese. The roll was decent, too. I didn't try the wings, but my son scored them as average. 

Eating in the dining car was a trip.  Although renovated, it still had the legit ambiance of a last century lunch wagon, with long counter and semi-swinging stools. It may date me, but I enjoyed this atmosphere even more than our meal.  

There are several diners along Frankford Avenue, some bigger, others smaller.  Some may have better food, but none do the "Diner Experience" better than Mayfair.

Those of us who remember and enjoyed the heyday of the Chambersburg section of Trenton, NJ, with Italian restaurants on practically every corner, felt a special sadness as one after another they began to close or move out of town to the suburbs. Over the last two decades as the neighborhood changed and the original families moved to greener lawns and better schools, they took most of their traditions and cultural institutions with them. When Amici's closed it's doors recently, the Italian era of this capital city was officially over. 

Yet, there is another casa Siciliana still going strong after 30 years at the same location. It might not be in the "Burg," but sure feels like it once you step inside. Enzo's sits almost invisibly on the northern end of Princeton Avenue in Lawrenceville, west of the Brunswick Circle. It is a small, cozy, darkly lit, romantic hideaway, where the Scozzari family has been running a pure Italian kitchen for two generations. I sure hope there is a third.

Park in back and walk past the outdoor dining area, through the front door and then a second one on the right. Step down into the small dining room and be greeted by Anna, daughter of the namesake Enzo, who will seat you at one of only dozen or so tables, and hand you the menu. Moments later, the head waiter approaches with water and description of the available specials. There is a small lunch menu with soups, sandwiches, and pasta plates. 

They didn't have the Italian Hot Dog I desired (being removed from the menu), but the suggested alternative, their "World Famous Meatball Sandwich," sounded about right. 

And, it was. Excellently garlicked, crusty toasty Italian loaf, stuffed with hand-rolled meatballs,  sauteed broccoli rabe, spinach and roasted red peppers, with a side a sweet tater fries, all on a large white round plate. Delicious! I like to deconstruction a sandwich and eat its elements separately to savor each ingredient. I did that for half and had a mouthful of flavor with each bite. It was unforgettable. The second half I attacked​ en masse. Cleaving through it and enjoying the texture and taste of each bite as they melded in my mouth. No red gravy here. Just each part doing its job to make me happy. Quite a total experience for a lunch. 

Got to go back for a romantic dinner soon with the woman of my dreams and a couple bottles of Chianti.

Enzo's is the real thing.

I am a fan of any new business that takes on the challenge of a major competitor with better goods, warmer environment and sincere service.  That Pretty Bird Coffee is about 50 yards from the green mermaid makes these folks heroic. That they are truly outclassing them is the stuff of legend. 

The space, although a small storefront, is well designed and cozy.  There are a few deuces, high communal tables and a counter for those desiring to maximize the experience by sipping in.  The staff is young and very friendly, with a few managers involved to keep everything flowing.  It was easy to engage in a pleasant conversation with them as I waited for my latte and strawberry donut (homemade). These guys are really making an effort to build their reputation and customer base.  

My latte was very good. No need for sugar or other adulterants, as it was strong and flavorful on its own.  The donuts were an indulgence, but they were sitting in the work area just staring at me. Impossible to resist.  When I took my first bite, I learned it was a cake donut with an interesting sugar/cinnamon/strawberry sprinkle topping.  Very good, but impossible to eat without a trail of crystals.  Slightly tart, too.  Liked it, but doesn't challenge Yum Yum or Mary's in the gooey goodness department.  

At $6.50 for the medium cup and the dunker, the price was okay. 

Pretty Bird is a nice place for meetups, and small conversations. 

Parking behind the building and in the adjacent lots.

Bravo Pho has replaced the earlier Vietnamese restaurant at this location, and all I can say is, "Hallelujah!" 

There is no comparison between the two enterprises. Bravo is the real deal, not just a reasonable facsimile for folks who don't know from authentic Viet cuisine. The menu is extensive, and the noodle soup (pho) and rice dishes (com) are excellent. The owners and chef are legit from Hanoi, and know their way around a Vietnamese kitchen. No excuses necessary!

I was in the mood for their version of wonton soup, which was basically pho broth with a large number of dumplings rather than noodles in the hot bath.  Same accoutrements (Thai basil, sprouts, jalapeno slices, lime wedge), and same great taste, but with beef/pork stuffed wontons. I thought it was a very good version of the classic. 

Why not five star? Well, because I am spoiled by visiting Vietnam and eating incredible food in both the north and south of the country. The small houses in Philly and Ocean Grove, California are often excellent, and this one may yet transport me to the Mekong River as those do. When that happens there will be five stars shining above its door. 

Bravo to Bravo for being as slurpin' good as it is!

China Gourmet is a very pleasant surprise if you, like me, love a traditional dim sum Chinese brunch every once and a while. 

Situated on St. Vincent Street in Northeast Philly between Brous Avenue and Roosevelt Boulevard in Mayfair, it is a large house in a developing Asian neighborhood that puts out trolley carts loaded with small dish treats both savory and sweet, at reasonable prices and with the expected hussle and flow that this dining style uniquely delivers. Admittedly, the aggressive nature of the cart ladies hawking their delicacies takes some getting used to. You have to be able to say "no" when you feel overwhelmed by the surrounding din. But, know that slowing down the onslaught is proper, and multiple opportunities will present themselves. Just take what you want in the moment and let the trolley women return when you are ready for more. 

The most important thing at China Gourmet is that they know from dim sum. There are dozens of choices and most of them are good to great. Shrimp and pork shumai, shrimp hargow, beef rice rolls w vinegar, fried stuffed buns, various dumplings, fish filled chili peppers, egg tarts and many others are well prepared and served hot or cold as appropriate. My bowl of congee was also decent with plenty of ground pork and fresh cut scallion on top. There is plenty more, but you get the picture. 

What's even better is the availability of FREE PARKING right in front of the restaurant, and the large Asian supermarket and Vietnamese kitchen right next door. The money saved is like getting a 25% discount off your check! Hard to beat! 

Now that we've experienced the fun and convenience of a strong dim sum morning with grocery shopping for dessert, Chinatown has lost some of its cultural luster for us (not completely). 

Gotta love it!

Andorra Ping Pong is the sibling restaurant to the Ping Pong Restaurant in Wayne, PA. It is similarly Szechuan oriented Chinese cuisine, but in a somewhat smaller footprint in the Andorra Shopping Center just off Henry Avenue very near to Wissakickon Valley Park, and just beyond Roxborough. It is family owned and operated, with husband running the kitchen, and wife, the front of the house. 

We were there for a small celebration, and thoroughly enjoyed our time there. We ordered enough to be able to sample a cross section of their dishes, and had plenty to bring home for our sons. We went with: Deep Fried Chicken, Fish Fillet Dry Pot, Cumin Lamb and Hot Sauce Pig Intestine; all melded together with the help of an excellent Charles Krug cabernet (BYOB). Each entre was a full load. The chicken was crispy, yet still moist within. The fish fillets, tender with plenty of dry Szechuan red peppers, cauliflower, lotus root and cilantro. The cumin lamb was well covered in dry cumin leaf and accessorized with green pepper, onion and good sized long hots pieces, while the intestine skin was dark brown, surrounded by celery, peanuts, scallion and more of those small red heat devils from Chongqing. All tasty morsels. 

If there was anything to talk about, it was the lack of numbing heat in any of the platters. A deep dive into the heart of each failed to discover any black peppercorn, nor star peppers - the two ingredients necessary for the development of numbing sweats.  When asked, we advised that they should bring the heat because we loved the sensation, yet it did not materialize. Spicy, yes. Numbing lips and tongue, no. 

But, aside from that disappointment, the meal was filling, satisfying and most enjoyable. We will still return, and visit the sister ship before too long. Perhaps, we will bring our own extra burn, just in case the kitchen lacks those key ingredients when we arrive next time.

Gotta like the name given to this roadhouse on Street Road in Southampton, PA. Makes it sound like an offshoot of Iron Chef in heat. This is the third incarnation for this rear entranced bar and grill. It is attractive with vaulted ceilings, tall glass, and substantial rectangular bar. Plenty of wood and windows all around. 

I liked my vantage point at the corner of the bar facing a kitchen door and HDTV. The beer taps were to my left. I appreciated being given samples of a couple of their brews when I seemed indecisive. I chose the Mango Cart, an obviously fruity beer that had a mildly sour mango flavor and beautiful yellow gold luster. Well worth the $6 pint. 

My classic cheeseburger was okay, but missed on its requested endpoint, coming out well done rather than medium. Too, the ground beef crumbled as bitten, giving the impression that it may have been frozen for a while before hitting the hot steel. Perhaps that explains why pink centers weren't an option. It would have been fine as an $8 puck, but at $11, plus $2 for the homemade potato chip swap from fries, it was overpriced.  Service was friendly and prompt. 

Plenty of sports available on the multitude of screens, and was fortunate to watch Tiger Woods win the Masters for the first time in thirteen years. Plainly, he had a far better day than I did. Wonder what was served in the clubhouse at Augusta on Sunday?

Still a great cheesesteak after several more visits over the past couple of years.  

The BIG STORY is the availability of a credit card processor that saves the time and expense of bringing enough cash or using the captive ATM.  

The sandwiches come to ten bucks with a drink, so it pays to be ready for the splurge.

Definitely one of the best burger joints in Philadelphia, especially if price plays into your taste appreciation. What used to be a food truck operation has now taken root on West Girard Avenue (2800 Block). Although, small in stature, their burgers, cheesesteaks and roast pork sandwiches are worthy of being called, "Philly Prime." At less that $10 per, they offer a strong value compared to some of the expensive burger houses. 

My Ponderosa Burger with grilled onions & mushrooms, Swiss, and fries inside the potato bun, topped with a drizzle of their secret steak sauce, was both a sight and delight.  Although slightly beyond my requested Medium finish, it remained juicy with a great taste profile from the added ingredients. The first bite told the tale.  It exploded in my mouth with so much forceful flavor, that some of it squirted out from my loosely closed lips. Glad I had grabbed enough napkins at the counter to deal with it. 

My lovely companion sampled the Manayunk Roast Pork Sammy (pork loin topped with American, coleslaw, pickle and BBQ sauce).  She could barely finish half!  Too, their fries were copious, crisp and freshly cut. 

Service, friendly and engaging. Order and pickup at the counter. 

Excellence all around.

On the same square as 1st Asian Supermarket in Mayfair, Philadelphia, in a corner brick two story, stands Marinucci's Deli. Those of you familiar, already know that it is a high volume higher quality Italian hoagie gold mine that creates stuffed sandwiches loaded with Dietz & Watson meats and cheeses, and a few signature pieces. Those of us who haven't been there before yesterday now know that this place is a legendary Philly landmark (30 years in this location) that turns out among the best Sammies in the city. 

I stopped in after a heavy afternoon of food shopping next door, and ordered two "small" 12" torpedos with Rare Roast Beef & Provolone and Roast Turkey & Swiss, both dressed with lettuce, tomato, mayo, oregano, hot & sweet peppers. Both To Go. 

Weighing in at about one pound each, we tore into the roast beef on the drive home. It was spectacular! The meat was fresh and tender, the provolone mildly tart and dry, that combined with all the accessories for a dynamic and delicious bite and chew. The best way to attack this zoftig big boy was with two hands and aggressive squeeze and stuff into the mouth, just like with a cheesesteak. We tag teamed it, my partner holding it in front of my face, while I grabbed with one hand and directed it into my mouth. It only worked at stoplights, but a couple of large bites did the trick. No fuss, no muss. Only a sesame seed from the roll jumping off the bread onto my lap before slipping to the floor. 

The Turkey & Swiss was just as good. Top flight ingredients and delightful eye opening taste. Both were good for two meals apiece, so we finished them later that evening with good brew and jalapeño chips. 

Marinucci's is one of those Philly joints that leave a lasting impression and a strong desire to return whenever in the neighborhood, which fortunately is about once a month. 

The corner of Brous and St. Vincent is a true destination for everyone seeking variety in their low budget culinary exploits. Vietnamese, Chinese, Boba and Marinucci's all in one square of Mayfair is a foodie's dream come true.

Croyden has its full share of divey bars and used-to-be-great taverns where a working person could belly up and grab a few mugs of frosty before heading home, or before bed.  Dog & Bull was one of those places in yesteryear, but is not THAT place any more.  That it is a way cool micro bar on the tracks next to the train station, is true, but what the owners have done with it brings it to another level of coziness and good grubbiness. 

It is now a favorite watering hole for anyone looking for a cool place for a few drinks or a better than good lunch or dinner.  It is tiny.  But, they have a great number of crafts on draft, plus a menu that keeps you entertained.  So, even though I walked in thinking we would have a drink and conversation, we ended up sitting at a high top over dinner. The place is intriguing. 

We both drank the hard Cherry Cider, a first for me, but likely not the last.  It was cool, mildly sweet, and oh, so, refreshing.  My Fried Chicken was done well with Mashed and lightly steamed String Beans.  It satisfied my recent addiction and it was interesting to see how different this dish could be from the standard KFC.  I did not taste my partners Salmon Wrap, but it was large and she stopped talking after she bit off the first chew.  Must have been good. 

Before leaving, the live music began.  An acoustic set by a local artist whose first cover of a Neil Young classic was decent.  He was game, but playing at the back end of the barroom is not the best way to grab everyone's attention.  While his guitar and voice were amped, it was not so loud as to disturb anyone who wanted to continue conversing.  Nice touch.

I really like what they've done to the place, and will return for more of the cool atmosphere, good drinks, and well produced bar/comfort food.

This was my first visit to Chili Szechuan since its relocation from Baltimore Avenue in West Philly.  It is certainly larger than before, and its booths and dark tones, more cozy than before. It has always offered authentic Szechuan spicy cuisine from Chongqing, China, but now it even adds the reality of many restaurants especially in the northern climes, of being chilly temperature-wise in winter.  We appreciated the cultural use of cold weather and wore our coats during the meal in honor of the reminiscent freeze in the house. Brrrr....

The food was as good as before. Spicy Lamb Chops, Szechuan Chili Sauce Fish Fillets, Eggplant in Garlic Sauce and Crispy Shrimp - Sweet & Sour, were our choices. They were all good to great, although our waiter admitted that even on the non-Americanized menu, they cut the heat for a western customer. So, even though we were mostly Chinese at the table, we all suffered through reduced burn and numbness. Next time, we will insist on the full monty fire treatment. We can all handle it!

The dishes arrived as prepared by the kitchen, and not all at once. Thus, the spicy lamb chops made the first impression of the night. They were excellent; with enough cumin and pepper to heat the tongue and gums, but not anesthetize them. Fun finger food.  Next came the eggplant in garlic sauce.  It, too, was a strong contender, with plenty of Chinese nightshade and a thick, rich dark amber coat. It could have been hotter, as the innate sweetness of the veggie dominated the other flavors, and needed more competition from Szechuan chilies. The shrimp was delivered next.  It was good, with 10 jumbos in an orange glaze. However, it was far more sweet than sour, and suffered most from Americanization syndrome. It really needed a blast from the smelter to bring out its hidden attributes. Finally, the Szechuan chili sauce fish fillets arrived in a deep dish to accommodate the soupy red hot bath it cooked in.  This dish was excellent and packed the most punch.  Tender pieces of boneless flounder is a beautiful orange/red conglomerated hot liquid.  Finally, a little numbness!

We passed on their dessert options, as they were not Chinese, and all came from an outside vendor.  The hot tea was from a non-descript bag, rather than loose pack.  Not so good. 

Overall, Chili Szechuan was a worthwhile trip on a cold winter night, yet it would do itself a favor by fixing the heating equipment, not making assumptions about "round eyes," and upgrading their tea choices. While these are mostly secondary considerations, they do detract from the experience.  As such, it really can't compare holistically to Han Dynasty or the other Hot Houses in Philly, where those details mean something.

Aldo's Pizzarama on Bustleton Avenue in far Northeast Philadelphia has been at the same location for a couple of generations, and has the reputation for making the best pie in this part of the city. Perhaps, it has changed hands since those opinions were expressed, but it was not our experience when we stopped in for dinner over the weekend. 

The guys behind the counter, although not busy, seemed unwilling to crack a smile or offer any service beyond taking our order and shouting out when the pizza or steak sandwich was ready, for us to pick up and deliver to ourselves. No silverware, no napkins, no courtesy offered. 

My son liked the steak, but said it was not worth the drive to have it. The pizza looked great with crisped sausage slices and well done crust. The problem was the overuse of cheese out of proportion to the sauce. It was such a heavy layer that the undercarriage could not support the topside. Lifted from the outer edge left the center of the slice on the aluminum pan with its contents sliding off. The work involved in folding the slices allowed us to taste how salty the cheese and red sauce were. Just not a good pizza, despite the decent crust. 

Won't be back.

I've been kicking myself for several days now for not dining at The Churchville Inn before last Friday night. Living in central Bucks County for decades, someone should have alerted me to how good it was; and after joining Yelp I should have scouted it out myself long before. Mea Culpa! 

Now that the boys and I have have broken the ice, we are in accord that we just had one of the best Bucks sups we can remember.  We mixed and matched the Whole Chicken Wings with Reaper (extremely hot) Sauce, Red Buds, Half Rack of Baby Backs, and the Maple-Bacon BBQ Grilled Salmon. 

The wings were about the biggest I'd ever seen; plump, juicy and scalding to near numbness. Big hit!  The Red Buds were an app, but enough for a meal, with a mix of braised bacon, pulled pork and melted cheddar. Nice take on traditional twice baked potatoes.  The salmon wasn't a large steak, but with the maple bacon thickened to a fire glaze, it was great. The mashed sweets were a mellow counterpoint.  The star of the show were the ribs. Meaty, tangy and suck off the bone awesome. There was no choice of finishes, but no one complained.  They were a great gnaw. We had no though of dessert.  

The inn facility is large and country comfortable, with downstairs and upstairs dining rooms and upside bar. No doubt we will have many happy returns.

There is little doubt that Rocco's is the best restaurant currently in Newtown. This may change as there are new kitchens opening up almost weekly in the community, but right now, this steakhouse has it going on full bore. 

I had dinner there with son and his girlfriend the other night. We sat in the glass enclosed porch that rings the first floor. The space is beautifully appointed in colonial style, and white table cloths and heavy stainless flatware. It is a pleasure to walk through the barroom and dining room to reach the porch. From that perch the Newtown bustle can be witnessed first hand. We were there to celebrate several occasions that had gone  unrecognized over the past 16 months due to Covid. We had much to be thankful for. 

Son o'mine loves his steak, and his N.Y Strip done medium was beyond excellent in texture and robust flavor. He cut me a piece knowing that this was not my normal diet, but that I was open to experiencing superior dishes. Yes, it was amazing, and it was easy to understand his attraction. I had to concentrate to appreciate everything that was going on in my mouth as I chewed and savored. His girlfriend went with a medium filet. It wasn't as juicy as the strip by observation, but she was clearly loving every bite of her medium round thick slab of beef. 

I went with the French Onion Soup and Prime Burger, knowing my diet couldn't handle a platter of solid beef. The soup qualified for possible the best of breed in a lifetime. It was rich, savory, onions, hearty beef stock, topped with french loaf under a thick layer of gruyere, seared to a near-blackened finish either in the oven or by blowtorch. The cheese had to be pierced to access the molten potage below, and to permit the superheated steam to escape. It was epic, and nearly a meal by itself.  Stupendous! 

After all this, the burger was a bit of a disappointment. True, it was a combination of ground beef, short rib and brisket, topped with onion, tomato, lettuce and melted provolone, in a brioche bun. But, flavor-wise it was a situation where more is less. I didn't get off on the mix of beef. It just didn't taste like a high end burger. I like short rib and brisket at BBQ joints, but prefer them separately, where each of their distinct attributes can be appreciated, and not muddled together. So, it was disappointing after the star quality of everything else. The fries were standard crispers. 

So, Rocco gets a less than perfect five stars here. Despite the burger, the rest of the experience was top notch, and the bar/dining area stunning In an understated way. On a less precipitous evening, eating outside would have been a legitimate option, but despite the umbrellas, we would have had to endure wet shoulders from the tropical storm brewing outside. 

No wonder Rocco's is booked solid every night. It is truly a first class night on the town.

State Street Kitchen is NO LONGER open Friday nights for dinner.  

The menu leaned toward Korean cuisine, complete with stainless steel bowls, chop sticks, and special hot sauces to heat your pallet and warm the soul.  The crowd is quite different than who you see at breakfast and lunch.  It seems like many of Micha's friends come down to hang out with her.  They bring wine or harder stuff for all to share, and often pick up a mix of desserts to pass around.  Sort of like a pot luck. 

This is a great direction for this small house.  With the right people working the kitchen, expanding to other nights would be a boon to nighttime State Street.

Hard Rock Café is an icon of the 20th Century.  It does feel dated and retro in the 21st. 

I hadn't been in Philly's franchise for about twenty years, and it felt and looked the same as I remembered.  Guitars on the walls, TVs everywhere the guitars weren't.  A gift shop that remains the heart and soul of the establishment.  Overpriced? Check. Gitchy? Check. Mediocre food? Check. 

My friends from Copenhagen really wanted to go so they could collect another Hard Rock T shirt. I remembered that their burgers were 'the thing.'  We went it to buy what they wanted first, and then grabbed a table for lunch.  The staff was professionally friendly.  The menu as expected. 

$14 for a Legend Burger and $3.50 for a Lemonade (no refill offered) were strictly based on what they could charge, not on quality, but I guess you have to pay for the atmosphere.  The Burger was right on Medium, but crumbled when cut due to freezing.  It wasn't bad, but they would have done better hiring a crew from Five Guys to handle this chore. The Onion Ring on top was over-fried, as was everything on the Appetizer Mix Platter. The Wings were not good, the Chicken Fingers were dry and tasted of yesterday's oil. I stayed away from the Spinach Dip. 

My friends are not foodies, and had no issue with the scene and grub.  This is what they were here to do.

Who was I to rain on their parade?

Maybe it was because I was there on a Wednesday evening, and the dining rooms were not crowded, mirroring the condition of the large buffet displays which were likewise limited in choice to few main courses, sides, breads and desserts, but there really wasn't much to enjoy about the dinner options that I had just paid in advance to consume, sight unseen. While $20 might have been reasonable for repeat visits to the buffet tables, that value proposition was shot to shit if the first rule of buffet dining was not accepted by the diner. 

Be prepared to chow down in extremis, or the whole thing is a waste. Healthy dining this is not. 

A half gone tray of meatloaf with choice of light/dark gravy, large pile of fried chicken as the only protein; a few macaroni/cheese elbows, Penni broccoli, mashed, stuffing and was that yams(?) as the heavy carb offerings, along with some nondescript bread; followed by copious amounts of jello, pudding, cookies, cheesecake squares and one last slice of dried out raspberry pie - all amounting to a heavy lugubrious carb centric plate. I neither wanted more after laboring through the first, nor would it have been wise for me to have attempted another helping. 

Beside that, that raspberry pie lacked any berries, but was a purple sweet colloid held in dry tasteless crust, and thus, without redemption. 

I just can't consume like that, nor was I really tempted to do so. But, I learned that my hunger is nothing compared to what the Golden Corral crowd is capable of.  Perhaps that explains why almost everyone there wore elastic waist sweatpants. They knew what they were there for, while I learned the hard way that it doesn't pay for people without that corpus and habitude to so indulge. We should know that the experience will be largely wasted on us. 

Pass the Pepto, please!

A party of seven can be a challenge for a popular and busy restaurant, especially when six of the guests have never eaten Italian food before.  Confusion, questions, blank stares.  But, when lucky enough to be handed off to a seasoned professional wait person, what might have been an eye-rolling chore, becomes an interesting and entertaining part of the evening.  

So it was at Carlucci's Grill in the Lower Makefield shopping center that is anchored by Kohl's Department Store at the corner of Oxford Valley and Big Oak Roads.  I was given the responsibility of ordering for everyone, so after studying the menu I decided to stick with the classics, so everyone would discover what Italiano was all about for the most people.  Parmigianas for everyone, except for the more adventurous who opted for Carlucci's "Princess" finish to chicken and shrimp.  Standard sides of pasta with red sauce, except for the aglio olio linguini I preferred.  

Gotta give kudos to our main man in black & white, and the kitchen.  The feast began with a puff bread with an olive oil garlic drip.  Never had that before, and it was very good fun to rip apart and devour.  The accompanying salads all had balsamic dressing, and were solid, if not exceptional.  We finally arrived at the entrees.  Large plates of veal, chicken and shrimp or eggplant, covered in red gravy and melted mozza or cream sauce (Princess), and sharing space with an ample load of al dente linguini, were placed before us.  

We all fell silent as we dove in.  The veal was fine, thin sliced and sautéed before dosing in ample thick and chunky gravy, with just enough cheese cover to allow the dueling colors to swirl without sealing the meat within.  Nice chew, better swallow. The eggplant could have been more tender, probably due to the thickness of the slices and not enough time in the fry pan to really soften the large circumference of the purple beast.  Still, a credible job.  The pasta sides were average. 

Carlucci's is BYOB, so we consumed Pinot Grigio and Corona in sufficient quantities to keep everyone lose and engaged.  Most importantly, we gave our guests something to talk about after returning to Asia.  

This is what Marco Polo had in mind as he returned to Venice on the Silk Road with his first shipment of rice and noodles.  He could not have fully realized what he was starting.  The Carlucci's have certainly carried the traditions that evolved from the Court of the Great Kublai Khan to us in competent hands.

Eleven of us showed up at 10:30 for a Dim Sum experience in Philadelphia Chinatown last Saturday.  I had selected Ocean City Restaurant on the north end of 9th Street from Yelp reviews.  A little out of the way. A lot more available tables than other similar banquet halls closer to the center of CTown. 

We were met near the front door by the owner/manager, who at first thought there were only two of us.  He was gracious, even knowing we could not eat enough to make his day.  Then, we explained there were actually nine more right behind us.  His face registered the glint of happy surprise as he swiveled and pointed to the large round table in the front corner with exactly eleven chairs around it.  Now, he was very happy, and walked with us and set up the lazy Susan in the middle of the table as we all gathered 'round.  Maybe, we would help his bottom line.  

Indeed, we did.

As the cart ladies approached, the titular hostess of this feast arose and began to order for everyone.  Nothing random here.  She pointed and placed, requested and demanded, served and bussed, and made sure everyone had an equal amount of every dish desired.  Truly, an amazing display of taking charge, and improving the experience.  She has a future in the hosting business.  

If you check the photos, you will see that we sampled a large amount of what Ocean City had to offer.  Everything was good to exceptional for dim sum.  Special mention to the Minced Pork Congee, Tofu Skin with Veggies, and the Seafood Dumplings.  Tasty and fun.  We didn't try everything, but enjoyed what we had, with even the rookies fully engaged.  We left enough on the menu for another visit.  

It always surprises me how much food you get at a dim sum, and for what a fair price.  Eleven of us (9 adults), gorged for under $150, and even brought a few things home.  

Ocean City is a traditional seafood house that does a splendid Hong Kong style 'small plates'.  Can't speak to the regular menu, but they do dim sum the old fashioned way. Full floor show. Totally satisfied.

Keep it coming!

Approaching Rozmaryn (Rosemary) Restaurant on a rainy January night takes a bit of courage.  The store front is a rowhouse with a neon "Open" sign in the window and an old unlit sign beneath it.  The front door is open and all you see is a long hallway with dim yellow lighting.  Sketchy characters on the sidewalk make you involuntarily prepare your fight/flight responses.  Be ready for anything...

But, first walk across Olden Avenue to the liquor store to pick up authentic Polish beer to make the experience complete.  In the back of the store is the Polish section.  More sketchy guys standing around - these 'packin' employees watch your every move.  But, the Xywiec Beer is back there in bottles or cans. I pulled out a six pack of glass and brought it to the counter. $10. minimum for credit cards, so I had to pull out my wallet (I really didn't want to do it).  Done. Walked back across the street and up the front steps of 925.  On the first door to the left was the restaurant sign bidding we enter.  What was behind the door? 

I went in first.  I was greeted by an apartment converted into a small eatery.  Yellow walls, stained wood trim. Wall sconces, but little other adornment.  No one else in the main dining area.  We stood a moment and waited to see if someone would come out to seat us.  A few long seconds later a woman appeared from the rear with a warm smile and firm voice welcoming us to her shop.  She was the owner, hostess, and chef.  Very big persona.  Lovely, and I immediately relaxed.  At 6:30 we expected other patrons, but we were the first and only folks there all night.  She sat us at a central table for 4, allowing us to spread out.  NFL Playoffs had depleted her clientele, but we were quite happy to have all her attention.  

After getting the lay of the land from the gracious Madame, we ordered off the rather small menu, which is in both English and Polish.  The Polish Plate to share as our appetizer.  It consisted of Meat Pierogies, Potato Pancakes, Kielbasa in Yellow Mustard, and Apple Sauce.  The Pierogies were the least enjoyable part of the dish. While the dough was lightly fried and was a good consistency, the meat was too dense and organ-tasting for me. The Potato Pancakes were large and thin, not very oily, and a good mix of potato and flour (to hold them together).  They were crispy on the edges and tasty with a dollop of Apple Sauce to mix a little sweetness with the mild saltiness of the latke. The Kielbasa was excellent.  Scored before grilling to help the heat penetrate and to avoid splitting, the outer skin was just firm enough to hold the link together, but when bitten, it gave way nicely to allow the very tender innards to meet the tongue, disclosing its softness and interesting spice.  It was the surprise star of the plate.  The mustard kicked up the flavor, but did not overwhelm the essence of the sausage.  

We had the Stuffed Cabbage and Breaded Chicken Cutlet as our entries.  The Cabbage dish came with Mashed Potato and Cucumber Salad.  The Cabbage was tender and the mix of beef and something else was good, but perhaps a little bland.  It needed something to sweeten it, or at least that was how my Polish-Jewish grandmother prepared them. The potatoes were not hot enough, and seemed to have been plated before visiting the oven. Mild disappointment.  The Cucumber Salad was a cream base and decent.  

My Chicken dish was excellent.  The breast was large, with a pleasantly hand dipped breading coating it.  I opted for Mushrooms rather than Tomato Sauce, and was very pleased with the freshness and amount piled on the chicken.  Very tasty and definitely something I would order again.  The mashed were again cool and I left most of them alone.  The Red Beet Salad finished the plate.  Served appropriately cold, it was a nice fit, bringing mild sweetness to the mix of flavors in the breading, chicken, and shrooms.  I was happy.

To complete the repast, we ordered the Blintzes stuffed with Farmer's Cheese, and dusted with Powdered Sugar.  These babies were wonderful.  Perfect crepe wrap, and a whipped sweet cheesy filling.  Light, and a perfect end to the meal with freshly brewed coffee.  

This is a one of a kind richly local ethnic urban place that is easy to love.  The entire experience from the sidewalk scene, to the liquor store, to the special charm of the owner/chef, make Rozmaryn worth a visit or two.  When a meal becomes the food for a short story you have found something remarkable. 

This was definitely that, and more.

Metro Diner on Street Road has the look of a cafe more than a traditional diner, with only a short counter with spinners overlooking the open kitchen, and a dining room to the other side. It is in a new building it shares with an as yet unleased commercial space. It is not the roadhouse a diner was designed to be. 

Still, the menu looked diner. So, what the heck. I was ready for breakfast, and I was already there, and in the hunt for some good french toast. That they had in abundance, although not just the plain egg bread fried with the hint of vanilla and sugar I was hankering for. But, when I asked the friendly server if it was available, she assured me it was. 

The coffee was strong, hot and free flowing. The main attraction was disappointing. It looked great on the plate, especially after melting some butter and running syrup over it. But, upon cutting and first bite, found its insides to be mushy and cooler than the surface. It wasn't eggy inside as you might expect, but almost watery, like the mix had been diluted to the point where it lacked the hen seed to thicken under heat. It just stayed wet. The flavor was about right, but texture counts, too. 

I suppose I could have given it back to them for another try, but wasn't feeling like making that scene. I ate what I could and took my leave. Just glad I hadn't asked for the heavy hitters on the menu, which would have put a bigger dent in my wallet.

It was probably a mistake that wasn't caught before reaching its final destination, but first impressions were damaging.

I totally get the cult of Federal Donuts; the lovechild of Zahav and Percy Street BBQ.  

The old corner shop is in a warren of narrow old streets in Pennsport, and the space itself has a tiny charm that could easily be a time warp to the 18th Century.  Standing in line or waiting for an order creates a sense that time has slowed down, and even the dust in the sunbeams may have danced for our forefathers. The combination of Korean style double fried chicken and deep dive dough balls is a natural fit for preparation, but I am not yet comfortable eating both at the same seating. The double dose of fats challenges my guilt. 

When we arrived mid-Saturday afternoon, all of the fancies were gone, but the 3 daily offerings were available.  Folks were gnawing on their chicken bones at the counter, blissful in their enjoyment.  We ordered a half doz mix of Vanilla Spice, Maple Brown Sugar and Strawberry Lavender to take with us on the drive home.  They were individually bagged while hot, and placed in a larger paper bag, and ultimately triple bagged in a plastic take out carrier.  

Opening the package, the heat and moisture has made the paper sacks damp, but still held in plenty of the essence of the dough wheels. We tried a Vanilla Spice.  It was covered in sugar and cinnamon, cake-like, and uber sweet. The bite and chew was pleasant, but there was no crispness due to the water vapors.  Very tasty.  A very good donut.  Over the next day, the rest were devoured, and although the taste varied with content, the general experience was the same.  A nice round piece of cake with a hole in the middle. 

Federal Donuts deserves another house call earlier in the day when the fancies are in stock, and again for a unique fried chicken experience, which seems as varied as the sweet fat tires. 
After those ingestions, an update will be in order. 

Until then, the consumed donuts themselves were not life altering, but were certain A-Okay!

This is a tough one to call. 

The premises of Three Monkeys Café is beautiful, both inside and out. A lot of thought and money was put into bringing the old saloon back to life. From tin-type ceiling tiles, through refinished wood floors, exceptional back bar, and zany monkey decorations throughout, the inner sanctum of this place is a pleasure to sit in and enjoy.  Great job!

The outer side patio/garden is likewise a wonderland.  Colorful, whimsical, tall treed, and full of monkey business.  On a spring, summer or autumn day or evening, it is no doubt an endearing space for a few drinks and semi-romantic meal.  Gotta love it!

The weak link is the kitchen. 

We were there for breakfast after visiting the USCIS facility nearby. It wasn't quite warm enough to dine al fresco, so we sat at a corner table in the barroom, and were served by a friendly management person.  We were introduced to Douwe Egbert Coffee, a Dutch brand in operation since 1753.  One of their spinoffs developed a novel approach to mass produced coffee that liquefies it in concentrate, and brews on site and when ordered, so every cup is fresh and strong.  Mine had a mild chicory flavor.  I really liked it, although I would need a lot more sampling and comparison to fresh ground beans to know if it was as good as what I grind/brew at home. Still, it was a pleasant cuppa Joe. 

The sausage, egg and cheese on seeded roll with side of home fries, were the main attractions.  They left me somewhat disappointed.  It was fine that they used cut up links rather than patties, and threw them in with a few scrambled eggs and slices of cheese.  It was very big, because the roll was from a cheesesteak sandwich; not a hard Kaiser.  But, it had not been grilled at all, and did not really work with the breakfast theme.  Too, the mix lacked spice, and would have benefited by being cooked with a pinch of salt, pepper, and maybe even a shake or two of Pecos Bill.  Finally, the potatoes looked great and greasy, but were completely cold.  

A little quality control at the grill, and perhaps retaining a real chef to handle the preparation or at least to train the staff, would make a world of difference.  Three Monkeys has a ton of potential. It just needs to polish the brass and sand the wood trim (culinary-wise) to become a completely enthralling experience.  

3.5 Stars

Hulmeville Inn was a dive bar before the term gained currency in the 21st Century.  

It sits at the crossroads of time, at the intersection of a stage depot between Trenton and Philadelphia in the 19th Century, and a cool and courageous crafty beer pour in the present day.  

Sometimes it feels like they are shooting an episode of Duck Dynasty at the pool tables with all the beards on display.  Still, even a clean shaven face is welcome in this throwback bar.  

The suds are amazing in their diversity from local to international, although the kitchen always seems a step behind in offerings and quality.  It is a fun place to go just to hang out and watch sports, or chalk up the old cue.  The prices can't be beat, and this is one of those places where they can sniff out pretension, so best to just be at your ease.  

I don't get down to Hulmeville often, but when I do the Inn by that name is a worthy place to visit. 

Walk in. Belly up. Buy a round. Shoot the sh*t.  Rack 'em up.  Break 'em. Set up shots for nightcaps. Head on home.

UPDATE. FEBRUARY 3, 2017 

Came in tonight for dinner and beer. Here, we normally order food and drink at the bar, and bring the glass back to the hightops in the barroom to await the cook delivery of the plates. Their brew list comes on sheets of paper and a wall screen. There were at least 40 choices from around the world and as close as Bucks. 

For drink we ordered Devils Double, a dark IPA, and Merry Monks. I guess we were feeling a little naughty and monastic at the same time. Both were strong mood setters. For nosh, we opted for a medium Firehouse Burger and their Boardwalk Cheesesteak.  We waited for our grub as the bar filled with Friday nighters. Nice, friendly crowd. Dates, friends, co-workers, fams. Bar Lady knew everyone's name and where they sat. 

My burger was a half pound delight on a ciabatta roll, loaded with red onion, romaine and a perfect medium finish. Needed utensils to consume because my mouth just wasn't big enough (I know. Hard to believe.). The Boardwalk steakwich was HUGE, with finely chopped onions, peppers and roasted reds and a layer or American. The roll was great for holding the massive beefy pile and it's drippings, so if you desired less grease you only ate the top of the loaf. But, if you craved full force cardiac compromising taste, you chomped all of it. Freedom of Choice! 

Hulmeville Inn has been tapping kegs for patriots for 200 years. You can feel it all around you, like a friendly ghost's embrace. 

Hoist a few together.

The return visit was even better than the first.

The Pho Tam Nam Gan, was absolutely crammed with thin sliced Roundeye Steak, Well Done Brisket and Soft Tendon, in addition to the nest of thin noodles, slivers of Onion and Scallion, plus the optional Sprouts, Thai Basil, Jalapeno and Fresh Squeezed Lime.  It was impossible to push down the flat bottom spoon to slurp the beef broth without causing spillage over the rim of the bowl.  

Hot. Steamy. Meaty. Delicious. 

(And not a hint of MSG.)

Ray's Café & Teahouse on North 9th Street on the eastern end of Chinatown, has been brewing incredible coffee since the mid-90s.  The ambiance is def Taiwanese old school, with Grace and son working the Hario syphon butane java makers with aplomb and verve.  The best locally roasted beans are used to make single cups of joe, that are delivered to the table on a small tray, with doily and excellent butter cookie aboard. Little spout of milk on the side. 

The Ethiopian Yirgacheffe beans from Main Line Coffee Roasters, were freshly ground the moment before their boiling bath and syphoning through the beautiful glass system, producing a superb cuppa joe. Not to put too fine a point on it, but this was among the very best coffee I have ever enjoyed. To watch Grace make my cup from grinding through pouring, was to see an artist at work. Perfect temperature. Perfectly balanced acidity.  A pleasure to imbibe. Easy to become addicted.  The Hario equipment was lined up on her counter, and the butane burner emitted a cool blue flame that brought the filtered water to a boil and flushed it up the tube and down through the coffee against a cloth filter.  Pure alchemy!
