Even the butter cookie with the colorful sprinkles was a winner. Hard and crisp, the way it should be. 

Yes. At $5 a cup, this is not for the faint hearted. But, for coffee lovers and mavens, going to Ray's is a trip to the mountaintop to sit at the feet of the javamaster.

Mugshot Diner in Fishtown, Philadelphia, is a classic urban diner, open 24/7 for the people of this north of Center City community.  We stopped in after a show at Punch Line comedy club the other night. Laughing so much made us hungry. We cruised around the block for parking and found a spot on our second pass on York Street. Thank you parking angels!

We sat in a booth along the front windows, where the hostess placed two menus and a specials laminated card. Our server came along promptly, introduced himself, and told us to let him know when we were ready to order. 

At 10 it wasn't very busy. Decent music in the background. We ordered one of their burgers and eggplant parmesan on ciabatta, after our server warned us off other ideas. Gotta trust the guy. Both sandwiches were decent - the burger grilled to a juicy medium, and the eggplant tender with adequate red sauce and mozzarella. They weren't awesome, but neither was that expected for the place and price. We were satisfied with this late meal. 

Mugshot has a sister house in Mt. Holly, NJ, where I have had several good breakfasts. If you like either one, your bound to like the other.

59 Almshouse is the address of an attractive roadhouse in Richboro, PA. It is all light wood and stone, with a cathedral ceilinged barroom that echoes with the sound of a full house at happy hour and a more sedate rear dining room for families and more intimate conversation. 

We stopped in for dinner on a Friday evening, just in time to catch the last five minutes of HH. My watermelon-tini and the bourbon barrel aged ale were both nice to get our appetites revved for what was to come. Blackened fish tacos and Southwest burger got top billing. We found both fairly well constructed and tasty, although my try at creativity, asking that the side of fries be poutine-ized was somewhat less than hoped. 

The cod in the tacos was fresh and well blackened in a frypan. The semi-authentic Mexican fixings (avocado, lettuce, aoili crema) we're on target. An enjoyable dish for sharing, although the tiny cup of black beans was cool and not flavorful. The burger was delivered partially medium (as requested), but partially rare, making for a hand packed patty that was partially quite good, and also half less than hot enough. Must have been grilled on the outskirts of the steel. Still, it was okay. The brown gravy that covered the fries was flavorful, but too heavy for the potatoes and turned them soggy, sacrificing texture and crispiness for something closed to chunky mashed. Didn't work for me, but it was my idea so I don't put that on the kitchen. Won't do it again.

We sat at a small booth in the barroom. Tight fit. The house was full of happy timers of mixed age, all having fun. It was obvious that '59' was a well known local hangout where everyone was welcome. We enjoyed the atmosphere. 

Nice place. 

3.5 Stars, rounded up.

Unfortunately, the first observation from my dealing with Pho & More in Montgomery Commons is that while it may be a Vietnamese house, it certainly is not a Thai kitchen. As I ordered from both ends of the menu, I found myself happy with the Roast Pork Banh Mi sandwich, but damned dissatisfied with the Lemongrass Coconut Soup (Tom Kha) and the Drunken Noodles (Pad Kee Mao). 

Why? Because although both those dishes have lemongrass spice as the key ingredient, there was absolutely no lemongrass to be found in either the soup, nor the wide flat rice noodles. The soup tasted of watered down coconut milk, with ample chicken and mushrooms, but without the strong bite that lemongrass provides. Very poor effort. 

And the Drunken Noodles were not hot and chewy at all, but really just Chinese Vegetable Chow Fun with a few leaves of Thai basil mixed in. I ordered it "very spicy," and the cashier dude repeated that request to me upon pickup. Yet, despite the reasonable quantity of noodles and veggies, it totally lacked the heat punch desired. Boring, semi-sweet fat noods without redeeming fire signature. Major disappointment. 

If I had to guess, I would venture that there was not a Thai person in the kitchen, nor even a real authentic recipe for Bangkok cuisine in the house. If they don't have lemongrass in stock, they just aren't Thai, and shouldn't misrepresent their abilities. Yet, the Banh Mi was decent and I grant that someone may have trained in Ho Chi Minh City or Hanoi to perfect their pho stock. 

Had I known the truth about this joint, I would have happily stayed in Vietnam, and travelled to Thailand another day. As it is, with dishonesty at their core, I will never return to find out what they are really good at. 

Fooled me once, shame on you!
Fool me twice; never happen!

While KO Modern Korean Cuisine does a tasty new take on traditional dishes from the peninsula, you must keep in mind that they call themselves a fusion restaurant that covers Japanese, Thai and even a pinch of Chinese in their kitchen. If traditional is what you want, then this is not the place for you. Try Mirim or the cafe inside of H Mart on Woodbourne Road for the real McCoy. It is only fair to judge based on their stated intentions, not on what they do not claim to be. 

To my tongue they do a very good job on creative contemporary Korean food. I thoroughly enjoyed the small plate KFC (Korean Fried Chicken) and BBQ Pork Belly Bao. The extra spicy wings were just that. Messy and delicious. The Buns a tempting pile of belly and greens atop a soft round pinchable white rice bun. Had I stopped there I would have been seeing multi stars. 

The Sushi and Bento Dinner from the Japan side of the menu were a different matter. Our Rainbow Roll ordered for a sushi neophyte, was less than inspiring. It appeared lifeless on the platter, and tasted less than brand new. When sushi is truly fresh, it has an inner glow. This did not. Perhaps, the use of dyed pink ginger was a tell, but it was less than optimal. I would like to see what they do with Gimbap, the seaweed and rice street food that most closely resembles sushi. I suspect it would have been superior. 

The Bento options chosen were teriyaki salmon,  Dynamite Chicken and a similar shrimp offering (tiny deep fried crustaceans in a gloopy sticky sweet sauce). Again, this Japanese combo plate missed the mark. The salmon was good, but slightly overcooked. The chicken was barely above room temperature, and the shrimp was lost in the heavy batter shell and thick clingy sauce. Just not what we expected from this kitchen. 

We agreed we would try again, but focus only on the Korean possibilities. This night, fusion could only be interpreted as confusion.

Oliver A Bistro sits in the middle of lively Farnsworth Avenue, Bordentown, NJ.  As such, it is one of the many culinary attractions that now predominate on this old main street along the mighty Delaware River.  On this beautiful Friday afternoon, the place to be is under a red umbrella on top of the red brick that are the sidewalks of this historic burg.  Failing that, the next best place to dine is in one of the large window wells on either side of the front door.  That is where I found myself, as all the outside tables were taken when I arrived.  

What is a bit disconcerting about Oliver, is that the inside dining room is rather dark and uninteresting.  Just dark brown tables and chairs with dark carpet and some wall hangings.  No real color, lighting, nor energy.  I directed my attention out the large windows and onto the street on this sunny day, but felt the welling darkness over my shoulders.  

My French Dip Burger with optional side Caesar Salad was very attractive visually, although the puck was a little beyond the medium finish requested.  The description of this opus was of Swiss & Havarti Cheese melt, with Bourbon Caramelized Onions, Sour Cream Horseradish Sauce, and a side cup of Oliver Au Jus.  All those parts were present, and contributed to a good tasting burger.  I have always enjoyed a horseradish alternative to ketchup on my sliders, and it was good to satisfy this long delayed gratification.  It all came together well, especially when I occasionally dipped the burger into the Au Jus and savored the implanted memory of roast beef done this way.  The Caesar side was fresh, green and mildly anchovied.  Liked it. 

At $12 for a full plated lunch, I was satisfied with the value received.  Come in closer to medium with pink center, and I would easily bump this experience up a star.  For a full blown 5 Star rating, something has to be done to lighten the gloom of the dining room.

Flip -N- Shakes is a 1960's-esque burger joint on 2nd Street Pike, Southampton, PA. It is a large room with tile floor and utilitarian furniture. Built for speed, not comfort. I was the sole customer when I walked in last weekend on a Saturday afternoon. I was mildly surprised by the lack of activity, but the staff was friendly, and answered by rookie questions with a smile. 

I opted for the Chop House Burger (horseradish, darkly sautéed shrooms, steak sauce, dijon mustard, provolone and onion frizzle on a standard bun), and an apple pie shake. I asked for medium, but then I read that all burgers were served medium-well. At $6.59, the price was a little high for the product presented. Quarter pounder without fresh taste, and a ton of spicy additions that were enjoyable (love horseradish on my sliders), but somewhat contradictory on the tongue. The interplay with the steak sauce and dijon was not harmonic with the radish, and appeared to have been absorbed by the mushrooms so that the original earthiness from the cellar dwellers was lost. Not a bad sandwich, but I wasn't in love with it. 

I had visions of a real slice of apple pie being placed in a blender with ice cream and milk to create the shake. Not exactly. There were a few small apple slices, and the cinnamon nutmeg flavor, but no crusty bits. The flavor was strong and sweet fun, but would have been completely off the hook with an actual slice of pie. It was comparable to a Shake Shack freeze at a better price, so no real demerits for the shortcut. 

The Five Guys nearby makes a better burger (with double meat), while the shake was very good here. Flip City sound track is mostly classic rock, so the atmosphere is fine. These guys have some tough competition in the burger wars. I wish them well in finding the sweet spot that will distinguish themselves from the surrounding hordes.

If you really like finding your way out of a maze, IKEA is your kind of fun store. One way in. One way out. Little signs with arrows point you in the right direction. A few unmarked shortcuts if your keen enough to find them. 

It's not that their products aren't good; they are. It's not that their Swedish meatballs aren't excellent; they are. It's all about their concept of how people think and learn. To IKEA, customers are to be lead around through the entire warehouse regardless of what they need, and forced to pass through every department on two floors until finally reaching check out cashiers at the end of a long and boring stroll. Once you've begun, forget about going back to the beginning. The human undertow will just drag you down. Need a restroom? Good luck with that. 

It helps if you are a zombie or dyed in the wool shopper when dealing with IKEA. If you don't particularly like the "Costco" warehouse experience, this place will wear you down. I mean, how many DIY furniture projects do you have in one lifetime? How often do you need to build shelves for your office? Not nearly enough to make this entertaining. 

Yeah. We did buy a few glass water containers for around the house, and the prices were good. But, how much better it would have been to be directed to the location where they were shown, and be able to go right to them, than be required to go on safari to find them. 

What a perverse trade-off.

Vic Sushi & Thai Cuisine is a small Asian house on Easton Road, Willow Grove. They have a split schedule with lunch until 2:30, when they close for a few hours to prepare for dinner at 5:30. I stopped in before the afternoon closure for a a plate of Thai noodles. 

I asked for lad na with chicken. The dish derives from Laotian/Chinese cultural exchange, with thick rice noodles and heavy brown sauce into which is stir fried carrots, snow peas, onion and egg. It isn't necessarily spicy hot, but can be made that way by adding lemongrass or chili sauce available in Thai kitchens. 

I guess the chef hadn't read the recipe, because what was delivered to me was something different. The noodles weren't thick and chewy, but of medium width and thickness. The sauce more a thin gruel than the heavy, clinging, noodle covering reduction it was intended to be. As a result, I was eating a drippy plate of lighter noodles and veggies, without the enjoyable chew and substantial flavor associated with the traditional dish. I had to request a spoon to deal with it. It wasn't awful, but a far cry from what it was supposed to be. 

First impression of Vic's is that it is really just a sushitorium trying to distinguish itself from the competition by adding a Thai tail to an otherwise Japanese fish. While the sushi may be good, the Bangkok piece really doesn't work well. 

One and done.

Careful as you approach Sophia Bella on Street Road Southbound, as you will drive past their small parking lot curbcut before you know it, and be forced to drive around the block to get back to the entrance of this Italian kitchen in Bensalem, PA. Worse, you might decide to just drive on, and miss a straight up very good meal. 

There are a few small dining areas in the building in addition to a large back kitchen and prepping/cashier zone up front. Attractively utilitarian, all. Room to stand and wait for your order without feeling cramped, as I was doing as my two hot sandwiches were working. 

These were taken to go, so when I opened the brown bag at home, I found neatly packaged long torpedo sammies (Boardwalk Sweet Sausage, Pepper and Onion/Eggplant Parm) in separate recyclable styro containers. Naturally, the enclosed bread absorbed some condensation so they were no longer dry and a crunchy bite, but were still delicious. Quality Italian sausage complemented well with the sweet and savory sauteed veggies. Eggplant breaded lightly and pan fried in extra virgin before placed in the roll with mozza and tomato sauce on top, and baked in the pizza oven until all melted into a savory layered tasty ensemble. 

I bought two to share, and everyone was happy, even the next day when reheated. Service was friendly and casual, and prices reminiscent of pre-pandemic days. 

Pizza looked good, too, but will have to save comments until I return to sample a few.

Very glad I went alone to check out Texas Roadhouse on Street Road, Bensalem, PA. The wait for a table would have been at least an hour given the size of the SRO crowd in the entranceway and milling by the front door. Solo I was able to find the solitary empty bar stool and jump right on without putting my name on a waiting list. This was a first experience with this outfit and I was amazed by the full house and amplitude of the noise. 

What was going on here to make it so popular? I soon found out.

No fewer than 3 bartenders stopped by to introduce themselves within the first ten minutes, with the first taking my order for a Sam's Winter Ale pint and a Smokehouse Burger. They all called me by name and seemed genuinely interested in my satisfaction. Despite the full house, and arrival of a few couples now standing around the small square bar hoping for a double vacancy, I never felt rushed nor put upon for ordering a sandwich rather than a large slab of grilled beef and dinner. 

And, the medium finish burger was exactly what I got. Half pounder. Hot pink core. Cheddar/American cheese blend. Tomato. Red onion. Mushroom. BBQ sauce. Sesame seed roll. Squirt of Heinz red and I was ready to dive in. 

It was excellent. Juicy and textured with luscious profile as I cleaved through it exposing a cross section of the large sandwich. Its 5 inch height was too much for my jaw to expand around, so I ended up using knife and fork to get the job done. Definitely fair value at $12 and change. The tag along fries were not as good, and I left most of them behind. 

Folks on either side of me were into their steaks, and seemed as content as me in their choices. Must admit that the aroma from all that sizzling meat was intoxicating. 

Leaving the house about an hour later it was even more crowded and louder than when I arrived. I wend my way through the peeps into the open air. So many families waiting to be fed; content to wait as long as it took to partake of the kitchen fare. Now I understood why. For meat lovers this was paradise on a budget. A place they could afford to take their families, have a filling tasty meal, and not break the bank. 

Del Frisco's it wasn't. Nor did anyone want it to be.

This was my first visit to Bonefish Grill. I guess I was always put off by their logo of a fish skeleton. Kinda spooky. But, we were nearby, and it was lunchtime, so for a moment I wasn't drawn to thinking about death when I saw the restaurant on Oxford Valley Road just near the mall. 

The atmosphere and decor was quite nice, with lots of dark wood, large bar and servers wearing white chef coats. We were taken to a booth in the barroom. It was comfortable, with last century rock & roll playing on their sound system. We were brought menus that included both light lunch options and more substantial dinner choices. We went with Fish Tacos (Blackened Cod) and Fish & Chips. 

Both were good, especially the tacos which included mango pieces for sweet juiciness to interact with the spicy salsa. Two were enough. The F&C was also good, but I wished that the outer breaded shell was less oily, as it didn't work as well with the lightness of the fish within. Still tasty, but the inconsistency was palpable. Service was excellent with our friendly white coat attentive and suggestive. 

We agreed that we would certainly give Bonefish another try when the mood for seafood struck us.

Aptly named Jersey diner on Rt. 206, Mt. Holly, NJ. 

The place appears clean and well maintained.  All the marble shines from polishing. The staff in black shirts and red ties look like a well oiled machine.  I sat at the counter for a late breakfast.  The service was friendly, but a little bit off.

I ordered a short stack of French Toast, with a side of Sausage and Coffee.  The Bunnomatic brew was good, and my request for milk rather than Mini-Moo was well met.  The egged bread was a thicker, egg based loaf with the consistency of Chollah, but not actually that species. It grilled up well with lots of caramelized edges and a huge capacity to soak of the Smucker's Syrup.  Wish they had a Maple Syrup alternative, but guess not. Glad it was only two slices, as they were big and filling. 

The breakfast sausage was four links that seem to have been cooked in the deep fryer rather than on the grill or in a pan.  They were uber oily and had a strange taste, perhaps from whatever had been deep fried prior to my order.  I tried, but could only eat half with max effort. Not good. 

I received my bill before I was finished from an escaping server who wished me a good day, but never offered a second mug of coffee.  I had to ask one of the other women behind the counter for more, and she sweetly obliged.  This small slight of courtesy set my attitude toward the place.  Plenty of potential, but lack of execution; especially in human interactive skills and short cuts taken to save time/money, but disrespect the paying public. 

This is one Pandora's Box I will not be opening again.

Provecho (advantage/good fortune) Mexican Grill on Philmont Avenue, Huntingdon Valley, PA, is a decent cafe style Mexican restaurant with a nice vibe, friendly service and kitchen that turns out a limited menu of traditional  platas somewhat tempered for the American palette. It is colorful with large wall murals and a few nooks with comfortable chairs and small tables right out of the Salvation Army store.  

We were there early on a Saturday night, grabbed one of those tables under a mural, and ordered their chicken soup, shrimp fajitas and chicken taquitos. The soup was excellent. Shredded white meat bird, chunky carrots and smaller pieces of onion, it had big flavor from simmering all day long. The fajitas had plenty of medium sized shrimp, well grilled and lightly spiced over slices of peppers and onions. Rice, beans, queso fresca, sour cream and a dollop of creamy guacamole completed the platter. 

Even with complimentary salsa added (not gratis across the board?!) the flavor was muted, and not the blast of spices and textures expected. The large amount of rice was offset by its blandness, although the refried beans were tasty. The three taquitos were stuffed with chicken, cheese and pepper and topped with the same finish as the fajitas. They were crisply deep fried and looked great. The chicken was again under spiced and even the chipotle salsa was too weak to kick it up to tickle the tongue. 

I have no problem with charging for chips and salsa, but add on cost for salsa (even homemade variations) is ahead of the curve of acceptable charges for accessories necessary for the fulfillment of the underlying dish. It's like charging for ketchup on your burger, or cream for your coffee. Never saw that in all my time in Mexico, nor in any of the dozens of very good Mexican houses around Montco. Perhaps, they need to do that to keep doors open, but it seemed ungenerous to these guests.

Carrabba's Italian Grill on Street Road across from Parx Casino, is a roadhouse with large bar, and substantial dining room. Although claiming to be authentic Italiano cuisine, it is really more of a hybrid with modern Americano thrown in to keep things interesting. We showed up on Super Bowl Sunday evening, suspecting that the game might suck, and we should be prepared with Plan B - a meal we could enjoy without need of huge HDTVs on the walls that demanded to be watched. 

Well, we were half right. The game was not worth watching. The food was somewhat more entertaining, but definitely not Italiano robusto. We ordered the calamari and minestrone apps/sides, and entrees of chicken marsala and lasagna. There was a side salad in there somewhere, too. Have to say, that while everything was okay, none of it was kickass. 

The calamari had an unusual breading that made it quite salty, despite the better than decent dipping sauce. No complaints about the soup, but the salad with house dressing, was, well, dull. Not worth finishing. My lasagna was middle of the road, with decent gravy, but the mozza and added Romano-grate were salty. There was not enough heft in the sauce, nor the pasta to give it any tasty substance. Finally, the marsala mushrooms were pretty good, but although we appreciated the large grilled chicken breast, it was not designed to be balanced with the sauce and mushrooms. The chicken was the dominant feature, rather than a melding with thin medallions, tender enough to mix perfectly with the marsala reduction. It was all about the chicken, not the dish. 

We ate in the barroom. It was cozy and our server was a quality dude with excellent skills. I sort of felt sorry for him working beneath his rank at this not quite good enough and salty restaurant.

"Anything worth doing is worth overdoing."
- Albert Einstein

And so it is with bubble tea shops in Philly Chinatown. 
You can't cross the street without seeing bobba signs on every corner. Tapioca is definitely having an amazing resurgence. I don't get why gummy sweet goobers are so popular, but I'm obviously in the minority. 

Still, I enjoy good milk tea as much as the next guy, and Vivi Bubble Tea has it's fair share of that. The space is larger than expected, with a large room with group tables in back for all your friends. Service is efficient and friendly. I had my almond milk tea in hand in under a minute. Impressive. 

The tea was good and exactly what I needed to continue with my shopping list and Artiva haircut. Steamy hot, mildly sweet, sufficiently nutty. $4. 

Noticed that Vivi offered fried chicken wings. Piquing my curiousity, I made a mental note to give them a try next time I needed a nosh while in Ctown.

Spice Rack on Knights Road, Bensalem, PA, is in a strip shopping center I had never visited before, called Bensalem Square. It is a small house with about a dozen tables, and courteous, efficient service and a rapid response kitchen. 

Our order of a chaat appetizer (Sev Puri), spinach soup (Palak), chilli chicken and cheese curry (Mughlai Sahi Paneer), with garlic naan, arrived on time and as ordered.  Each had its strength and weaknesses, but overall was a good meal. The chaat was their take on traditional Indian street snacks, with a crisp cracker base, ground veggies and spiced crispies on top. Very good and fun to eat. The spinach soup was sort of a flat dark green broth with interesting flavor, but little body. I bit of cream would likely have really brought it to life. The chilli chicken (dry) was okay, but although said to be dry, was still fairly moist in a heavy goopy sauce. I have had this in several other Indo/Chinese fusion joints, where the chicken had a drier coated finish and a better texture/flavor profile. The paneer dish was rich and flavorful, and was the star of the show. We asked for it moderately spicy, and thought it hit the mark. Finally, the garlic naan was very good. Thinner and crisper than most I had eaten before. The mango lassi was a thick smoothie with crumbled cashews on top. A tad expensive, but a delicious suck. 

Spice Rack is pretty far out of my way, so it is unlikely I will return. There are many better and more consistent Indian kitchens in and around Bucks County, so unless your in the hood, there are plenty of other choices. 

Hidden? Yes.  Gem? Not really.

Cheesesteak Review -

Dino's is primarily a take out pizza joint on Street Road in Warrington, PA. We wanted to eat while the food was prime, and opted to mange at one of the three tables in the front of the house. Son and I were in the mood for steak sandwiches, although the pizza looked appealing.
 
This Saturday night they had a three person operation in the kitchen, with Dino on the grill. The room was a bit chilly on an early December night, even with the little space heater. Still, hunger and strong aroma of the beef being chopped and tossed by the chef overcame any temporary discomfort.  

The sandwiches were excellent. Fresh crusty rolls, huge load of grilled beef made in house and sliced just before touching hot steel to guarantee juiciness and surprisingly good flavor. A work of culinary art. 

We congratulated Dino for hitting the cheesesteak sweet spot, and assured him we would return. Never too far to go for a great Philly steak sammy. And, if the pizza is as good, the beginning of a long delicious relationship.

Met up with a friend the other night at Hot On D Spot, a Trinidadian Restaurant at the western end of Nottingham Way in Hamilton, tres close to Trenton.  Don't know about you, but I had never tried Trini cuisine before; and in fact while I knew that Trinidad was an island in the Caribbean, I knew little of its history and culture.  My loss. 

Trinidad was settled by a mix of folks who really did not want to be there - African slaves and Indian indentured servants (almost slaves).  They mixed together into a very interesting and spicy society.  The food evolved into something that did not look or taste like either's home cooking.  It was sort of like Indian with similar breads and curry orientation, but with meat on the bone dishes that were of a different continent.  

Regardless, the food was great. We had some Doubles - basically Chickpea and Potato mash with Curry in small round Naan-like soft breads.  Very tasty and definitely a cousin of Samosa.  Next I ordered Roti with Boneless Chicken, while my companion went with Roti and Goat.  Both had a side of the same mix of Chickpea and Potato found in the Double.  I thought the Chicken outshined the Goat.  It was tender and in small pieces long cooked in a spice pot.  The Goat was still on the bone.  It required more work to eat it, and to my palate, was darker and more gamey than I like.  

The accompanying Roti was superb.  It was large and folded up on the plate, but as it was taken out and ripped apart to be used to pick up the meats and veggies, it had elasticity and a ground Chickpea and spice dusting on the inside that added taste and a curiously fine grit to the experience.  I could not finish it.  

I hope to learn how to eat with one hand without using utensils and just pinching the food with the Roti.  It is much harder than it looks, especially if you try not to get your hand dirty.  

The owners and staff were very friendly.  We engaged in a running conversation about the food and life in Trinidad.  Fascinating.  The house only has four tables and a fridge with cold drinks.  I stopped beforehand to pick up a six pack of Red Stripe to add to the festivities. 

This one is a definite keeper.

While the Banh Mi (BBQ Pork) was first rate, due especially to the French baguette loaf made in house with great texture, taste and crunch, the rest of the show leaves something to be desired.  

We sampled the Egg Custard Tarts that came in packages of two and wrapped in plastic.  The result was that the crust was soft and soggy, while the custard filling seemed to be under baked.  The Durian and Jackfruit Smoothies seemed from a mix concentrate, and not based in fresh fruit which were available nearby in local supermarkets.  Overly sweet and sealed so the actual drink could not be viewed unless the plastic top was cut away. Once opened, the distinct rotten egg odor of the durian fruit wafted out.  At least it had been authentic when the concentrate was first prepared. 

The biggest shock at Nam Son was how dirty it was inside.  A floor that hadn't been cleaned in a long time; car tires stored next to the drink display case, no gloves used in food preparation, reused woven wicker baskets that bore the stains of past meals. 

Best of Philly Award in the category Banh Mi may be warranted, but it has some serious competition around town. Owner was friendly and engaging with customers, but he really should make an effort to upgrade hygiene in his shop.

Pho Viet HOA on Welsh Road, Willow Grove, sits in the middle of a modern strip center right next door to an Italian restaurant; one of the beautiful things about the melting pot we live in. Its modern utilitarian decor makes room for a dozen tables along both walls, with enough seating for social distancing in these Days of Covid. Service was prompt and efficient, with a suburban smile. The menu was primarily Vietnamese as would be expected, but also delved into a broader culinary universe found in neighboring Asian kitchens like Chinese and Thai style noodle dishes. 

I ordered Veggie Fried Rolls as an appetizer, Wide Noodles with Veggies "Wet" in a light brown sauce, and two Banh Mi sandwiches, Grilled Beef and Pork (for family take out). I hesitated on their Pho based on the luke warm reviews from respected Yelpers and the price compared to favorite pho houses in the City, which were a few bucks less. 

The four Veggie Rolls and dipping sauce were very good, crisp and full of real chopped veggies, and not just cabbage. The garnish of daikon and carrot were a nice touch. The large plate of fat noodles was supplied with ample broccoli, carrot, onion, mushroom and sprout, but lacking in spice. My mistake for not requesting lemongrass be added, but I squirted on Sriracha from the table rocket to compensate. Not precisely the flavor profile I hoped for, but decent enough to satisfy. I took half of that home. 

The uncompromising winner were the Banh Mi consumed by the family later in the evening. They were both stuffed with excellent roast pork and beef, cucumber, daikon, carrot, cilantro and a tasty mix of hot/sweet sauces, all barely contained in fresh (if not exactly French), rolls. Baguettes would have been near perfection. Compared to what we ate the week before from another Vietnamese/Thai house, this was Blue Ribbon. 

So, go for the Banh Mi for sure, perhaps not for their specials noodle list, while the jury is out on the Pho. I wouldn't hesitate to give it a try as long as the sammies were the primary focus. 

P.S. The Banh Mi were eaten before photos could be secured. Apologies.

Las Margaritas on 2nd Street Pike, Southampton, PA, isn't bad for a casa Mexicana that serves mainly an American audience not necessarily familiar with the deep choices available in a kitchen that caters to its own nationals. The space is large and dimly lit, with plenty of colorful cues of its South of the Border cultural heritage. It is very popular as witnessed by the long wait for people walking in looking for a table. Luckily, as a solo diner, I was able to grab a barstool and take my liquid and solid choices right there.

I have been somewhat spoiled by the wide variety and authenticity of all the casas Latinas in and around Trenton, which has become a very ciudad Centro Americano. All those formerly Italian corner restaurants now speak Espanol, and they put out amazing cuisine. 

Still, Las Margaritas is a good place for a reasonably priced cocktail by the same name, and the well known dishes found in most Mexican houses catering to gringos. Lots to choose from in terms of nachos, tacos, burritos, chimis, and tortas, and even a few decent dinner platters, like the chili rellenos ordered by me.  I found the two large breaded and fried poblano peppers to be nicely loaded with melted cheese and queso fresco, and topped with a thin, but well spiced, ranchero sauce. I tossed on the salsa from the chips to add texture and heat, and enjoyed the refried beans and dirty rice accompaniments. 

Not a bad meal at all. Bartender service was fine and muy amable. The only hiccup was being tendered the wrong cuenta for a couple of bucks more than what I ordered. El hombre tried to tell me it was the same price as what I got, but I knew that was not the case. Still, it wasn't worth a challenge to his manhood, so I let it roll, and adjusted the tip accordingly. 

Honesty is always the best policy when it comes to restaurant tabs.

I understand why so many people enjoy dining at Café Michaelangelo on Bustleton Avenue in the Far Northeast, Philadelphia. While most customers are local to the area, we were coming down from Bucks County, and this Italian haven was just a few miles over the county line. 

It doesn't look like much on the outside. A narrow parking lot separating the building from heavily trafficked Bustleton. The façade a worn brown wood with narrow doors and confusing signs.  Still, we found our way in through the side entrance and walked into a small lobby, followed by a large glass-walled dining room with high exposed beam ceiling and vistas overlooking a back yard that was treed and green - more like a tree house feel, than a structure anchored to the ground. Although aging, it was very attractive. Positive first impressions. 

We were seated at the first table in the dining room.  Although closest to the door, there was a half wall with trellis protecting us, and we soon forgot we were sitting on the edge. The menus were brought out quickly and we settled in to scour it for that evening's delights. While reading, we ordered a Stone IPA and River Horse Raspberry Tripel Horse Belgian-Style Ale. (You're wrong! I had the fruity beer, and my beautiful companion the very stout IPA.) We decided to go light. Fried calamari as a shared appetizer, and roast pork and Italian sausage sandwiches as our mains. Alina was our excellent server. She took very good care of us first timers. 

Although the calamari was almost exclusively cut into bands, with only one set of tentacles, it was quite good; especially the dipping red sauce which was spicily chunky and required a second helping. While I might not get it again, it was a fine vehicle for sauce delivery. 

The sandwiches were both first rate. They were served on decent Italian rolls which supported their passengers from plate to mouth without hesitation or flopping. The meat was tender and flavorful, with dipping sauce to enhance the experience. The sausage was cut into smaller slices for ease of ripping off chunks of the sandwich, and had ample onions and green frying peppers mixed throughout and more of that wonderful red sauce.  Really liked both plates. And, there was a plentitude of stuffing in each - so much so that we could only eat half of each sandwich and brought the rest home for stepson to enjoy.  We had planned to order something separately for him, but we had so much that it wasn't necessary. Alina brought us the takeout containers and bags with an easy smile, despite the loss of the extra sale to the house. No doubt, she had seen this happen before. 

We thoroughly and zestfully partook of our Café Michelangelo meal, and commented as we ate how good it was. In warmer weather, eating on the back patio would be a worthy addition to the program. 

An exceptional find on the wild streets of Bustleton. And, the prices didn't hurt either.

It was a cold, windy, city morn when we reached Washington Avenue, and I still hadn't had my first cup of java. I was trying to maintain my good mood, but it would be a losing battle without some caffeine soon. 

Desperate times called for desperate measures. 

I remembered there was this Bambu shop nearby, so I Yelped it and realized it was right across 6th Street from where we were. We walked over and found it in the inner corner of the shopping center. It was a small shop, with short red sofa, three cafe tables, and a few chairs along the window. The walls were covered in menus and photos of their signature Che fruity concoctions. 

Colorful, but I needed something stronger and hotter. Farther down the drinks list was the coffee. I asked for Vietnamese coffee, hot. I normally drink it in VN cafes or after meals, so this was my first takeout. 

It was exactly as expected. Strong, hot and sweetened by condensed milk. I missed the whole drip experience but it was great to be able to shop the market with java in hand.

Can't say I was impressed with this Iron Hill Brewery in Abington, PA. 

While the Pumpkin Ale was tasty and refreshing, our menu choices were fair to middling at best. We ordered their Calamari appetizer, Asian Salmon Burger and Country Schnitzel as main courses. The Calamari was all small rings (no tentacles) and overly oily from deep frying. Our guess was that these little things came from a large bag of frozen seafood. Nice to have slivers of hot peppers mixed in, but the ranch dressing dip really didn't contribute to the experience. 

My dining mate didn't offer a taste of the Asian Salmon after she took a bite and put it aside. "Too much garlic," she explained. Those fries were quite crisp and crunchified, however, and I had a free hand with them. 

The pork fillet Schnitzel was good; nice breading, pan fried with chunky Andouille Sausage white gravy over top. We ended up sharing that after she turned aside her salmon. I found the cutlets to be better without the gravy, and was able to push most of it off the entree. The sides (fresh spinach sautéed in garlic and oil, and the mashed sweet potato) were very colorful and also tasty strong contributors. Fair to say this plate was our dinner's salvation. 

The space felt somewhat worn out. I don't like carpeted dining rooms, as they tend to hide the accumulated dirt that collects in the fibers. This wall to wall definitely had been down too long. 

This was my third Iron Hill in the past month. Overall, unless very new, these breweries just don't seem to maintain high class facilities and appear worse for wear compared to their competition.

Three STARS is as far as I can go.

While Gay Street in downtown West Chester, PA, is way cool, with outdoor cafes, taverns and breweries competing with pedestrians for sidewalk space, this Iron Hill Brewery & Restaurant seems a bit out of sync with its very popular competition. Perhaps because it is older than many, the overall impression is drab and worn. 

We were a small group celebrating a new member of the firm. Staff put a few tables together for us, giving us complete command of the main dining room late in the afternoon. We ordered drinks and a few appetizers and smoozed for a couple of hours. We had good conversation as we consumed a plate of hummus/pita, sweet potato fries w dipping sauces and roasted Brussel sprouts in balsamic (?) dressing. 

The drinks were fine, if unimaginative; the same being true for the food. We consumed everything with a couple rounds of booze, and had no complaints, but it could have been so much more to keep us interested in their dark auburn atmosphere.

This Iron Hill just felt tired compared to other of their siblings I have visited and enjoyed. They occupy a key corner in town and it was easy to imagine how much more interesting and inviting it could be. How about an outdoor presence like everyone else? How about better marking of the main entrance door? How about better lighting around the bar to accentuate the back bar display?

Just saying...

The owners of Pin Wei Chinese Restaurant on S. Henderson Road, King of Prussia, PA, may be Taiwanese, but they have taken the time to understand and produce first quality Szechuanese cuisine in the heart of Montgomery County. They have mastered the mysteries of extremely spicy sauces and cooking techniques that create the unique numbing style that finds its source in the history of Chengdu and Chongqing, China.  There aren't many of these authentic houses around, and when one is found it automatically shoots to the top of the list of great dinner spots.  From the size of the crowd waiting for tables last night, the secret is out. 

This was our first visit, after looking mostly in vain for a Szechuan chili joint that knew what it was doing.  There are a few in Philly, and a couple in nearby Jersey, but by and large, the art of flamethrower dishes is a lost art.  We were very happily impressed with Pin Wei. 

We ordered more than we could finish in one sitting, so we would have enough to take home and enjoy a second time.  Our choices consisted of: Scallion Oil Cucumber as an appetizer, and entrees of Chicken Dry Chili Peppers, Lamb Dry Pot, Twice Cooked Fish, and Deep Fried Longhots. 

In a word; FIRE! 

The cucumbers were served cold and marinating in the clear scallion oil.  Crisp, cool, mildly hot and a great introduction.  The platters arrived as they were finished in the kitchen, not all at once, in the traditional Chinese custom.  The longhots arrived next.  They were beautiful to behold - like dark green snakes coiled on themselves waiting for someone to bite them to release their venom.  Awesome, as each chew released more toxin, burning the gums and walls of the mouth, and bringing tears to the eyes.  Eventually, the scald tempered, and the underlying flavor of these peppers emerged transcendent. 

The chicken dry pepper was a sight to behold, with a huge amount of small red Szechuan chilies, garlic, ginger, onion and small pieces of breaded and twice deep fried chicken mixed throughout.  The chili powder on the morsels was a powerful, sinus clearing, blast.  With every wonderful crunch more capsaicin was released, bringing the mouth to near full numbness.  Got to love that feeling to appreciate its otherworldliness. The lamb dry pot arrived next, and we were thankful for a little relief from the conflagration.  The meat was tender with a gentle sweetness beneath the cumin and other stimulants.  Plenty of mushrooms to absorb the dark sauce at the bottom of the heated metal bowl.  Excellent.

Finally, the twice cooked fish arrived. There was a small glitch when after waiting a while, the wrong dish came to the table - twice cooked pork (belly), which looked good, but, alas, was not what we ordered. Ten more minutes to get the right platter.  It was terrific, saving best for last.  Fish fillets, slightly crisp, yet also soft within, with a dark sauce that hinted of vinegar in addition to the less dominant burning powders.  I had to ask our server what that unusual taste was, but he just smiled and demurred.

Inscrutable. 

The secrets of Pin Wei were safe with him. After all, he was the owner, and he didn't want us trying to replicate his magic elixirs at home. He didn't want to be responsible for what might happen.

HOT Damn, people! 

PRO TIP - How does Pin Wei compare with Han Dynasty in Old City?  Food wise, it is a very close call.  Both are excellent, and there is no point in picking one over the other based on the kitchen.  Where there is some separation is in the atmospherics.  Pin Wei is a small place compared to Chestnut Street.  The dining room is very crowded and thus quite loud.  It is a bit distracting. HanDynasty is in an old bank building, and although busy, possesses more nooks and crannies where it is possible to feel some level of  privacy, even in the crowd. The front of Pin Wei was packed with people waiting for tables, and we almost had to fight our way out after dinner. The bar area was SRO, while Han has a larger bar zone, which seldom feels overwhelmed with people.

It is obvious than the success of Pin Wei, is also its shortcoming.  It needs a much bigger space.  Whether it wants it or not is a separate question.

Our very personable waitperson described Jones as serving, "American Comfort Food."  Even before seeing the menu my mind was wandering about what that would mean to my Chinese friends experiencing local cuisine for just about the first time.  For me, a brownie and a glass of milk is comfort food, but for anyone lacking a database of experience, they might have some fairly wild ideas.  

Turns out, they didn't have a clue and relied on me to order for them.  Okay. I was up for the challenge.  How about a good burger for the 19 year old, and a turkey club for his mother?  Handled.  I've been curious about the chicken & waffles craze, so when I saw it on the menu, I stopped reading.  

We were all satisfied with our lunches.  The burger was a big hit with the young guy.  He believes burgers are the height of American culture.  He could be right.  Turkey is not well known in China, but the combination with bacon, lettuce, spicy mayo and tomato seemed to captivate my friend.  I moved quickly to remove the long wooden picks used to hold each quarter together, as she was unaccustomed to this shiv and nearly poked her eye out.  

The fried chicken arrived as a breast/thigh combo with golden brown crispy coat.  It was good, but perhaps a little too salty.  The waffle was the better companion, done well on an iron and still steamy soft within with a hint of sweetness to counterbalance the NaCl on the bird.  As a lover of Southern Fried Chicken, I did not truly appreciate the passionate embrace of these two carb loads on one plate.  Call me old fashioned, but I will stick with waffles for breakfast and fried chicken for other meals; although I might be convinced to change my mind if someone poured pure maple syrup over both and allowed me this sticky indulgence. 

Jones is a very nice facility with high ceilings, which make the brown sandstone columns around the house quite attractive and draw eyes upward, giving the sense of a mountain lodge in Red Rock, Sedona.  

Made the saying of "Grace" seem totally appropriate.

It's great to have a high end Napolitan pizza house in Newtown!  It's even better that the enterprise is owned by Pasquale and Anna, the proprietors of Osteria Vecchia, the excellent casa Italiana right down the street. This shop is for the daughter and son-in-law.  Thus, begin empires. 

The building is on the site of the former Minuteman Press.  That old structure was taken down to the foundation, and a new Euro-Country Casual establishment arose.  Attention to detail is obvious, as the space is beautiful, with quality stone, wood, glass and a "just off the boat" wood burning hive oven covered in red glazed tile and contrasting white ceramic lettering that shouts, "Pasquale & Anna/Acqua e Farina!"  

We were greeted by Sal, the maestro de la casa, who sat my son and I at the corner table where we could see the whole operation.  We ordered a Siciliana pie, and as we waited, other servers brought thin slices of red sauced bread, and a small plate of Brussel sprouts that were soft and delicious from their time swimming in olive oil and spices.  I was even offered a glass of red wine on the house. Very cool touch!

The pie arrived with steam shimmering above it, on a large white platter.  It was cut in quarters, and covered in mozza, afterburn peccorino and chunks of eggplant.  Truly, a work of art with the bubbled crust and scorched undercarriage.  The special deal with these ovens is that they hold extremely high heat, such that the raw pie is placed in the oven for less than three minutes, while baking everything quickly and capturing all the flavor of the ingredients before they burn off and escape. The result is a wonderfully textured and tasty crust that is flavored by the ingredients you choose.  It is all about the dough (thus, the name, Water & Flour), and secondarily about the toppings.  Quite different than the better known pizza experience provided by most joints. 

So it was here. A beauty to behold, and a pleasure to consume.  Of course, there is a downside to this approach to baking.  While the crust is excellent, the more ingredients you put on top, the wetter the center of the pie will be on the plate, because it is not possible to fully cook the veggies and meats in such a short time, and as a result of the lack of evaporation in the oven, the finished product will be softer that normal, and the drip from the collected moisture under the hood will be noticeable, and require care to avoid making a mess. 

The secret is to order a simple pie with minimal topside accessories, so that the crust, cheese and sauce have the maximum opportunity to vent off the moisture.  This provides a drier bottom and optimal crustiness. 

Dining at Acqua & Farina is very different than eating at pizza parlors.  It is designed as a feast for the senses.  There are more moving parts, and the resulting cost enhancement is noticeable. There is a time when "two slices and a soda," is what you want, but there are also times when although you yearn for pizza, you want a more rousing experience.  

At those moments, Acqua e Farina will be calling your name.

Not sure how Chickie's & Pete's is considered a café, as it seems much more like a dark and dingy sports bar with a huge collection of tap levers hanging from walls and exposed beams.  There seems to be plenty of suds to choose from, and the menu is adequate, especially if you like shellfish as your main course.  

Problem here is that there are no side dishes with your meal.  Everything is a la carte, and the expense climbs rapidly.  If you want a beer with that, your tab will gouge you at least $15 for a sandwich lunch.  

My Chicken Parm Sandwich was pretty good; deep fried and crispy outside, still soft and tasty inside.  The Tomato Sauce was mildly salty, but still a good blend.  Would have been even better if they figured out a way to give a small amount of Crab Fries with the platter, rather than charging another $7 for a full basket of taters.  The House Salad @ $10., was a large plate full of Romaine and some other veggies, and a reasonably good vinaigrette, but underwhelming at the price. 

If you're into tired looking sports bars with ample brew (not necessarily craft-quality), and a menu that forces you to be very selective about the cost of your nosh, C & P is for you.  Otherwise, there are much better sports houses around with better food, drinks, atmosphere and prices.

Adams Avenue in Northeast Philadelphia is a center for the Vietnamese community. The neighborhood is full of pho and com (noodle & rice) houses that are about as authentic as you can find on the East Coast. No, it is not yet as diverse as Garden Grove, CA, with little differentiation between southern and northern style cuisine, but what they do have, they do well by and large. 

Pho Ha Saigon benefits from being a fairly new structure; well designed and spacious enough (in a post industrial sort of way) to attract and hold your attention, with a respectable and capable kitchen. The service staff is generally bilingual and large enough to stay on top of their work. Their HVAC is strong enough to suck the front doors closed and create a semi-vacuum between them, making prying them open to enter or exit a chore. Hopefully, that also means there is sufficient circulation to be sucking out any Covid suspended in the air. 

I went with a smaller bowl of Pho Ga (Chicken Noodle Soup), Spring Rolls, and takeout for the family of Grilled Beef w Vermicelli, and Roast Pork/Beef Banh Mi). The bowl was still large enough for a few goldfish to swim comfortably. The chicken broth had very good flavor profile and there were plenty of accessories (Thai basil, sprouts, jalapeno slices, & lime wedge) to adapt to my tastebuds. The sliced breast meat was downright generous, and the under the surface nest of thin rice noodles, more than adequate. 

While the Spring Rolls were generic, with standard sweet dipping sauce, the pho was a pleasure to slurp with flat spoon in one hand and chopsticks in the other. It filled me completely. I suppose the broth could have been somewhat deeper in secondary seasoning and simmer time, because I found myself suffering a mild case of MSG poisoning on the way home. I am allergic to it, and I should have warned them when ordering. Still, MSG really shouldn't even be in their kitchen. Chalk it up to my oversight. I won't remove a star, but reserve the right to let people know in case they are also sensitive to it. 

That evening my family went after the Banh Mi and Vermicelli dish with gusto. The sandwiches were stuffed and had great taste with strong roll contributions. The Grilled Beef was succulent and in small thin sliced pieces. Delicious. 

But for my bout with the food additive, I totally enjoyed my meal at Pho Ha Saigon, and will not hesitate to return with memo to self about inquiring about MSG.

I always feel a bit out of my element when invited to a good steakhouse like Capital Grille in King of Prussia. Not a steak lover, I can appreciate the clubby atmosphere, the dark wood tones, and white jacketed servers always where they should be, attentively taking care of their beef obsessed customers. I even love the aroma of grilled sirloin and the menacing glitter of oversized serrated knives slicing through medium rare filet mignon. For me, the odor is the best part. 

So, I ready my excuses for not joining in the carnivorial feast, yet always manage to find plenty of good things to enjoy on the menu outside of the main attraction. Nobody really minds that I am the guy who goes with calamari, wedge or Caesar salad and a tapas approach to the many veggie sides available. Give me interesting brussel sprouts, cauliflower or roast/mashed potato, and I go to town. 

Capital Grille does everything well, and the servers are always on their game. The New England Clam Chowder, Wedge Salad and large plate of calamari (tentacles included) were all tasty and left me full even without the heavier meat load. 

I mused as I worked through my choices, watching my office compadres cut bloody paths through their perfectly finished steaks and chops. I knew we were appreciated by the powers that be to be treated so well.

White Dotte Dairy Bar & Grill is an old school roadside attraction at the intersection of Rts. 38 & 206 in Vincentown, NJ. It produces good soft serve ice cream and an assortment of burgers, cheesesteaks and other  fast food that take your mind off the drive through pancake flat Burlington County. 

I stopped by for breakfast earlier this week to find out what they were doing to be in business for 70 years. It is a small custom made railroad car like wooden structure with small counter and a few tables. Clearly their success relies on take out. Yet, I enjoyed my time on one of their stools at the green paisley lunch counter. The menu is All Americana standards. I asked about the french toast, and when the friendly server said she really liked it, I went with it.  I sipped their generic coffee while waiting for it to come off the grill in back. 

The walls had pictures of the farmstead and family since inception. Curious about what "Dotte" meant, I asked whether it stood for someone named, "Dotty," or something else. I was surprised to learn that it had nothing to do with a person, but that "White Dotte" was the name of the chicken breed raised there. I googled that and found that the actual breed was Wynedotte,  an American egg layer developed in the 1880's to produce brown eggs. Beautiful bird, too. Very cool.

And, the french toast was very good. The mix had excellent proportions of vanilla, sugar and cinnamon, that completely saturated the three slices of their bread, and caramelized the edges. Surprisingly tasty. 

White Dotte turned out to be much more than expected. Historic enterprise from one family. Cozy building. Esoteric name that added to the positive impression. Decent grub that made this a stop well worth repeating. 

A chance to learn something unexpected and captivating.

Folcroft Diner sits on Chester Pike (Rt. 13) in the northern panhandle of the borough by that name in Delaware County, PA. Before the interstate was completed, it and Rt.1 were the primary roads north and south between Philly and Baltimore. Driving it last Friday on the way back from UDel to Bucks County due to jammed traffic on Rt. I 95, was an historic tour of yesteryear America when roadside attractions were often the best part of a family car trip to the intended destination. 

Cruising north with son after school was declared closed for classes for the remainder of the spring semester, it was natural to reflect on the drive with my parents between New York and Washington when I was a student in D.C. Felt like an unfortunate right of passage to be experiencing this due to the curse of COVID-19. 

The diner was the perfect stage for a lunch stop to stretch and grab a quick bite of Americana. A cup of New England Clam Chowder and Petty Melt (medium, fries, slaw & pickle slices), were the way to go. Our booth was comfy, our server friendly and attentive, and the space around us sufficient to allow us to feel socially distanced. We considered whether restaurants would remain open for sit down business in the days and weeks ahead. If this was to be a last meal in the Age of COVID-19, then we would soberly celebrate the moment and pray our angels protected us. 

The chowder was thick creamy and loaded with diced clam. The cup was very filling and more than enough for a sample. The burger was a half pounder, finished as desired, bracketed by quality rye toast, melted Swiss and filled with sauteed onions and mushrooms. A long red squirt of Heinz Ketchup and I had a fun, satisfying meal. I could only down half, and took the rest home. Prices were surprisingly reasonable for the quality and quality of the plates served, almost like the menu was printed in the last century. 

Maybe it was.

I was thinking "Mykonos" as we drove to Mikonos Restaurant on Scotch Road in Ewing, NJ.  The Aegean island is a place I hung out for a while in an earlier life, drinking Gerovasilliou and Agiorgitiko to excess in the harbor side tabernas by day and surrendering to the liltingly haunting Bouzoukis by night.  I couldn't share my reveries, but I wondered how close to my recollections this Greek house by the same name would come to those wild Hellonic daze. 

 It wasn't fair to even entertain the possibility that there would be any similarity; after all, that was life in a mystic age long gone from this coil.  Still, it did serve to awaken something long dormant, and while this is the age of dark cynicism, the place had enough pictures on the walls and aromas wafting through the room to allow for a moment of silent appreciation. Wine saturated memories are sometimes enough.

The food was pretty good, too.  

Our opening salvo of Avgo Lemono Soup was Star Dog Champion delicious. Creamy, Lemon bite, soft Chicken chunks, and Rice.  Our three spoons fought for each drop.  

The follow up for two of us was the tour de force Liga Apo Ola for 2, a huge platter with ample Moussaka, Spanakopeta, Pastitsio, Dolmades, and maybe something else I have forgotten, served with a metal spatula to aid in distribution.  They were all exceptional, although the Stuffed Grape Leaves had more  dry rice filling than I recall from past experiences.  My guests had never eaten Greek cuisine before, and they were so impressed that they tried to duplicate the Lemon Soup at home the next day.  

Our third member ordered a Chicken Souvlaki Platter.  It looked great (see photo), but my taste of the chicken surprised me with the strange toughness of the meat.  He gamely ate everything, but I could tell he was struggling with it.  A large slab of Moussaka from our plate was the least we could do to help him out. 

But for that last bit of news, this was a 5 Star dinner.  We will return in due course for the Avgo Lemono and further exploration of the menu.  Those Gyros that went by looked amazing!

With a sign under the peak of the roof reading, "Circa 1734," you get the feeling that the Newportville Inn is pretty old. Approaching it as it sits on Lower Road running along Neshaminy Creek, it is easy to imagine it looked more or less the same 250 years ago when it was a pre-Revolutionary War weigh station between Philadelphia and Trenton. Historic lore mentions the likes of George Washington, John Adams, Alexander Hamilton and even Thomas Jefferson in the vicinity as they sought safe places to meet to plot the course of independence while the British Army occupied New York and threatened Philadelphia. This historic structure was there to offer room and board to the wayward revolutionists. 

Aside from newer additions and the outdoor beer garden, the building is basically unchanged since back in the day. Sitting at the old bar in a small chamber with low beamed ceilings and deep well windows, time can seem to stand still. Yes, it could stand some renovation and deep cleaning, but not at the expense of lost charm and legendary significance. I enjoy such time warps on occasion. 

Besides, the German menu and beer choices are hard to duplicate in the area. My Wartmeister Pilsner was cold, smooth and refreshing. The footlong wiener house special with potato salad and sauerkraut, a delectable authentic meal. Dining at the bar with Johnny Bartender working his magic, and the 76ers on the tube, was a very satisfying interlude. The hot potato salad was great, and the sliced apple in the sauerkraut a terrific idea, adding a touch of sweetness to the briney sourness. 

While not a lover of all German cuisine, wurst and schnitzel I like, and Newportville specializes in them. Given how friendly everyone was to this stranger, I can see returning as the mood for a brat or breaded/fried chicken or pork schnitzel moves me.

When a comfort food restaurant is empty at 7:30 pm on a Sunday night, there is reason to think that perhaps that is saying something about the operation there. That was what we faced on a damp March night, but we were already inside, and as the old saying goes: "What the hey?!" 

Turns out that with the smoker out front, and a good chef in the kitchen, the food was pretty good.  Only problem was the slightly weird attitude of management that wanted our business, but at the same time had a series of rules they felt compelled to enforce while we ordered. First, they were closing in 30 minutes, which meant we had to order quickly.  We could eat inside while they cleaned up.  Second, our sandwiches came with fries, but any other side order was an extra buck. I wanted baked beans. Okay, bud, but fork over the sawback. Third, a medium burger wasn't possible because the health code required everything be grilled to well done.  What if I didn't like an over cooked burger?  They couldn't help me officially, but they did ask the chef to take it off the heat while still pink.  He said he would with a wink. 

Ultimately, the brisket sandwich was quite tasty, with a nice rub making a flavorful bark.  It might have benefited from another hour in the smoker to make the beef more tender, but it was decent as it was.  My Firehouse Burger was very good, with nicely sautéed/grilled onions and peppers.  Half pound of ground beef was truly pink at its core, and proved a challenge to consume despite its excellent juicy profile.  The baked beans were also solidly flavorful, but could have used a few chunks of burnt ends or pulled pork in the mix to max out the texture and provide more twang. 

The dining room was small, but comfortable, with Texas collectibles hanging for ceiling and wall. I would return to try the ribs or another burger, but not before I visited other nearby grillmasters to check out their goods.  I wasn't blown away by Fat Jack's, but neither was I repelled by their chuck wagon grub.

Unofficial Yelp Events (UYEs) are always just about as good as a party among social media friends can be, and this was no exception.  The meet up at Tired Hands Fermentaria was my first opportunity to visit this well known brewery in Ardmore, Pa., and to sample its wares.  I've got to say that sitting at a table with about 20 peeps, surrounded by the acoustically challenged corrugated iron-roofed warehouse and close to the stainless steel fermenting tanks where the magic is done, made for a loud amplified afternoon. Yet, sitting with folks that I look forward to seeing, and the new ones that I am about to meet, made it bearable. 

Arriving late, I was still in time to find a seat and order a Shamabalac mystical ale and a veggie Banh Mi wrap.  Our server was cool and competent, keeping everyone in suds and sustenance, while allowing us to maintain separate tabs.  Quite a trick that she handled with aplomb. 

The drink was blond and had remarkable fruity notes.  Liked it, and ordered a couple more. The Vietnamese interpreted sandwich was hardly banh mi at all, given that it was in a wheat wrap rather than a French baguette.  True, the daikon, carrot, tofu and siriracha were present, but the concept was wrong.  Better to just called it Vietnamese inspired, and leave it at that. It was okay, but the image in my head was abandoned unfilled. 

Truth be told, I am not a beer maven, although I enjoy it in small creative doses.  Bourbon is my downfall.  Still, I see what people like about Tired Hands, and brewery clubs in general.  The capacity crowd on this late Saturday afternoon, certainly did, too.

El Barrio Cantina y Tequila Bar is a 5 Star facility with a 3 Star kitchen. 

It was a very pleasant surprise to walk into a large warehouse space with corrugated iron ceiling, long bar with attractively bottled backbar, and Dia Del Muerte personality.  Skulls everywhere.  Plenty of booths in the three dining areas to feel comfortable.  Acoustics were trouble, as every sound was amplified by all the hard and harmonic surfaces.  Pleasant service. 

We ordered pretty standard fare.  A beef burrito for son. Chicken flautas for the old man.  Shrimp Molcajete for stepson.  Chips & salsa as forespice. Everything was okay, but not memorable.  The burrito was stuffed with mildly spiced shredded cow, cheese and peppers.  My son drowned it in the available salsa to bring up the burn.  He ate every last shred, but announced it wasn't very different than what he had recently at Taco Belch.  My fried chicken, cheese and spice stuffed flutes were fine. It was an appetizer, but enough for me last night. Crisp shell. Decent bird mix. The molcajete was basically their version of fajitas - served in a hot volcanic rock, with only six medium sized shrimp and a load of sautéed colorful peppers and onions.  Small sides of black beans, rice, guacamole and sour cream.  He wolfed down the crustaceans and played with the veggies before declaring himself full (bored).  At $15., it was more floor show, than gut filling meal. 

We left agreeing that the joint had potential, but that the food wasn't its strength.  Too young to partake of the bar offerings, we suspected that all the tequila on display might offer a clue to where the magic lies in El Barrio Cantina & Tequila Bar.  

Next time I'll come with grownups and sample their tequila flight and margaritas.

Eagle Diner on Street Road, Warminster, PA, is a traditional Greek food emporium with broad multi-page menu covering all three meals, plus a significant salad bar. It is open 24/7.  The only thing missing is a counter with stools for those who prefer that old line dining experience, like me. 

I stopped in for diner last weekend, hoping for a good meal for this solitary traveler. I had to wait about 15 minutes for a table, as the place was SRO when I arrived around 6 pm. A stool at a counter would have eliminated the wait, but I did not mind standing in the entrance area and observing all the scurry from the staff. It also gave me the chance to check out the cakes, pies and other bakery goods made on premises. Certainly did not hurt my appetite. 

I was eventually shown to a table in the back, and handed the short novelette menu. So much food; so little time. I chose their meatloaf mini dinner, with mashed and cup of soup or salad bar. I grazed over the greens for a while and returned with a full plate of various salad components. It wasn't a stunningly broad spread, and a lot of it was processed and not fresh, but it still provided many colors and flavors that worked well on top of a lettuce base. Three bean salad, beets, red onion, macaroni and potato salad, baby spinach, pickled everything, cheesebread and 1,000 Island dressing, kept me munching while waiting for the mains. 

When my entre arrived, I was confronted by two huge slices of baked/grilled beef loaf and a dish of white mashed, with brown gravy on the side. The meat was tender and tasty, but better with a jet of ketchup, than the brown sauce (a bit salty). The slices were about 1.5 inches thick. I couldn't finish the meal. Absolutely no room for the luscious looking desserts.

At a price around $10., the value was evident in every bite. 

I'm told Eagle does a good job for breakfast, too. Next time I'm in the area that time of day, I'll stop in again to check it out.

On the corner of 13th & Snyder in South Philly, AmeriThai was a pleasant respite on a steamy late June afternoon. Although as colorful as a Thai temple with rusty orange hues and elephants abounding, sitting in a quiet corner with the air cooling only ourselves, it felt a chill oasis. 

The menu offered plenty of choices from soup to noodles, curry to bigger game like chicken, pork, beef and duck. We order Chu Chee Duck and Crazy Noodles, with appetizer of Curry Puffs. 

In reverse order; the Curry Puffs reminded of Indian Samosas -  Sweet and White Mashed Potato, Onion, Peas,  mixed in mild Curry powder, deep fried, with semi-sweet/spicy Chili Dipping Sauce in a small brass dish. Excellently golden. Crisp shell. Tasty innards. Tart sauce. Liked it a lot!

The Crazy (Drunken) Noodles with tender Sliced Beef was a load and a half with big Fat Noodles, Veggies, and hot spicies. Plenty of dry Chili Pepper flakes in the mix. So glad we had Thai Iced Tea to tamp down the flames. 

Chu Chee Duck had wonderfully crisp skin, moist delicious meat and a pale orange cream curry sauce. This became slightly sloppy finger food, as every morsel was too good to miss and required close examination and tongue probing to suck it all off the bone. 

There are many very good Thai houses in and around Philly, and AmeriThai is certainly one. It is a little frayed around the edges, but it fits well with the neighborhood. Others mentioned that the kitchen is inconsistent, but I don't know about that yet. What I know is that when they get it right, it is an excellent place for dinner.

Surprising good Chinese cuisine at this basement kitchen associated with the Asia Market on North 11th Street, Chinatown, Philadelphia. There may have been change of ownership and this is a first visit, but if the past owners were even better on the wok than these folks, then I missed something pretty special, because I was quite happy with what we ate this night. 

Amazingly convenient if grocery shopping of Chinese ingredients is your reason for being there in the first place. Just go hungry, eat, and then shop.  Worked well for us. It is not too far fetched to think that if the Tasty kitchen runs out of something, they just walk a few feet into the supermarket and pick up what they needed. Symbiotic. 

We ordered the wonton soup, salt baked squid and roast pork on rice. All were very good to excellent, despite the somewhat dank surroundings. The large bowl of soup was loaded with more than a dozen freshly handmade wontons with ground pork filling.  The beef consume was hot with a pleasant flavor.  Made for fun slurping. The squid was cut into fairly large pieces and coated with a light flour, salt and pepper breading.  It was tender and juicy. Especially enjoyed the scallion and sliced jalapenos the dish was mixed with.  The flavor/texture profile became quite animated on the palate. This was the star of the show.  The roast pork had a nice ruddy bark and was lean cut.  Not quite Ting Wong Restaurant level, but close enough. We ended up taking about half of the dry dishes home.  

With all the wonderful alternatives on the street above, there is not that much reason to go subterranean for a solid meal, unless price motivates you highly. The numbers on the menu were very reasonable, and it is easy to imagine that Tasty Place does a large business with students and others on a budget.  

You certainly get more than you paid for here.

One door closes and another door opens. 

We were in Mayfair to check out the Italian food at Emma's Cafe on Frankford Avenue, but when we learned it was booked up on Saturday night we decided to roll with it and pop in to the Aja Asian Fusion Restaurant right next door. The mental gear shift wasn't that difficult. 

It had a big dining room and we were led to a booth against the wall in the middle of the room. It looked to be clean in the dim semi romantic light and our server was pleasantly efficient. Their menu made it clear that Aja was primarily a Chinese house with a cross section of sushi related dishes and a very few Thai choices, like pad thai and two curry options. My concern that it was more confusion than fusion was born out when we ordered the shrimp pad thai (only form it came in) and teriyaki salmon bento box with shumai and California rolls, with choice of miso soup or salad with ginger dressing. 

The noodles were far too sweet and bereft of peanuts to have ever been touched by Thai hands, although there was alot of it on the plate. The grilled salmon was a very small steak, but had the right taste and texture. The miso was fine, but the shumai seemed a frozen, cheaply produced variety and the Cali roll was just okay, tasting mostly of avocado and seaweed. From what we saw at the sushi bar they didn't move enough fish to keep it all daily fresh. There was an awful lot being stored in plastic wrap. 

Unless you're satisfied with generic sushi rolls that can mask the flavor/freshness of the fish, Aja Asian Fusion is better wokking up Chinese dishes for you. Leave the Japanese and Thai cuisine for more talented kitchens. 

Once was enough. 

Will make reservations for Emma's next time.

Viet Thai Cuisine is a well designed Asian house just off the Pa Pike in Horsham.  Lots of stone and metal, and even a wall of pussy willow branches. A semi-private dining room was off to the side.  Service is warm and precise, and the menu offers a fairly broad cross section of dishes from Vietnam and Thailand.  In such "fusion" locales, the question always is whether it is really "fusion," or more confusion?  

The staff we saw was Thai, and we took that as a suggestion to stay close to the menu from their homeland, just to be safe.  Besides, we have been to many very good Vietnamese shops in and around Philly, and our Thai options were always more limited.  

We ordered Coconut Soup (w/ Tofu), Summer Rolls (Veggie), and Salmon in Red Curry Sauce for sharing.  The soup had the sweetness from the coconut and the hot bite of lemongrass, with plenty of veggies.  It was quite good, and was slurped away quickly.  The summer rolls were also top notch, with a thin strip of tofu holding the rest of the contents together.  The peanut dipping sauce was excellent with thin chili shavings and ground nuts sitting on top, looking like calligraphy (see photo).  If there was anything that missed the mark, it was the salmon, which was slightly overcooked, and was drier than desired.  Still, the presentation was lovely, and the surrounding elements on the plate along with the red curry, redeemed the fish to some extent.  

We were enjoying our time here, and decided to extend it with a fried banana dessert.  It came in the guise of spring rolls with a large scoop of Bassett's Vanilla Ice Cream melting on top.  It was a creamy sweet ending to our evening at Viet Thai.  

3.5 Stars

I am new to Maryanne's Homestyle Cooking, although I know they had another location in the past.  I am glad I finally made it, and that it is now closer to home.  

This is a modern version of the old style small town luncheonette that was prevalent across the USA in the early and middle part of the last century.  It is more than a simple place to have a good meal, but also the unofficial town center, where people meet to discuss their lives, community and nation.  It has a warm and comfortable Americana feel to it.  I enjoyed my first visit sitting in a booth behind two senior gentlemen who were doing movie reviews and political analysis at a fairly sophisticated level.  At least 75 each, they gave nothing away to younger minds.  

The service was solid with timely walk bys asking if I wanted more coffee.  My French Toast was above average, but not among the best I have had.  The java was hot and tasty.  

If there is a weak link in Maryanne's armor it might be the way they approach providing the accompaniments to the dishes served.  Their syrup came in a small plastic cup.  It seemed to be watered down to be just maple sweetwater, rather than anything close to authentic commercial grade maple syrup.  It was completely soaked up by the bread because it lacked the viscosity to sit atop the short stack long enough to allow for cutting and consumption.  It made for soggy French Toast half way through the meal.  I would gladly pay extra for the choice of syrups.  The butter was likewise very thin and airy and had little buttery taste.  

Maryanne's could be a real HOME run if they decided to provided an upgrade to these items, or at least the choice to patrons.  Their prices are very reasonable for the clientele, but even folks on Social Security enjoy a little pampering now and then.
