Hawkeye's Country Tavern is a modern roadhouse on Route 113, Perkasie, PA. It has a decent, but limited beer list, and talented hands in the kitchen. The menu is primarily American classics, with a large sandwich page and multi component entrees for those desiring a bigger meal. 

I sat in the step down barroom that felt like a basement with low ceiling and large rectangular bar. I didn't see the dining room. My server was prompt and friendly, bringing the draft Stella Artois to me in seconds. My plan was to have an early solo dinner while the family worked into the evening, and to bring home food for them so they had something interesting to eat when they arrived.

The chips & salsa table nosh was a nice touch. 

I liked the homemade meatloaf dinner that came with mashed potatoes and fresh steamed zucchini. It was def a step up from a burger, with texture and flavor coming in part from the dark brown gravy on top. Washed it all down with the cold Stella. 

I ordered the Brisket and Cuban Sandwiches and their Original Burger (grass fed locally w cheese, grilled onions and avocado) as takeout for the fam. Later that night I tasted the brisket on brioche and it was quite tender with a nice almost sweet BBQ bite. The Cuban disappeared without an offer from the stepson, while the burger was devoured by son after the rest of us went to bed. Told me he liked it, with special mention of the creamy avo adding interest when I saw him in the morning. 

Overall, although labeled as a roadhouse tavern, Hawkeye's felt like a family restaurant (although I didn't see any kids). It did a very good job with the cuisine standards, and with a better curated brewery component and deeper whiskey shelf, it could attract a more rousing crowd and rock out.

F. W. Woolworth built a retail empire at the end of the 19th into the mid twentieth centuries, out of the "Five & Dime" store concept. In its heyday it had over 5,000 stores on 4 continents. One of those iconic enterprises was build on Haddon Avenue in downtown Collingswood, NJ. Today, the high tintype ceiling, wood plank floored space is where Sabrina's Cafe holds court. Walking in from the rear parking lot the room feels cavernous and a real blast from the past. 

It sounded that way, too. Without acoustic softening from all the cheap clothing Woolworths used to sell, the crash and clang of scraping chairs, dozens of conversations, kitchen noise and background music, made for very discordant uncomfortable ambience. If they hung tapestries rather than blackboards, and placed sound panels strategically along the ceiling, Sabrina's would be a much more pleasant restaurant to visit and hang out. As it is, regardless of food quality it is not welcoming enough to be worth a return.

What about my breakfast last week? Well, it left a lot to be desired. My server was pleasant and efficient, but never brought the milk requested with their good coffee. She probably couldn't hear me. Their signature Challah thick cut french toast looked great, but the egg/sugar/cinnamon mix had not penetrated into the body of the slices, making it dry and tough chewing. There was sweetness baked into the bread, but even melted butter and poured syrup did not significantly reduce its lack of moisture within. I took half home thinking I might be able to salvage it in my kitchen, but by the next morning it had lost all freshness and couldn't be revived. RIP. 

I wonder what good old Frank Winfield Woolworth would do about this situation? It was he and his brother Charles who added the lunch counters to their successful stores and made them a new part of American culture. They would no doubt figure out how to perfect the experience and make more money doing it right.

Bagel Train remains my favorite bagel vendor in the area. 

Always a curiosity why people from Bagel City (born and raised there myself) think they know rounders better than anyone else, or that there is any uniformity among Big Apple bagels. There really isn't. I've had great ones on the Westside, and crappy ones in Soho. I've bitten into rock hard dense losers in Canarsie, and lovely light crunchers in Elmwood. 

So, don't listen to anyone who says they know what's best for anyone but themselves. If you love them, that's all that matters. Even if you never spent a day of your life in the City That Never Sleeps!

Zaika on Grant Avenue in Northeast Philly, is one of the best Pakistani/Indian restaurants I have ever had the pleasure of supping in.  I mean, there are some strong reviews from people I respect, but I didn't think I was about the experience a gastronomic wonder. Chef Mohammed has it going on!  

Somewhat surprising that we were among the very few customers on a Sunday night, but no complaints. The house was recently renovated with a larger dining room, and a touch of class with comfortable seating and sparse, but attractive décor.  Our server, Nema, was excellent.  She knew the questions to ask to make sure we got what we wanted.  Correct level of spiciness, and the right dipping sauces for the dishes ordered. No ice for the water. When undecided about whether to go with garlic or chili naan, she had the ready solution of having the tandoor bake up a combo of the two.  Garlic chili naan, indeed, was a winner. 

The rest was a cavalcade of wonderous dishes that expanded my understanding of what was truly possible in an IndoPak kitchen.  There were only three plates requested; a Samosa Chat app, Chicken Kashmiri and Bhaingan Bharta (eggplant). Each was uniquely distinct from similar plates in other restaurants, and each was outstandingly better.  

The Chat was a deconstructed Samosa, with the crisp fried dough on the bottom of a mass of tender chickpeas, potatoes and spicy homemade Masala sauce.  It was ordered for medium heat.  Auspicious beginning!  It had a complex flavoring and texture that was similar to other samosas, but somehow better, with a subtle sweet undernote to the usual fritter-like taste.  Delightful. 

The Chicken Kashmiri was ordered because of familiarity with this dish elsewhere; knowing it to be cream based and a lightly sweet alternative to all the curried heat coming from the other sources.  This version was that, but so much more.  Rather than just the combination of the heat from the cream sauce, the sweetness was supplied by raisins, pineapple and dried apricots.  A complete and unexpected surprise, that was in turn a mystery to be solved.  It took a while to figure out what those flavors/textures were.  But, when realization dawned, so did a big smile at the elegantly simple, yet creative genius at work.  Pineapple and apricot discovery was better than a game of charades. I loved this masterstroke. 

The Bhaingan was not as wildly original, but an excellent mashed roast eggplant, green peas, onion, pepper and tomato mixed with traditional herbs and spices.  Ordered hot, it was a nice counterpoint to the cooler sweetness of the Kashmiri. 

Last, but far from least, the Garlic Chili Naan, was a knockout bread sensation.  A bit oily, but the interplay of the two main ingredients so well seared to the surface of the naan, and the chewiness and absorption of the lightly crisped dough, made for great taste and the perfect utensil to pick up the sauces from each dish and slowly devour every last drop.   

Yes. There was a Mango Lassi, too.  Best way to cool an overheated tongue is to bathe it in cool mangoed yogurt drink.  

Zaika - The best meal I have had so far this year.

Noodle Eighty-Eight (Lucky Noodles), is a surprising hybrid house in Souderton, PA. Nicely renovated residence, the dining rooms are simple, but well appointed for comfort and utilitarian style. We were there for Sunday lunch, although there was no special menu. The main attraction were the Xiao Long Bao, the Shanghai soup dumpling specialty that I had been Jones-ing for. We added mushroom filled spring rolls as a second appetizer, and General Tso's Chicken and Short Ribs as entrees. 

In order of appearance the meal ran from excellent to ordinary. 

The XLB were very good, with steaming tasty pork truffle oil bouillon and filling. The gingered vinegar was a nice complement to pour into the pouch once the top knot was bitten off and the mixed contents sucked out. Such a tactile fun experience. 

The Spring Rolls were deep fried and stuffed with ground mushroom and sweet dipping sauce. They were crunchy, but the filling had little flavor nor interest. Wouldn't get this again.

The side greens salad was small, but had a pleasing sweet vinegar finish. It's unusual to get a salad in a Chinese house, and this was a tip of their chef's cap to their hybrid intentions. Far better than the ginger goop dressing on iceberg found in almost all sushi zones. 

General Tso was the weak soldier this day. The pieces were large requiring cutting to consume (thus, the need for western flatware). The breading was thick and not at all crisp, and the old man had spent too much time being woked. It was dry and lacked any verve. Disappointing.

Luckily, the day was saved by the Short Rib dish. More western than Asian in presentation and taste, it was tender, juicy and packed a tangy punch from the excellently reduced sauce. It pulled off the bone easily. But for the baby bok choy, this reminded of a good pot roast or sauerbraten. Regardless, it was nearly perfect.  

We made the drive from Newtown in 40 minutes on a rainy afternoon. Given the overall experience it is doubtful we would do it again. The dishes were inconsistent, but priced for perfection. Service was good, but without expected hot tea, nor rice. Also true about the parking situation. Not good unless you park across the road, around the corner or find one of the few that hug the building. 

3.5 STARS

For a Bucks County vineyard, Crossing Vineyards is as good as it gets in terms of beautiful scenery, comfortable surroundings and quality of wines available for tasting and purchase. It reminds of the wineries in Napa and Sonoma with small acreage producing some of the best vintages. It is easy to relax , sample the wares and at least for a few moments be transported to the left coast. 

This hacienda has been in the family for two generations, and the colonial home they live in looks the same as it did 200+ years ago (with better plumbing, electricity and fresh paint). Take a free tour of the grounds and production facilities, followed by a sit down on the patio in good weather to sip their award winning reds, whites and blushes. 

The most engaging choice is the dark rouge and somewhat sweet and dusky Chocolate Cherry Truffle. The Viognier white, Cabernet and Merlot also merit consideration. While head on comparisons with California wines may not grade out well in every instance, they are competitive, and save the time and treasure of traveling west. Sometimes a pleasant afternoon is all you need to get away. 

If you enjoy Crossing Vineyards it can be just the start of a magical mystery tour of the other Bucks County wineries that can make for a great weekend.

Blooming Grove Inn occupies the space of what was Lieggi's on Upper Ferry Road in Ewing, NJ. It is a pleasant converted mansion on the slopes of the eastern side of the Delaware River Basin.  My visits have always been at the bar for after work meetings and light socializing.  The crowd is forty and fifty-somethings; all well behaved.  The bartenders are excellent.  Noah remembered my face, if not my name, after an absence of at least six months.  Impressive.  

Last night, my margarita had the right touch of Padron and Cointreau, and my friend and fellow court gladiator enjoyed his aged malt whiskey.  Behind us at the end of the bar, a mellow guitar vocalist played gently and sang from a decent list of soft rock standards. It was just enough to fill the gaps in our conversation, but seemed to disappear when we spoke again.  

We decided to have a bite at the bar, rather than score a table.  I asked for the Meatballs I had seen brought out earlier, and Sam went for the Tapas plate. My dish was excellent.  Tender, airy meatballs in a tart, garlic tomato sauce, sprinkled with dry Italian grated cheese.  I only skewered a few pieces of cheese, greens, mushrooms off his plate, but thought everything was fine, if not enthralling. 

So, why four stars?  It has nothing to do with the quality of the house, the kitchen, nor the bar.  They were all fine.  Blooming Grove just isn't my cup of tequila.  I prefer a less well kempt, more outside the box, more diverse, kind of place.  It felt too tame.  More a place to take your aunt and uncle, or business associates, when you don't want them to know who you really are.

Stopped by for breakfast this week and sat at an otherwise empty counter.  The place looked refreshed since the last time I was here several years ago.  My server was friendly, courteous and prompt with the large red coffee mug, keeping it full throughout my meal.  

The Sausage, Egg & Cheese on Croissant was a special this morning, and included a side of Hash Browns for a price under $6.  I was pleased that my waitperson pointed that out to me when she heard I was heading in that direction.  

The sandwich was constructed with double Sausage Patties, American Cheese, and a nicely Fried Egg.  The Croissant was fresh, and had a pleasant sweetness with every bite.  It was very good.  Yet, the half plate of Home Fries were room temperature at best.  They were overcooked and dry.  Add cool temperature to that, and I found them inedible.  Not sure why the grill chef didn't know that those taters were left in the corner of the iron for too long.  Just as well, as I didn't need the extra calories turning into sugars.  

The coffee came from a Bunn Double Drip.  It was a good bean, and I enjoyed having a large, heavy mug to sip from, rather than a smaller vessel to be constantly refilled.  

Overall, the environment was attractive and comfortable.  A little more attention to detail would certainly make Blue Fountain a more positively memorable experience.

Emei Shan is a holy Buddhist mountain in Szechuan Province, China. It is a difficult climb up steep trails and even steeper stairs. On the way, monkeys drop out of the trees seeking donations from the faithful, sometimes quite aggressively.  Still, once reaching the summit, you stand above the clouds and look out at a timeless world of sky and mountaintops.  Breathtaking.

E Mei Restaurant takes its name from this mountain.  

When I made my first visit over the past weekend, I was impressed with the effort made to upgrade the floor with quality tables and chairs, as well as table clothes and an overall sense of wanting to treat the customer well.  It worked. The cuisine is slightly different than the better know superheat of most Szechuan style dishes.  The owner is from Chongqing, a major city in China, that was formerly part of Szechuan Province, but is now an Autonomous Zone, carved out of its former province.  Their food is spicy and often hot, but more subtle than the blast furnace approach found in better known Chengdu-ese molten flavors. 

My companion and I started with apps of Dan Dan Noodles and Eggplant with Pepper. Both were well done, and only mildly hot.  The beef sauce on the noodles was plentiful. The eggplant more shredded than sliced, yet even with the ample peppers, did not raise a fire alarm.  Both were quite enjoyable. 

Our main courses consisted of Fish Fillet in Hot Spicy Sauce, Diced Rabbit with Peanuts in Chili Sauce, and Saute Squash.  Here's were the thermometer began to rise.  The fish came in a deep dish with a ton of fillets.  The sheen from the chili oil in which the fish swam was very noticeable, and its red color contrasted nicely with the pale yellow of the odd shaped fish.  This dish was about 4 alarm, meaning my tongue instantly reacted to touching the sauce and began to numb a bit. Just the way I like it! 

Rabbit is not my fave, but having had it in Chongqing I wanted to celebrate the opportunity.  The meat was on the bone, and cut into small pieces.  The peanuts were a strong presence, helping to control the overflowing chili and star peppers attempt at an insurrection. It was 5 alarm even with the peanuts holding the worst elements at bay.  For me, rabbit is a lot of work because of all the bones and small morsels of meat attained.  Still, it tasted very good, and all of it was gone by the time we called it quits on more eating.  The small green squash was a pleasantly sweet counterbalance to the rabbit's "hare" raising. 

All in all a very enjoyable and authentic meal.  Definitely worth a return visit.  For those of us who love Szechuan heat, this place is worthy, even if not at the apex of the volcanic chili scale.

Climb E Mei and taste the view from the top.

All this for under $50. plus tip.

Legend tells of a mythologic Blue Moose that traveled the spiritland and Doan hills around New Hope and the north river highlands. From time immemorial it was the guardian that helped those hurt by natural, supernatural and even manmade acts, survive and repair their damaged bodies and souls.  Its gifts to all were amazing strength, nurturing support and a supply of local foodstuff to aid in recovery. It was also known for dexterity on the mandolin.  It seldom took sides. It was only there to observe and assist with sustenance and music.  

Over the centuries Blue Moose has taken various forms animate and inanimate. An accomplished shape shifter, it appeared when the need was dire in a form acceptable in the current cultural milieu. It helped sustain our men during the Revolution, and helped build the longboats that made the Christmas eve crossing. Currently, it assumed the guise of a restaurant in a small old house on Mechanic Street in New Hope, Pa. Always brash, it has not bothered to hide its identity. 

It sits in plain sight.  Café Blue Moose welcomes all to rest within its aging walls and taste its well honed victuals at any of its tables. 

It was within these atmospherics that we arrived for an early dinner last Friday evening, climbed the stairs to the second floor and took control of the middle table overlooking the open space down to the front room.  Open paper umbrellas hung down gently spinning in the air currents.  Stars were painted on the exposed cathedral ceiling.  Period pieces on the walls completed the sense that we were encouraged to take leave of normalcy and enter the world of whimsy, where we could best appreciate the decompression from reality.  BYOB aided the transformation. 

Our servers were lighthearted and sincere.  The menu a prix fixe affair allowing choices in any combination of Apps/Salad/Soups, Entrees, and Desserts that added up to 2 or 3.  Our choices were to share a Warm Goat Cheese Salad; Braised Short Ribs and Sautéed Salmon; and a Apple Crisp finale. The salad was a nice green plate with local leaves, Hazelnuts, sliced tart Green Apple and Dried Cherries in Balsamic Vinaigrette .  A round fried Goat Cheese ball was indeed hot, smooth, and subtle.  The parts played very well together and was a delight.  

The Short Rib was already off bone having bathed a few hours in red wine and garlic.  The meat was sitting atop Garlic Mashed, and under a strong helping of Pickled Cabbage and Carrots.  The taste was mildly sweetly vinegar inspired, and completely pliant.  The Mashed and Rib sauces were blood brothers, bringing the best of both when combined.  Symbiotic to the max.

The Salmon was a reasonably sized steak on top of small grain White Rice Risotto.  It, too, had a pickled topside that tasted of onion/mango, but was likely something else.  It was finished well and easy to eat, although there with an unidentifiable aftertaste that was less enjoyable than the primary sensation.  A small nit in an otherwise inspired meal.  

Finally, the Warm Apple Crisp was a fun crunchy a la mode mess with an oat/brown sugar crumble that was a joyful indulgence.  

All the while, Blue Moose played his music in the background, completing a near-epic experience.  His mandolin put aside for a heavy bass line for rock melodies that soothed and awakened appreciation of meal and history.  

As we stepped out into the snowfall and gathered our memories of what had just transpired, the sense that Big Blue was with us in deed and spirit was palpable.  We thanked him for his faithfulness and skilled metamorphosis into a shelter that was exactly what was needed in this age of doubt and cynicism.

I don't know what it is, but gambling doesn't appeal to me. I understand the enjoyment some seem to have risking and most often losing their hard earned money, but I don't share the feeling. I also see that most lose what they come with, and would have been better off going bowling. But, I am not adverse to observing the mostly self-destructive behavior close up by sitting at a Blackjack table for a while and playing a few hands. 

Some feel comfortable in a casino. I never have. Yet, Parx is very big and often so crowded that I feel invisible. That allows me to wander around close to the action, yet not be part of it. The occasional whoop from winning a big pot, or cry of angry frustration losing one are part of a tragi/comedy that plays out hundreds of times a day. The staff seems well trained to deal with the range of human emotions, and nothing gets out of control. 

The best things are the number of food choices at reasonable prices. Happy hours are extensive and often late at night. It is possible to grab a drink and decent snack or dinner without handing over a $20 without change. If your not losing too much, Parx can be a decent date night, with live entertainment and lots of people watching. 

Biggest negative - This is a smokers space. Anxiety increases the habit. The air system is not totally effective, so health is an issue. No doubt the employees are involved in risky behavior. Healthcare is not available to most workers unless they reached full time status, which is strictly formulated. You just can't afford to accept the exposure for very long. 

Once a year is more than enough. 

2,500 employees. That is a lot.

DJ Kitchen offers Szechuan cuisine on City Line Avenue, Philadelphia. 

Well, sort of. 

It has the red Szechuan peppers down in large quantities, and many other hot spices that bring the willing cognizant diner to the brink of tongue burning ecstasy. Yet, like most other Chengdu facsimiles around town, it stops short of the authentic 'flavor of numb' brought on by only the traditional black peppercorns and star peppers that grow in the hot humidity of the ancient Du plains in the plateau region of the central and western parts of the province. 

Without the Numb, it just isn't true Szechuan. It is still quite good, with quality ingredients and plenty of meat, veggies, spices and sesame oils, but it isn't the Full Monty. The portions are substantial with leftovers for the boys at home. 

We thoroughly enjoyed the Cumin Lamb and Long Hots with Beef. They were colorful with powerful aromas. The meat was tender while the peppers and onions, crisp. The red onion was particularly sweet in contradistinction to the growling bark of the green long hots. Both damn good. The only shortcoming beside the absence of numbing essence, was the saltiness of the Dry Pepper Crispy Chicken. It was an unnecessary distraction to an otherwise entertaining platter. 

We enjoyed chatting with Ming, one of the owner/managers, who took time to explain some of the history of the restaurant. He and his partners have created an interesting haven for those seeking an alternative to the regular Chinese American grub, and although it doesn't travel all the way to to the numbing mountaintops, it does take us a long way up that winding spicy road.

Cheesecake Factory may be the quintessential modern American diner. Huge diverse menu and awesome desserts. Yeah, it doesn't exactly look like a stainless roadside palace; designed to appear more like a massive adobe warehouse on the outside and something out of the fantasiful Arabian Nights, within. While not a regular visitor, sometimes it is exactly what I am looking for, especially when the answer to every existential question is, "cheesecake!"

It certainly filled that bill last night. We weren't sure what we wanted for dinner, but knew what we didn't. Tired of checking off all the ethnic styles available within driving distance and eliminating most of them, we came to Cheesecake Factory. It had dishes from all continents, a bar, and those awesome creamy sweet cool desserts. Perfect cure for indecisiveness. We drove to Willow Grove in about 30. The expansive hall was busy but not full. We were seated immediately near the bar.

We caught the final minutes of happy hour and celebrated with half price glasses of an excellent cabernet. We selected the Crispy Brussel Sprouts for an appetizer (wonderfully done with bacon and maple syrup), and their Southwest Chicken Sandwich (strong contender in a crunchy baguette and spicy aioli), and Shepherd's Pie (savory ground beef and veggies in mushroom gravy topped with a load of mashed potatoes and melted cheese). Toasting our way through the meal, we completed with a flourish of a thick slice of shared almond cheesecake (they bake them right). 

This was a full and fun dinner that permitted us to chose cravings that we didn't know we had. We couldn't finish any of it, and brought enough home for another meal. Cheesecake Factory may not see us again for a while, but it's good to know it's there when we need the modern American diner to help us decide what to eat.

Pho Le Lai is a Vietnamese restaurant located on St. Vincent Street in the Mayfair neighborhood of Northeast Philadelphia. It is found in the same building as 1st Asian Supermarket, making it convenient to eat and shop for our Southeast Asian grocery needs. Both are closer to our Bucks County home, saving time compared to either Chinatown (traffic & parking) or Washington Avenue (traffic). 

I was the sole customer when I walked in around 3 P.M. The cordial manager got up from reading the newspaper and seated me at the table next to her and handed me their multi page menu. Another friendly woman came out of the kitchen with a pitcher of cold water, to answer questions and take my order. That was simple - Pho Tai and Roast Pork Banh Mi (This is a pho house, after all.) 

Ten minutes later she was back with the "Small" bowl of steaming beef noodle soup requested, and a side plate of exceptionally fresh standard accoutrement (sprouts, sliced jalapeno, Thai basil sprigs and lime wedge). I took a pair of new wood chopsticks and flat bottomed spoon from the table holder and doctored the pho to my taste, paying attention to pull apart the nest of noodles lying beneath the surface of the dark broth (Northern Vietnamese style). 

The flavor profile displayed some depth and had been simmering in a large pot for a long time. It wasn't quite as rich as Pho 75 or Pho Ha, but it was very good and didn't require help from the Sriracha bottle rocket on the table. It was plenty spicy with the addition of the jalapeno. 

I was content to slurp away and patiently lift noodles out of the caldron and fold them onto the spoon before shoveling them into my mouth. 

The Banh Mi arrived minutes later. It was a full sized sandwich on decent French baguette, cut in half. Like the pho, it was larger than anticipated, especially for $6!  It was loaded with dark roast pork, daikon radish, carrot, aioli and cilantro. I added a long squirt of Hoisin to bring up the savoriness of that combo, and took a bite. From crusty roll through crisp daikon and ultimately tender pork, it was delicious and captivating. It was a complete oral and tactile experience. One of the best sammys I've enjoyed since Ocean Grove, California, the capital of Vietnamese America. 

Along with China Gourmet, the excellent dim sum emporium also in that building, the presence of Pho Le Lai make St. Vincent Street a strong destination for your Asian taste buds and culinary needs.

The Dining Car is an old style stainless steel diner on Frankford Avenue, Northeast Philadelphia. It has a small private parking lot behind the structure, with much more space available in the Mealey Furniture lot next door. There is a dining room as well as a large counter for folks like me who are eating alone and enjoy watching their employees as they work. 

The staff is friendly and efficient. I had menu in hand and a mugga joe before me within a minute of sitting down. Traditional diner fare, with a few things for which they are noted - chicken croquettes and Jewish apple cake - among them. It even had a moment of fame when it was the subject of Guy Fieri's Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives show on the Food Channel. Of course, Guy is all about spiked hair showmanship and excessive exuberance, and not necessarily honest assessment of the food he is mugging for. Here, his enjoyment was legitimately entertained by the urban nature of this part of town having its own stainless palace, but also likely uninformed by the other Philly Special joints in the same neighborhood that far outshine The Dining Car (The Clown House, for example). 

I was there for a French Toast breakfast, although I was tempted to see what the fuss was all about with the apple cake. Doubt it was better than grandma's. 

Still, I enjoyed my morning repast, even if not outstanding. Two slices of decent white loaf seemed a bit light if it wasn't a short stack. Although advertised with "maple syrup," I'm fairly certain that the sticky sweet colloidal liquid pouring out of the container on the counter was not from a maple tree. Tasted a lot more like a generic Mrs. Buttersworth. Still sweet. Still a decent companion to the fry bread. Just not Grade B Dark. The coffee was strong, hot and free flowing from the Bunn brewer. 

The place was humming on Thursday morning. A definite community gathering spot.

There are things to like about Brick House Tavern & Tap, and a few other things that detract from the overall experience. 

The space is generally very nice, with an open floorplan, and brick wall along the back of the house. There are booths, high top large tables, sofas, and a bar - each offering a different comfort level. I was there as a solitary traveler, and chose to sit at the bar. This may have been a poor choice, as the design leaves a lot to be desired. 

Although square with barstools along each side, lines of sight are obstructed on each side by the beer tap hardware that extends down from the ceiling and spreads out it large apparatus just above eye level so it is impossible to see the HDTVs behind the bar. Also, after a pour (I had a Summer Shandy), the individual tap continues to drip onto the metal splash guard above the drain, spraying droplets of beer in all directions - especially toward me, the customer. While it didn't make me wet, it did reach the wooden bar top, making it damp and causing damage to the finish. There must be a better, cleaner, more sanitary way to deal with drippy taps. 

The bar ladies were clearly selected for their fit in jeans, more than their tending skills. While I am not complaining about the view, the dropped and broken glasses, cut fingers, and spillage was not the most fun to observe. And, it happened twice during my hour there. 

The Brick House Cheeseburger seemed a safe bet.  It looked good on arrival. Yet, the medium grill requested was much closer to well done. The fries were fine. It was an average burger, at best. 

The overall sense of this joint is that management does not run a tight ship, and should spend more time training staff to be sure the customer is the center of attention, rather than the interaction between the workers. The menu is pricy for this level of roadhouse experience, and the quality of the menu and service should reflect that. Otherwise, what you get is a dive bar trying to pass itself off as elite.

BREAKFAST @ TIFFANY (Diner on the Boulevard)

Happy New Year (2022) Everyone!

My last Yelp of the old year was at this fine establishment in the Great Northeast, Philadelphia. It had been closed an extended period of time for renovations, and the effort appears to have been worthwhile. The facility has a new outer shell and the main dining hall is bright, attractively utilitarian and very clean. Staff from management to servers are courteous and helpful. The menu is a diner's long list of nearly infinite possibilities. 

But, I was there for a New Year's Eve Day breakfast, and while prepared to be tempted, knew what I wanted - French Toast & crisp bacon. There is a long counter along the back wall, and when I arrived it was unoccupied. I sidled down to the third from last spinner, past the last booth, and found myself in the perfect Covidly socially distance spot. No one with ten feet of me. I ordered coffee and my Frenchie. and perused my phone for the latest news while I waited. These days that is always a risky thing to do and expect to keep a good mood, but old habits die hard. (Good riddance 2021!)

So, my plate was delivered with a warm smile. I beheld two slices of thickish bread well grilled and sided by four slices of heat curled bacon. Both good to the naked eye. First bites told the tale. 

Although described as "Challah" bread, the texture was more a yellowish thick slice with extra sugar baked in. It lacked the rougher consistency and swirl of true Challah. Okay. I'm being picky, but the mental image of the real deal had excited my tastebuds and I was a little disappointed. Too, it came with those industrial corn syrup sweeteners, that are just empty calories and not conducive to good health. No Log Cabin nor Mrs. Butterworth in the house. True, it was edible and the bacon was fine, but these days I have reservations about putting such ersatz materials in my body, and would gladly pay extra for pure Grade B maple syrup. 

I get that corners must be cut to stay ahead of the game, but I would prefer the choice. 

But, that's just me. 

Let's have a better 2022! Lord knows we need and deserve it.

Tony's Place Bar & Grill sits on Greeley Avenue, Ivyland, PA, across the street from the terminus of the New Hope & Ivyland Railroad.  It has an interesting history coming out of Philadelphia in the last century to set up shop in the wilds of Bucks County. The place is very attractive from the outside, with lots of slate and stone, and outdoor canvas covered patio to one side, and large bar/dining area within. Lots of HDTVs to establish its bona fides as a sports bar. 

On a early Sunday evening in December it was about half full when I arrived around, but the crowd grew as it neared kickoff for the Eagles-Seahawks game.  This is definitely a good place to take in games with friends and family as the beer options are pretty good, and the kitchen cooks up a lot of comfort foods. Although high end steaks are also on the menu, I did not see any brought out. My pumpkin cider tasted like autumn and had a nice kick.  

I was impressed with their Tomato Pie. Very thin cracker-like crust, mozza cheese under a nicely balanced sauce.  Similar to the pies found in New Jersey, and not the "upside down" thing that often is called TP, but is nothing like the real McCoy. So, congrats on getting it right. 

Service was okay, but there were long stretches of time when no one stopped by to see how we were doing. Long wait for the check, too. The customers seemed to be mostly locals who were there for the games and party time, or to pick up a few pizzas to take home.

Pretty much a standard Pennsylvania roadside diner down on Street Road, Bensalem. It is well maintained, has friendly professional staff, large menu and reasonable prices. 

I stopped in for breakfast recently, and sat on a stool at the traditional counter. Coffee was immediately available from the Bunn-O-Matic, and my request for milk over creamer was met with a small glass of moo juice. The daily special omelette was described well, and server and I agreed quietly that ham, bacon and sausage was just too much meat for three eggs to handle. Opted instead for short stack french toast and java only. Lately, it seems I am not as hungry in the morning, which helps explain the increased bagginess of my pants. 

The thick white load was good with adequate saturation of the egg/vanilla/sugar mix into the heart of both slices. The soft butter and Smuckers table syrup finished off the plate. It was all grilled well, but providing a pour of pure Grade B maple would have been so much more satisfying. I would pay a buck or two extra for that sweet smokiness soaked into my bread. The cuppa joe was decent and refilled frequently. 

I departed $10 the poorer, including gratuity. Not bad for this part of Street Road, right down the street from Parx Casino.

Recently returned to Buffalo Wild Wings Langhorne plant for a family Friday night.  While I didn't walk in with fond memories of my past visit, my son was in the mood for hot wings, and BWW certainly had plenty of those.  

Truth be told, this experience was far improved.  The house was far from crowded.  All the other customers seemed to be families with teenage/early twenties boys who wanted the gorge on wings and watch sports on huge HDTVs.  We fit right in!  

Service was better than remembered.  Our guy was over the top solicitous of our satisfaction; so much so that I jokingly asked him to calm down or he wouldn't make it through the night with his hyperactivity.  He was not so far gone as to not appreciate that I noticed he was working hard.  Even a small glitch in the cooking of the Alaskan Cod sandwich was handled with aplomb, with the house manager stopping by to apologize for the delay in bring the fillet to proper temperature.  

Drinks were ample and fairly priced.  Can't object when a 12 oz. cocktail comes in at $6.50.  

The chickens who sacrificed their flight for us came to us both Blazin and Thai Curry.  They were meaty, deep fried, and bathed in some impressive chili mix.  The former took the enamel off my teeth (much to the merriment of young man), while the latter had great south Asian flavor. Liked them both, but would never be challenged to eat a extra hot one again.  The fish sandwich on brioche roll was surprisingly decent, with the fish large enough to withstand the cooking process and still be crispy and tasty with aioli mayo and melted cheese.  

Glad we decided to return to Buffalo Wild Wings on Rt. 1, Langhorne, Pa.  We enjoyed ourselves, and didn't feel the need to apologize to ourselves for going.  

Improvements noted.
I've been back 4 times since my first Thai experience. Food is amazing. The service is very good, always friendly. This has become one of my favorite places to eat.

Over the weekend some friends and I were able to have a veritable celebration of bubble teas, or as I would call it, a Boba Fete...  *cricket, cricket, cricket*

Ahem, anyway...
This is a really delightful spot for some really delicious treats.  Though it took a while, I have grown to enjoy boba drinks with those chewy little orbs of tapioca floating in them.  It was sort of a niche thing for a while, especially in Reno, but I am glad it has taken off, and we now have Bubble Tea Station right in the heart of Midtown.

They are hard to miss, being set up in a tiny stand near the intersection of Virginia and Center Streets.  There are a few parking spaces in their own lot, and plenty of others in the surrounding blocks.  Walk right up to their windows, and you can see their impressive selection of flavors and and additional options.  And once you order, it is pretty interesting to watch as their machines shake and seal your drinks for you.  Outside there are several tables and umbrellas, which are no doubt great to hang out at during the warmer months.

We ended up going with three of the milk teas, the Matcha, Thai Tea, and Taro flavors.  All of them were sweet, but not overly so, especially the matcha, which actually had a very prominent green tea flavor.  The Thai Tea was likewise very good.  But what really impressed my was the Taro flavor.  This funky-looking purple brew is just phenomenal, and definitely gets a high recommendation from me.  Though we didn't get a chance to try them this time, we did see there are fruit teas, as well as more standard cafe drinks like lattes and cappuccinos available, too.

The service here was exceptionally friendly, and the teas were handed off to us very quickly.  Price-wise you are looking at about the same range you would for a sugary blended drink at the Green Giant or other big chain coffee stores, but I think for the novelty of it, and how yummy they turned out, you are getting a great deal.

So if you are cruising through Midtown, especially if it's a sunny and warm day, I can for sure say you got to stop by and snag a boba tea.  Great work, guys!

Normally I try to steer clear of reviewing chains, or places I have been to only once, and I usually give myself some time to mull over experiences before writing.  But since MOD Pizza opened right near my work literally in the last few days, it seemed a good time to be spontaneous.  It's a chain I knew pretty much nothing about, another sign of the increased presence of different companies and brands flooding into the Reno area.  Located in the Firecreek Crossing center, their grand opening vibe is very strong, with decorations and balloons, a hearty crowd of customers, and staff stationed to help new customers navigate their menu.

You walk up to the counter, and you see that they charge a set price for the size of pizza you order, not the amount of toppings you put on it.  You select your sauce, and as many toppings as you want to create your own custom pie.  Or, they also have a menu of recopies you can choose from as well.  You watch from your side of the glass-enclosed counter as the crew assemble your meal, moving it down the line from sauce, to meat, to veggie stations, finally sliding it into the oven to bake, and serving it up to you with a few finishing garnishes.  If this model sounds familiar, it should, as it is the same sort you see at Subway or certain other joints, only now applied here to pizza.  It never ceases to amaze me how people can come up with new adaptations of existing methods, and more to the point, how the staff here can utilize it to crank out customized pizzas so fast.  Seeing all this, I was a tad nervous that this would be pretty bland and generic, certainly nothing to Yelp about.  But after lunch today, I decided that, yeah, it can be good to be wrong.

From when I placed my order to when it was dished up, total time elapsed was about ten minutes.  This is insanely fast for a fast-food, tailored-pizza, and yet there it was.  I had built my 11" pie with tons of cheese, olives, and bacon.  Oh, and now would be a good point to reiterate that they do not charge by the amount of toppings.  So theoretically you could pay the exact same price for a plain cheese as you do if you were to get literally every topping they had.  This would normally send up warning flags for me, but after sitting down and taking a bite, I was pleasantly surprised.  The pie was pretty tasty, I have to admit.  Granted, I've certainly had better pizzas before, but for fast-food, this is really impressive quality.  I would certainly take them over some of the more traditional and well-known pizza chains.  The crust is pretty thin, though, but not overly crisp.  The dough is kept that way, I guess, which helps them in making sure their cook times are way down and they can get a good turnover rate with orders.

In addition to their pizzas, they have plenty of bottled and fountain drinks, a few dessert items, and setups in place for beer taps. (which they promise are coming soon)  Good amount of indoor and outdoor seating, ample parking, and amazingly friendly and energetic staff are also some good plusses.  And getting back to the price, my 11" pizza was only about $9.  Pretty good value, pretty good quality.  So definitely a sold four stars.  Welcome to Reno, guys, and good luck with the rest of your opening week!

Probably one of the worst restaurant going experiences I have ever had. It was sad for my friends and I too because this was our last spot on our trip in NOLA. This place is rated so high on Yelp and it definitely threw me off. One thing to note is that this place has been open for a very long time, so I definitely think the quality and customer service has taken a hit. 

First off, you can't share a meal or do family style without getting charged extra. Seriously?? Why? I've never been to a restaurant that does that and either way I just don't get why you need to be that complicated and greedy. It was about $4 extra for each extra plate. Really dumb! That itself should make you not go here, but don't worry there's many more reasons. 

The prices are insanely high but it is fried chicken/ soul food so I get that just not this high. We ordered a good amount of chicken and got some mac and cheese and greens which comes with it. I think we asked to switch the greens out and we couldn't for some reason (seriously...) 

The waitress didn't seem like she even wanted to talk to us or serve us. Not sure what we did, we asked questions but nothing over the top. She wasn't happy and not one bit nice. There's more that happens too so keep reading! 

So the chicken and food come out and we are so excited and happy! We start eating and obviously the first couple of bites when you are striving is good, but then it hits you. The chicken is insanely oily and greasy. Obviously it's not bad but can't anyone make good or even better chicken like this? Especially if you gonna charge that much, come on man!!

Here is what topped it all off and why I would never recommend this place!! Multiple pieces of chicken had a piece of hair in it!! How disgusting. That grossed us all out and we just couldn't eat after. We told our waitress and she responded by saying everyone wears hair nets. So?!? The hair was fried in to the chicken, lady!! I don't care about hair nets it's in the freaking chicken!! Then, she reimbursed us with a small piece chicken leg. Hahah, come on! You gotta do better then that. 

We were so upset with everything and when we get the bill, the waitress already included a 20% tip. It's a party of 5 (I know some restaurants do this but dang 20%?!?) super upset because she didn't not offer us good service at all nor did the restaurant. 

So in conclusion, if you finished this post, I saved you from making a huge mistake. Trust me, do not go here and don't read the old reviews. A great restaurant can become garbage if they don't keep the consistency and not offer good customer service.

This is just like Abuela makes. Being Cuban makes eating Cuban food at restaurants less appealing. Ropa vieja, tostones, mariquitas con mojo, all these are dishes I took for granted for so many years. This place is as good as anywhere I have been. The dishes are authentic, the atmosphere is a little bit touristy. It's not a copy of or has the same feel as Versailles on Calle Ocho but the menu is excellent. Bistec palomilla con maduros and arroz con frijoles. All of it is the real deal. The only thing missing is an ice cold Iron Beer, but Malta Hatuey takes me right back to sitting in my Abuela's kitchen while she is preparing croquetas and bacalao. This place takes me home.

Pat's King of Steaks is a tourist staple for cheesesteaks in Philly. It's always a ton of tourist here because of their popularity from different television shows. Pat's is one of the first cheesesteak places I ate at in Philly (along with Geno's). I got a cheesesteak with onions and Cheez Whiz. It's important to know what you want to order before arriving at the window. I thought Pat's cheesesteak was decent. I prefer Cheez Whiz over provolone. There are peppers for customers at the napkin area. Pat's is usually busy on weekends. Expect long lines during prime hours (moves fast).Street parking can be a hassle at times. If you're a tourist, check out Pat's at least one time. Pats rival Geno's is a few feet away. Both restaurants are located in a busy section of Philly. Deciding who has the best cheesesteak is fun for foodies or cheesesteak lovers. I give Pat's King of Steaks a 3.5 rating.

I was leaving Sonny's Famous Steaks and stumbled upon Happily Ever After (located next door). I'm a dessert fiend,so I had to satisfy my sweet tooth before coming back to VA. I ordered a slice of Nutella cheesecake. Happily Ever After  cheesecake was tasty. The smooth texture was perfect. Nutella and chocolate is a good combination in my opinion. The dessert shop is small with some seating throughout (cool decor).Its a cool place to socialize with friends. Staff was friendly during checkout. Happily Ever After sells drinks and other desserts as well. I'll be back to explore the menu more. Parking can be a hassle at times (street). Happily Ever After is a good choice for cheesecake in Philly.

This Mexican restaurant in Clearwater has a lively vibe with fun interior decor, attentive staff and top-notch Mexican cuisine.  The clientele seemed diverse and everyone looked to be enjoying themselves. I read they also have live mariachi band on Sunday but sadly I was there on a different night. 

The star here - the Mexican cuisine - carries a good mix of authentic aromatic flavors with hand made tortilla. I tried Guacamole Maya, a chunky guacamole mixed with corn, grilled jalapeño with airy fried Pork Skin as chips for dipping. This is a must try of the three guacamole combo they carry.  My jalapeño margarita was well mixed with the right portion of boozy and spice served over ice. I drank two orders of these.  My chorizo tacos came piping hot along with perfectly cooked and moist Mexican rice with a side of black beans.  The chorizo had the perfect balance of smoky flavor and kick all wrapped in those moist yet firm hand made house tortilla.  The flan as finisher was nice but this item is nothing to write home about - the standard flan taste. The quintessential chips and salsa starter had much room to improve. The salsa was pretty bland and watery, the chips seemed a tad too crisp / burnt. 

The menu here is tight in a good way, not too many items to overwhelm you but not too few to restrict the variety of types to hit the spot for everyone's Mexican cravings.  

I will definitely come back to Hacienda Corralejo Mexican Kitchen, there are many other items I want to try, that other reviewers are raving about,  ie Guacamole, Burrito, Enchiladas, etc.; all of this paired with great customer service, and great margarita to boot, this place is definitely a top winner in my books.

Street Side is a new and hidden gem at the nexus of olde kensington, fishtown, and northern liberties. It's a tiny little spot that may only have seating for maybe 14 diners at a time, but what it lacks in size it makes up for in heart. I'm happy to be the place's 2nd Yelp review, after being tipped off about this place by the wonderful Sophia I., who got the coveted 'first-to-review'. 

The Banh Mi is just as good if not better than QT in chiatown, and that's some high praise. The complexity of flavors paired with the perfect roll at a price point that was more than reasonable was simply fantastic. 

Since this was my first time here I opted for spring rolls and also a bowl of pho - for scientific yelp purposes of course... I'm not a fan of soups in the summer, but I just had to try it and I was impressed!  

Possibly the best thing to point out is the reasonable price for any of the items on the menu. I'm dog tired of spots opening up in the neighborhood with an average plate cost of 15-20$. Street Side is easily half that cost. With all of these positives, I'm pretty convinced that this place will grow in popularity quickly and become a quite successful addition to the 'hood.

In one fell swoop, Cafe La Maude has shot to the top of the charts as my favorite brunch in the NoLibs/Fishtown area. The menu is a daunting wall of text with what seems to be no rhyme or reason, but from the little bit that I had (Waffle Chicken Cordon Blue) I can tell that they've got talent. 

I'm very happy to have gone here (thanks for the invite lindsay v., Smrithi D., Kathleen D.) and will be back again next weekend to work my way down the menu.

I ate here 5 hours ago and I'm considering making the 25 minute drive to eat here again right now. 

Lots of vegetarian options, so you're good there if you have a ton of vegetable eating friends like I do.

Places like this are why I yelp. Without Yelp, I wouldn't have heard of it and so when I found myself near china town and needing a bit of a pick me up I decided that it was time that Audabon and I met. 

This is a new little bakery (opened march 19th!) and has been growing in popularity since it's opening. Inside you're greeted with a wonderful pillow that tells you you're handsome (or beautiful if that's what you want to hear), and some pretty cool signage with Audabon spelled out in nails. 

The specialty here is the macaron -- thats MAH-KAH-RON... These little treats come in all sorts of colors and flavors and I believe Audabon has a weekly rotation. It was my first time in, so I will have to go there again next week -- for scientific purposes of course. 

I got a chance to speak with the owner for a moment. I almost felt bad because she's so busy making these little pieces of sinful heaven. I saw some batter in the back and I saw a tray up front that was getting the fillings put in. Combine that with customers and she's furiously busy with her successful new bakery! 

Stop in if you get a chance, I'm sure you will enjoy it!

One of my favorite spots to eat brunch. I'm attempting to dethrone Dan A. as the check-in leader. Shhh! It's a secret. They have a special menu (located in the middle of their menu) that changes on a weekly basis according to whatever the theme is. Most of these options are slight variations of the same item and are always delicious. The place is quite friendly to vegans and vegetarians too!

BBQ is something that every person should take seriously. 
I mean.... I'm pretty sure many people literally have been in a life or death experience with good or bad BBQ being the determining factor for survival. Let me be clear - this is Alabama BBQ 

Moe's is a hidden gem in New Orlean's BBQ community. I've only known about it for a month or so... and I can't stop telling people about it. 
Here is how I sell it.... 
1. Meat options - seriously so many meat options! And every single one that I have tried has been delicious. The chicken makes my mouth water just thinking about it. 
2. The sides...they have their staple sides, but they also have a large list of rotating sides. There are even so many gluten/dairy free sides that I get choices. Trust me - that is hard to come by. 
3. The vibe - somehow, it never seems crowded, always feels like you are at home, the drinks are cheap and the space is clean. 
4. Kids eat at a discounted rate on certian nights... my goddaughter loves it! 
5. The final way - is the fact that I rave about it. There aren't many things I rave about randomly at work when it is getting close to lunch time... and this is one of them.

Are you trying to win me over or convince me to watch your ferrets (I hate ferrets)? Well, Red's would be a clutch move in a negotiation.

- Their eggplant balances the flavors and spices that dance on your tongue.
- They cater easily to dairy free and gluten free needs, which is not something easily done at Chinese food.
- I have watched friends literally lick the plate with the General Tso's chicken and not feel an ounce of shame. 
- The cocktail list balances nicely with the food and still holds some creativity. Don't sleep on the daquris'. Those flavor blends are freshly made and promise to make you smile.
- Don't be turned off by the hard to find sign or the lack of ventilation. It is part of the experience.
- If you are up for some free entertainment, sit at the kitchen bar and watch the open kitchen. Those people working up magic for your mouth can be quick entertaining.  


PS  - I made the discovery of Grubhub delivering Reds.... my world might be changed forever.

After all the attention Pizze Real is drawing to itself via a personal campaign against yelp and its reviewers, I came to the Pizze Real Yelp page, and I noticed I have never written a review for here. The following is an honest, unbiased review. 

I have been here four times.  I have never  experienced bad service. I have been served by the same person each time. An (and I hope she doesn't mind my description) elderly lady. She's always been a good server.

The decor: I had no problem with the interior design, or artwork, or furniture. 

The food: I have usually stuck with pepperoni and sausage, and adding garlic each time. The pizza is definitely NOT the worst in all of Nashville. That title belongs to Soulshine Pizza in Midtown. But Its not the best either. The crust is definitely too thick. -Just a personal preference. And it could use a little more sauce. Not bad, but not great either. Its pizza, and at least the ingredients are of a higher calibre than other pizza places I have eaten. The only reason I came in here in the first place was because of location. If you are hungry and in five points, then it does the job. Five Points Pizza is just better in my opinion. Its not that I am being paid to say this, its not that I am biased. The basis of this review is on food alone. The Yelp description of two stars says it all: "Meh. I'v experienced better."

That sums it up.  

Anyone of average intelligence can filter through the obvious planted reviews (five star and one star alike). The furniture and decor, and interior and patio - there's nothing wrong with that. I personally haven't had a bad experience with the service. Nothing would really prevent me from returning here. But with Five Points Pizza just a short walk away, they seem to be getting all my money instead. 

And that is as honest a review as ever.

This place is amazing! Absolutely delicious and great service all around.

I have been here twice. This was my first venture into trying Colombian food and I found the tastes very new to me. The ceviche appetizer was tart and just perfext with the plantain chips. The corn is pretty aesthetic and the toppings with lime complement the corn. The sangria is one of the best in the city for sure too. The arepas themselves were excellent. I have tried the chich-arepas and the skirt steak arepas. They are the favorites for sure. Can't wait to go back again!

I live 2 blocks from Goose the Market, yet it has been over 6 months since I have purchased anything here, despite the fact that I love charcuterie, meat in general, high quality seafood, gelato, cheese, and craft beers. 

Why? 
1. I have a latex allergy. When I smile and politely request that the the counter guys remove their gloves, wash their hands, and make my sandwich or slice my food gloveless, I am met with hostility EVERY. SINGLE. TIME. Yes, I know that there might be some latex cross contamination...don't roll your eyes at me. Yes, I know that it's "against health board regulations" to handle my food without gloves. I'll take the fall if they walk in and catch you. Every time...rather than serve me the food that I am requesting, they get rude and the attitude is "if you're going to be difficult I'd rather not serve you at all." Except I'm not being difficult. I just don't want my lips to crack and my tongue to swell. It's a simple request. 

2. BEYOND THAT!! I must have gone in close to a dozen times and requested "Do you have any non-latex gloves?" NO. "Could you please remove your gloves to make my food?" WE'D RATHER NOT. What kind of ownership doesn't care about that kind of stuff? What kind of employee doesn't pass along "Hey...maybe we could get a box of non-latex gloves to use for the people with allergies?" The kind that doesn't care about their customers and only cares that latex is cheaper than vinyl, nitrile, or other options. 

3. And that brings me to the 3rd reason. I've seen the exact same products that Goose sells...elsewhere...for LESS! I'm not just talking about a nice Marsh, Whole Foods, or The Fresh Market (chains which have bulk-buying power)...I'm talking about Goose-esque boutique meateries in Chicago and Milwaukee, selling Purple Haze chevre for 10-25% less than Goose is selling it. The "Indiana food book" that was published the other year? It's called An Indiana Harvest. It's a great book, beautiful photos, I've bought it twice as a gift. Everyplace sells it for $25. Goose? Oh...$30. Cheerfully. Well...maybe not "cheerfully"...after all, this is Goose. I will rephrase that to "gladly in a surly manner". 

4. No one ever says "Next?" or "I can help the next customer," or really, makes any effort to help you. No effort what so ever. They stand there, and talk, or look at something behind the glass case, or mill about by the long cutting board, so that you think they might be helping someone else...except that isn't the case. When you're finally pushed over the edge and holler over the case (which is about 5 feet tall, so it's not easy for someone my height) "Am I next?" Someone will acknowledge you, not politely, and grudgingly prepare your order. I always feel sorry for the first-timers, because they might stand there for 45 minutes or more as the calloused veterans step ahead of them to aggressively pursue a meat slicer to serve them. 

5. The bread is so hard and tough it cuts the roof of my mouth. There's a difference between "crusty" and "would leave a visible bruise if you were hit with a loaf of this bread". I actually looked in my mouth with a mirror and saw blood and skin flaps after eating half of a Goose sandwich. They need to take a lesson from Patachou or Bluebeard as to what crusty bread should be. 

I shall continue to walk to Mass Ave to get my gelato from Best Chocolate in Town. Where they smile, are conversational, and are not jerks to me. Also, where they don't have latex gloves. I shall also continue to hope that Goose the Market decides to give their employees a level of customer service training equal to that received by your average McDonald's or Taco Bell employee.

I've heard nothing but great things about Lee's, and every time I pass by I think "I really need to try this place." I stopped by during the dollar stroll (and loved what I got), but I wanted to give it a fair shot and have a real "meal" here.

We walked in and were immediately welcome and offered a printed menu to look over by the owner (Lee, I presume.) I was really blown away by the variety of the menu (from standard things like cheesesteaks and club sandwiches, to a ton of vegetarian/vegan options, Asian fusion dishes, and breakfast all day).

I opted for the Seitan cheesesteak w/ american cheese and Old Bay fries. My BF went for the Chicken & Shrimp Stir Fry/Fried Rice (I forget the real name...) We tried to pay then, but the owner politely told us to sit down and enjoy ourselves first, before paying. The food came out pretty quickly, but not before one of the cooks came out to drop off a few different home-made sauces (the home-made Dijon sauce, he insisted, was "great on fries".... spoiler alert: he wasn't lying.)

My Seitan cheesesteak was HUGE, piping hot, and loaded with extra veggies. I added some ketchup and some of the house made sweet chili sauce. So good. The Old Bay fries were crispy and well-seasoned (I think they are just frozen crinkle-cut, but not a problem.) My BF's Stir Fry/Fried Rice came out on a giant plate, and he only ate half, saving the rest for lunch. He enjoyed it a lot.

The exterior and interior aren't much to look at, but the people behind the counter, the extensive menu (can't wait to try breakfast), and the overall experience made me a Lee's fan, for sure.

Webster's definition of Yakitori is Japanese marinated meat skewers.  However, personally it means an assortment of well-seasoned, perfectly cooked deliciousness on a stick.   Yakitori Boy is a hidden gem, found in Philadelphia's Chinatown district.  We came here on a whim on a cold Wednesday night and were greeted by $6 Martinis, $2.50 sushi rolls and $1 - $3 meat skewers.   

Atmosphere: A- (lounge vibe, soft background music, candle lit).

Service: A (friendly, prompt and ready replace your empty glass)

Food: A+ (Awesome)

A few of my favorite $6 drinks were the Smashed Monk, Lychee Pomegranate and the Saki Tini.

The pork Belly, short ribs, rib eye, chicken skin, Chicken and scallions. , Salmon & scallions skewers were delicious.  

For the more adventurous souls, try the chicken gizzards, chicken liver and the quail egg wrapped in bacon.   

If you're reading this review and it's a Wednesday evening, stop reading, drop what you're doing and head to Yakitori Boy right now.

My fiancee picked me up for lunch today and we were looking for something quick and easy, and ended up at the Trolley Stop.
We both ordered a club sandwich (one on wheat, one on white), which came with fries.  The sandwiches were very good.  Bread was toasted, right amount of mayo, lettuce, tomato, ham, turkey, and cheese.  Fries were decent, some were a little soft, but not big deal.
Our only knock was that it seemed to take a little longer than should.  Two club sandwiches seem pretty easy to make, and it wasn't crowded.  
But it was a very good sandwich and the service was good also.

5 stars all around! No wonder Cafe La Maude has such rave reviews, they deserve every single one. My husband and I came for a New Years Day hungover brunch and it seemed like the rest of Philly was doing the same. It is a very tastefully decorated intimate cafe that turns tables around with impressive speed. When we arrived, there were maybe 4 other parties ahead of us, all standing closely at the entrance to not have to wait in the frigid cold. Within less than 15 minutes we were seated and promptly served. They are BYOB and have delicious fresh squeezed orange juice for mimosas. 

Being the big eaters we are, we started with the parfait and espresso/americano. I don't know that a parfait is ever something memorable, but this one will linger in our hearts and stomachs for a long time. The creamiest yogurt topped with strawberries, banana, and tasty chunks of homemade granola. It was a very generous portion and could definitely be eaten alone by one person, so I'm glad we shared it before our entrees! I ordered the sweet potato Benedict and an order of French toast and unfortunately I cannot remember what my husband ordered. I'm so happy so many other Yelpers have taken pictures because I regret not doing so with these beautiful dishes!! We were so hungry that we dove right in to enjoy our meals. 

I'm not exactly sure, but I get the vibe that the menu is a fusion of Middle Eastern and French cuisine, two of my favorites. I'm biased coming from a Turkish family, but the combinations of dishes on this menu were so interesting that we cannot wait to come back and try everything. What sold me on the sweet potato benny, other than being a fan of any sort of Benedict, was that it was served with Sujuk, a spicy breakfast sausage my dad would always bring home from the Turkish market. It's not something you see many places and I was excited to see it included in a few other dishes as well. What an incredible meal... the perfect medley of flavors harmoniously mixed. My husband was blown away by his meal as well. I saved about half of my benny in order to still have room for the beautiful French toast we also ordered. To no surprise, the French toast was perfectly prepared and beautifully served with fresh fruit. 

Something we loved was how involved the owner was in his cafe. He was keeping track of waiting parties, kept tables moving, ran food, and was extremely personable with all his guests. His love for his business showed and he should be very proud of this amazing gem in Northern Liberties. We're already planning our next visit! What a great way for us to start 2018!

Urban Cookhouse is a casual eatery sitting in the heart of Midtown with quick/counter order service that serves Americana style food with a highlight on their sandwiches and wraps, however they do serve appetizers, dinner plates, salads and even brunch. Additionally, they do feature alcohol with select beers, wines and cocktails. UC is a small chain with most of their locations being in Alabama, this Nashville location is the only one in Tennessee currently. 

Parking - Free during certain times, 10:00 AM - 8:30 PM and outside of those hours you can scan to pay or use the pay station. Parking is $11 during those hours. 

We came this way for lunch as we waiting on our nearby hotel room to become ready. We walked in from the back, passing the cute Dolly mural and circled to the register/ordering counter. The menu hangs above the register for your to study in the event you don't know what you want just yet. After we scoped it out we quickly saw a few things to grab. I got the White BBQ sandwich, which was a chicken sandwich with housemade white sauce, cheese and bacon. My partner got a wrap, the Buffalo Chicken which came in four pieces and featured grilled chicken, buffalo sauce and cheese. Both of us sided our sandwich/wraps with their fresh fruit. 

For both of us the sandwiches were just ok. The chicken on the White BBQ was dry and chewy for me and the buffalo chicken was not very buffalo-y, which made it a dry wrap. Additionally, the fruit was not as fresh as expected, as the apple pieces were mushy and off-putting. Not the best showing for a place we had higher hopes for.  

Seating was great as you had booths and tables, along with bar seating inside and then you had the great covered patio! We landed on the patio and it was perfection! They gave us a number for our order and each table is fitted with a wooden block to display your number. It did not take long before our food hit the table via one of the runners. 

Overall, Urban Cookhouse was just ok for us. I can see myself coming back for a casual lunch now that I know what to expect.

So, I will be honest and say that we were in search of after dinner cookies on our last night in Nashville and of course, we hit Yelp and Five Daughters popped up. However, we arrived about an hour before closing and they were already out of cookies for the day, so we reluctantly and with an upside down bottom lip selected a few donuts that they had left for the evening. Turns out that it wasn't the worst thing that happened to us on our trip to Nashville! 

Apparently, Five Daughters Bakery has a cult-like following around Nashville, so we happened upon it searching for an item they are not even remotely famous for and ended up walking out with one of their most popular treats, donuts! This particular location in East Nashville sits in a fairly new mixed use plaza with a couple of shops and other eateries. 

As mentioned, we stopped in about an hour before close on a Friday evening. We expected it to be a little busier, but we happened to be the only ones in the shop. So, once we accepted that there were no cookies, we scoped out the few selections of donuts they had remaining and ended up with a strawberry glazed and the King Kong. Both turned out to be solid choices! 

The donuts or cronuts in this case are definitely sturdier, more dense yet flakier than your average donut. This is due to 100 layers that are packed inside of these tasty rings of goodness! These layers make them a perfect vessel for creams, sugars, toppings, drizzles, chocolate chunks, and more! I personally had the King Kong, which is rolled sugar, infused with vanilla buttercream, topped with maple glaze and candied bacon pieces. It was a pretty heavy duty donut! I am more of a purest when it comes to donuts, so this was stepping outside of my norm and while I did not absolutely hate it, it did have a lot going on. It was a very decadent donut and between the buttercream and maple glaze, it was quite rich. Again, it was tasty in its own right and I can definitely see why it is one of the signature donuts that keeps folks coming back! 

Service was great as well! They could sense our sadness about the cookies and turned our frowns upside down by being really nice and helpful as we blankly stared at the donuts in the cases and asked about each one of them. 

Overall, I can see why Five Daughters is a fan favorite in and beyond Nashville! Upon our next trip, we will have to make it in well before closing so we can get a full glimpse of all the goodies this place has to offer!

*This Review is based off of a drink and the service...I sadly did not partake in the namesake bagels...at least not yet!"

We recently stayed at an AirBnB that located a few blocks away and while we were waiting to check in, we explored the Sylvan Heights area and came across Star Bagel Cafe, which sits in the restaurant row area of the neighborhood. 

I was just after an iced coffee of some sort and luckily they had just what I was craving, an Iced Mocha! I placed my order than wondered around the small café to see what they had going on before eventually settling down at a table to wait. They asked me my name, so I figured they would call once ready, but after about 4 minutes of waiting I walked up to the counter and saw my drink with my name ticket on top of it. Not sure if that is the process, but seemed odd as I was one of only two folks waiting so a heads up I was good to go would have been nice. But, at the end of it all I got my Iced Mocha. Speaking of said beverage, you could definitely taste the mocha! It was almost overwhelmingly mocha. 

The ordering counter is essentially made up of the bagel case which showcased around 17 different variety of their homemade bagels! We did not partake this visit, but those bagels looked delish and then you add some of their house made spreads, boyyyyyyyyy! Speaking of the spreads, while I was waiting I canvased the cooler case where they held water, juices, granolas, salads and several varieties of their homemade cream cheese spreads! 

Service was ok. The person who took my order was all business and again, I did not interact with the person who made my drink...but maybe that is by design? 

The layout of the place is solid. You walk in the main doors and walk into the front counter. There are a few high tops tables in this area and then on the other side of the drink station you have a few low tops and booths where you can hang out. They do also have a cute patio with umbrellas as well. 

Parking could be problematic as there are limited spots in front and on the side, but given the nearby businesses and street parking, you should be good to go.

Overall, my visit here was limited on time and product, but given the status of this little spot in the neighborhood, I can definitely see us coming back through on our next visit!

My friend who lives here in Reno recommended this place knowing I love a good pie! I gave up my dinner plans on eating at La Strada (whose pasta was named top ten in the U.S.) so I could try this pizza! Was it worth it? Heck yeah it was! This is what a great pizza should be like. Quality crust, sauce, and cheese are the foundation of a great pizza and topped off with quality ingredients. This restaurant does all that. I tasted a quality crust, which had great chew, cheese, and sauce with every bite. There are few pizza joints that does this right. How many times have you experienced either no to little sauce or no to little cheese when biting into a pizza? I experienced this too many times. Well, you don't have to worry about that with Smiling Hope Pizza. You'll be content with every bite. The pizza here is exceptional and made by even more exceptional people!

Nektar is very warm and welcoming. Nicholas, the owner, makes sure the bar/restaurant is well stocked with great tasting wines of many varietals. He personally may taste 20 different wines each week and will rotate as he feels is necessary for the enjoyment of his customers.
Tony, the bartender, was very professional and friendly. He is very knowledgeable about whiskys, bourbons, and of course, wines. It was a pleasure and comfort to have Tony serve me.

The food is also spectacular. I sampled the scallops, shrimp and portabella fries on the small plates menu. Lots of good flavors within each dish.

Nektar also has wine tastings from time to time for customers, but they also take the time to educate their staff on the many libations and food offerings.

Great experience for me. I feel you should give Nektar at visit too!

What a fabulous hotel resort in a great location. We had visited the hotel to determine where we would like to stay the next time I was in town. The views from the Infinity Pool and the lobby restaurant were beautiful. 

My favorite room i wanted to stay was room 902 that also had great views and was quite spacious. They did have plenty of other bungalows further away from the main lobby. 

The hotel is a upscale high end resort that provides relaxation in a luxurious fashion.

In less than seven days I have visited three Mexican Restaurants which is three more than I have had a meal at in five years. Yes, I did love the Mexican Restaurant choices that my friends were introducing us to for lunch while in California. La Playa Azul Café was one of my favorites  but that might have been because I am a seafood lover and they had many selections on their menu to choose from. 

Our party wanted to be seated at their outdoor patio along the main road. The patio had high umbrellas with comfortable seating. 

For lunch, we all shared and enjoyed the crab salad, chicken salad and Chile Relleno while washing everything down with their well-known potent margaritas. Everything was wonderful including the service.

A friend of ours invited us to Brix 33 restaurant for dinner where he is a regular. When we arrived, the restaurant owner greeted us when we were seated.

The restaurant has a casual cozy ambience with roomy seating. Our waitress was quite pleasant and attentive.  

It was happy hour, so I immediately indulged myself in a couple of cocktails along with an stuffed pasta appetizer which was delicious and we all shared. 

For dinner, I ordered the Hot smoked Salmon that I also enjoyed very much. It was a delightful dining experience with friends.

The food is good. The Bo nhung Vi is the best. However, the owner doesn't appear too friendly, especially towards the Vietnamese customers who are regulars. She also has a habit of reprimanding/being harsh to her waiters/waitresses in front of customers which I consider rude and downright mean.  The food is decent, but I mostly come for the Bo Nhung Vi. I just wish the owner treats her workers with more respect, especially in front of customers. It gives the impression the workers aren't treated right, which makes me question why I should support this establishment.

Found by accident.  That is how I come upon my review.  A friend and I were headed to the Phil's Grill on Camp Street and when we arrived, we noticed that it was GONE and in its place a new establishment called Rebellion.  Honestly, it being unknown to us, we almost walked away.  After a read of the menu, we thought "why not, let's give it a shot!"

The Gastro Pub Genre seems like a very wide and somewhat undefined category.  Food with alcohol I guess.  However, for the first time in NOLA I really kind of get it after experiencing Rebellion for the first time.  (Maybe that is where the name comes from?)  Anyway, the food was simply fantastic.
