I ordered the crab eggs benefit on tomato instead of English muffins with hash browns and a side of bacon. My husband ordered a breakfast sandwich. After about 30 minutes, our food came out! We enjoyed the food since we were hungry from the long wait.

Then we paid, and the girl that took our card disappeared. We looked for her for about 10-minutes then the hostess brought us our card. We found that a bit weird, and the hostess informed us that she added an extra charge since I had tomatoes instead of bread. I found that very sketchy that it wasn't communicated prior to them running my card. I told her I wouldn't have gotten the tomatoes had they been transparent with me when ordering.

Customer service here was a HUGE issue for me. The $2 didn't break the bank, but the principal of the sketchy charge bothered me. I certainly wouldn't come here again just because of the service, but the food hit the spot.

The Rex family businesses, both The Wylder near downtown and Certified Kitchen & Bakery in the North End, fed us multiple delicious meals during pandemic months.  Many repasts came from Certified since they delivered a delightful dinner meal for two (or four) every Thursday for many months and to our west of Boise town of Eagle for a mere ten bucks delivery fee.  But during pandemic months we also discovered a great 'to go' option offered as curbside pickup at The Wylder called "Wyld Night at Home".  Certified has ended their Thursday dinner deliveries (with many thanks to them we say alas) but Certified's excellent breakfast, lunch and bakery options can be had at their storefront  to go.  And it looks as if The Wylder is continuing to offer "Wyld Night" along with all other menu items for curbside pickup. 

TO FIND OUT MORE:  If you need a great take out meal, customizable by you to include the options of your choice, whether to take home or back to your hotel room, to learn more about "Wyld Night" do this:

*Go to The Wylder's web page, choose menu from the top bar where you'll see the menu and also an "order online" link. 
 https://www.thewylderboise.com/menu
*At that link scroll across to find Wyld Night and click on that to learn the options.

You can order anything on the menu to go, but the Wyld Night packages - there are multiples - are a particularly good and delicious value.  As in the "Wyld Night + Cocktails" we enjoyed which was only $55 before tip to serve two and included a pizza, a veggie, a salad and 2 custom cocktails - all of our choice .  (There is also an option for only $35 to serve two sans libations.) As example, here are the choices we made for a fav combo.

*Seasonal special pizza "Basque in the Sun" - parmesan base with sweet potato, Spanish chorizo, kale, goat cheese
*Market romaine salad, seasonal veg, white cheddar, house ranch vinaigrette
*Oven fired acorn squash with walnut-chard pesto, ricotta, brown butter breadcrumbs, pickled red onions
*Libations: Rose's Luxury - Rittenhouse rye/Carpano Antica/Kirsch/Aperol &
House Arrest - rye/ Amado Nonino/ sweet vermouth

EATS DEETS:  While The Wylder is best known for their pizza, the veggies and salads here are top notch and we can - and sometimes do - make a meal out of those.  Oh...and the mushroom toast...yes...  As for the pizza, the combinations of first rate toppings have always been excellent and where once I was not as keen on the crust I now think it is darned good. Did they change it or did my taste evolve?  BTW, I ask myself the same question about Steve Martin who I did not as much appreciate in his younger years and my high school age youth but whom I think is a darned sexy and talented man in his older age and mine not that much younger than him.  Things evolve.

IF I COULD WAVE A MAGIC WAND:  One of the reasons The Wylder wasn't often on our 'go to' list in pre-pandemic days was for tight seating.  Not only do we find that uncomfortable, for me it is sometimes impossible to get to a table since I am an enthusiastic gourmand / diner / ardent local food fan with mobility limits due to Multiple Sclerosis that onset in my college days.  I appreciate good food, I am an undemanding guest and appreciative one to tip 25 - 30% and yet many eateries make it from difficult to impossible for me to get a seat at a table due to too tight spaces.  If I could wave a magic wand I'd have all eateries, The Wylder included, put 36" clear floorspace behind  chairs of seated diners - only 3 feet - this is the ADA standard - so one doesn't have to be able to stand and "squeeze in" to get a seat.  Essential for ADA equal access, more comfortable for everyone, and we've all become aware during pandemic months how it is also a good thing to have some "breathing room" around us.

FINAL TIPS:  Among the finest mixologists in Boise work here.  Perhaps the best breakfast sandwiches in Boise can be found at Certified.  If you like The Wylder's lasagna (who wouldn't) you can buy it frozen to cook at home at Certified in their freezer case in store.  And yes, the lasagna makes a lovely gift for someone.

An unpretentious and funky, all people are welcome vibe coffee house with a truly neighborhood sensibility that I wish was closer to my neighborhood because I'd go in often.  

DRINKS & EATS
I have not strayed from black coffee or Americano, although they make all kinds of coffee / espresso beverages.  The coffee is good.  The Americano is really good.  

Baked goods are created in house.  I am a fan of their biscotti in particular.

Can you say "share" boys and girls?  Of course you can.  And you should plan to do that if you choose a cinnamon roll as your goody because they are big.  The guy sitting next to my hubby and me this morning paused on his way out to say, "I admire the way the two of you are working as a team to attack that roll."  I laughed and told him "Pull up a fork, there is plenty for three."   And here's a tip; the cinnamon rolls often sell out by 10:30 a.m.

There is a sour cream chocolate sheet cake that seems to be a signature / staple and I hear it calling my name every time I'm here.  Maybe next time I'll succumb to the Siren's song.  Calories be damned.

Prices are reasonable.  

THE DRILL & SERVICE
Stand in line, place your order, wait while they make the beverage and plate up your eats.  Then carry it to your table.  Bus your own when done.

People behind the counter are friendly and pretty darned efficient too.. 

SEATING & VIBE
Seating is at tables and chairs, all standard height on the main level and also up one step to a raised seating area.  There is counter seating that is also standard height with chairs, another high counter height table with stools and a sofa near the front door. 

In the mode of all people being welcome here, let me say I wish I had my phone to take a shot of the cars in the parking lot the day before yesterday.  Left to right in the first three spaces :  a) car with Trump bumper sticker...next to that b) car with Obama 2012 bumper sticker...and one car over from that c) a car with Bernie 2016 window sticker.  

To be truthful, I imagine it might be a tad uncomfortable for anyone transferring that Trump sticker from car bumper to themselves and walking in here.  This feels more 4th Street Berkeley than Main Street Coeur d'Alene for audience.

Still, there seems a sense of grace filled detente here and people from all stages in and walks of life. 

GIFTS & THINGS
There is an area for buying cards and giftee-s too.  You know, like if you wanted to sit in a coffee house and write an actual long hand note in a card to mail to someone.  Ahhh...love it.  I used to be a prodigious sender of cards and handwritten notes.  I have lost that that practice.  

Free wifi too.

THIS N THAT:

PARKING: is on street and also in a very small lot in the back.  One space of accessible parking, although to my wheelchair using friends I point out it is only van accessible if you back in. 

ACCESSIBILITY:  Level in at the front door and in the back /side door.  Mostly on one floor although a few tables are up one step.

LOO:  Down the hall.  It is accessible.

Will we go back?   You bet.  There is still wood to chop for service protocol (as in getting the food out of the kitchen without overly long waits even when the restaurant isn't busy) and finesse in the dishes.  One expects hiccups in a newish place (open only a couple of weeks).  

There were more pros than cons here.  The greeting at the door was warm welcome, the server was knowledgeable and cordial, the menu was intriguing (even for we who lean to vegetarian), the food was good, the ambiance was industrial hip but still comfortable and the prices were reasonable considering the entire dining experience.  

VIBE
High black ceiling, industrial minimalist interior.  I loved the white cloth napkins with beet colored striping. Surprisingly comfortable seating at  spartan looking tables and chairs in the dining room which is separated into two parts.  Left of the door as you walk in is main space, right of the door is smaller space (which should be great seating in summer as a garage door there will roll up).  Bar is straight ahead with two circular booths and the remainder of seating all high perch seats at high tables.

"All people are welcome" vibe was a happy surprise from the "hipster central" I was expecting.  We saw people of all ages, from kids through seniors, and all walks of life come in during the roughly 75 minutes it took for lunch.  Both my hubby and I noted how many were "the guys who lunch" in groups of all ages as the place started to fill as opposed to "the ladies who lunch" one might find at some other venues. 

MENU
See photo.  Menu included a few apps (roughly $4 - $10) and salads (roughly $7 - $14) and sides (around $5 or under) but the focus is on burgers.  In addition to the specially aged beef used in the ground beef burgers in creative combinations ($12 ish) there were also chicken, salmon and vegetarian options (around $10 ish).  

Libations (on back of the menu) include beer (the focus here), a modest list of decent wines by glass (between $7 and $13 each) and speciality cocktails ($7 to $9 ish as I recall).  Coffee is local Dawson Taylor. 

FOOD
We shared Asian chicken lettuce wrap app ($9), the beet-veggie burger ($10) and buttermilk panna cotta ($6).  We'd order them again even though there were some 'needs work' surprises in all the dishes.

As example, the chicken dish (it is ground chicken, btw, like Thai larb not diced chicken more like Chinese restaurant wraps although the menu didn't make that clear) was nicely flavored and served hot,  But with Bibb lettuce leaves that while fresh and dry (good things) were  too delicate to stand up to the filling and wilted and wilted apart to need knife and fork to eat.

The beet-veggie burger was earthy - flavorful and served on an excellent Gaston Bakery bun with top notch mustard and fresh onions,  But the patty fell apart making it difficult to eat.

The panna cotta had good  buttermilk flavor and was just sweet enough,  Yet it had too much gelatin in it to be the barely set delight that we're accustomed to from the many panna cotta we've sampled everywhere.  There was even a little layer of gelatin on the top which is not a good thing.

VALUE
I note some reviewers think the price is too high for burgers, but you get what you pay for in the quality of the ingredients here.  Still, it is a good expectation to set that if you're looking for a bargain burger joint, this isn't it. This is a quality place with prices that are fair with that in mind from my perch. As grounding example, our meal for two without beverages was $25.00 before tax and tip.

SERVICE
Service process here is something on which I hope they'll focus.  It was easy to see in looking at the layout of the space how the protocol for servers from order taking to placing the order with the kitchen to getting it delivered to the table was made awkward.  Also one wonders if the kitchen might be too small or under staffed given how long it took for orders to make it to table even when the place was less than half full.

THIS N THAT:

1) ACCESSIBILITY:  Level in and throughout.  Standard height seating in restaurant.  Only high perch seating in bar; problem (equal access means to in bar seating too - ask my young disabled vet friends about that) that could easily be corrected by swapping out a couple of high perch tables with standard ones.

2) PARKING:  On street.  Not sure if lot across is public or private.

3) HAPPY HOUR:  Yes.  Discounts on apps 4p - 6p.

4) BREWFORIA:  Around the corner.  Connected ownership but not the same owner.  It's complicated.  Shares hall and bathrooms with Grind.  Grind kitchen also provides eats for Brewforia, we're told,  which might add to food delay issues when Brewforia is open.

Chandler's will be CLOSED FROM 11/5 UNTIL 11/13 due to covid19 issues.  "Taking a breather..." as the owners / management said in public announcement.  This from their announcement via social media and email today:  "We have had our first positive cases of COVID19 in the Chandler's family.  Therefore we are suspending service immediately.  Thanks for your patience and understanding.  We look forward to welcoming you back on November 13."

Expanded hours.  Friendly people.  Sparking clean if awkward space in lousy strip mall. Good food even if not the best for us.  Moderate prices.   Order at counter and carry your food to table service format.  We are wed to another local full service barbecue spot but there was a lot to like here for some folks even if not our thing for repeat visit. That's the nutshell view.  Detail follows.

A TIP - THE HOURS:  Originally open only for lunch Tuesday through Friday; recently added dinner on Friday and Saturdays.

THE DRILL:  The service format of order at the counter, food served on disposable paper ware, pick up your eats when ready and carry to your table, is not our thing for eat in.  We don't do fast food for similar reasons.  Different service format strokes for different diners. 

SKEPTICS WON OVER:  We walked in with skeptics' view given our hearts and taste buds belong to another local BBQ place.  But we were won over by warm greeting as we were offered a rib to sample while we decided on what to choose from the big chalkboard menu over the order counter.  Aroma of barbecue as you enter is winning too.  We liked the unpretentious vibe.  We liked the absence of loud music; one could carry on a conversation.  We liked that nearly all of the seating was standard height tables and chairs that works for everyone, no need to perch on a bar stool here.  And we appreciated that the huge and awkward space (reclaimed from Mickey Ray's) is clean.  All in all, pride of ownership shows.  Still, the location in a woeful strip mall and space layout is uncomfortable and that is what that is.

THE EATS:  Almost all is a la carte.  Be aware of that when ordering for a group.  I notice some reviews not flattering for Rib Shack that seem fueled by diners not understanding the a la carte set up.  Sides do not "come with".  

Sides are offered in a few size options like 1/3 pound and 1/2 pound.

Meats come by half pound, pound and other options I think (like maybe a rack for ribs).

We appreciated the menu has both rib ends (pork) and pork ends among their offerings. (Also burnt ends for beef eaters, which we are not.)  They also offer baby back ribs and another cut which I'd say is like a St. Louis style.

We chose spicy red potato salad, coleslaw, rib ends and  baby back ribs.  They have over a dozen different house made bbq sauces.  They are all available to sample and all good enough.

BARBECUE AND SIDES ARE LIKE BUYING JEANS: Even if you wear the same size as the guy or girl next to you, different styles probably fit each of you best.  So for the food here as fit...

...we like that serve meats dry rubbed with sauces to add as you choose and each of the three sauces we tried fit us for being not too sweet, vinegar forward, and lots of chiles in the mix.  

...pork rib ends were great.

...baby backs had a LOT more fat than we prefer; we would not order them again.  

...spicy red potato salad was for us perhaps the best potato salad we've had at any barbecue place in Idaho.  

...coleslaw was fresh and crisp with celery seed (yahoo) if too sweet for us.

THE DAMAGE:  Prices are competitive.  We were full to capacity on that meal and it was just about twelve bucks a head without beverages.

THIS N THAT:

1) LOCATION:  This is one of the most poorly maintained strip malls in the this part of the Treasure Valley, imho.  Not the Rib Shack owner's issue for sure. I hear the mall owner is a commercial builder.  Shame on him.  He knows better. 

2) WHEELCHAIR ACCESS: The parking in this strip mall is woefully in non-compliant with Federal ADA civil rights law and Idaho Building codes for mere minimums for accessible parking. The law and code is 26 years old.  The mall owner has had plenty of time to fix this.  I imagine it will only get changed if the mall owner gets sued.  Sadly but seriously.  But once you get in the door at Rib Shack it looks like the restaurant owner has his piece right;  all on one floor with ample aisle space and several standard height table options.  

3)  OUTDOOR SEATING:  Patio in the front of Rib Shack with tables set up for good weather dining.

The tacos were even better than the buzz!  The tastiest street-TexMexAmerican-style tacos we've had in all of Treasure Valley.   Arguably anywhere north of Austin.  If you need more than that recommendation, here are things  to know before you go...

BACK STORY:  The friendly guy behind the counter told us this was started by a couple of sisters who relocated from Texas to Boise and noticed the absence of street-style taco places here.  Filling the niche, they opened Tin Roof.  Aren't all of our taste buds tickled for their entrepreneurship!   (I'd love to know how the nifty name came to be.  If I have a chance to meet the owners, I'll ask.)  

FORWARD TIP:  I hear another Tin Roof is planned for Meridian.  El hurra!  Times two for that cheer since it will NOT be in the Village mall.  (Who wants to go to a big shopping mall and fight the parking to eat?  Not you?   Me neither.)

VIBE: Located at a little strip mall not far from downtown and with neighbors that include a dry cleaner and yogurt shop, this is a sparkling clean and 'all are welcome' kind of place.  For seating there are several long communal tables with chairs inside and also some high counters and chairs on one wall and at kitchen.  There are more tables and chairs outside on a covered patio with a funky-fun-firepit.  They have allowed ample room at the order counter and in the aisle way to get from food pick up counter to the tables. Seating at tables may be a tight squeeze in busy times.  One TV in the corner (with sound off when we were there - thank goodness.)

SERVICE:  Do friendly folks make terrific tacos taste even better?  Maybe.  The people at the service counter and in the open kitchen space sure are delightful.  And the time from placing order to calling our name for order being up was "flash fast".

DRILL:  Menu is posted on big, clear to read signs on  the wall to the left of the order counter.  It lists six breakfast tacos (available all day) and fourteen others including two pork, two chicken, three veggie (yahoo! says me), two seafood and five beef options. Order at the counter and when your meal is ready they'll call your name to pick it up to carry to your seat at a table...or to go with you.  

EATS:   We shared four tacos between two of us; one of the pork and all of the veggies tacos.  Each was delicious with fresh ingredients and flavors on very good corn tortillas.  (The tortillas came to them formed and par baked and they finish them off on the in house tortilla 'grill'.)  The tacos were very tasty just as served.  Next time we'll also try some of the sauces in squeeze bottles at the counter...tomatillo (mild), red chile (spicy), and orange (habanero hot).  The tacos are served inside cardboard containers and all placed on a nice round Tin Roof tray to make it easy to carry and eat them.

VALUE:  Breakfast tacos are only $2 each, seafood options are $2.50 and the others $2.25.  A bargain for this great product!

ACCESSIBILITY: I have MS so pay particular attention to equal access. (I bet the Governor of Texas, a man who uses a wheelchair due to an accident, does too.)  Level in the door and all on one level.  Tables are standard height with chairs that can be moved if necessary for wheelchair access.  Patio is fully accessible with some tables there as well.  Good for them. 

PARKING:  Parking is at a premium in Boise so a big advantage for this location is the small strip mall parking lot.  ADA parking spaces included.  

TIMING IS EVERYTHING:  Want to avoid the long line which can sometimes form here (for good reason) or to be able to have a group find seats together?  If you're going at lunch be in by 11:20 and you'll be good to go.

I was craving Thai summer rolls.  Had I not remembered reading some decent Yelp reviews for this place I would have passed it by given the location in a seedy strip mall.  Bottom line from our experience: Chiang Mai isn't a bad place to stop if you're in the area for food that is Southeast Asian or Chinese in concept if not authentic in execution.  It isn't a place we'll go back to again but glad we tried it.  Once.

Let's start with the GOOD THINGS:. 

1) Summer rolls were freshly filled and expertly rolled.  I would have been a bigger fan if they contained some SE Asian herbs in the mix, like cilantro, Thai basil and mint instead of only lettuce as the greens element.   I liked the dipping sauce served with them was a vinegar tart, sweet, salty offering (although not fish sauce prominent as one might find for traditional nuac cham)  instead of  peanut sauce.  I used  red chili paste on the table to add spicy heat to the mix. 

2) Very friendly service.  It seemed virtually a wave of people were leaving through the narrow entry as we tried to enter just after 1:00 and  we had the then advantage of few tables being occupied and attentive servers.  Food was delivered promptly with hot food served hot and cold food served cold.

3) Decent seating options including booths with elephant pattern woven tablecloths topped with glass or formica topped tables and chairs all at standard height.

4) Music selection on the sound system of rock ancients like Jim Morrison and Mick Jagger.  (Embarrasingly, I know all the lyrics to all the songs and wanted to sing along.)   Set at at a low enough level to know it was there but not to override all else.

5) Prices were low ($19 before tax for three dishes at lunch) and servings were large.  But I'd rather have higher prices and smaller servings of better food. 

Now the 'NOT SO MUCH' things:

1) Like many Thai restaurants in the area the menu seems an amalgam of Chinese - American and Thai items with the latter tamed down from the robust flavors I have enjoyed at Thai restaurants in cities like Portland, San Franciso, Las Vegas or even my former hometown of Bend.  For a city of Bosie's size it is surprising to find so many Asian restaurants don't "pick a lane and drive in it" for authentic food.

2)  The food is just OK "minus".  Pad Thai is one of those dishes I am almost ashamed to hear myself order as it is sometimes so poorly done, but when it is well made it is a treasure.  It was on the lunch menu here and so I ordered it as a good litmus test for any Thai restaurant which arguably ought to get this rice noodle dish right.  (Like say an Italian restaurant's ability to turn out spaghetti marinara right.)  This was not the worst Pad Thai I've ever had, but it was not good either.

My husband veered to a Chinese food item selecting Hoonan (not a typo, that is how it appeared on menu) vegetables.  The mix of veggies, which included bok choy, napa cabbage and pea pods, was cooked to just right  toothsome doneness.   Oversauced, but that seems to be a trend  in Chinese - American food service,  with too much soy sauce in the mix of things, another trend, and just barely a hint of the Hunan heat as promised on the menu. 

3) The infrastructure of the restaurant looks like it is falling apart, from the parking lot through the door and all around.  Which may be nothing the restaurant owners can do anything about unless they own the building.

4) Getting in the door can be a challenge at the narrow entry as people are going out and you are coming in given they have a host station set up as "traffic stop".  It is awkward and uninviting.  This they could fix.

THIS N THAT:

1) PARKING:  The ramshakle lot shows looks rode hard and put away wet, but it is a lot with parking and that is a good thing in spite of the condition.

2) NEIGHBORS:  Bar to the left, Asian Market 2 to the right.  The latter is an interesting place if you're trying to find some harder to find SE Asian ingredients like shrimp paste or a choice of half a dozen plus brands of fish sauce.

3)  ACCESSIBILITY:  One blue wheelchair marked spot in the entire lot is outside the Asian Market.  It is not van accessible.  Restaurant is level in and throughout.  Table seating is standard height.  Adequate path of travel to several tables.

You know the "Tell me about the chicken" scene from Portlandia?*  Well. That's us.  Hubby and me.  So a drive through burger kiosk in a strip mall parking lot is a highly unlikely place to find us given we have long been of the "know what is in your food and where it comes from" types.  To make it even more unlikely that we'd end up placing our order at a kiosk with "Burger" in the name, I share the "he" of we won't eat beef in any form and the "she" won't eat it ground - unless "she" sees it ground in a butcher shop from a range raised cattle cut of her choice. 

But here "we" ended up at a drive up burger kiosk after reading about the owner, Shad Cupp, who range raises the Scottish Highland cattle at his BVR Highland ranch and who started the ranching enterprise after having an epiphany about the flaws in our food supply when he saw "Food, Inc." and was then wrestling with his own health problems being compounded by a fast food diet.

Learning he also had pork products from his pasture raised hogs, this kiosk was a destination dining choice even though we knew the only place to eat would be at picnic tables in the parking lot given we didn't think our "little piggy" brats would hold up all the way home.

THE EATS:  Eat the brats we did at that picnic table, every single bite - the "he" in a spicy Italian rendition (he is Sicilian after all) and the "she" in the classic with mustard and kraut - and licked our fingers clean of the yummy black pepper rich salt on the french fries too.  Another unlikely sighting for us given except for the true pommes frittes at Bacquet's in Eagle or Petite 4 on the Bench we don't eat french fries either.  And given both "he"' and "she" are lighter eaters with a lifetime of weight control challenges in the mix it is also unlikely to see us eat an entire dish of anything - sharing being usual MO - but a whole brat each was consumed with gusto.    Fresh made sausages using BVR ranch raised pork are served on local baker Gaston's buns and with local MFT ketchup for the fries and all at only about $10 each.  (The price includes a large soft drink, but on those we passed.) 

THE OWNER:  Maybe it was seeing us lick our fingers that made the nice guy who owns this come out to ask us how we enjoyed the food.  It gave us a chance to talk about our shared perspectives on the importance of humane and sustainable practices in animal husbandry and learn more about his business.  With his adult son, Hoss, now largely running the ranch Shad has the time to run the kiosk and associated food truck.  He'd like to be able to expand for other kiosk locations in the area so that people don't have to eat bad food to eat convenient food.  And while his animals are currently dispatched and processed at the only USDA approved facility in the area, he would one day like to have his own on ranch facility to do that to have end-to-end control of his product.  (If he does that, I'm on board for one of those burgers too!)  He realizes a kiosk isn't ideal - no seating or loo for customers and all - but it was the affordable place to start.

THE DRILL:  Drive up to the window and a nice young 'un (on our day a delightful young woman who we assumed was a relation) will take your order.  Then if there is a car behind you, the same young 'un will go to that car to take theirs so the delay is minimal for waiting for food to be cooked (on our day Shad was doing the cooking).  But this is cooked to order eats, not McDonald's drive through, so set expectations for a little time being needed.  If you're planning on eating at the picnic tables, they'll offer to bring the food to you or you can walk up to the window to fetch your own (our choice) when it is ready. 

THE SCENE*: Sure, you know it.  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ErRHJlE4PGI

PS:  God bless small ranchers and farmers who use sustainable agricultural models to provide good and healthy things for people to eat.

This "mom and pop" breakfast and lunch spot provides a good option for eats if you're in Meridian.  'Joe' is the same person as Joe Momma's in Eagle.  He is no longer part of that business (divorce settlement, I'm told) but for context of what to expect here, you can see the roots in 'neighborhood place' orientation and menu too. The food here is better, imho, than the other venture and the interior is brighter and there is somehow a feeling of more welcome for me by the staff here, so of the two this is my choice.

LOCATION & VIBE:  Tucked at the back of a Meridian strip mall, it's not visible from the main drag and a little hard to find on the first visit.  It is worth finding.

Bright space with high ceilings with exposed duct work in new industrial style space.  Big windows in the front and on one side.  Some booths line two walls, tables and chairs the other and still a few more tables and chairs down the middle of the room.  Enough space between them to avoid "sardine can seating" and room to navigate from tables to loo too.  I also love that when there is music it is barely noticeable and on some days, like today, there is no music.  Better yet for conversation to take center stage.

SERVICE:  Friendly and efficient.  Sometimes there are delays in food coming out of the kitchen, like today when the place was about 70% full on a weekday late morning.  But that seems to have to do with limited cooking staff not with any lack of attentiveness by the servers.  One (or two) cooks can only do so much at one time.  The servers clearly enjoy their work and have a lot of pride in the restaurant and want their customers, their guests, to be happy.

FOOD:  Garden Hash from the "Specialty Hashes" section of the menu, is a new-ish add and my current favorite.  It includes tender nuggets of roasted garlic cloves in enough quantity to repel a vampire - so you know if you want to ask at order for them to adjust quantity.  It is delicious with 'just so' freshly cooked fresh veggies including spinach, peppers, zucchini, mushrooms and artichoke hearts nestled on a bed of Joe's potatoes along with Swiss cheese and fresh avocado.

I'm normally a hash-browns-kinda-gal but Joe's style potatoes could make a me a convert.  Also worth noting the dish comes with two eggs of your choice and they get my "poached, hard like golf balls" just right every time.  (Harder to do than you think.).  The dish is ample enough size to expect to ask for a 'to go' box unless you're an Amazon-appetite-eater.

I also enjoy that Moe Joe's offers the opportunity for half orders of eggs Benedict (they have about half a dozen options on the menu) which is swell since I can never finish a whole order.  I'll also suggest if you order a Benny here that you ask for some lemon wedges on the side as in the vernacular of "different strokes for different palates" the hollandaise is much lighter on lemon than I prefer.

My husband likes the early bird breakfast offerings of a handful (or so) for $6.99 that is offered only until 9:00 a.m. (Tue - Fri) unless you are over 55 in which case it applies all day.   He's way old enough to take advantage of the all day time frame and he often chooses the pancake option from that menu.

Moe Joe's makes their own  biscuits and you can substitute a biscuit for toast with your order.  I recommend you do that.  And when they ask if you'd like Marionberry or strawberry jam, they bring it to you in a container, not in a sealed package.  Nice. 

Still, not all is perfect for me.

Coffee is just OK and since it is served from carafes, while one's cup is always kept filled by the really nice servers it is often warm not hot.

They don't have an option for real maple syrup.  I don't mind paying more for it.  I would like the option to order it.

The cinnamon rolls while homemade are a bit doughy and under-baked in two tries. 

But on the whole, I'm a fan.

VALUE:  Two breakfasts + two coffees = $25.00 "minus" for us most of the time.  Good value.

THIS N THAT:

1) PARKING:  Mostly more than ample in the strip mall lot except at peak breakfast hours on weekends.

2) ACCESSIBILITY:  Accessible parking (two spots laid out just right with one van accessible) in the lot.  Level in the door and throughout.  All seating is standard height.

3) ALLERGIC TO LONG WAITS?  Simple antidote is to avoid weekend breakfast hours.

Tony makes not only the best pizza in all of the Treasure Valley, he makes the best pizza anywhere.  Full stop.  Period.  If you search far and wide you may find pizza as good as Tony's.  Maybe.  But you won't find any better.  Ever.  I am a person not given to absolutes or hyperbole, so trust me when I tell you with certainty that Tony's pizza is penultimate!

Pizzeria Teatro was our destination dining stop as our first dinner meal on our first "should we move to Boise" tire kicking trip almost six years ago.  My husband, who is Sicilian heritage and grew up in an Italian neighborhood in Brooklyn in a household where his grandmother spoke only Italian, said "I'm home" when we walked in the door then.  We feel the same way now.  (And this is a coincidence, my hubby and Tony went to competing high schools in Brooklyn.  Although decades apart for my old'un hubby, he still considers both of them to be guys from the same neighborhood.  As New Yorkers are inclined to do, I guess.) 

No matter what pizza you choose, it will be excellent.  The same can be said for the salads.  Not to mention a wine list that is 'perfetto' for Italian fit.   And it is also the friendly service, lovely art on the walls, and great jazz classics music on the sound system that season the experience.

See my first review from 2013 if you find details helpful.  But I figured it was worth a review update as it surprises me to find how many people we talk with about superior places to eat in Boise have never heard of Tony's, including people who have lived here far longer than we (of our now five year residency.)  Tony's continues to be on our recommendation list for others for destination dining.  

Also as praise for Tony and his pizza, I share that a few weeks ago while dining at another eatery where pizza is on the menu, the owner sat down with us to ask what we thought of the pizza coming out of his kitchen.  This man, who also shares Italian heritage, said he too thought Tony's pizza was extraordinary and if Tony ever retired he was going to ask him for his pizza recipe.  "Ah", we said, "But if Tony retires the pizza would never be the same, recipe or not, because there is the hand of the pizza artist in the making of Tony's pies that makes them so deliciously special."

The only thing I would change here if I had a magic wand is the location.  Parking in this part of downtown is a bear  for anyone and in particular for me as I have MS and rely on accessible - aka complies with ADA - parking to be able to park and get out of my car and there isn't much of it in this part of downtown.  Plus, I live out in the west side wilds of Eagle.  So, if Tony ever wanted to move his pizzeria out to my side of town somewhere with a parking lot, I would be on auto-pilot for weekly dining.

A fan of locally owned Form & Function coffee when having it at Boise eateries like The Wylder or Txikiteo, when recently in the neighborhood of Form & Function's bricks and mortar store, I moseyed in for a cuppa from them directly. I was not a fan of the metaphorically lukewarm service I received or the literally lukewarm coffee.  Which the person behind the counter clearly had to have known was almost room temperature when she handed the cup to me.  And yet, I had to take a sip to figure that out for myself.  Given the prices of coffee here, not to mention their reputation of which they are proud, I asked to have it replaced.

"Oh, it isn't hot?" (Delivered in tone rich in ennui.)  As if that was a surprise to her.  

The interior has seating at high counter stool height and some at standard tables.  There is more up a flight of stairs to a loft.  But, feeling entirely unwelcome, I took my order to go.

Overall the vibe  inside is as lacking warmth as was the service and coffee.  It isn't that I don't appreciate spare, modern-minimalism because I do.  It is just that the entire space is 'chilly' and add in service issues it is the antithesis of the "all are welcome here" I prefer regardless of décor.

One and done for me.  

PARKING:  Good luck with that in this neighborhood on street or street level lots down the block...but there is a parking garage associated with The Fowler apartment building at which Form & Function sits at ground level so perhaps that garage is an alternative.  I didn't check it.  The street Form & Function faces has no parking allowed.

ACCESSIBILITY: Level in the door from sidewalk, ample floor space inside, limited standard height seating, didn't check the loo.

NEIGHBORS:  The Wylder on one side, Boise Brewing on another, Law School across the street.

Newish eatery with same owners as Tavern at Bown Crossing and Owyhee Tavern.  Knowing the mode of those others and assuming similar menu and food quality here we went in with expectations set on low side of mid range.  But even at that the experience undershot the mark.  Neither ambiance nor eats would bring us back under our own steam.  If others suggested meet up here, we'd suggest alternates.  We left with a sense that if Applebee's were a kindergarten kid who ascended to third grade it would be this eatery.  We are big fans of supporting locally owned restaurants but this isn't one we'll choose again.

LOCATION: The highly visible intersection corner in a strip mall at the border of Meridian and Eagle - this is the venue as Blaze Pizza, Fred Meyer, CupBop Korean and Flatbread Neapolitan Pizzeria among others - near a slew of housing developments is likely a prime location for the owners to have selected to bring in the demographic of diner they're looking for and as alternate to the sea of chain eateries in this area.  They will likely be packed at peak times once their audience - maybe Eagle Bardenay fans and folks still 'California dreamin' - finds them.

VIBE & SEATING:  Dark space  with brown paint paneled walls and windows only at far end.  Tight booths on the opposite side of the room from the bar, high step up tight booths in the bar - which is the location with a sense of light - and three'ish small tables right inside the door for those who require table seating or prefer it.  Music of not unpleasant '70's - 90's mix but set too loud, 3 TVs showing sporting events scattered around the room with none easily visible from many of the booths on the opposite side of the bar.  And in the mode of "what WERE they thinking" in a business where focus is on bar / liquor / beer sales they have but one stall loo each for guys and girls.  Imagine the logistics on a busy night.

EATS:  Maybe the chaos is to get people not to notice the food is just ho-hum.  The lunch menu of appetizers ($8 - $15), sandwiches & burgers ($12 - $16), salads ($8 - $13) with a soup or two ($6 bowl).  The folks who ordered the tomato basil at an adjoining table left it uneaten as they said it was so bad so it waved us in another direction for our lunch order.  The two dishes we chose were enough to eat but sort of C+ at best - clams were chewy and salad drowning in dressing. 

Dinner menu is similar to lunch but expanded to include other things (like steak & chops $24 - $45 or poultry and seafood options $17 - $28) and with some specific to the Eagle location in the "Tavern at" series.  (Owners said they design each Tavern menu to include some things unique to the location.) 

Dessert menu is straight out of Sysco Sweet Things offerings (literally) and about half a dozen at $8 in options like Mud Pie, Flourless Chocolate Cake, Berry Cobbler...

If you're interested in seeing all the menus, here is a link.  https://www.tavernateagleisland.com/menu

LIBATIONS:  Full bar service (it may be sad commentary that the cocktails were the best part of our meal), beer and a wine list that is laughable for the laziness or ineptness to have omitted vintage years on the vintage offerings including among them high end wines. (Bottle prices roughly $22 like Sycamore Lane Chard to $350 for Opus One.  Limited number of wines by glass about $10 - $14.)  What audience of customers would order a bottle of Leonetti Reserve Cab ($260) or Pepperbridge Merlot ($75) without knowing vintage year?  And if our experience with the very nice but not fully trained servers was any indicator, they wouldn't know wine information either if one asked.  Happy note is that coffee is Stumptown and served hot.

STAFFING:  Servers were pleasant and trying.  The hostess was working hard to bus stables as customers left, sweep floors under tables and still answer phones and seat customers by going up on her "tip toes" to try to keep an eye on the distant door where customers entered.  Suggests owners are cutting staffing corners.

ACCESSIBILITY:  Barely mere minimum for accessible seating here and awkward for sure.  Were I a person using a wheelchair, I would note that all of the booth seating in the dining room and all of the high step up booth seating in the bar is not usable and "you are not welcome here" in design.  Only three small tables in the odd traffic pattern entry space seem accessible.  The bathroom is accessible but soap dispenser set above the 48" max reach range of law and code.  Only accessible parking spaces in the lot are at the far end of the sidewalk. 

SERVICE HOURS: Open straight through from lunch (11:00 I think) through dinner (starts and 4:00) and have a Happy Hour beginning at 4:00.  There were plans to introduce brunch on weekends in October.

The food is delicious.  It seems as might be served at an abuela's kitchen table.  The splendid service makes it taste even better.   The young women waiting on the booths and tables inside the strip mall located modest space were warm and friendly from greeting at the door through the meal.  You sense the hearts of everyone involved here, from cook to servers, are vested in making the guest experience a good one. Our expectations were exceeded.  We look forward to returning in spite of the awkward location with an awful parking lot.  

TIP:  If you read no further than this, here's a tip.  Flatware in the form of knife and fork are delivered to the table wrapped in a single, small paper napkin.   Ask for a spoon and extra napkins.  You'll thank me.  Reasons why follow.

VIBE:  The glass door of the strip mall store front opens into a modest sized interior with a handful of booths lining each side wall.  There are three additional four-top tables down the center of the room.  Bright colored sombreros and art with Mexican themes adorn the walls.  My husband commented on how much he enjoyed the fit of the decor.  

SERVICE:   Welcoming greeting at the door followed by smiles throughout the meal from the charming young women waiting the tables.  They knew the menu, could answer questions and conveyed genuine delight that we had decided to eat at Mi Casa.  The stellar service is a reason we will go back.

But a note to set expectations here regarding pace.  There seemed to be one or maybe two cooks in the little kitchen.  When tables are full and  roughly 40 diners arrive at roughly the same time, as at lunch hour, there can be delays in food arriving at the table.  You will be well cared for by the friendly staff as you wait, but if you're in a hurry this may not be the best fit. 

MENU & FOOD:  Chips with little bowls of salsa and refried beans for dipping are delivered to your table along with multi page, laminated menus.  I appreciate that each diner got their own little salsa bowl.  I love salsa and prefer not to share.

And here is the first reason you may use that spoon I recommended you ask for.  The salsa is yummy  with fresh minced onion, tomatoes and jalpaneo but it is thin in texture and I wanted a spoon to eat it.  No kidding.  That extra napkin will also come in handy to wipe up "oops" salsa spots on the table when using vehicle of the chips.

Dinner options are on the inside pages of the menu.  The lunch menu on the back offers smaller sized and lower priced versions of some dinner options.  You can also order from the dinner menu for lunch.  When my husband did that, for sopas, they provided him with a lunch sized portion at a lower price without him even asking if that was possible. 

The menu runs the gamut from standard fare on Mexican-American menus, like burritos, to specialties like mole and carnitas and tamales and sopas.  There were several seafood options and three or four soups.  Everything is made in house, including tamales and sopas.  And here I'd offer that the potato soup that has a vegetarian broth with roasted pasilla peppers and cojita cheese is delicious.

You'll find that  spoon handy again when you ask for a take away box in which to put your leftovers of any entree you order.  Portions are so generously sized, even at lunch, that neither my husband nor I could finish ours but the food was so good we wanted to take every morsel to eat as leftovers. 

If I could wave a magic wand, I might step down the salt in the dishes just a bit.  But that has more to do with my personal preference and no fault of the kitchen.

PRICES:  So reasonable that I wonder how their metrics work to be profitable.  Two people sharing a large bowl of soup plus two entrees, plus delicious chips and salsa was under $20.00 before tax and we had leftovers to boot. 

THIS N THAT:

1) LOCATION:  I am not a fan of strip malls in Meridian housing cheesey chain restaurants (as in the Buffalo Wild Wings which is Mi Casa's neighbor).  I conclude I am of minority opinion given the poorly designed parking lots at strip malls like this with too tightly spaced and small sized spaces to pack in as many cars as possible seldom seem to have an open space to park.  I avoid these lots as there is typically nothing to make me want to be there.  I will brave this location though, to visit Mi Casa.  But if I could wave a magic wand, I'll move the restaurant out of this strip mall.

2) ACCESSIBILITY:  Whomever built this strip mall, which is clearly less than ten years old, completely ignored ADA parking standards, which have been the law for twenty five years, given there are but two in a parking lot that has over two hundred spaces. Shameful.  And illegal.  The restaurant itself is level in and throughout, all standard height seating.  In spite of close quarters, it seemed as if wheelchair access could be possible.

Applause!  Owners have modified the service model in place at opening that didn't work well given the awkward interior layout.  Much improved for service now with order at counter followed by them delivering to table.  So - Hooray - "High Four" stars.  All the other high praise in previous review applies.  See below:

Botanically speaking, lemon trees have a tough time growing in Boise's climate.  Culinarily speaking, Lemon Tree eatery should thrive because sandwiches here are delicious.  Creatively "twistier" than most with options for omnivores, vegetarians and vegans alike and at good price points. Kudos to the owners and Chef Diane Dalton.

A tip if you read no further than this - if a sandwich has apple-lime-pecan slaw on it, order that thing!  You're welcome. 

VIBE:  Sleek and crisp with neutral walls, black ceilings and yellow accents (like the logo mural on wall and lemons on the counter).  Sparkling clean - pride of ownership shows in the best way.

Owners are husband and wife, transplants to Boise from Los Angeles (might that be the root of the Lemon Tree name?), he with restaurant management experience at chains like Meridian located Yardhouse, Freddy's Frozen Custard and local eateries like Owyhee Tavern.  The well thought out concept here reflects his retail food expertise.  

SEATING: Three or four tables seating about 12 people total on main floor, about half a dozen high stools at the open kitchen counter (also pre-ordered pick up location) and more high stools along front windows. More seating at tables up a flight of stairs in balcony.  Seating on sidewalk area too in good weather months. 

DRILL:  Chalkboards adjacent to order counter list many sandwich and side options.  Order taker was "all business", not unlike a fast-casual-chain interaction.  They may warm up with time but we missed friendly welcome of local-owned-style.  They opened with "call your name when ready' but recently upgraded service to deliver to your table.  And awkward warpy-wooden planks used for food when first open have been replaced with sturdy metal trays lined with parchment. 

EATS / VALUE: Sandwiches are the stars but there is one soup (tomato-basil and a good 'un) and a couple-three salads including one made of "savory oats".  Sandwiches run $8 - $10.50 and come with a side salad or chips or, for $1 upcharge, soup.  Sandwiches are on local baker Acme bread in focaccia or ciabatta and in sizes not too big to be eaten by one but big enough to share if a side is added.  The options for vegan and vegetarian sandwiches are arguably among the very best in the area.

Dee-luscious vegan Brussel Sprout sandwich on focaccia with roasted brussel sprouts, roasted red peppers, apple-lime-pecan slaw, caramelized onions and whole grain mustard was excellent.  Each element so well done, filled just enough and OH THAT SLAW!  ($8.50)

Examples of others include:
*Yam & Cheese - roasted beets, red onion confit, whipped goat cheese, greens, blood orange vinaigrette 
*Ham, Yam & Jam - Ham, roasted yams, cherry preserves, sharp cheddar, jalapeno-dijon aioli, apple-lime pecan slaw
*Salami & Artichoke -  Genoa salami, house-made artichoke spread, roasted red peppers, greens, fontina, Kalamata olivada

LIBATIONS:  Several kinds of house made lemonade.  Raspberry-Lime was tart-delicious perfect. ($2.75)  Served in "mason jars".

ACCESSIBILITY: Level in the door passage space to seats can be tight if all seats in use.  About half of seating is up flight of stairs.  Three of four tables down might work for wheelchair users for 30x48" ADA rule.  Didn't check loo.

PARKING:  On street. Good luck with that.

TIPS:  Lines can be long here for lunch time.  To avoid crowd, recommend be there at 'opening bell' or wait for early afternoon.  Or they take call in orders so call ahead to grab and take away.

Some Yelp reviews have expiration dates because restaurants are fluid - things change over years.   With that in mind, time to back up a bit for opinion about Andrade's.  Once our favorite Mexican food eatery in the Treasure Valley where we have enjoyed a dozen-ish meals over the past three years and recommended it to scores of other diners. this last time in it was such a poor experience for food that we left not only disappointed but embarrassed. Because along with us was a friend who was in for her first Andrade's visit based on our unwavering recommendation.

Alas, all three meals were so dry and lacking flavor that they were little edible.  So little so for my plate that our friendly server took half the cost of the dish off the bill.  Nice of her to do as none of us complained but we were honest when she asked, given none asked for take away box in spite of ample remainders on plates, "Didn't you like the food?" 

Every place can have a bad day.  This I know. And as update note 2/18/19, I share that I heard from the owner who was good to be concerned.  See my UPDATE comments embedded to try to fairly address his comments. 

But for three poor to nearly inedible dishes served at the shank-end of lunch hour (they make the turn from lunch to dinner menu at 3p, although dinner can be ordered during lunch hours too and dinner plates were ordered by two of us), was disquieting.

Also worth noting the salsa and bean dip that accompanies chips arrived in 'tasting sized' little cups nearly impossible to use.  Our friend asked if we could get larger serving vessels as are normally used here.  The friendly server subsequently obliged with apologies that the dishware was dirty when we arrived and she had some washed for us.  This at a time when I recall fewer than eight people in the eatery with the lunch crowd long gone.  A little thing but nonetheless another thing suggesting things are not as fine tuned as before.

The menu has much expanded in the last months.   Is that why the food was not now as good?  Could the kitchen be over stretched? I don't know.  But we all ordered standard offerings like enchiladas and tamales.  The dinner plate portions were huuuuge but less of better quality is more in my view. 

Also in the several months between our last visit and this one there has been a full bar added inside the main dining room.  Has the focus on food been lost in the transition?  I don't know.  But worth noting this addition for those interested.

All of this may not have been enough for me to give up on Andrade's without a follow up visit before deciding to take it off my 'favorites list' but for two other items in a perfect storm.

The first of these was, as we exited, raw big sink in the kitchen piled high with what looked to me like raw chicken.  It was an 'ugh' moment making me wonder if I wanted to eat here again.  (UPDATE:  The owner let me know this was a tray of thawed, raw breast meat which they use and on a tray over the sink getting ready for being washed / cleaned for safe use.)  Uncertainty reinforced the following week with the restaurant inspection news in the Boise paper (I read the report weekly) called out a handful of violations at Andrade's, a couple of which I considered significant on their own but in context of the several more disquieting still.  (UPDATE:  I assumed in my original comments that readers know how the process works.  For those who may not know here goes;  periodic health code inspections are unannounced and eateries are given X days - typically 10 days -  to correct the violations itemized by inspector and then there is reinspection.  So these were corrected.)

On the plus side, the people who work at Andrade's are have always been, most friendly and it remains a welcoming interior.  And more plus, although I didn't check it out, there is now a sign up at the entry with "Family Bathroom" which has unisex symbols and also a wheelchair icon and arrow pointing direction through an adjacent space. 

But 'thinkin' bout my Yelputation' - to borrow and butcher the lyric from The Who's tune - I have to say I'm lukewarm about returning to Andrade's after this visit.  

What to you mean you don't know the tune?  Sure you do.  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qN5zw04WxCc

Good news and bad news.  Good news first: owners of Bleubird are opening a new place, on the Bench, to be called Petite 4.  Now the bad news: Bleubird is closing as of the end of January.  So you have until then to enjoy the splendid sandwiches and friendly people at Bleubird before they fly off to create a new place for their customers to enjoy.  Change is bittersweet.  As we say farewell to Bluebird downtown we can look forward to Petite 4 in the Bench neighborhood.  The greater Boise area can sure use some honest to goodness neighborhood restaurants.  I'm hoping they do something other than stand in line at the counter to order at the new place and improve the space planning layout for accessibility and tables.  But I'm sure they'll create wonderful food and maintain their friendly service!

The hospitality here is as welcoming and the ambiance as warm as the food is delicious.  Lovely all around.  We leave after a meal, a feast really, feeling nourished in body and lighter in spirit.  Open for lunch and dinner, we recommend this owner operated Iraqi food eatery where pride of ownership shines.  

DELICIOUS FOOD / TRADITIONAL MENU / SOMETHING FOR EVERYONE:  My husband and I are longtime fans of Middle Eastern food and appreciate there are many regional variations.  We are most familiar with Israeli, Lebanese and Iranian food so we have had fun learning about the differences in Iraqi cooking by enjoying dishes at The Goodness Land.  The gracious and friendly owner, Salam Bunyan, is also the excellent cook and every dish we've ordered has been delicious. 

The menu appears above the order counter with numbered, color photos and English and Arabic subtitles.  It is divided between appetizers (#1-12) and entrees (#13-32).  (Fold up paper menus are also at the counter and on tables.)

This is for us unarguably the best hummus (#2) in all of Boise and the flatbread that comes with it is excellent.

If you're a lamb fan, try the traditional entrees of lamb and rice of both Bryani Lamb (#19) or Lamb Qwzi (#21), each unique from the other for seasonings and presentation and both delicious.  (Rice here is as excellent as the proteins.) 
 
The eggplant salad (#3) is one of our favorites and so is the fatosh salad (#6).
  
We also enjoyed being introduced to Iraqi Felafel (#28) which is different from the Israeli version most of us have probably have as Felafel in most dining spots that serve it in the US.  Iraqi Pickles (#11) are a great option to enjoy with the Felafel.

There are lots of options for both vegetarians and omnivores and you can have a feast to enjoy no matter what you choose.  But this is a Halal kitchen and you will not find pork or alcohol on the menu. Our plan is to eat our way through the menu here on the advice of people we met today who have done nearly that in the course of their regular visits to Goodness Land in a year!   

One note to offer, although not listed on the menu in all cases, fries are added to some dishes.  I suppose this is a nod to American dining habits but so you know if you prefer not to eat fries (we don't as example when we have other food this delicious) you will know to ask to have them left off. 

Try the Arabic coffee which is cardamom infused and simply delicious in beautiful presentation and also the Iraqi tea which is lightly spiced and also beautifully presented.  They are wonderful ends to the meal.  

WELCOMING HOSPITALITY /  WARM VIBE:  Salam seems to great everyone warmly when they enter and he remembers folks who have been in before.  He is delighted to answer questions for people unfamiliar with Iraqi food.  And this is the kind of place where as a diner you want to share with people too.  As today when a young woman, a newbie, was waiting on her to go order we invited her to get a plate and come join us to taste some of the things we had on our table about which she had asked questions.  She came to talk to us, and said "a feast" when she saw he beautiful dishes.  (Exactly right, it always seems so.)  And there was Salam right behind her to offer her a plate of samples to try.  He is that kind of gracious host.  

The vibe is warm and welcoming too.  The sparkling clean space has tables and chairs as well as lovely fabric traditional, deep banquette seating and also a few booths along walls. Table coverings are red and green fabric with plastic on top.  Traditional music plays and adds to the ambiance.  A couple of TVs with sound off are on one wall.

THE DRILL:  Order at the counter and Salam or folks that help him will deliver it to your table.   When you're finished, return to the counter to pay your bill.

GREAT VALUE:  Price points are very reasonable for such high quality, delicious food and range from $3.99 (for some of the appetizers) to $16.99 (for the Lamb Qwzi entree).  The servings are so generous in size that we have leftovers for take away meal.  

THIS N THAT:

1) PARKING:  Private lot shared by other businesses like a Euro deli, a vape shop and a sports bar mean there are times when parking is tight.

2) ACCESSIBILITY:  Level in the door, all on one floor, standard height seating, ample space in aisles, accessible bathroom.
PERMANENTLY CLOSED per sign on door 8/6/21.  Greek restaurant said to be gearing up to be next up at this location at some date TBD.

Today is Thursday May 14 and Yelp HQ is encouraging Yelp Elites to write Thankful Thursday notes for businesses about which we have been thankful during this covid19 period. My first thought of a business that deserves praise is Bacquet's.  Although my 5-Star worthy applause here is redundant given the multiple reviews I've written since my hubby and I first discovered Bacquet's to share about their ongoing excellence so more and more people might have the chance to experience it for themselves.

But in particular during this challenging time for all of us during the roughly 8 weeks of Idaho "stay home" orders that also shut restaurants for in-house dining, we so appreciate how Chef Franck Bacquet and his wife and partner Michele, have kept offering excellent to go fare, introduced a daily "family meal" (Tues - Sat), have offered easy no contact pick up in the parking lot and even home delivery to a limited area by their delightful staff...and one night when we needed it we were grateful they provided delivery...and taken care of their staff to keep them safely employed.  

Ironically, although we didn't know at the time that our dining-in meal at Bacquet's on Sunday March 15 would be our "last supper" out, turns out it was because the next day relying on data and CDC advisory, we stopped eating out as personal choice while we watched things unfold (we follow science data) and then on March 25 the Governor's orders made that impossible to do.  I can't think of a better place for us to have had our "last supper" than Bacquet's.  It has been our 'go to' of choice for about 85% of our take-away meals during this pandemic period and it has nourished body and spirit to have the excellent meals and warm hospitality - even when order by phone and deliver to car is the modality.  

We also admire that they are following the Governor's directives and are not jumping the gun on re-opening as some in their industry are so they are showing respect both for governance and for their colleagues in this business.  

We also admire them for helping people in the community.  As example, during this shut down period they started offering for sale at the restaurant things that folks in the community may have had trouble finding in stores, especially early on, like flour, yeast, eggs, chicken and other things becoming a sort of "corner store" for local folks who needed a resource.

Since my husband and I follow the science data closely we know we are in a demographic that has been urged by scientists to continue to be cautious in making our choices of where we go as things re-open.  And as things reopen, Bacquet's will be one of those places we trust to do the right things for all their customers who dine there in the "new normal" just as they always have in all times.

One man. One wok. One dish at a time. That's what the server told us.  It is true. The seventy-six year old owner / cook is the one man. When he retires, so will the restaurant I assume. If you haven't  been in yet, what are you waiting for? 

We peeked in to the kitchen.  But for one young woman assisting to put food into containers for to go orders and moving the plates for dine in customers from kitchen to server, it was a one man show. Sometimes in evenings or at busy lunch hours there is a line of customers or longer waits for food.  Knowing how hard this cook / owner works to produce the dishes all week long should help make one patient and then some.

FOOD & MENU
Not all execution is 'chef perfect'. For example, the shrimp in the shrimp and veggie noodles were served with veins still in. 

My husband and I seldom eat poultry, in particular at a restaurant, but the House Special chicken and noodles with ginger sauce sounded delicious. The sauce was addictively good but we might have appreciated the dish more had the chicken pieces been skinned before the cooking since for us they had an odd texture. 

But the house made noodles are wonderful, the vegetables are wok cooked perfection, and the sauces on our dishes were not only delicious with distinctive flavors but not over applied.  In many American focused Chinese restaurants it seems the trend is to drown food in sauce when it should really be only smooched by it. Like this.

The noodles are fresh made every day. The cook makes the dough, it gets run through an ancient looking noodle machine six times to stretch it out (our server's daughter runs that machine and it looks pretty labor intensive) and then noodles are cut to use. 

Order any Chinese noodle dish and you'll be happy. Order noodles with vegetables included and you'll be even happier. This food is clearly cooked in a hot wok by a person with the experience to get that very difficult to achieve skill right!

A note worth sharing is this:  you'll have a choice of heat levels.  Medium was just right from two hot dried chilis being part of the cooking.

Also note:  Pad Thai is on menu That is a Thai dish using rice noodles.  It may be good.  But the house made Chinese style noodles are "it".

THE DRILL
Take a seat at a table and order from the laminated menu. A pot of tea and a cup of soup is offered with your meals. The soup was a delicious one of vegetables cooked only in the broth created by their cooking. That is the Tuesday / Thursday soup.  On Monday / Wednesday / Friday Hot and Sour soup is served with "cook's choice" on weekends. 

Forks are on table and diners are offered chopsticks. These are noodles perfect for eating with chopsticks. Even my hubby, chopsticks skill challenged as he is, had fun with it.

VALUE
Portion sizes are ample, we had leftovers to take with us, and the price is a bargain. I think our lunches clocked in at under $9 / each.

THE VIBE
The window in front looks into a hodepodge area of chair and table stacked high with food magazines and dusty cookbooks and plants. I'm thinking this might be the cook's retreat as it didn't seem to be seating. 

The dining space itself has black and white lino floors and red topped tables with paper parasols hanging on the ceiling. The space is an old one but clean and inviting.  But expectations in synch for what this is, it is bare bones. 

As you walk in you are greeted by the aroma of a hot wok and fresh food. Further sensory delight was provided on our visit by ability to hear the "chop, chop, chop..." rapid fire of knife on block and the sizzle of food hitting the wok.  We could hear all that thanks to no music in the dining room. Hooray! There were strains of classical music (like Scheherazade) wafting from the kitchen. The nuances of sound made this even better. 

SERVICE
Our server, although clearly over busy as the dining room started to fill up, was very friendly and refilled the tea pot for us too without us needing to ask. She checked in with us during the meal and thanked us for coming in.

She also paid attention when one of the two women at the table next to us didn't finish her noodles. She asked if something was wrong. No, said the diner, it was a large serving and she couldn't eat that much at one time. Good to know, said the server, because the cook does not like plates with uneaten food coming back to the kitchen.  If that happens, he expects her to know if there was a problem and what can be done to make the guest happy. 

Delightful.

THIS N THAT:

1) PARKING: In private, aging, poorly maintained strip mall lot.

2) ACCESSIBILITY: Level in door and throughout. All seating is standard height. Enough clear floor space to get to most tables. Accessible parking in the lot does not meet Federal Law and State Codes. 

3) NEIGHBORS: Chiang Mai is next door.  Outpost of Asia Market at far end of lot.

Soup Kettle Grille delivers tasty food and "soup-erior" service in a fast-casual-order-at-the counter format.  The restaurant is not a franchise or chain, as the name might suggest, but a locally owned 'mom and pop shop' where you feel warm welcome the minute you walk in the door.  Serving scratch-made soup and grilled sandwiches (which may be the star here) for eating in or taking out along with frozen soup by the quart, this has potential to be a gem but for woefully uncomfortable "sardine can" table set up. 

THE DRILL:  Walk in and straight ahead to the counter where the friendliest person will answer your questions, take your order and offer you a sample of soup(s) of your choice if you're undecided on which o choose from the roughly half a dozen they have listed on their menu board.  (Note:  Buffalo Chicken is their best seller.)

They make more than 30 kinds of soup, half a dozen or so available hot for in-house or take-out in options that change weekly with many other varieties frozen by the quart in a case near the counter.

Place your order for eat in, take a seat, if you can get to it at the tables in the sparkling clean but sardine-can-tight dining area and they will deliver to your table.  Soup is served in heavy duty plastic cups or bowls with plastic spoons and a slice of bread in a paper sleeve. They'll clear the table for you when time permits, or you can easily bus your own to a 'service counter' at the window wall near the front of the eating area.   If your order is to go, they'll call your name when ready.  

THE EATS:  The grilled sandwiches smelled great and looked really tasty as we saw other people enjoying them, but 2/3 way through a two week diet, we opted for 3 cups of soup to share 2 ways.  For the record they were Roasted Tomato, Potato Leek and Buffalo Chicken and we would order them again although I did wish there was sea salt on the table to add to the former.  Cost: $4ish each ordered like this, about $3ish if you add a cup with a sandwich.  Soups that are Vegetarian or Gluten Free are marked, soups with dairy are marked, and there are also options that are noted as Vegan.  This is easy dining for Ominvores to Vegans and people with food allergies too. 

We picked up a couple of quarts of frozen soup in other flavors on the way out. Caribbean Black Bean (vegan) was surprisingly bland when we had it at home.  Spicy Sweet Potato Chipotle (vegetarian) had a hefty smokey chili kick. 

LIBATIONS:  Do not miss the Carrot Lemonade (@$2.80 for @16 oz)!  It is just barely sweet and uses fresh squeezed lemon juice with carrot juice.  A treat.

THE VIBE:  Ahhh...roma as you enter from cheese grilling in sandwiches almost seems to tug and hug you through the door.  Warm greeting from the people at the counter add to the sense of welcome.  As downside, I realize they need tables with chairs to put diners' fannies in, but the sardine-can sense of so many in a small space is the thing I'd wave my scepter to change were I 'The Queen' and have them remove a four top and rearrange for more "breathin' room".  It is the way too tight seats that will keep me from going back to eat in.  They've jammed seats for about 42 inside what would better hold 36 and be tight at that.  

THIS N THAT:

1) PARKING:  Private lot for the little strip mall has a good amount.

2) ACCESSIBILITY:  ADA compliant parking in the lot.  Level in the door. All on one floor.  Accessible loo (says my spouse, I didn't check.)  Tight table seating and aisles would make wheelchair access impossible.  I talked to the owner.  She realizes this is a problem and says staff would move furniture as necessary for a disabled customer to get to a table.  But the 28 year old civil rights law that is ADA says equal access to tables for disabled diners must exist as standard, not as workaround moving of furniture.  If US Rep Tammy Duckworth, who uses a wheelchair after losing her legs in wartime service as a Blackhawk pilot, were to come in here, she shouldn't have to be embarrassed and need to wait for 'musical tables'.  She should be able to take a seat like everyone else.

3) GOOD NEIGHBOR:  Sofra Bosnian is right next door.  It was empty as we walked by both to and from Soup Kettle Grille, which was doing a brisk business including folks waiting in line.

With apologies to Rodgers and Hart.  

"We'll take Manhattans, 
New twist Old Fashioneds,
Housemade Eggnog too,
It's lovely sipping through
Red Feather's menu."

OK.  I'll stop.

But a timely tip to say the Eggnog with Buffalo Trace bourbon and a kiss of fresh grated nutmeg is a treat with a true limited time offer as it is likely to come off the menu after New Year.  It was worth every calorie of indulgence and may be the best eggnog I have ever enjoyed.

All cocktails here are luscious.  These are skilled mixologists at work.  The drinks menu has both new twists on old favorites as well as completely new combinations and drinks are listed on the extensive menu in order of light to dark. 

There is a lot to like here outside of the beverages.  This is not just a bar with food.  This is a restaurant with delicious food that also serves cocktails and wine.  It has advantages that its' sister enterprise of Bittercreek, right next door, does not.  The Achilles here may be service.

VIBE
The space is small and tight but somehow they have avoided the gawdawful noise levels and cheek to cheek (as in south cheeks) crowding of Bittecreek.  The music is a good, unusual mix that fits the space and while it is at an assertive level is not the overwhelming level of Bittercreek. 

There is a two story lighted wine cellar display offset by wood tables and a casual feel that is just a little sophisticated too.  One is at home here in jeans but one could also feel this is date night setting.  There are low tables and high stool seating both on the first floor and more tables and chairs up a steep flight of stairs.

SERVICE
I wouldn't say this is "all people are welcome" vibe as our host and servers while cordial did seem a bit unsure of us given we are likely outside the usual demographic.  Follow up was minimal.   But "nolo timere Boomers" is my motto.  We old people who remember exactly where we were on November 22, 1963 eat and drink too!

EATS 
Red Feather shares a kitchen and menu with Bittercreek Alehouse until 5:00 so you'll find delicious food using locally sourced ingredients.  Happy hour from 4:00 to 6:00 is as Bittercreek's menu.  After 5:00 p.m. Red Feather has their own dinner menu. 

This is easily some of the best food we've had in all of Boise and while some may do as good a job for Farm to Fork sourcing, none do it better than Bittercreek and Red Feather.  They even list all of their local suppliers on the back of the menu; something I very much appreciate.

Prices range from as little as $2 for happy hour tacos (these both my husband and I highly recommend) through entrees priced at around $20 minus.  These are really fair prices for the quality and portions.  Tis a mystery how they do it.  

My Brooklyn native husband called the Manhattan Clam Chowder among the best he's ever had.  Leaning vegetarian in most things, we note the menus (lunch and dinner) are great ones for those who like to graze through a menu as omniovores, but in particular a good set of options for vegetarians.  I'd say order anything with chimichurri sauce. And if you think a wedge salad is a ho-hum thing, try it here as transformed with butter lettuce heart, gorgonzola, candied bacon, oven roasted tomatoes and crispy fried onions.  Just over five bucks on the dinner menu and it is a meal in itself.  

HAPPY HOUR
OK.  I'm going to be a crumudgeon about their Happy Hour drinks special. (HH is 4 - 6 / M-F).  This is a policy used by several Boise establishments.  A "two for the price of one" on certain drinks.  That does not mean you can order two drinks for two people to have one each and pay for one.  It means the same person has to order both drinks for themselves.  Drink one, your second one is free.  For some people two cocktails and a drive home is not a good thing.  I think this policy encourages over consumption.  I'm much more a fan of HH policies that offer a discount on one beverage. 

VINO
We have yet to order wine here and we need to fix that shortcoming on our part because they have a great list of fairly priced wines by the glass and by the bottle with Idaho and Northwest options well represented.  Salute!

THIS N THAT:

1) BREAKFAST & OTHER SPECIAL FEATURES:  I hear they serve breakfast, although have not been in for that meal.  They also have a wine cellar that is available for special events I hear.  Also a cocktail club in which one can enroll, so if you're a frequent imbiber here that could be fun to know more about.

2) ACCESSIBILITY:  Level in but path of travel spaces are tight.  Some seating at standard table height if you can get to it.  Upper level seating is by stairs only.  No accessible loo.  There is no accessible parking on this street.  

3) GOOD NEIGHBOR:  Bittercreek next door. 

4) WHATTYAMEAN...who is Rodgers and Hart?  ;-)   https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_jHwgfRGTq0

"Big enough to meet your needs.  Small enough to meet your neighbors."  That sign was painted on the Co Op window when I started shopping there six months ago.  Recently removed as part of a front spruce up, it is worth memorializing the phrasing here since since it seemed just right..

While we're on phrasing, to riff on the old Amex slogan...

...MEMBERSHIP HAS ITS' BENEFITS:

You don't need to be a Co Op member to shop here but, really, if you Co Op shop just once a month why wouldn't you?  It costs only $65 to join, a one time fee with no annual dues.  But if you join on the first Friday of any month you get a $15 discount and membership is only $50.  Why one would join other than a first Friday, I know not.

Members are entitled to periodic specials.  Better yet, once a month on any day of your choice you can receive a 10% discount on your entire order.  You will very quickly recover that $50 membership fee!

On that same day of the month you also will receive a 10% discount from any purchases at the Co Op Wine Shop or the Co Op Pet Shop just  across the parking lot.  The 10% off the Wine Shop discount one day a month sure comes in handy for my hubby and me.

Even if those other two shops don't beckon to you, there are...

...SO MANY THINGS TO LIKE HERE:

PEOPLE:  Friendly staff, including the young woman checker who went out of her way when it was evident I was a stranger in a new land on my first few visits to talk to me each time, make you feel welcome.

PREPARED FOODS & DELI:  They list local purveyors used in their dishes, all of which are made in house.  (Try that at Whole Foods...you won't find it.)
