Gin is still on trend so I have been trying to introduce more of it to my palate as I am not a natural gin fan. This boozy cocktail could convert me, though. A generous pour of the herby booze (served in a Collins/Highball glass) was deftly mixed with lemon, simple syrup, lime, and cherries. Lime & cherry go well. Lemon and gin go well. The simple syrup brought out the citrus notes and dulled the sharp juniper qualities of the gin. I was a fan. It was a very nice way to start the meal. With my entree, I kept it simple and seasonal with a vinho verde.

The menu is seafood (duh) with a French twist. So, expect bouillabaisse, mussels and frites, rillettes, beurre blanc, and the like. Since the mussels were steamed in beer, they were off limits to me. That didn't stop me, though, from going all in on the frites. The very generous portion came with three aiolis: olive, garlic and... I'm blanking. I'm blanking because I don't do mayo, aioli or any other of the devil's condiments. The frites were perfect on their own: thin, addicting texture, well seasoned... You'll need to share (due to the size) but you won't want to share. Being in the mood to eat a substantial meal, I opted for the fish of the day. It was a monkfish. I know. Bottom feeder. Poor man's lobster. Potentially troubling fishing methods. All of these thoughts raced through my head... But it's very French and when in Rome...* This preparation came with risotto, crawfish, kale, and a balsamic (?) reduction. It was absolutely incredible. Savory but slightly sweet, the creamy risotto paired nicely with the buttery (slightly oily) fish. The crawfish added to the sweet flavor but the firm texture complimented every bite. The kale wasn't an afterthought but a necessary component of the dish. What looked like an easy plate to get through had me struggling by the last bites. That said, I couldn't leave without dessert. The flourless chocolate cake, adorned with strawberries, blackberries and whipped cream was a huge hit. Had the sundae not come with a brownie (ohh, I miss you gluten), I would have ordered that. It sounds like a decadent delight.

For all this food (plus my dinner companions), I paid a lot less than I was expecting. The price point + quantity = wonderful value. You won't leave here hungry. You will leave satisfied. It's worth noting, too, the staff was fantastic. Remember, this is a brand spanking new restaurant. My server was very affable, the manager was a delight and the owner was incredibly gracious. My only nit would be to address the music. While Sea Salt isn't a stuffy eatery, the background pop music doesn't quite fit what you're going for.** Maybe some Edith Piaf instead? Also, ladies: check out the bathroom. My dinner companion raved about it.

*I did feel slight guilt pangs, however.
**Even though I was dancing in my seat to 'Bang Bang.'

I've just been informed this area/neighborhood of town is called 'TMAG' and it might have ruined my whole day. Nashville, stahp it. TMAG? Has this always been a thing? I knew that once you crossed 24 on Murfreesboro, things got a little wild west-ish but I can't with this tomfoolery. TMAG.

I say all this because when I found myself in this part of town, I was really surprised/impressed with the growth. With new shops adorning both sides of Murfreesboro, I imagine that new people/opportunities have moved in as well. It's good to see Nashville growth that has nothing to do with Downtown or places out east. Although, is this still Nashville or have we crossed into Davidson County? I though 'Nashville' ended once you crossed 24 but maybe that is an old rule. I don't know. I can't keep up. OMG. Focus. Pizza.

Pizza. I wanted pizza and when you eat gluten-free, that can be a challenge. A quick search of the Jelps led me to this new-ish eatery. The see-saw reviews made me a little nervous but I decided to go for it. I'm pleased to report that the venture was a good one. This is a family business (high school kids were working phones and expediting orders; I love seeing stuff like that) and the operation looked legit. The build out is comfortable so feel free to eat-in or carry-out. My large veggie lovers on GF crust was ready exactly at the time it was promised and rather than the square slices I anticipated, the pizza was served in a traditional circle. All good. The GF crust was the thin/cracker crust, not the harder/denser one. If texture matters, I want to give you a heads up. I like both. To my pleasure, the pizza was packed with ingredients, not too much cheese and had a 50/50 savory/sweet sauce that should please most everyone. The only caveat I have is that while the crust is GF, I don't know that the oven is. If you're celiac, inquire before buying. Otherwise, Nashville metro, you have a new pizza place. For the night birds, this one is open 'till five' so have at it. It's not artisanal fare but it's not Godfather's either. Try it. I think you'll like it.

Baja Burrito is an institution -- and I am just now checking it out. There are reasons. 1. ) I am not in Berry Hill that often. 2.) Because of the flour tortillas, I don't eat burritos anymore (and I miss them a lot). 3.) It's always crowded and I don't like to head face first into crowds these days.

But, it came to pass that I was finally going to get some Baja Burrito goodness in my life. I just leaned in. I knew that I was going to have a good experience when I found parking in the lot. There's a reason why people complain/write about the parking situation over and over again. It's horrible. It's a small lot and there's a small city's worth of people trying to come here at all hours AND Nashville is a driving (not public transit) city. All of this combines for a frustration parking experience. Unless you're me. On a Friday. At lunch time. I should have bought a lottery ticket. As easy as parking was, though, that line was every bit the monster I'd heard of. The good thing is that the folks behind the counter are pros. No matter how intimidating the line looks, it moves quickly. This means you should be ready with your order when you make it to the front. Don't gum up the line.

Since flour tortillas have made burritos a thing of the past for me, I ordered a chicken burrito 'in the buff.' This is just a burrito without the tortilla. I enjoy that Baja Burrito offers so many topping gratis. So, along with my chicken, I got Mexican rice, black beans, olives, lettuce, tomato, onions, cilantro, pico de gallo, and cheese. I also got a dollop of mild sauce but there are plenty of off-line salsa bowls to get your fill of mild, hot, green, and/or pineapple salsa. No, this isn't a street fare taqueria. Think of this as a SoCal burrito joint (complete with fish taco expertise) and you're on the right track. To complete my order, a carton of chips and a grapefruit Jarritos. Done.

Scanning the dining room, I spied an empty four top for my party of three. I asked my friend to nab the table while I took care of utensils, napkins and salsa. In a place this crowded, you have to think strategically. We snagged the table and scooted in to the tight environs. This is not a place for the girthy. Be warned. Finally ready to eat, I understood why BB has so many fans and why it's a Thunderdome-esque experience to have lunch here. Fresh. Delicious. Filling. I greatly enjoyed my plate and -- between it and my chips -- I had the perfect amount of food. Given its reputation and product, I don't know that there's ever an off time to come here but I think I am willing to find out.

4.5

Looks are deceiving, people. What appears (on first glance) to be a sports bar is the deft home of some of the Crescent City's most delicious (and affordable) fare. It's a fantastic reminder that New Orleans is a global culinary capital and there's phenomenal food to be found in every neighborhood. You might not find yourself on Carollton but you should.

My unruly group arrived on a damp Valentine's Day and I can just imagine the reaction the kitchen and wait staff must have had. I would have had it. On Couples Day, I would not have been in the mood for a big group. But there was no attitude from the one server who was tasked with taking care of us. Nor were there any delays and backups from the kitchen. This is a machine, people. This is a machine that creates delicious food that you might not expect to come from the kitchen. Really? How so? Vietnamese Shrimp Bisque. Were you expecting that out of a Southern kitchen? I wasn't but it was on special and I tend to gravitate towards specials ('get it while you can'). I was very pleased with my choice. Packed with just enough heat to tickle the back of my throat, the bisque was a layered presentation of slightly sweet, lots of savory and round comfort. It was perfectly beautiful on a damp, misty night. How would I follow such a show starter? Why, with another special, of course. This time, I chose the roasted herb chicken. Chicken? Really? Really. This giant meaty bird was succulent, juicy and seasoned so well my eyes and nose benefited almost as much as my mouth did. Paired with the protein, healthy portions of onions, mushroom and truffle spoon bread... wow. Just wow. While you may expect something like this to come from a Southern kitchen, the execution could have been messed up seven ways to Sunday. It wasn't. For the entirety of the savory portion of my meal, I nursed a single glass of pinot grigio. 1.) I was still slightly hurting from the night before. 2.) The pour was very generous.

Needing to see if the meal could bring it home, I ordered the flourless chocolate cake. Yes. This wonderfully black and perfectly decadent slice came on a chilled plate and offered all sorts of chocolate therapy. If you have a sweet tooth and need to avoid gluten, make sure you spend some time with this bad boy. New Orleans is a food city. There are chefs throughout the metro who are doing serious things in the kitchen. For as much as I enjoy the white tablecloths and coordinated service of the Quarter and LGD, make sure you take the time to seek out and experience all the thrills NOLA has for your tastebuds. You mouth won't regret it -- even if your waistline might.

2.5

I find it interesting: 417 Union is one of the most reviewed restaurants on Yelp Nashville but I didn't know much about it until recently. The folks I know who have dined there did so years ago. AND it's not hurting for business. Interesting. Undoubtedly, the location plays a big part of the last interesting tidbit. Closer to the government buildings than the honky tonks, it makes sense that all sorts of gov't workers make their way for a nice sit down at 417 rather than a grab & go in the Arcade. It also makes sense of the hours. 417 Union knows what works for it. It has a distinct point of view. I can respect that. 

My experience, however, ranged from odd to okay. Some of that is my fault: I ordered a Southwestern Chicken Salad rather than something Southern. I was planning on ordering something 'meat and three-y' or breakfast-y but my server made the ordering process a bit strange. I arrived earlier than my dining companion and just wanted to peruse the menu and wait. I was forced into ordering something. It was... odd. We were in before the lunch rush so there were plenty of available tables.* But, my server was insistent on me ordering immediately. Flustered, I went for the salad. Being a salad, it was served to me before my dining partner made it to the table. Not to leave her out, though, she was rushed and cajoled into an order. But, at least she was given the specials of the day to choose from. I was not so fortunate. My salad was okay, if not a bit bland. My 'grilled' chicken had no grill marks or taste of smoke. It looked and tasted baked... which is fine... but it's not grilled... which I ordered. The salad is served in a giant tortilla shell... which is a fine idea... but said shell is too big for the plate on which it's served... which makes eating the salad difficult at best and tiresome at worst. The ingredients were on the chilled/cold band side: my mixed greens were umixed (just green), my corn & black bean salsa was just black beans, the cheese was hard to find, and the tomato was fine. The chipotle ranch dressing was fine. Served on the side, there was just enough for the salad. I declined getting extra. Looking at my friend's fried green tomato sandwich, though, I didn't have much fomo.

Throughout the meal, my dining companion and I were routinely interrupted by our server, given the wrong drinks, given our checks early, and asked why we had yet to pay when he came by (minutes later) to collect our bills. I think had it not been for the off service, I would round up on the 2.5 rating rather than round down. But the experience was so off-putting, rather than enjoying lunch with a friend, my table felt rushed, uneasy and out of sorts. It wasn't an enjoyable dining experience. Perhaps if I worked in the area it would be on my routine but as it stands I can't imagine returning. But it *is* one of Nashville's most reviewed restaurants so there's gotta be something there... right? I think I missed it.

*By the time we left, it was pretty much packed to capacity.

I avoided coming here for quite some time because all I could recall was review after review, complaining about this, that and the other. Either those reviews were off base or Tower has really gotten its act together. Based on my experience, I have a new entrant in my sandwich rotation.

Tower (as it says in its name) is both a market and deli so you can come here for a couple of different reasons and have a good experience. If you come here to shop, be forewarned that the market is more bodega than grocery store. Have your expectations set in reality and all will be well. Or, they can be *really* well and you can come here for a sandwich. I popped in on a muggy Thursday night thinking I was going to grab a burger. I'd gone elsewhere but that proved to be way too much trouble for such a simple request. Wandering, I found myself at Tower and I just decided to go for it. Since I had already committed to breaking up my routine, I decided to go rogue on my sandwich order. Taking the time to full peruse the menu, I found what I wanted: the lamp philly. Yes, that would do quite nicely.

I paid and browsed the market as I waited. I am quite alright to wait for freshly-prepared food. Before too long, my sandwich was snatched off the grill and wrapped in paper, ready for me to eat. 

Oh. Wow. This was good. Philly cheesteaks are a weakness (college years spent in the Philly metro will do that to you) but *lamb* Phillies... wow. Next level. This philly came with the trappings you'd assume: provolone, onions, peppers, fresh, chewy, bread but, in addition to the tender and well-seasoned (and, generously portioned) meat, the star of this bad boy was the harissa that lined the bread and kissed the lamb. Outstanding. Truly, this was a sandwich to remember. I look forward to returning to see what other sandwich inventions await me. If you were holding off on Tower because of previous reviews, forget that. The shop is firing on all cylinders and putting out an impressive product. I love seeing more winners dot this stretch of Gallatin. Keep it up!

3.5

Despite living in Chicago for many many years, I never had a kolache. I know, right? It had been on my agenda to stop by Yeast and remedy this situation. One mid-fall Saturday morning, the stars aligned and I was set to try the treat. 

Actually, I was set to try all of the food. The menu at Yeast is outstanding. If you have a weakness for baked goods and breakfast food, this might be one of the most dangerous places in the city. I gladly spent $20 on my specialty/seasonal biscuit, chai tea, black & white cinnamon roll, and blackberry kolache. The specialty biscuit was a fresh-made, over-sized biscuit filled with egg, bacon and pimento cheese. I could have stopped there. Not only was it delicious, but it was substantial in size and I, happily, ate until it disappeared in seconds. My chai tea was prepared on site with tea bag and milk. It was appropriately spicy and smooth. I asked for my black & white cinnamon roll to be warmed up and that was, absolutely, the right call. Again, the good was extremely generous in size and the warm dough topped with the sugary sweet white and deliciously chocolatey black was almost too much. I shouldn't have eaten it. I should have saved it. But, I have no will power so it, too, was devoured on site. I didn't have the stomach real estate or pride to go for the kolache but it was a Sunday morning delight, paired with herbal tea. The years-long wait for the kolache was worth it. I won't call it a danish and it didn't change my life but it definitely satisfied my belly. I'd like to try all the fruit-filled varieties.

Sounds like an awesome experience. Why the 3.5/3? The service I received was dismissive at best and rude at worst. It was my first time to darken the door at Yeast and I took some time to get the lay of the land. I didn't get in line until I knew what I wanted and had observed others order so that I knew the flow and wouldn't gum up the works. When I asked questions and made conversation (about the product and neighborhood, respectively), I received averted glances, blank stares and a plate snatched out of my hand (the aforementioned heated black & white cinnamon roll). Keep in mind that I'd watched others receive conversations, smiles and the normal pleasantries. I don't know what it was about me that made me receive such a 'winning' reception but it was alarming. As good as the product is (and it is, I can't deny that and will star accordingly), I can't say that I'm in a rush to ever come back. That's a shame.

4.5

Come here ready to eat and come prepared to come alone. While Las Americas may not have a ton of reviews on Yelp, the local community is very aware of how fantastic the food here is... and that means crowds. The parking lot is a bit harrowing (steep, backs up on to Nolensville, tight spots), but once you successfully navigate it, the hardest part of your visit is out of the way. Don't make the mistake many first-timers make and walk into the store. Look for the tables and walk in to the restaurant. 

I came on a Sunday afternoon and it was standing room only. After a few minutes of looking at semi-full tables of families, friends and singles, I eventually relented to sit at the bar. I'm glad I did. Ten minutes later, there was a line of hungry folks at the door, glowering at people who weren't sitting at tables packed to capacity. I was happy to not be taking up more space than needed. I walked in not feeling 100% (had a ROUGH night downtown the night before), so I thought I was going to go for a bowl of pozole and keep it moving. After all, it's a tried & true hangover cure. But once I caught a whiff of a papusa, I knew what I must do... and hope that solid food had the same curative properties of soup.

In my semi-decent Spanish (the waitresses are bilingual but you get your order across quicker and more succinctly in Spanish), I ordered a bean & cheese papusa, tamarind agua fresca and a combo burrito with chicken. The papusa was as good as I smelled and read about. It was thick, substantial, tasted great on its own, filled with delicious cheese & beans, topped with fresh, crunchy cabbage, and came adorned with wonderfully spicy sauce. I almost never turn down an agua fresca and this tamarindo was no exception. The glass must have been 32 oz. It was one of those huge red Pizza Hut cups you might remember from your youth. By the time my gigantic (seriously, very very large) burrito came out, screaming hot and sizzling with cheese (almost like a chimichanga), I knew that I had chosen wisely. The kicker (in addition to fresh chicken, hand-made tortilla (I could watch the kitchen making everything to order) and cool veggies, was the bowl of fresh-sliced avocado that came with the burrito. In moving to Nashville from Miami, I knew I was trading in Caribbean/South American fare for Central & North American cuisine but this was the first time since moving, I really grasped what this meant. This is authentic, real-deal, incredibly delicious, and affordable food. If you eve *think* you like food from this region, make a bee-line and gets ta eatin'.

Red Pony is indicative of why - when the wife and kids part of my life starts - I'll move to Franklin. It has enough small town charm with all the proximity of city life that you need. Plus, with restaurants this good at the ready, hopping up and down 65/Franklin won't be as necessary as one might think. If you drive and you enjoy good food and you live in Nashville, you have no excuse not to have patronized Red Pony.

The drive down from the city was relaxing as always. Love coming down here. I don't know what it is about driving due south, rather than southeast that makes life less hectic. I-24, you need to figure your life out. In any case, after a relaxing drive and easy parking (there's a huge parking structure around the corner; I can't fathom how anyone has parking issues around here), my dinner guest and I made our way to the double brownstone (redstone?) that is Red Pony. Even though we came on a Tuesday, I'd recommend reservations. Red Pony is no secret. You don't want to wait for this goodness. We were seated upstairs and the fun began.

The menu changes seasonally so be aware of this. You don't need to be concerned: everything is delicious. I just want to prep you for the evening. Steven was our waiter and he took fantastic care of us. Not only was he affable and knowledgeable about the menu, he was extremely helpful in instructing first-timers in best enjoying the menu. Plus, he started us off with some complimentary crab hush puppies. Done. I was done right then and there. The hush puppies were fantastic. I mean, hush puppies and crab. How can that be bad? I started the meal with a cocktail of Steven's recommendation: the Easy Goer Martini. I was a bit dubious despite his enthusiasm as it was a gin-based cocktail and I'm not, typically, down with juniper. I shouldn't have worried. The pamplemousse and strawberry masked the herbal qualities and brought a nice sweetness to the fore. The name was incredibly accurate. Thanks to the hush puppies I forwent a salad. Instead, I splurged on a larger entree. The sesame tuna was a generously-sized fish dish, crusted with sesame and served with noodles and vegetables. I paired it with a pinot grigio and was quite pleased with myself. Since I didn't get a salad, I felt completely justified in getting dessert. Do this. The Chocolate Trio was a revelation: chocolate pot de creme, chocolate tres leches and a boca negra. I didn't know where to begin. I just wanted to put my face on the plate and wiggle it all around until the food was gone. I might have done just that. There might be pictures. I might not be embarrassed. 

Red Pony is well worth the drive, your time, your money, and your consideration. Whether you are on a date, celebrating a birthday or because it's Tuesday, any reason is a good reason to come to Franklin and eat at one of the best restaurants in the metro. I'll see you there.

We were warned. LeAnn Rimes tried to tell us. You can't fight the moonlight... or, escape from the deliciousness of Five Daughters donuts.* You can't say you didn't know better. Well, I can't say that because my mouth is full of delectable donuts.

Now, before I get into this review, I have to let a couple of things be known: 1.) I didn't pay for these bad boys. 2.) I can't speak to the controversy of whether these baked bounties truly originate in middle Tennessee or - as with many items of this sort - in Cali-forn-i-ay. I can't speak on that. And I can't speak on whether my mouth and belly would be as happy with the food had I spent $50 on a dozen or some witchcraft of the sort.** But, as a recipient of the donuts, sparing nothing more than calories and additional nights of pitch-dark amorous relations (light is the enemy; there's a reason touch is a sense), I was more than happy with them. In fact, I may have squealed, moaned and clapped while stuffing this goodness in my face. Chocolate cream filled. Inside Out Caramel Apple. Chocolate Coffee Cocoa. 100 Layer. The Quinn. I speak your name(s).

I fully recognize the foolishness and - let's be honest - waste of spending this much money on donuts. I get it. I do. I'm even open to future mockery if we discover a Mast Brothersesque twist to the phenom.*** But, there's no denying the product tastes really damn good and with three locations and counting (all in high-rent districts), 5 Daughters has to be doing a lot of things very right. Bring on Federal and let's see if the market corrects pricing or keeps it as is. Who wants to buy me one?****

* You have to listen really closely to the sound to hear this lyric.
** Probably not.
*** I never fell for that one.
**** Ten.

Before you write Mas Tacos off as a hipster paradise/fad, try them out. Guaranteed, you're in for a treat. My entire experience at MT (from walking up to the building, to ordering to eating outside) reminded me of Austin. I don't know if the owners are from there, but it's definitely the vibe I got. This isn't a bad thing. Rather than the most authentic Mexican food experience possible, I think Mas Tacos serves up some very yummy Mex-texish (my word) fare that's decidedly more 'blue dot and weird' than anything else the Lone Star state has to offer. Add in a healthy dollop of 'San Diego' for good measure.

Be warned: you will order more than you can eat. Everything sounds so good and is (relatively) fairly-priced, you're going to be tempted to order a ton. Take it from someone who ordered way too much: plan your order and then order one thing less. Your stomach will thank you. I started with the watermelon-lime agua fresca. Whatever you do, avail yourself of agua fresca. Whenever it's on a menu, I order it. MT's didn't disappoint. Packed with flavor but light and refreshing for a late summer day, I could have consumed gallons of the stuff. It's a good thing I didn't, because I ate way too much as it was.

I started with the chicken tortilla soup. Far from what you might remember from a popular fast(er) food chain (which, if I'm being honest, has decent soup for what it is), this is without-a-doubt homemade and magically delicious. You'll want to drink the broth. The soup is filled with tortilla, cheese, cilantro, tomato, corn, and shredded chicken. The avocado which topped by soup and filled the bowl was a welcome addition. I found the soup a touch lime-y but I like citrus. If your taste isn't accustomed to tartness, ask for a sample before diving in. For the main event, I ordered the fish tacos. Freaking awesome. HUGE pieces of tilapia, surrounded by onion, cabbage and dill. Perfect. My mistake came in ordering three of them. I was expecting the small, wimpy fish tacos you can get at other places. Not so here. These tacos are substantial. Order wisely. The only bummer of the meal came from the eating environment. Since the day was nice, we ate outside... and were swarmed by flies. They were everywhere. It made eating tough and not the least bit appetizing. Granted, it's getting colder now but in the future, I'll make sure my MT meals are conducted inside.

Eighth & Roast offers a coffee shop experience that doesn't alienate. I know the preceding might be an odd sentence but, if you admit it, you know what I am talking about. Coffee can be as intimidating as beer or wine. Depending on where you go to get it, you might feel unwelcome, out of sorts or unsure of what to get. No worries. It's just coffee (or beer or wine). It's meant to be consumed and enjoyed. If the process of doing so becomes any more involved than that, you (and the place you're patronizing) are doing it wrong.

Eighth & Roast does it right. From the moment you walk in, you feel comfortable. It might have something to do with the homey wooden & brick touches or good, laid-back energy inside the Waverly shop. I think it has much to do with the fact that the baristas are friendly, smile at you once you step inside and don't seem as though they hate the fact that you breath the same air as they do. #thelittlethings Not being much of a coffee guy, I was pleased to discover the breadth of their tea program. Not only does 8&R have an abundance of (loose leaf) tea to choose from, you have the option of getting it hot or cold, so you can, happily, patronize the shop in the middle of summer or winter. I opted for an iced chai berry tea and every sip was a joy. I have plans on coming back and trying their entire line of teas.

But don't be so quick to take your drink and run. Remember the homey wooden touches I spoke of earlier? Yeah, take a seat. The wifi signal is strong and plenty of other patrons are tickety-tacketying away on their computer thingies. Join in. Or, if you'd rather forgo the work and concentrate on eating delicious things, you can do that too. Eighth's blondie game is legit. Seriously. If you have a sweet tooth, order one. Don't share. I don't know if these delights are made in-house or imported from somewhere else in town. All I know is that every time I darken those doors, a blondie will make its way into my belly. Every.time. 

For a coffee shop, the hours aren't very accommodating  to a later night crew so I'd advise you getting here earlier than later. Thursday-Sunday seem to be optimal days. Waverly is more of a residential than commercial neighborhood (for now?) so look for nearby street parking by the pretty homes.

3.5

It's right there in the name: come here for the music, stay for the drinks and patio after the set... you can probably skip the food. The Listening Room can give you a pretty decent night out (especially in good weather) but you have to know why you're coming and choose your experience accordingly.

As anyone who's visited can tell you, it's a cool venue. From the moment you walk in, you can feel the musical electricity. The stage is the real deal. It's not overly fancy; it's just legit. You know it when you see it. Other venues may have more cache, but the LRC is no slouch. If you're set to see a show here, be excited. Parking can be a bit of an issue but they have a (free?) valet. If Tom is working, he'll take good care of you and your vehicle.

Since it's a music venue, one would hope the drink program is up to par. It is. I came here on a Wednesday night in early autumn and was on a red ale kick. The only one I saw on draft was Fat Bottom's Ruby -- which was a-ok with me, as I'd been drinking a lot of it... but that's when I saw the rest: there were four tubs of hooch! Forget the suds. I can get that anytime. Bring on the hooch! Since I needed to be presentable (at least, that's what I told myself), I decided on the tasty but not knock-you-out Fancy Lemonade: vodka, simple syrup, lemon, soda. Very drinkable. Good for a hot day. I wanted to try the watermelon drink that had moonshine or the Blowin' Smoke drink which had whiskey but the bartender told me both were pretty strong and, again, I needed to be coherent so...

When the music's in between sets or you need to talk (don't ever talk during a performance), take your drink and hit the patio. There's not much of a view right now but once the amphitheater gets built up, you've got a game changer on your hands. The only real letdown is the food program. My Caesar salad was mealy and my portabella burger was cold & rubbery. The food would have been a rather unfortunate end to a decent evening had I not observed a woman spitting the worst game I've ever heard to a guy who couldn't care less. I thought only dudes did stuff like that. The beautiful disaster that woman brought to my life made me almost forget about the bad taste in my mouth.

4.5

This is how you do upscale coffee. At Steadfast, you'll find no pretension or derision. Instead, you'll enjoy a great product and fantastic service. See? That wasn't so hard, was it?

As others have mentioned, the space is very inviting -- despite its simplicity. The sparse Scandinavian feel makes for clean lines, no fuss and a dining room that takes the focus off of it and onto the product and allows for patrons to concentrate on interacting with each other rather than being distracted by everything happening around them. In warmer months, take advantage of the outside eating area. You might need to: the word is out about SC and seating is at a premium. My party had to hover over a singleton taking up a four top.* Eventually, he meandered away and we were able to sit. In the time he took to be a good neighbor, though, we had time to engage with the nice folks behind the counter, study the menu and make good ordering choices.

I opted for a butterscotch latte, mixed berry muffin and a peach salad. It was late summer, so the food choices seemed seasonal and like good choices. They were. Oh man, they were. The butterscotch latte is one of SC's signature drinks -- and there's a reason for that. The drink is rested (meaning they sit and the flavors percolate) which allows for a more mellow approach but a more pronounced flavor. The butterscotch isn't cloying or overwhelming. For those with sensitive stomachs, no fear ordering this drink. I liked it more than I thought I would. The mixed berry muffin was an oversized explosion of fruit packed into a soft, sweet, bready delivery vehicle. I don't know if these delights are made on site or shipped in, but they're in my SC rotation. The peach salad (I believe) sports The Peach Truck peaches. Done. It's a green salad with an abundance of peaches, walnuts, arugula, pepper, light dressing, and burrata. It's not at all what I expected and a perfect late summer salad. I loved every bite. If more businesses like Steadfast Coffee are what we can expect as Nashville strains to match the expectations set for it by internal and external press, the city has a bright future ahead of it. See you soon. 

*Don't take up a four top in a busy place when you're flying solo.

Suzy Wong, how YOU doin'? Forgive me, but a restaurant whose name evokes images of the future cast member of a RuPaul show *has* to have a Wendy Williams connection (I am not convinced that she isn't RuPaul). But, that's as far as I am going to go with tales of the she-beast in the review. Suzy Wong's is a house of happy and mirth. I shall not sully her reputation with images of weave and HGH. The food, drink and service are too fabulous (had to be said) to not concentrate solely on it.

The food: everything I ate was fantastic. I know SW touts itself as a bastion of small plates. Well, the bowls are more than enough for a person to eat by himself. But don't limit yourself to just eating one bowl (coconut chili fried brown rice with egg). Go with a group of people and experience as much of the menu as possible. What should you get? Start with anything with cheese. Yes, I know that cheese + Asian food sounds disgusting and it usually is. BUT when the cheese is of the red curry variety and the added Asian element is a bowl full of wonton chips... well, are you following me? Awesome. Delicious. Delectable. Don't share. SW is fusion, so expect some mindfreaks and some old standbys. I was a fan of the wonton nachos (topped with pork and cheese; slap somebody), pork ribs, coconut-chili chicken wings (stupid good), various makis (thumbs up for crab and avocado), moo shu chicken wraps, and gyozas (even though I was tricked with veggie fare). You can't go wrong with the food.

Or the drinks. They're strong. They're colorful. They're strong. You'll drink several. You might pass out. I'm not judging.* The cool thing about the cocktails is that each is paired with a 'traditional' Asian influence but nothing (despite the name) is kitschy. It's not unusual for a drink to be made with lemongrass, basil, ginger, hibiscus (drink this one!), or lychee. Whiskeys (this is TN not KY), sparkling wines and vodkas serve as the base, but these cocktails are so expertly made, no matter what your taste preference, you'll be hard pressed not to find a drink you like. So, choose on color or fruit or fizz and sit back and get ready to fall in the rabbit's hole.

Service is fantastic. It's a well-oiled machine. I came in with a gaggle of hungry folks and everyone was well served and attended to. There wasn't a question that didn't get answered, a request that wasn't handled or a concern that was left hanging. I was a little concerned about what the service would be like. A restaurant named for a celluloid prostitute and that evoked images of an eastern Wendy Williams is, by-definition, awesome but it could also be the home of attitundinal service and side-eyes. No. Not at all. The staff couldn't have been more of their game. Their knowledge of the food and drink menu was expert. Their attention to empty plates and finished drinks was uncanny and the charm in the face of a mob of people was admirable. Their efforts did not go unnoticed or unappreciated. 

*I am judging.

4.5

A house of pizza sounds like a pretty awesome place in which to live. Since moving back to Nashville, I'd heard over and over that I needed to check Joey's out. Thing is, the hours didn't really match well with my schedule. When I had occasion to have a post-event lunch meeting somewhere, though, I knew just where to schedule it. At least, I thought. You know how I mentioned earlier that I'd heard over and over about Joey's? Yeah, well that translates into a packed house (of pizza). Parking can be a bit tight and seating can be an issue. The wait isn't all that bad relative to demand to crowds. So, plan on parking on the street somewhere (don't even think about the lot) and keep an eye out for open seats at any table and slide in where you fit in. Oh, and don't bring a bunch of people. This is a 2-3 (tops) person place. Got all the rules? Good. Now, gets ta eatin'.

I don't eat as much pizza as I used to. These days, the abundance of cheese turns my belly a bit. I think it's because I'm no longer 22 (it's hard to believe but true). I wanted to attack the Gladiator but I knew my gut didn't have it in me. So, while I was waiting in line to order, my lunch companion walked me through what I should try: pizza rolls, pizza by the slice, calzone, and/or salad. This was useful. At a place as busy as Joey's and with as many regulars, don't gum up the works by asking questions, hemming and hawing. There's a machine at work. Be a part of it. I ordered a slice of pepperoni and a slice of cheese. I figured if this was a NYC-style pizza joint, I should get NYC-inspired slices so as to get the full on experience. I also ordered a root beer because it's a scientific fact that root beer is the soda that pairs best with pizza. As I ordered and paid, I chatted up Joey's daughter a bit (she was working the line/register). What a nice person! In fact, everyone with whom I interacted was really nice. There's a family feel at Joey's and it doesn't take much to be a part of it. That' a huge plus.

Within no time (relative to my expectations), my food was ready. My lunch partner and I spied a four top being used by one person so we asked to sit and the singleton agreed. Good form. Before I could dig in to my slices, my buddy ordered me to try either some of his pizza roll or the Gladiator. I opted for the roll. It was legit. It was a full on NYC memory in my mouth. It made me excited for the pizza. Yep. This is it. NYC-style, without a doubt. As I folded and ate, I wondered if Joey had a reservoir of NYC water in the back. For me, my favorite part of a NYC slice is the crust and Joey's delivered admirably. The sauce to cheese ratio was perfect as was the flavor/seasoning of the sauce. The pepperoni were plentiful and fresh (not that hard, chewy things you sometimes find in pizza joints). This is the real deal. 

The limited hours are a sign of the success of the shop. When you can close by 3 during the week and not open during the weekends, you're living right. It may be an effort to get to Joey's but the reward is worth it.

Ugh. I know. Right now I'm the vegan in the steakhouse. And after years of reading/writing reviews, I know no one likes the vegan who complains about the steakhouse. I get it. I, someone with gluten issues, came to a bakery. BUT one would think that in a city like Nashville, there would be *some* option available to a sizeable portion of the community, especially one so aligned with the demographic of Dozen Bakery. Allow me to elaborate.

I brought my assistant here for a coffee/snack while we discussed business. I'd read of Dozen for years and was looking forward to visiting. We planned on meeting up at 3 which -- I thought -- would give us plenty of time to enjoy the bakery, seeing that it closed at 6. Well, they stop serving food at 3. That was a confusing let down. Seeing that we were there at (a little before) 3, though, we had a few options available to us. I asked about gluten-free pastry or bread options. Unfortunately, I was told, there were none. Bummed but not out, I decided on a salad. A salad would do just fine. But then I was told that the salads weren't gluten-free either? Huh? Whaa? It's vegetables. How and when are raw vegetables not gluten-free? I was told there wasn't anything on the menu that was gluten-free. Ugh. Okay. Whatever. Liquid sustenance, it was. Looking over the small drink menu (I know it's a bakery, not a coffee shop; I was just a bit surprised by the dearth of options), I decided on the Moroccan Jasmine Mint tea. I wasn't given an option as to whether to have it hot or cold so imagine my (non) surprise when I was given a cup of hot water and an 'artisan' tea bag. Did I just spend $2 on a tea bag? I did -- and I was displeased. I asked how long I should steep the tea. I received a blank stare back. As I settled on a 5 minute steep time, I realized my table was covered in water. The tea bag was leeching water from the mug, through the 'artisanal' bag and out the other side. Awesome. I sopped up the mess and grabbed extra napkins to allow for the future/coming mess and steeped. And stewed.

After 5 minutes my tea was ready and... soap. It tasted of soap. The tea was almost too floral on the nose but the mouthfeel was soap. I felt like I was being punished. Maybe I was. I leaned into the experience and laughed. Raging against it would have made an unpleasant experience that much more uncomfortable. Two final points: 1.) I didn't take the poor service personally, as I observed patron after patron get similar counter service. 2.) The wifi was strong.

If you can digest gluten and arrive by 2, I think Dozen should provide a much better experience for you. Again, I knew that I was going to a bakery but I assumed given its location and demographic that my particular issues wouldn't be that difficult to overcome. Couple with timing and execution, though, this was textbook struggle. I'm sorry to be the vegan in the steakhouse.

Wow. I am all the way late on this one. I told y'all I hadn't been to New Orleans in 10+ years. It seems as though I am the very last person to have heard of and eaten at Lüke. #fixed

My experience at Lüke reminded me of why, even after that damned storm, New Orleans is the center of American culinary awesomeness. It just can't be helped. When I lived here, no matter if I was at a shack or an upscale, coat-only establishment, I don't think I ever had a bad meal. Ever. I'm serious. Lüke keeps the streak going. 

I came here to meet and upon recommendation from my mentor. Yes, I have one. You should as well. This fellow set me on way wrt career choices, timing and strategy and it had been far too long since I'd seen him. Plus, he has fantastic taste in food/drink. We sat and were immediately greeted by that warm, chewy bread (with butter) I'd missed for so many years (yet instantly remembered once I smelled it). To my surprise, neither my mentor nor I wanted a drink. Where was I and who was I? No drink at lunch... in New Orleans? Something was amiss. I think I wanted to stay fully present in the conversation and meal. I stuck with my tonic and lime and availed myself of the $17 express lunch of the day. For less than $20, you get a cup of soup and the entree of the day. Being that it was Thursday, that meant my choice was the jambalaya. Done.

In no time, I was slurping on a bowl of hot, spicy, filling, decadent crab bisque. OMG. I'd missed eating like this. Eating is such a joy/(first world/privileged, I recognize) pleasure. To eat food that make your endorphins light up and mouth sing... it's a blessing. It is. The sweet crab meat was the star of the bowl. Not to be hidden amongst heavy cream, the shellfish was up front and present in every spoonful. I was feeling a wee bit full when my large plate of jambalaya arrived. The description said something about green onion sausage and andouille cracklin'. I dunno. All I know is as soon as the smell hit my noise, I couldn't get it in my mouth fast enough. Wait. I lie. I took a bite. Then took a bite of the corn bread. Then I crumbled the corn bread into the dish. Then I topped everything with a metric ton of hot sauce. THEN I put it in my mouth as fast as I could.

Our waiter was pleasant, accustomed to the lunch crowd and delivered the type of service that I remembered, service that helped make New Orleans restaurants famous. Bellies protruding and mouths achy from laughter, my mentor and I bid farewell to Lüke and got on with the business of the day. I was not even four hours into being back in The Big Easy and I didn't want to leave. A good meal and good conversation will do that to/for you.

I'm the 50th review! Nice! I know, I know: I didn't believe it either but this spot truly lives up to the 5-star average. A cafe like Little Mosko's is exactly the reason why this site/app exists: to connect people to great local businesses... especially businesses one may not know of ordinarily.

Without Yelp, it's hard to know how you'd know about/find LM. It's a part of the SoBro Peabody Street campus that houses Pinewood, Emmas, etc. And it's a direct descendant of the old Mosko's & the Muncheonette (which came to an end in the late 90s and that's all I'm going to say to date myself). The set up is just like you might remember/imagine and it fits very well within the hustle and bustle of the EC... but you don't need to be an entrepreneur to eat here. You just have to have an appetite.

The menu changes weekly so you have plenty of reasons for returning. There's also a breakfast and lunch menu so you can eat here a ridiculous number of times per week and not get bored. I came to LM for a lunch menu. As soon as I sat and started looking at the menu, I got a little sad. The cakes, cookies and sandwiches looked so good but this %&*%^ gluten thing I have going on makes that a pipe dream most times. And then I saw it. I could 'GF yourself' for $1. Can it be? I went to the registers and talked to the owner and she told me that the innards of all sandwiches are GF and the bread can be subbed out AND THE BAKED GOODS ARE ALL GLUTEN-FREE! I almost got dizzy. She explained that she's part of the GF tribe so she knows the struggle. AND if you check in on Yelp you get either a free coffee or cookie. Done. DONE! IN ALL THE WAYS, THIS IS DONE! I couldn't control myself. I ordered a Pomodoro Pork sandwich, Buffalo blue cheese chips, a clementine San Pelligrino, and a chocolate chunk cookie. Why not, right?

Before too long my made-to-order (as they all are) sandwich was ready. I should have taken a picture but I couldn't control my need to eat it immediately. This was a mountain of a sandwich. House-roasted, super tender pork, slow-cooked (pomodoro) tomatoes, garlic butter, basil, and salty pecorino romano cheese all generously portioned between two slaps of soft, multi-grain GF bread. I ate my sandwich with a knife and fork if that gives you any indication on how big this bad boy was. With every bite, I became happier and happier. With my soda and chips, I had the perfect lunch. I was so stuffed that I couldn't eat my cookie. My friend (who was experiencing her own lunch nirvana) told me to go ahead and eat the cookie because it was too good not to. But I fought my piggy instincts and gave in to delayed gratification. Later that day when I needed a pick me up, I had the cookie. I was instantly regretful that I didn't buy more. This was an explosion of dark, rich chocolate in a soft, slightly chewy cookie. With every chew I was, like, 'seriously?'. Unreal. Delicious. My friend committed to coming to LM weekly and I might have to join her. Believe the 5-star average, folks. It's real. It's deserved. It's fantastic. Little Mosko's is the breakfast/lunch joint you've been looking for. Dang. Just writing this made me want to eat another LM sandwich. This is obsession.

The first thing you'll notice at G'z is the smell. The smoker sits outside the restaurant and does the best advertising G'z could hope for. One whiff of that sweet smoke and I knew I was stopping in. Secondly, you'll notice the crowds. This is a small restaurant in a strip mall and there are plenty of folks in the place waiting for all sorts of delicious bbq. Thirdly, you'll take note of the nice guys working. G'z is a small operation and every fella behind that line is chatty, respectful and appreciative of your business. No one is too cool for school here. These fellas appreciate your dollar and - as such - you'll want to give them more of them.

On the busy Saturday night I stopped in, the fryer was down. That meant no fries for sides. Oh well. That didn't stop me from ordering a half chicken with pickles (no bread) and a side of smoked cabbage. I was very satisfied and very full after going to town on both. The chicken is white meat, smoked expertly and surprisingly juicy. The bird is packed with flavor and moist enough to eat with your fingers, although you can keep it classy by using a fork and knife. Whatever you do, though, use some of those famous sauces. The chicken doesn't *need* them but they add so much depth and flavor to the party. I alternated between sweet heat and honey gold. I liked sweet heat but I loved honey gold. I might drink it if it were in a glass. I'm serious. Not content to be ignored, the smoked cabbage brought heat of its own. Of solid texture and juicy sauce, the cabbage holds up to the meat and, quickly, becomes a side you'll eat on its own rather than an afterthought to the meaty main event. Look at how many reviews mention the cabbage. There's a reason.

G'z is not worried about being cool. G'z doesn't care about being trendy. G'z simply offers solid bbq (and a lot of it) at very fair prices. This is how you eat bbq out east. Don't be fooled.

3.5

Acme's biggest strength is its biggest liability: size. The sheer size of Acme makes it exciting to explore but it also makes it necessary to have it packed to the gills to justify the expense. And, unfortunately, when it's packed, your mileage is gonna vary.

There's so much to enjoy about Acme. From the moment you walk in on the first level, you know you're in for something special. The live music on stage makes you feel at home. The local craft brews on tap will make you feel at ease. And, the southern-twisted menu will make you feel full. I was gonna go for the catfish but so many people raved about the hatchery, that I had to try it. I'm glad I did: curried chickpeas, coconut rice, cashews, cilantro & fried egg with fry bread. It's the perfect amount of food and unique enough that it should be your first stop on the menu. The build-out is gorgeous. The bar is beautiful and you can get some country store shopping in near the entrance. The second floor boasts shabby chic seating, big booths, huge tvs for sports watching, craft cocktails like the Back Porch (moonshine, lemonade, Grenadine) and sushi (not from Sam's/Sam) in the form of eel avocado and crunchy crab. The third floor is a blank slate made for private events. The rooftop is the money. Sweeping views of Broadway, the river and east Nashville, I defy you to not be in awe of the sights. On a good weather night, forget about it. These are all the positives. Now, for the not-so-greats.

I, too, have found my service to be disinterested at best and rude at worst. I didn't enjoy the sushi I had on the second floor. The overwhelming reaction I had to both my rolls was that they were mealy and fishy. Yes, it's probably my bad for ordering sushi at a feed & seed but I didn't expect to actively dislike the experience. You can skip it. If there's not a crush of people in the building, the second floor won't be open. I don't begrudge Acme that decision. After all, it costs money to staff, stock and run an entire floor that might not have the customer base to justify it being open. It's too bad, but I get it. Acme can't control the crowds it attracts but on a busy Friday/Saturday night in good weather, forget about it. The line snaking up to the roof is maddening. The a-to-e experience of moving around is no fun. And, each time I have been there on a busy night, I've seen some permutation of a bro fight. Not fun. The views that make the rooftop so alluring get obscured by the cluster that it the unholy union of Lower Broad tourism, locals dead set on bringing out-of-town guests and fraternity/sorority members of all ages. It's an odd mix that doesn't seem to mix very well. Add a cover on top of that and... well...

I've come to learn that a successful visit to Acme is all about timing. I would give you those times in this review, but I don't want to mess up my chance for continued good experiences. When they're good, they're very good. When they're not so great, they're a bit painful. I don't know how to rectify or advise Acme as a business model. The rent has to be astronomical. The space is huge. The bills have to be staggering. The elements are there for a fantastic experience each and every time. Here's what I would suggest: control what you can control. Managers -- take note of servers. Servers who aren't getting the job done need to go. Plenty of people are looking for work. Acme is an attractive place to do so. Good servers/service = return business. Reconsider the sushi menu. I like the idea of different experiences on every floor. I think the second floor menu already offers that. The sushi addition might be overkill. Again, you can't control your clientele. What you can control, however, is how they act. If you catch bros broing out, fighting, being a nuisance, escort them out. Think about ways in which you can better control the amount of people on the roof. Consider back entrances to control for bunching. I offer the free advice because I want you to succeed (and it's part of my job). Feel free to take it or leave it. I hope you take it. Acme could and should be 5 stars across the board.

4.5

It wasn't even a contest. Shortly after touching down in Nashville and putting my things away at the hotel, my belly started rumbling and there was only one way this fever was being cured (well, two ways): more cowbell and some Hattie B's hot chicken. As annoyed as I was by the line leading out the door and wrapping around the corner, I was pleased that I chose to come here solo. That meant that I had a greater likelihood of getting a table for my spoils. Unless you come here at an off time (and I don't know when that would be), it's difficult to find seating for, say, a party of four. My suggestion: leave 'em behind. Besides, you don't want witnesses for what you're about to do.

And what are you about to do? Destroy some food, that's what. I don't know whether it's because I've lived in Miami for too long but I was pleasantly surprised at the prices. For $17, I received: a large dark, mild (that's two thighs and two legs; who eats white meat?), pimento mac & cheese, black-eyed pea salad, white bread (I could do without), pickles (so good; pair 'em with the chicken), 64 oz. of sweet tea, and peach cobbler (served with ice cream!!!). Do you hear me? DO YOU HEAR ME??? Ugh. Soul food, you have killed my people for centuries but you just taste so damn good. I can't allow myself to make this a regular thing. But, anyway. Back to the story. $17!! For all of that. I can't even begin to process it.

There's no need for me to describe how everything tasted (spoiler alert: incredible). If, after reading what I ordered, you need a description of what these plates are and how they tasted, it's too late for you. There is no saving you. There's not a Southern bone in your body. The appropriate response is to see the listed items, figure out how long it will take you to get to Hattie B's, order them, bloat, curse the sky, writhe in pain, eat some more until it's all gone, stumble home, and pass out.

Well, that didn't take long. There's still a lot to like about LA Jackson but I'm not as gaga about it as I used to be. It's far too crowded these days and the crowd is... interesting. It's as though people are here because *other* people are supposed to be here. Does that make sense? The scene the space used to make feels far less authentic than it used to be. On a recent Saturday visit, I was shocked at how empty it was. Remember back months ago when there were lines to the lobby on weekdays. Additionally, the tax/tip trick that's going on with the wine/cocktail program is not a good look at all. Rather than incorporating tax into the drink price (as usual), you're getting hit with paying $16+ before tip for a $13 cocktail. Nope. No sir. The view still stuns but the gild is off the lily.

3.5

It's interesting to re-visit Tin Angel as a bona fide adult. I think most people who have any history with Nashville can share in the above sentiment. Back before the days of celeb chefs and pricey Southern staples, Tin Angel was one of the chief go-tos for anniversaries, brunches, Barrister Balls, etc. So, now that the city has changed around it, I thought it might be cool to revisit what used to be one of my out-out-towner choices.

It holds up pretty well. The beer list won't win over craft beer lovers and the menu isn't as adventurous as some of the other nearby options but Tin Angel is what it is. I enjoy the fact that it's managed to stay true to self in the midst of rapid (and, all around) change. Parking is *still* a hassle (pro-tip: go for the street; not even think about the lot). The restaurant is *still* really dark (this could have advantages). The staff is *still* very nice (save for a bumpy start - no greeting at the hostess stand - the evening was perfectly lovely). These are elements that Tin Angel has held on to and it helps retain the 'fundamentally Nashville' feel it has.

Since I didn't find the sour or fruit beer I was looking for and because my friend didn't want wine, I opted to drink water with my meal. The water here is crisp, very cold and not filled to the brim with ice. My glass never emptied and, personally, it was a nice change of pace to concentrate solely on the flavors of my food and not my beverage. I should try this experiment more often. I wasn't very inspired by the appetizer options but we settled on the bacon-wrapped figs with honey & goat cheese. They were quite tasty but that's the expectation, right? Bacon. Figs. Goat cheese. Honey. The components are all delicious. They should be (and, were) delicious together. Where I think the menu oversold itself was my entree option. I went for the Chicken DaVinci and think that the description was better than the execution. On paper, it sounds lovely: Roasted chicken breast stuffed with prosciutto & provolone  
cheese on grilled Parmesan polenta; sun-dried tomato & mushroom Marsala sauce served with roasted broccolini. Heavenly, right? Despite the heavy cheese description, I tasted very little cheese throughout the dish. My chicken breast was small, tough and dry. The broccolini was more wilted than roasted and the accompanying sauce wasn't as bright as I expected it to be. The star of the plate was the polenta. Despite the lack of cheese, it was very nicely prepared and served as the unifying element of the meal. The dish has potential (it sounds lovely) but the execution was just alright. Where Tin Angel won back points (and my overall impression) was dessert. Since we forwent booze, we'd earned dessert. They were both fantastic. We talked about splitting but wound up concentrating on the desserts we chose. My friend spent time with the apple blackberry crisp. Served piping hot and exactly what you'd expect it to taste like, the dish was elevated by the cinnamon ice cream. I would have been very happy with it... had I not been pigging out on the Chocolate & Caramel Indulgence. The dish lived up to its name. I found it to be more on the caramel side but that's quite fine with me. The dessert is a chocolate cake with a milk chocolate, sea salt and caramel center -- served warm with vanilla ice cream. Tin Angel finished strong. Well done. 

I might not be back every week but I'll be back. With almost 25 years in existence, Tin Angel's earned the right to have a stumble or two. I think I'll investigate the prix fixe next time.

Annnd, just like *that*, the prophecy was fulfilled.* It shouldn't be this hard to spend money. Walk in. Order. Wait short amount of time for the food paid for. Receive said food sans attitude. It should be easy. Here, it is not. Wish I could say I didn't see this coming.


*See tip.

It seemed as though everyone I knew (in certain circles) had gone to Bourbon Steak or been invited to go to Bourbon Steak... except for me. I wasn't too put out as I'd been to the Miami (well, Aventura) location and I am not much of a beef eater but still. We're in the South. Appearances matter. I hadn't been in a big rush to check it out due to the... miscommunications... but I had a friend in town who fancies nice things so off we went.

To access the restaurant, enter the JW Marriott from 8th, cut right, go past Stompin' Grounds and turn left to the elevator. It's on the 34th floor. Hit the button and wait. You won't feel like you're ascending, but you are. Step off and it's all systems 'go.' We weren't coming for dinner, so we headed straight back to the bar. On either side of the bar are 'balcony views' -- seats that abut the windows and give perfect views of the city (much to the chagrin of the Westin; #noshadefact). Finding the scene a bit crowded on a Saturday night, we posted up at a small table next to the bar. Rather than fight the crowd, Godfrey took care of us. He was excellent. Chatty, personable but not a hoverer, he walked us through the menu and made sure that we were adequately hydrated. Keep in mind: there are two different menus (with varying prices for wine). Make good decisions.

One thing I enjoyed about the menu was that it offered a graphic of the glass the drink came in. Something else I found kitschy was that you could order cocktails either as they existed classically or change them up to get Bourbon Steak's twist. I began with the Indigo Bunting (chosen for the tiki glass as much as the ingredients). It was bold and very heavy-handed on the pour. J'aime. My next drink was the Junglebird. Again, the glassware played into my decision. Despite the gin and fruit juices, it wasn't too sweet of a drink. The pour was heavy but so was the ice element. For $17 (!), I was a little put out. Wanting to switch to wine, I tried a corked syrah (yuck; it was replaced without charge) and settled on an interesting frappato. Again, I appreciated Godfrey's deft strong hand when it came to the wine pours. With glasses abutting $20 a piece (holy markup, Batman!), you're going to want to get more than four sips out of it.

I can't speak to the food, but as a scene-y place to be Bourbon Steak is a good pick. Be aware and advised: the crowd is specific. This isn't a hip/hipster crowd. It skews older, more touristy and despite the setting, the dress code was all over the place. Plus, the drink prices are a wee bit shocking. Come either for one drink or be prepared to spend the rent money. The view makes it worth it but... know before you go.

Considering its address, I was expecting a pretty disastrous experience at CL. But then I remembered who was captaining this ship. A [redacted] hotel is no match for the culinary genius of Nina Compton. The Old 77 needs to thank the [redacted] gods it worships that this NC milkshake brings all the boys to the yard.

Walking into the bar area with rattled nerves from my hours-long frustration with the hotel, I didn't even want a drink. I just wanted to stink-eye all things associated with The Old 77. My colleague, sensing that this was about to go *very* wrong, convinced me to try a pina colada. I obliged... and everything changed. Damn! That drink, literally, turned my frown upside down. For the next couple of hours, I forgot where I was and leaned in to good food and drinks.

At least, I was prepared to. As mentioned by another colleague, our waitress wasn't the friendliest. She forgot orders (my beer was no where to be found until the end of the meal). She was short tempered with the table. I'm always shocked to experience this in New Orleans restaurants. When I lived in New Orleans (pre-Katrina), hand to God, I never once had nasty service. Not once. Anywhere. I don't know if this new crop of servers are New Orleans natives and/or know what the deal is, but it's troubling that the tradition of incomparable service has been so sullied in the aftermath of that damned storm. For the sake of all, I tuned her out (but made a note to self to side-eye her on the street) and got back to concentrating on the menu.

The menu. It's fantastic and everything you would expect from the rightful* winner of Top Chef. The dishes (we shared many dishes but I don't play the shared plates game when it comes to my entree. I like to feel full after a meal -- not polite) that stood out to me (nothing was bad or, even, average) were the tuna tartare, brussel sprouts and curried goat. The tuna came with avocado (standard) and crispy bananas (whoa, mama!). The temperature was perfect and the combination of the flavors and textures led to one of my favorite preparations ever of that dish. As hackneyed as brussel sprouts have become, these were served seasoned, crispy and with a light buttermilk dressing and finished with chicken skin. Child, yes. Everyone knows the best part of fried chicken is the skin. Again, the preparation knocked my socks off. I sheepishly admit to enjoying goat. I feel badly because goats are such awesomely smart-assed, honey badger animals. I don't often eat them but sometimes I can't help myself. I couldn't help myself. The meat was lovingly seasoned, impossibly tender and paired with sweet potato gnocchi (yes! change it up.), peanuts for crunch, and cilantro to round it all out and surprise the palate.

I knew to expect a good meal. I was shocked at how wonderful it was. But for the waitress who distracted from the experience, I would have said the evening was perfect.** Still, though, if in the mood for outstanding food that lives up to the New Orleans (celeb chef) tradition, you'll be quite pleased with your meal at Compère Lapin. Well done (as usual), Chef!

*Mhm. I said it.
** Well, that and the location. #thecortez

I don't often eat cased meats but when I do, odds are I'll be doing so at I Dream of Weenie. I'd passed the VW van for a year before some friends finally convinced me to try it out. I don't know what took me so long. It probably has something to do with always being in a rush as I sped down 11th. Stopping for a bite to eat at the side of the road wasn't always something that came to mind. It so happened, however, that after an evening of carousing, looking at art and drinking my body weight in delicious local beer, I was in need of a laid-back meal to fill my belly.

First thing I noticed, the employees are really really nice. For working in such a tight, hot space and dealing with all manner of denizens, I was shocked at how chatty and genuinely friendly everyone was. Major kudos to the IDoW team. That can't be easy. The second thing I noticed, IDoW has a legit soda program. As someone who loves all manner of sody pahp that dares to go beyond the big two, I was pleased as punch to spy so many delicious options. There might even be a secret stash. You didn't hear this from me. The last thing I noticed, IDoW has some seriously awesome flavor combos when it comes to hot dogs. This isn't your average ballpark frank. Speaking of franks, I ordered the Flamin' Frank (after a much-too-long inquisition about the choices; I apologize, patient IDoW person). Not only do I not, typically, eat hot dogs, I don't, typically, eat a bunch of hot food later at night. Oh, beer. You lead to so many good choices. This dog was covered in chili, cheese, onions, mustard, salsa, and jalapenos. And it only cost $4. And... it was delicious. I inhaled it. I tried not to. I tried to savor it. But it was so good. Oh! Here's another thing: rather than having to eat your hot dog along the side of the road like a tragic figure, you get to relax at picnic tables under trees and feel 100% about giving in to your childhood wants. Perfect. I realized that night that a near-perfect late summer day in East End requires a stop in to IDoW. And if a perfect day isn't on your agenda, just stop in for some delicious, easy-to-eat grub.

Lookit me: eating Slavic fare like I'm back in Chicago. It's been a while since I had been around all things vegetables-I-don't-regularly-eat and meats-I-shouldn't-regularly-eat. It was a nice reminder of a diet from long ago. New Orleans, you offer so many culinary surprises.

And Kukhnya is a surprise. I *never* would imagine to eat at a music venue, much less have the food be good but here we are. Walking in, I wanted to show off my Cyrillic skills but I'm rusty and we were walking too fast to the back (party/music is up front) for my brain to rightfully translate. My glory robbed from me, it was time to drown my sorrow in booze. Who am I kidding? It's not a New Orleans trip if I'm not liquored from sun up to sun down. You have to order drinks at the bar (even if you're eating in back) but the bartender is a pro and he'll get you handled right away. I ordered a Louisiana Mule (which adds satsuma liqueur to give it a unique taste) because when it's late and I'm cold (and a little buzzed), I'm fine with being basic enough to want a copper mug. The drink was potent, a bit tart and extremely drinkable. I'd order it with a meal but not if I was hanging out at a show because copper mug. 

I'd been eating and drinking all day so I was fine eating fries off other people's plates and drinking when I caught a whiff of kapusta. Kapusta is braised cabbage with vinegar and spice (think: sauerkraut). I wanted some. And if I was getting that, well, I *had* to get a kielbasa to go with it. Again, if I was going all Chicago-style and having cased meats, I was darn sure to have sauerkraut and spicy mustard to go with. I didn't order the bun because gluten-free when I ignored the voice inside my head that said most sausages aren't gluten-free. Well, at least it tasted good going down. Drunk decisions aren't always the best. Who knew? Back to  my plate, the sausage was served cut into small pieces and set atop the cabbage. Once I slathered that mustard all over the meat and paired each bite with a vegetable, I was in Slavic street food heaven.

I could have chosen better given my dietary restrictions. I should have chosen better given my dietary restrictions. I didn't and I learned the outcome of such folly... but, man, it tasted good! If you don't have a funny gut, have at it!

When ya get me thinking, "Miami did it better," I get a bit cranky. And, in all fairness, this is probably a case of unfairly heightened expectations. Y'see, everyone I'd met (up to that point) told me that the booze purchasing experience I'd been waiting for was waiting for me at FM. 'It's all in one! They have everything!' Okay. Cool. Great. I hadn't been a fan of the separation of boozey goodness that makes up the Nashville beer, wine & liquor scene. I know it's no one's fault but the legislature's but moving back to Nashville after so many years away - and where I can buy what I want with selection & impunity - is annoying.

So, it came to pass that a Saturday found me with time to, finally, make my way to FM and... this is it? It's one large room. Granted, it's a really big room... but one large room. For the size, I found the beer selection to be inadequate. Again, I can read. I know the name sez 'wine & liquor warehouse.' Thing is, if you're the biggest and baddest, I expect the biggest & baddest. There are more than a few smaller stores serving up better selections and service. Yep, I said service. I guess it was my bad luck but the two folks with whom I spoke couldn't have been less interested in helping me out. The first gentleman was the beer expert who looked nonplussed to confused when I mentioned my desire to make my own six pack of red ales. From the singles/loose collection, I was unable to do so. I soon gave up on beer and decided to try my hand at wine. The selection/quality was much much better but when it came to searching for a salesperson to answer some questions and help me out, I was left with nada. So, I left with nada. No sale. I'm sure FM offers a fantastic wine & spirits experience for some and that (coupled with the size of the store) leaves me at a 2.5/3 rating... but I doubt I'll be back. For my purchasing needs, there are other places in town that are doing it better.

There's been a lot of confusion in my reviews of late. I simply can't understand the lack of attention some local businesses get (especially in light of the heaps of attention others get). Long before the hipsters, out of town coverage and increased congestion, there was Margot -- complete with a 1930s building, ever-changing menu and distinct point of view. I might raise some eyebrows in so saying but... this is my favorite restaurant in Nashville. I don't understand why there aren't mountains of reviews for this true Nashville gem.

The restaurant is a converted gas station in the middle of the 5 Points intersection of East End. It's, literally, in the middle of one of Nashville's most (currently) exciting neighborhoods. Perhaps it's hiding in plain sight? I was looking for a restaurant for a special occasion and I stumbled across Margot's reviews. What intrigued me the most was that the menu changes daily. That kind of commitment to the dining experience is admirable -- and tough. Many many visits later, I can say with complete confidence that it delivers upon its lofty goal. While the POV is rustic French and Italian, I would say the rustic nature of the dishes transcends region. It's exciting to discover what's on the menu and how the experience will be different for the evening.

By now, I have the Margot experience down to a science: seasonal cocktail and appetizer, main dish and wine, dessert and tea. If you order your food in this manner, you're sure to have an excellent experience. Try to sit upstairs if you can. The vibe and decor lend themselves to a homey, comfortable environment suitable for reunions, business dinners and dates. Yes, Margot can be very romantic: the lighting, food, brick walls, and high ceilings can make a gas station the right setting for love. But, booze may have something to do with it. The cocktails are seasonal, interesting, diverse, and well-crafted. One of my favorite cocktails was an orchard punch. It was an apple-forward libation, perfect for the fall. I tend to favor the brown liquor cocktails here. After all, we're in Tennessee. WRT appetizers, ask for suggestions for the perfect pairing with your drink. I have found the seafood options to be wonders. From crawfish pizza, to complex soups to kale salads with cheese and fruit... there's a lot of attention to detail to ensure your first bite will be a fantastic one. The wine list is a marvel. Again, ask for suggestions. The main courses will always feature a meat, seafood, chicken, and vegetarian/vegan option, so you can bring anyone here. Yes, ordering the chicken dish at Margot isn't a wasted order. That said, one of my favorite mains was fried soft-shell crab served atop cheese grits with tomatoes, peppers and bacon. Think about that. Concentrate on it. Weep that you didn't eat it. It's a wonder how I have room for dessert at the end of the meal. These dishes are hearty, substantive, generously-portioned, and extremely rich. I shouldn't have room but I will myself to do so. Pro tip: peppermint tea helps with digestion... and eating more food. This is important because you're going to need dessert. Whatever's available in chocolate, get it. I still dream of the chocolate cappuccino cake. Heavenly *and* sinful. On one occasion, my belly couldn't muster the strength for a rich dessert. What to do? Why, order the Hurricane sorbet. Hurricane sorbet. This is what you expect at Margot. Every time.

The service is outstanding as well. It begins with making reservations (and you should make reservations). Everyone on the phone is so pleasant and helpful. There's never any whiff of arrogance or rudeness. I wish this wasn't such a special circumstance but after enough RSVP attempts at 'top' local restaurants, you'll see what I'm talking about. The host is a consummate professional. Not only does he have complete mastery of his dining room, he's friendly, chatty and accommodating. I've never had to wait for a table upon my arrival. Again, one would think this wouldn't be a big deal with a reservation. One would be wrong. Throughout all of my visits, my worst service was 'good.' Every other time it was stellar and in one circumstance it was above and beyond. If you have the chance to sit upstairs and have William A as your waiter, do it. In a restaurant full of excellent servers, he stands out. It's high praise but he's entirely worthy of it. When I have out of town guests, there's never a question of where I bring them. Each and every one has raved about the experience. If you haven't been to Margot, you're missing out. If you haven't reviewed it, you should do so. It's my go-to restaurant and I am so grateful that it's here.

4.5

It's a Nashville institution for a reason, folks. There are a few things that always seem to happen when friends/family visit Nashville. I won't belabor the point by writing about them because we've all been through it. Many of these tasks cause me to shuffle my feet and groan. A trip to Monell's, however, is reason enough to invite visitors. Even Southerners enjoy Monell's -- and that's sayin' something. Sometimes restaurants like this cater to folks from outside the region who wouldn't know the importance of cooking with bacon grease if it hit them in the head with your grandma's skillet. No such slight of hand, here. Monell's is the real deal.

You might be surprised, then, to realize that this Southern feast isn't found in some hideaway shack. Monell's food is housed in a gorgeous Germantown Victorian, complete with a koi pond and bridge. Yes, it's true. We even wear shoes -- regularly -- down South, as well. I know! Stereotypes blown before you even walk through the door, Monell's is bringing it. Walk in, tell the hostess how many are in your party and get seated with strangers. Take off your hat. Turn off and put away your damn phone and get ready to share a variety of Southern goodies the way you would if you were a guest in someone's home.
