If sitting with strangers and having conversations puts you outside your comfort zone, I don't think you'd enjoy yourself. But, if you have a lick of sense and can act right in public, you'll be just fine.

One of the things I enjoyed the best about Monell's is that the two pitchers of tea are labelled -- so as to AVOID the non-sweet tea. That's how you do it, folks. That's what you signed up for. On the Saturday afternoon that most recently rocked my world, we started with biscuits & cornbread (with butter and hot sauce, 'natch). This led to: slaw, cheese grits, cucumbers, squash casserole, pulled pork, fried chicken, white beans, potatoes, sausage gravy, green beans, and meatloaf. The plates kept passing and I kept eating. If something ran out, our waitress was on the ball and we got a new helping of it with no wait at all. You know that mechanism in your brain that tells you you're full? I think there's a machine at Monell's that disengages it as everyone at my table ate until they were uncomfortable... as you should. My only disappointment was dessert. I have never been a banana puddling fan. I was in the minority at the table as everyone else dove in to it and didn't come up for air until it was gone. Had there been some apple pie, yellow cake with chocolate frosting, pecan pie, etc., my inner fat kid would have been fully realized. It is was, I could barely walk so, perhaps, it's best that I didn't have dessert. 

The price for this feast? $15. FIF-TEEN BUCKS. Yeah, it's a Nashville institution for a reason, folks.

4.5

This is Whole Foods done right. I mean, it's Whole Foods. You know the drill by now. Enter. Give your wallet/purse to the nearest employee. Pray s/he leaves you with something by the time you want to leave. Go home and enjoy your cage-free, air-fed, humanely-raised emu, and call it a day. Yep. You know what's up.

But this... THIS Whole Foods... well, it's the best I've ever been to.* To start, let's talk location. The Hill Center is nice enough to convince city residents and transplants alike to move to Green Hills. It's also the perfect location for a Whole Foods. Admit it, you'll never be able to visit a strip mall Whole Foods again now that you've experienced high-end furniture, clothes made by a boutique in Urundi, Burundi and parking a female friend of mine described as 'cute.' Cute parking. It's a thing. Luckily for all you hearty shoppers, garage parking is a thing as well and it's mere steps from the Whole Foods entrance. Take *that*, Mother Nature.

Once you've entered, keep your wits about you. This Whole Foods is massive and the selection is extremely complete. Take your time and choose wisely. Enjoy the high ceilings, good lighting, wide aisles, and overall cleanliness. The produce department is lush, fully stocked and exotic. The bakery will prove undeniable with its cupcakes, pies and such. PLUS, there's a separate case for cookies, scones and donuts. You're not getting away without getting fatter. The craft beer collection is impressive. For a land-locked location, I was shocked at the quality of seafood. The butcher will make your lunchmeat slices from the actual animal. There are no slimy, pre-packaged lunch meats here. While you're at it, pick up a made-just-for-you sub sandwich or slice of pizza. The salad bar is four or five bars long. The prepared foods are gourmet and delicious. The salads and dinners behind the glass case will make you feel fancy and healthy. The cheese... oh, the cheese! Heavenly. And the people are very, genuinely nice. From the lady in the bakery, to the fellow in the deli, to the chap who instructed me on which fruits to buy and why, to the young woman who checked me out, I encountered real smiles, personalized small chat and excellent customer service. I know it's a chain. I know it's expensive. But, know this: there's no beating Whole Foods. Pound for pound, it's got the grocery game in Nashville on lock. 

*And almost replaced the memory of the third-world, flies-on-bloody-meat-slicer Miami Beach Whole Foods. Almost. That was some serious trauma, y'all.

As someone who was skeptical of this '12 South' thing just a couple of years ago, I find myself in the neighborhood more than I ever would have imagined. Places like the 12 South Taproom are why. For most things social, shiny and palatable for a certain demographic in the city (a bit more universally welcoming than other parts of town), 12 South hits all the right notes. 

So it came to pass on a summer Wednesday evening when I had a guest in town, beer on our minds and a need for food -- but what kind of food? Rather than driving around aimlessly, my subconscious took us to 12 South. I think I had another place in mind, but as soon as I drove past the Taproom, I knew what time it was. If it's your first trip to the rodeo, it's a wee bit confusing how to enter and how to grab a table. But, at the time of night it was and with our collective hunger, we made some executive decisions that seemed to work out well (go to the far end of the patio and grab an open table). Within a few minutes of our sitting, we were approached by a waitress. She asked what we wanted to drink but we didn't yet have menus. Ah. Right. That. She grabbed some off another table (efficient) and took off. A few minutes after that, a gentleman came by to take our drink order. We told him that we thought we had another server. He replied that they switch off. That was good enough for us. Since we were outside, it was warm and I was in need of tripel refreshment, I ordered a La Fin Du Monde (always a good pick -- especially in early summer). Buoyed by my beer (and a bit shamed for adding to my belly), I went with a healthier dinner item: the Southwestern Cobb with extra ranch.* The menu is fairly extensive for a taproom and the quality is decent for one as well. I was happy to see that my salad was of the 'large' variety. From the romaine lettuce base, there were ample amounts of bleu cheese, bacon, black beans, avocado, almonds, chicken, and pico de gallo. Did I mention the ranch was/is spicy? Yeah. Delicious. The beer/salad combo was the perfect dinner for an I-don't-know-what-I-want-to-eat-but-I'm-hungry-want-to-eat-outside-and-don't-have-a-specific-taste-for-something. My Belgian beer and very large salad came out to $21 before tip. Granted, not fast food prices but fair considering what I had.

I'll be back.

*We're in the South. Healthy is relative.

So, here's the thing: if you come here and get their specialty, you're going to be happy. You will. This is a fried chicken & beer joint. Says it right in the name. Stay on course and all will be well.

My first time here, I ordered the rotisserie chicken and it didn't go so well. The portion size for the price was off and I was left feeling some sort of way. I reviewed it. The universe laughed and made it so that I worked with the Waldo's folks soon after. After seeing the hustle, love and hard work they put in to their product, I started to rethink my initial impression. After witnessing the overwhelming response to their food, I knew that there was something there. I had a good reason for not partaking of their specialties before: I have a gluten-sensitive gut. When I eat it, bad things happen. Bad things. But that's on me. It's the reason I no longer frequent breweries and bakeries. I can't have their offerings without consequence. 

Unwilling to explain this whole song & dance, I, instead, asked the proprietor what he would suggest as his restaurant's standard dishes. Being that we are in the age of the chicken sandwich, he suggested The OG and The Roost. Knowing there would be hell to pay (in my gut) but that I didn't have to be around people for a couple of days, I threw caution to the wind, ordered both (with sides) and drove home with my bounty to eat and watch HBO.

I started with The OG. I paired this with fries and I don't know which I liked better. Waldo's does fried chicken really really well. I appreciated that it wasn't masked by a lot of random toppings, just pickle, lettuce and herb mayo. Sounds simple. Tastes incredible. I was a big fan of the fries as well: shoestring thin but loaded with flavor and there were a lot of them. Win. As much as I liked The OG, though, I liked The Roost better. Think of it as a 'younger' chicken salad sandwich. This was fire-roasted chicken, tossed in Alabama white sauce and loaded with pickles. Sounds simple. Tastes incredible. Plus, there was a LOT of chicken. As picky as I was about my initial rotisserie offering, I definitely got my money's worth with the sandwiches. The slaw that came with The Roost was a nice touch, too. I can see that being a good topping to/for The OG.

I broke my own rule at Waldo's: when first trying a business, try what they do best and go from there. I, likely, won't be a regular customer due to my belly not being a good fit for what they do well but I have to say that what they do well... they do really well. There's a reason for all the love.

3.5

I don't think I did this the right way. It took me a while to finally step foot inside the CAMH and by the time I did, I'd heard that the restaurant was on its second iteration of kitchen leadership (as the name talent is prepping for her new Nashville ventures). I came for brunch and not dinner which, going by reviews, is the stronger service. Lastly, I didn't choose the right dish. Yeah, I didn't do this the right way.

I'll get to the mistakes I made but I want to start with the positives. The space is very cool. I like that Chef Maneet took a chance on this part of the city before it was overrun. As another yelper notes, in six years, this area is going to be unrecognizable and CAMH will be an anchor of the neighborhood rather than the lone wolf (sorta) it is now. Also, the drink program is fantastic.* I began my meal with a Dirty Laundry (pimms #1, raspberry brandy, lime, and ginger beer) and ended it with an Ol' Chauhan (their take on an Old Fashioned). I hoped for larger drinks/more generous pours but I could find no fault with the preparation of the cocktails.

On the food side, though, it was a bit disappointing. To start the meal, I tried an order of deviled eggs (combined with bites of some neighboring monkey bread). I'll start with the bread: it was more greasy than sweet/satisfying. I kept waiting for a culinary revelation and it never came. Actually, I think that's a fair assessment of everything else I tried during brunch. The deviled eggs were boring and bland. That's a sin in the south. Rather than ordering The Chicken Or The Egg like I'd thought about (I had major plate envy when I saw my dining partners chowing down in pure bliss), I ordered the Biscuits & Gravy. I'm a huge biscuits and gravy fan and love the super-stuffed feeling I get when devouring a plate of these bad boys. I was not a fan of these biscuits & gravy. Truthfully, I found the plate to be unexciting. The description had a lot of promise -- curry flavored biscuits, poached egg, ham, grilled tomato, and gravy. The execution/reality, though, was a small plate of lukewarm protein. I didn't discern any curry flavor in my too-hard biscuit and while I understand the trend of small plates, when it comes to brunch, I, like most southerners, appreciate big. When done right, brunch is usually the only meal you need on Sunday. I had dinner that night.

It's entirely possible that I screwed up my CAMH experience by coming at the wrong time and ordering the wrong thing. Our service was nice and, as I mentioned, I enjoyed my drinks. Next time, I think a smaller dinner group and going with my gut wrt ordered plates should make all the difference.

*Made even better by the addition of Mantra beer. Mantra has transformed the beer scene in Middle Tennessee and forced everyone to step up their game or get left behind.

3.5

There's a lot of potential here. What's most disadvantageous for Bearded Iris is timing. There are some breweries -- both new and old -- catching fire right now. Starting slow with a promise to build is a positive thing but, in comparison, you're not going to do yourself any favors. That said, I think Bearded Iris will get there. There are some good bones.

Let's start with the tap room. I love the fact that it's so unique. Set in a part of Germantown that's more industrial than super gentrified (those rents!), it's hard to anticipate that once you take advantage of the generous parking situation, you'll walk into a room that's more saloon/bordello than cold, hip tasting room. There's plush seating, a fancy chandelier, bar seating that's out of the wild wild west (a good thing) and a bar area that's more reminiscent of Miss Kitty than Hello Kitty (again, a good thing). I like the fact that BI isn't afraid to do something unique and stand out on their own. I think it bodes well for the future of the brewery, taproom and fan base.

As of early spring, there weren't that many beers on tap but I am hoping this is soon to change. As mentioned earlier, it's a newer brewery and, sometimes, things take time to work out. I was pretty excited to note that despite the relatively few beer offerings, there was a petite saison on the menu. I've said time and again that I enjoy starting the spring beer drinking season with a good saison and, as of this writing, that style isn't always easy to find in town, so things were coming up Milhouse... until I tasted it. I'm sorry to report that I didn't care at all for the saison. It was watery, bitter and had a disturbing aftertaste. It was akin to going in for a big dollop of whipped cream only to discover it was sour cream. I was more saddened than angry. I was excited to be here but really let down by my choice of beer. I was here later on a Saturday and there weren't that many customers. The bartender was more into hanging out than working. I get it and no one was, in any way, rude. But, making sure the patron was in to his beer... not such a concern. Since I was here with a friend to celebrate his birthday, I went in again. This time, asking for a sample first. I opted for the biere de garde... and this was much much better. Robust, amber, malty, and sweet enough to intrigue, I happily sipped this beer and wondered what other surprises might be in store at BI as time goes by. In the current landscape of Nashville breweries and at their velocity, I think BI is a bit behind the rest but if Local Color is indicative of what they have in store for the (near) future, I think this is a brewery to watch.

One of the (VERY) few things I miss about Miami is the abundance of Caribbean fare. When the skies are overcast and things are hum-drum, there's nothing quite like some variance of calypso music and permutation of rum, beans and pork to liven the mood. Living in Miami Beach and in Downtown, I took quality, cheap and tasty Cuban food for granted. Moving to Nashville, I had come to accept that my media noche days were at an end.

Or, were they?

Who would have thought that in this part of the metro (Crieve Hall, right?) one would find a real deal slice of My-am-mee? Readying myself for a dose of Miami 'tude, I was pleasantly surprised to find none whatsoever. Refreshing. I came for lunch on a busy Wednesday but as long as you know what you wanted, the process was efficient and fairly quick. After all, your food needs to be prepared. This isn't a grab-n-go or a sit-under-a-heat-lamp sort of place. You'll appreciate the freshness. After studying the menu, I ordered (in Spanish) the pan con lechon with a side of moros y cristianos. The lady behind the counter told me to cop a squat and wait for the goodness, so I did so. It was hard because the air was filled with delectable aromas. I have mentioned that I am trying to get away from eating pork but that becomes a real hardship when eating this sort of food. That is, a delicious hardship. Oy. This non-pork thing...

In no time at all, my food was ready. I paid, grabbed my sack of grub and hit the road. Once I got home, I tore into that bad boy. Oh man. I'd really missed this: pressed, crispy bread, wonderfully seasoned, tender pork, onions, MOJO!!! Oh man. Every bite was pure bliss. Man, Miami. Why are you such a messed up place to live? I need to eat your food on a regular basis. Not wanting my moros y cristianos to get cold, I broke out the hot sauce and started in on them. For those who might not know, moros y cristianos is black beans (moros) and rice (cristianos) made with garlic, onion, pepper, some sort of pork product, and herbs. It's a fairly ubiquitous side that can go wrong very easily (rice & beans ain't easy, y'all). I'm pleased to report that Back to Cuba's myc is well-made and I'd, gladly, order it again. 

Despite Nashville's growth, it might be a while before there's an abundance of Latin Caribbean eats in town. Fortunately, until there's more, Back to Cuba offers up a real deal menu to keep us all full & happy. Next time, I'm eating in.

4.5

Before I get too into this love letter, I have to say that the address has always been a concern of mine. For tourists interested in coming to LC or new transplants eager to see what the fuss is, y'all should all know that this isn't Nashville proper. You will drive a good ways away from the city limits to come here. Whether you want to call it Bellevue or Pasquo, it's all the same to me. You just shouldn't call it Nashville. Doing so, you're going to be surprised why you're so far away from all the other Nashville attractions you've read about and want to see.*

Logistics out of the way, The Loveless Cafe is everything that's wonderful about living in the Nashville metro area. To begin with, driving to it on Hwy 100 from the city is something that's pretty in every season, but early fall is my favorite time to do so. The winding road and turning leaves leave no doubt that you're in the southland and you're about to enjoy some fantastic eats. The drive really prepares you for the experience. Once you arrive... yep, you're here. TLC is an old motel. I think that adds to the charm. It looks like a movie set. Having the cafe and motel unchanged (where it counts) since the '50s is a testament to the power, honor and necessity of tradition. I am so pleased to know that no soulless developer (from out of town, no less) has been able to destroy what should never be touched. I wished the city of Nashville followed suit. So, charm, drive, motel... you're caught up. Park out front or along the back and get ready to do some serious eating.

This ain't the place to be if you're on a diet or (unfortunately) have dietary restrictions. This is heavy, sugary, fried Southern goodness. A steady diet of the stuff WILL kill you so only come here on special occasions. Give your name to the nice people up front and take your seat. Pro tip: don't come here on the weekend or for brunch. That's amateur hour. Come here for dinner during the week and you won't suffer through the pain of waiting behind a family from Modesto eager to take a group selfie with a gingham tablecloth background. I have to let folks know how to do things...

Okay, you're seated. Get ready to eat all the food. Remember, no diet/restrictions. Start with sweet tea and keep it coming. Next, say 'yes' to the biscuits and keep them coming. You're going to want to try all the preserves AND the butter, so save (at least) a biscuit half for each type. They're canned on site and they're delicious. I can't choose between the peach, strawberry or blackberry. They're all addictive. Okay. Strawberry. But I wouldn't turn any of them down. Next, you're here for dinner so go all in. Depending on the day of the week, you'll be able to choose from a special menu. I don't need anything special because if you're going all in on a Southern feast, you gotta go for the chicken. Get the half fried chicken. It'll come with the back, breast, wing, and drumstick. You won't be able to finish, so eat half of the half. Why won't you finish? Well, you're going to consume a gallon of sweet tea. The biscuits are coming to your table as fast as you can eat them. Oh, and you get sides with your chicken. The choices are awesome so choose wisely. As much as I wanted to go for cheese grits and greens (man, I could go for that now; I'm hungry), I chose the fried green tomatahs and mackincheese. I was very happy with both choices. The tomaters were crispy, nicely-breaded and flavorful on their own. Plus, the serving was generous. You're not going to receive one lone, sad tomato. The mac was a bit creamier than I like (I prefer the southernized, post-church baked and a wee bit crispy mac) but it was tasty nevertheless. I wanted to end with peach cobbler but I couldn't be a hero. I was stuffed to the point of discomfort and I had a long drive back to the city ahead of me. I am pretty sure I was food drunk. It's a thing. Next time, dessert. Next time.**

*Seriously. Look at a map. Does this look in town to you?
**Next time to be determined upon consultation with my physician.

3.5

What makes the experience at TTJ so memorable is the scene. Let's be honest. As excited as I am to have an izakaya in Nashville and have people, regularly, exposed to the awesomeness of Japanese pub culture, my food was a bit inconsistent. That said, what was good was really good and I'm happy to bring out of town guests here again and again. But, what excites me about doing so is the scene.

I've never been to Japan but I have been to a fair number of American izakayas in food cities, I assume, know to get it right (SF, NYC, Chicago). As far as the lighting, hum and drinks go, TTJ nails it. I like the fact that it's a bit dim. It's not 'get your mack on' dim. It's 'I've had a long day at work and want a drink' dim. And when it comes to drinks, TTJ delivers. The drink program is well nuanced, interesting and accessible to all tastes. I had a hard time deciding on what my poison for the evening would be... but I knew I wouldn't be able to resist anything called 'punch' for long. Yes, the sake punch drew me in and didn't let me go. When in Rome... er, Tokyo, right? Truth is, you'd be hard-pressed not to find several drinks that didn't press your buzzer and ring your bell. After work drinks with friends + TTJ = win.

Eating is a pretty good experience as well. I think you just need to know what to order. I started with the sunomono and it was a wonderful starter. Light and hit with the right amount of vinegar, the seafood (octopus and scallops) and vegetables (thinly sliced cucumber, and crunchy brussel sprouts & radish) married well to create a dish that made me feel healthy and worldly. Where I might have screwed up came with my choice of ramen. Instead of going fancy I should have kept it simple. But, I'm in Nashville, right? Chicken's a safe bet, right? Well, sort of. My broth was wonderfully seasoned and I happily slurped it and my noodles with abandon. Unfortunately, my tsukune was uneven. There's nothing not to like about (and, yes, I hear what I'm about to say) chicken balls except when they're uneven. My bites ranged from easy to bite to I-have-to-hold-this-with-my-fingers-to-bite-and-chew. You can guess that wasn't a pleasurable experience. It got to the point where I concentrated on the broth (the chili oil, egg, mushrooms, and greens added delectable depth and flavor) and avoided the protein altogether. My friend was going to town on his chashu so, maybe, that's the better option. I'll know for next time.

There will be a next time.

I finally got around to trying Silo and it didn't disappoint. When Nashville was establishing its 'it' status, there were a handful of restaurants/places that were helping to elevate the city past its mid-South borders. It's a bit much to try and hit them all (especially with new 'it' places popping up monthly*) but when there's an occasion, one should take the opportunity.

So it came to pass on a busy-ish Sunday in late spring that I had friends in town and a need to impress. Silo had been on my list but I thought it was closed on Sundays. A brief trek through Germantown revealed that to be a mistake and in a short amount of time, we were at the bar awaiting a table. This 'elevated Southern' trend is a tricky thing. I suppose for tourists from either coast, it can be a sure-fire way to experience 'authentic' Nashville but for anyone from Kentucky to Alabama, North Carolina to Arkansas, the thought of paying $30+ for shrimp & grits is a bit daunting. We eat this stuff all the time at family dinners for free. Why pay big money for something we can make? The answer: because you can't make it. At least, you can't make it like this. I am not a defacto fan of elevated Southern. In fact, I think much of it is a scam. But when it's done right, you'll savor every bite.

Silo does it right. Waiting at the bar for a table, I started my journey with a Smuggler's Lemonade. It had a subtle punch and wasn't too sweet. It was a nice way to start a meal and a very accessible cocktail. Reading the reviews about where to sit, we managed to snag a table in the back side room. It offered a private experience that enabled us to talk easily without screaming over each other. For my meal, what could I order but the shrimp & grits. It's my litmus meal at these sort of restaurants. With the first bite, I couldn't speak. The shrimp were succulent. The grits melted in my mouth. The sauce, onions, chives, and pork added depth to this low country favorite. I was hooked. This was a shrimp & grits dish I couldn't make, couldn't get at a relative's house and didn't flinch at all for paying ~ $25 for. Being that the plates are served solo, we got some sides to add to the reverie. I found the mac & cheese to be a bit gummy, gloppy and disappointing (definitely not worth the price tag) BUT the jalapeno corn bread and the greens more than made up for it. You can't just eat anyone's greens. To make them correctly takes time, finesse, seasoning, and experience. Bad greens can ruin your whole day. These greens will make you want to sing. Even if you think you don't like greens, order these greens. The side was large enough to be an entree portion. I was happy to split it. Nashville's current iteration owes a lot to places like Silo and the transformed Germantown. It's not too late to discover why.

*YMMV.

2.5

I was going to be generous with three stars but the odd accounting on my bill forces me to round down. I want Liberty Common to work much more than it did for me but I definitely don't want to leave and feel taken advantage of. That's a bummer. It has some key highlights (namely: location and decor) but the overall takeaway was that there are some things lacking. I'll explain.

I met some folks for brunch and, on Sundays, there's a live jazz band to add to the ambiance. I appreciated the effort but the acoustics were overpowering. LC is blessed with beautiful floors, high ceilings and windows and/or mirrors on the wall. That makes for gorgeous 'gram photos. It also makes for a deafening sound trap. For as talented as the musicians were, I was glad when they finished. Through no fault of their own, the music was just too loud and not at all conducive for having a conversation.

Sitting down, I knew eating would be a bit of a chore. The brunch mention is very gluten heavy. Even though my waiter tried to dissuade me of the notion by suggesting the quiche, when I asked if the crust was made me with flour he acquiesced that it was. I also made a note not to trust his gluten-free suggestions. So, as much as I wanted to get pancakes, waffles, fried chicken, or a burger, I settled on the cheese grits and pomme frites (online menu price $5, I was charged $6). These pomme frites were much thinner than I was expecting (no freshly cut potatoes here) but they were seasoned nicely and very addictive. Everyone at the table enjoyed their serving. Mine didn't come with a dipping sauce. I was fine with that but if you need ketchup or mayo, know to ask for it. The grits... were not successful. I just can't abide a restaurant in the south that can't execute grits. I don't trust the chef. These grits were neither creamy nor seasoned. The cheese was not integrated into the dish, rather it was served melted on top (like a French onion soup). I don't mind a coarse grits preparation but these were almost... pebbly? The other fellow at the table who got grits didn't care for his either.

The drink menu was much more successful and, in hindsight, I should have had a liquid brunch and kept it moving. I began with Le Dernier Papillon (online price $11, I was charged $12). Served in a coupe, this was a balanced and boozy gin cocktail (aided by the absinthe-adjacent genapi, color from the sour cherry and tart kick from the lime). I looked and tasted great. I should have stuck with it. Instead, I moved on to the Jean Tonique (online/menu price $10, I was charged $11). Served in a highball, this was/is a nicely fizzy strawberry-hibiscus gin & tonic. It was a bit sweet for the mouthfeel but nothing offensive. Coming from the previous drink, however, it was a bit jarring. 

My tablemates had some billing/accounting errors that I, obviously, should have paid more attention to. Of note: the taxes are broken up/itemized but they add up to the standard 9.25%. So, two drinks, grits, fries, tax, and tip came to just shy of $50. I know SoBro rents are high but this was a surprising price point for what I received. I'd come back to Liberty Common for post-work drinks but I'd keep an eye on the bill. There's potential here but I can't say that it makes sense just yet.

It had been years since I'd been to the 12 South Burger Up. I enjoyed my experience so it wasn't like I didn't return because I was bitter. I just wasn't compelled. Well, fast forward many years and a much closer location to me and the compulsion hit. I don't know that it was a good thing, though.

First off, this new complex in Edgefield is quite nice. I never would have known this was the old Turnip Truck. Kudos to redoing the space in a way that's inviting and attractive. I worry about over development in many of the historic neighborhoods (hi, City Council; are you there?) but this was a nice re-imagining of what could be. Well done. But, try as I might, I can't eat buildings. I was hankering for some type of burger and was willing to pay marked up prices to get one. Considering I first discovered Burger Up with a vegan, I didn't think anything of my order for a turkey burger on a GH bun (extra charge) with no mayo. For this side of town and this sort of business, this is a pretty standard order. And, I didn't receive any pushback for the order so... that's great.

I called it in and it was ready in 15 or so minutes. I paid my $15.50 (for a burger and fries; I should be slapped) and headed on out the door. The burger came with onion, romaine, tomato, and avocado. Standard ingredients that skew on the bit of the wet side. The GF bun didn't like any of this. It disintegrated into a mushy, unpalatable mess. The consistency and taste was very off-putting. Annoyed but not discouraged, I soldiered on, eating the burger in pinches, not bites.

Fast-forward a few hours later: pretty horrendous gastric distress. I felt ill. I was ill. I stayed ill. Cue the unhappiness with paying $15.50 for a burger that fell apart, had a bun that tasted awful and, ultimately, raged against my body. The Burger Up building is pretty but you can't eat buildings and I won't be eating their food again. Perhaps the universe was punishing me for pay $15.50 for a turkey burger. Lesson learned the hard way.

The fries were fine.

A million years ago when I used to live in Nashville, Fido was a regular on my Finals circuit. Cramming for the big exam? Red Velvet cake and coffee. Pulling an all-nighter with the study group? Red velvet cake and coffee. B!tching about certain professors? Red velvet cake and coffee. Stalk... er, follow... um... Red velvet cake and coffee.

The years have marched on and I no longer live up the road, but I still have fond memories of Fido. My, how you've grown. I wandered into Fido after a decade away (d'oh! Gave away those million years) and was pleased to see that it's still a staple of HV life and the food is as fantastic as remembered. I'd just gotten off a plane, so I wasn't in the mood for red velvet cake and coffee. I needed big boy sustenance. But, first I needed to visit the little boy's room. Why am I including such a detail? The bathroom is clean, spacious and awesomely green (the color). Clean bathrooms = happy me. Attention to detail here = great attention to what's on your plate. It matters.

The generously-portioned (and perfectly savory) salmon scramble was a nice welcome back to my old stomping grounds. The egg and fish cooperated well in the form of big chunks with every bite. Herb cream cheese and capers acted as support staff (taste?), while the red onions brought it all together. Rarely can one go wrong with hash browns in the southland. The ones with this dish proved me right. Toast is toast but tea isn't just 'tea.' There's tea and then there's brown water. I was served tea.

Nashville, I missed you.

I'm the 800th review? Nice! There's a reason why Etch is on the lips (literally?) of so many locals and visitors alike. It's only been 5 or so years (for Etch; not Zola) but in that time, Deb Paquette has helped to define what the new iteration of Nashville dining is. Look around town and you'll see her (and a few others') influence in plates, decor and POV. If you live in Nashville and are in tune to an elevated foodie culture* Etch has been part of your journey.

And since so many flock to the SoBro eatery, reservations and seating can be tough. So, what to do? Come for lunch. You're a local. You don't have to wait for the evening or a weekend to enjoy the spoils of the city's food scene. Come for lunch and enjoy the restaurant without any of the traffic jam that awaits during the evening hours. Since I'm a physician who enjoys healing myself, I took my own advice and met a friend for lunch. Even though our reservation (yes, make one) was for 11:30, I was surprised by how busy the dining room was. By the time we left, it was respectably full. Our two top by the window offered great light and enough space/privacy for a lunch meant for catching up and trading notes. Just what I ordered.

And what did I order? Well, it was five o'clock somewhere so a glass of wine needed to be in my hand. I was in the mood for a vouvray or vinho verde but didn't see either on the menu. Much as I was afraid of a potential spill, I opted for the cab blend. I greatly enjoyed it. A trip to Etch isn't fully realized without the cauliflower so we started with that. As soon as it hit the table, it was an experience for the eyes and nose. The beautifully roasted cauliflower complimented the vibrant orange and green on the plate. The decadent truffle oil filled the air around us and we dug in to the signature dish. It's as good as advertised. People mention it because it's a must order. So... order it. I was vacillating between the Latin Chicken salad and the Indian Chicken when our server's reaction pushed me over the edge. She was extremely helpful in every regard but when I mentioned I was thinking about the Indian Chicken, her face lit up and she gasped a bit. What can I say? If a dish elicits that sort of response, you order it! The plate was very tasty. The chicken was generously portioned and the meat fell off the bone. This being Etch, the sauce heightened the already-seasoned chicken to a new level. Expect spice without heat or an overpowering aftertaste. If you *are* sensitive to spice, the caraway mint yogurt sauce is there to cool you down (and add more flavor). The kale and fig added a nice depth to the plate and I found myself doing my best to combine all the flavors in every bite.

In my effort to one day be a laddie who lunches, Etch will be a permanent member of my rotation. After my friend and I were finished, we wondered why we didn't do this more often. 'This' being lunch at Etch. Indeed. Why?

And that, my friend, is 2000 reviews. Boom. Bring me some wine.

*Admittedly, a troubling turn of phrase.

2.5

I didn't get it.

I didn't get the effusive praise of some of the 5-star reviews. Unfortunately, my experience ran more along the lines of the majority of reviews. I don't know what's off here, but things are not clicking. Wait. I do know what's off. Well, some of what's off.

Product: My party came here on a Sunday night around 7. During the course of our stay, multiple dishes were no longer available. They were out of turkey. They were out of brisket. Heck, they were out of brownies. I don't understand why and how you can be out of so many various items on the menu. For a restaurant of this size and at this time of night during service, it doesn't make sense. Having to go with a third or fourth choice of item leads to a frustrating experience that many aren't willing to give another chance. 

When it came to the items we were able to taste, it was a mixed bag. To begin with, my daiquiri was painful. I know the description lists black pepper as an ingredient. For that reason, I wasn't going to order it. Our server, however (more on him in a bit), pushed the drink on me, downplayed the pepper qualities and spoke of the popularity of the libation. It was horrible. It was not at all suitable to my tastes. It was like drinking warm mezcal with black pepper. Any fruit notes were lost on me. Terrible. The papas bravas were boring. I was never asked how I wanted my burger and received a medium VERY rare patty to choke down. Given the service issues (coming), I decided to deal with it rather than send it back. The brussel sprouts were a better option and the beans were very good.

Service: It's been mentioned time and again as an issue here. I don't know why the front of the house isn't addressing this. It's been proven that people will go back to an establishment with okay food but good service but will rarely ever patronize a restaurant with stellar food and horrible service. As of my experience, the food quality did not make up for the forgettable, dismissive experience we had. 

As I mentioned, my group came here on a Sunday night. We did not have reservations. At the time, such weren't a possibility. We waited for 45 minutes and were seated up front by the kitchen, rather than in the belly of the restaurant. Oh well. I came to the restaurant with a friend from college who was contemplating moving back to Nashville from NYC. I brought her and her husband here in an attempt to convince her the move was a good choice. She's still in NYC. Our server was dismissive, inattentive and condescending -- from the very beginning. His behavior made no sense. Water was hard to come by. He didn't explain the menu or how plates were coursed. He talked over our decisions and talked us in to plates we weren't quite sure about. He didn't ask about allergies. He never inquired how we wanted meat items prepared. He paid no attention to service requests (say, bringing my beer out to the table with my burger; he brought my beer during a lull in the service so by the time by medium rare burger came to me, my beer was half-consumed and warm). Ultimately, he did nothing to add to the dining experience and, in fact, detracted from it. It was a frustrating experience for the table and an embarrassing one for me (since I suggested the debacle of the evening).

I didn't get it.

The Thompson has come out of the gate doing a lot of things really well. I haven't stayed at the hotel but I am impressed with the properties they have on site. They're all different but they all adhere to the same standard. As crowded as The Gulch is, there are now many more reasons to Lyft your way to the neighborhood.

One of those reasons is Killebrew. Set just off the lobby of the hotel, this upscale coffee shop has everything you need: friendly baristas, excellent drink choices, pastries, a great soundtrack, comfortable seating, and interesting decorative elements that invite you in to the space. When I went, there wasn't a menu so the barista rattled off an impressive list of coffee choices. I can't imagine that doing so over and over again is fun so, I'm guessing, menus are forthcoming. Not being much of a coffee guy (I'll drink the stuff but I don't go looking for it), I opted for a chai... as did my friend. But, here's the rub: there were two chai choices. One was the typical masala chai (I got). My friend got the tumeric variety! I loved the fact that there were two, distinct chai options in addition to all the various coffee varietals. There was a slight mix-up and we were given our orders in to-go cups, despite saying that we planned to stay in the shop but that's a trifling matter. The shop *is* small so I would warn against posting up with a laptop and taking valuable real estate. If you *have* to do something like that, the hotel offers seating just outside the shop that should accommodate all your won't-work-from-home needs. 

The two chais with tax came to just shy of $10. Yes, it's overpriced but it's The Gulch. You have to expect it. I'm not much of a coffee guy and I don't go seeking it out but when I am in the neighborhood and I want to rest for a bit and warm up in the coming winter (if it ever gets cold), I know just where I'm headed.

This rating is an improvement. After my first trip to Top Golf, I was pretty determined to not ever come back. As is described in far too many of the reviews on this page, the service was horrible. Not one person with whom I interacted (or observed) was friendly, kind or gracious. I didn't take it personally as everyone around me had a similar experience. Again, I know the Nashville service industry is going through a rough patch but management has got to stay on top of these problems. An nasty staff will drive away customers... which will tank your business.

So, yeah. Mean. Nasty. (Unfortunately) typical of this TG location. I wasn't coming back and I was alright with that. Fast forward to a recent Sunday night and the party I was with didn't want to go home. We were in the general area and no one (except for me) had been here so... here we go. I didn't tell anyone that I'd had a not-so-great time here before (I didn't even review it) so the expectations weren't skewed. We had... an alright time. Coming off a terrible time, that's a win. I still experienced AWFUL service at the main floor bar (eye rolls, sighs and minimal spoken words) but the upstairs bar was a much better experience (friendly, talkative bartender who, although busy, realized that a smile = good tip).

On the main floor, we sat in one of the hitting bays. I wasn't in the mood to hit balls* so I sat at the table, sipped my drAnk and made commentary. Wanting to maximize my dollar, I went with the Mai Colada. The description described a mix of two rums, orgeat, pineapple juice, lime juice, a rum floater, and a popsicle. I know I got the popsicle. I didn't get the floater. I'm unsure of the rest. The drink was boozy and my friends were having a good time so I didn't want to rock the boat. After the game, most left but my buddy wanted one more drink. Unwilling to go back to the mean bartender, I suggested heading upstairs to hang out at the open air bar. This was a better call. The bartender here was nice, the air was surprisingly decent (not humid) and the people watching was hilarious. For my upstairs/outdoor drink, I went with the melon cooler. Vodka, St. Germain, cane sugar, lemon juice, watermelon made for a crisp, refreshing drink. I think there was a cucumber component (it's in the name and the drink is green) but I might be making that up.

I left Top Golf slightly buzzed (rideshares FTW all the time!) and in a good mood. This is a win. The bar may be low but when things have been BAD in the past (just look at some of the lower-starred reviews), I'll take a win where I can find one. I might be up for a return visit... upstairs.

*Grow up.

Official 'no tipping' has arrived in Nashville. So, 'no tipping' doesn't really mean 'no tipping.' It means that the price point is higher on the front end, so as to achieve a living wage to the folks who work there. So, think of it as 'tip included.' I spent $35 (including tax) on my cocktail and entree, if that gives you a sense of what to expect.

TKO is brand-spankin' new and needs to work out some kinks. That said, they're surprisingly put together for such a new venture. The building is just the one you're thinking of: the new brick complex that sprung up out of nowhere on Gallatin, towards the northern edge of Inglewood. Without even looking at the address, I knew that's where I was heading. The dining room is a bit sparse and without personality. As time goes by, I expect that to change -- especially given the unique POV (Southern + Chinese?). What is full of personality, though, is the wait staff. Our server was funny, engaging and very involved. She made us fell welcomed and explained the menu quite well.

And, let's talk about the menu: it's small. Again, TKO is new and it makes sense that they start small with tried and true plates that customers like and grow from there rather than having to edit a large menu. I started the meal with a No. 3 cocktail. It's a combination of Rye icepick Rittenhouse, lemon, ginger, apple, and angostura. I felt the taste was a bit muted and muddied. I wouldn't order it again; I want some punch when it comes to my cocktails. It was fine but at $11, I want to know that I'm going to enjoy my drink. Points for an interesting combination, though. I wrestled with a couple of entree options but ultimately decided on the lamb mapo tofu. After being shocked at how quickly our food came to the table, I was able to enjoy the smells from the plates that surrounded me. This is a decently spicy plate of crumbled lamb, chili paste, fried tofu, onion, and szechaun pepper. The rice (this dish definitely needs rice) was $3 extra. I was a bit put out by that. I don't think you should create a dish that needs rice -- and, then, charge extra for it. I also agree with another yelper that the portion size doesn't quite add up to the price point. I am going to give TKO the benefit of the doubt because they're new and trust that as time goes on, either the portion size or price will change (probably the former). But, if I am honest, I just crossed the line into 'full' but was nowhere near 'stuffed.' Depending on how you eat, this could be a good or bad thing. But, no matter how much larger my belly became, my mouth was very happy with the food.

TKO's an interesting addition to the Nashville culinary landscape. I'm curious to see how neighborhood folks and food fans (I hate the 'f----e' word) take to it. I'm also eager to see what crops up around it. That Nobel Prize winner was on to somethin' when he wrote about changin' times...

Eastwood? Porter Heights? Rosebank? I never know what to call this part of town. The boundaries tend to change depending on to whom you ask. I'm gonna say TC is on the Rosebank side of the Eastwood/Rosebank border. I could be wrong.*

The reason I mention all of this is because you are going to want to make sure that you can find TC without issue. It's a great addition to the city's coffee scene and, especially for its neighborhood, stands alone in offering great breakfast and java options. Now, with all the cheese-stands-alone action going on, know that the parking lot is a bit on the Mad Max side (Nashville drivers, please do better) and the actual cafe is a bit tight but if you know these things going in to the experience, you'll do just fine.

The owner, Khalil, is a really affable chap and it doesn't seem like he has a stranger in his life. During the 3.5 hours I posted up at the Cafe, person after person came in to great him with a smile and hug. That says a lot, people. His warm personality is infectious and will make your frown turn upside down. Guaranteed. The standout accent of the airport terminal-themed cafe is the rounded pink bar. It grabs your attention and makes you want to sit there. If you do, I recommend sitting a couple of seats over from the soda dispenser. The other side of the bar is directly beneath the vent and the cold air is not shy about blowing on you. Sitting there can also offer a bit more arm room if you're eating and not just sipping on coffee. There are a few small tables and some small chairs in the entry. If you have some girth to you, you may want to avoid those chairs. Jus' sayin'. Oh, the soundtrack. I don't know if it changes everyday but my Friday was made better by listening to all the 80s hits that flowed one after another.

3.5 hours? Did you eat? Yes. Of course. I can't stand people who sit up in coffee shops, take up valuable real estate and wifi (it's free here) and gingerly sip on water. Get.Up. This is not your house. Khalil is too nice to read you so I will: either spend money and keep spending it or leave. You want to hang out? Go to a library. Read a book. This is a business. After I side-eyed a good number of people complicating my ability to tickety-tackity and eat and sip, I was much better. For breakfast, I decided on a seasonally-appropriate honey vanilla chai latte and the classic waffle. The waffle is a handsome selection of 3 GLUTEN-FREE wedges, powdered sugar, maple syrup, butter, and jam. It also comes with candied applewood bacon. Pour the syrup and butter over everything and eat the waffle with the bacon. You're welcome. My chai came in a large cup (my favorite) and was a taste of autumn with every sip. When i took the time to glance up from my meal, I took in some Star Wars playing on the wall. You read right. Before leaving, I ordered a Ploughman's Plate to go. This is a meat & cheese lovers' dream: four kinds of meat, 3 kinds of cheese, olives, and pickles. Be serious about meat & cheese or don't order this. It almost did me in. I am not a meat & cheese pro.

I'll be back for more. Terminal Cafe fills some serious holes re location, coffee and meal time. It's time is now. Check it out... just not when I want to come and spread my arms a bit. I needs mah space. 

*I rarely am.

Absolutely lovely. This is the high-end restaurant Nashville's been waiting for. May this be the beginning of a trend of similar spots opening throughout the metro. I've had the pleasure of eating at many Besh restaurants in New Orleans. Marsh House stands proudly among their crowd. If you love food and haven't been here yet, you're wasting time.

The menu may harken back to a Louisiana made from swamp-myth and Spanish moss, however the reality of the decor is a vibrant, yet coolly modern take on what restaurant scene looks like in the here and now: high ceilings, impressive bars, intimate tables made of heavy wood (and heavier chairs), light fixtures that promote conversation and a color scheme that instantly relaxes. You may wonder why I am spending time talking about such 'secondary' touches. You have to realize: a restaurant like Marsh House doesn't leave these details to chance. They are deliberate and deserve to be noticed. Notice them.

But don't spend too much time on the environment. You have drinks to drink and food to eat. I began my meal with the Millwood cocktail. This purple rum delight took me back to my Lower Garden District apartment and made me want to stay there for a spell. It was delicious. Yes, it lingered a bit too long on the sweet side but the drink was distinctly Louisiana: in color, taste and punch. Bayou drankin' is no place for 'oh, that's too sweet' protests. Git diabeetus or git out of the way. I balanced that drink with some vegetables... and pork. The brussel sprouts were about the best I have had. These petit cabbages were drenched in honey, pecans and pork cracklins. They were sinfully good. You won't want to share but your [anything] levels demands that you should give, at least, one or two of those bad boys away... if for no other reason than to gloat that you have a bowl of goodness in front of you and many more to scarf down.

I wanted to get the seafood stuffed flounder for my main but the bready stuffing chased me to my number two pick: the pork. Three cheers to bread because this piggy dish was dyn-o-mite. The vehicle for the pork was dirty rice. The sweet succulence of the pork was balanced by the fermented crunch of the 'southern' kimchi. I know it's gauche of me to admit but I wanted a pour some Louisiana hot sauce on my plate and ask for a side of red beans. I'm not a huge fan of making southern dishes expensive (low country is, by definition, cheap food; that's how the people who lived there could afford to eat it). But this dish, elevated and redefined for a fancy setting, was a heap of food for $22. In this context, that's a steal. I paired this plate with a red (Roero?) that was lighter than the Cab I thought I wanted but proved to be a perfect compliment to the food. And, speaking of compliments, the staff is extraordinary. From the hostess who greeted & sat us, to the bus boy who attended to our left overs, to the som who suggested the wines, to our outstanding server Amy/Violet... Marsh House has put together a team of winners. 

This is not a joke, Nashville. This is not a test. Marsh House has come to dominate. Game on.

4.5

I hadn't been to Uncle Bud's since law school. Honestly, due to the ravages of time/age, I'd forgotten about it but I found myself in Donelson looking for some rare books. Once I stumbled upon UB, all the giant mason jar memories came pouring back. I knew I had to return to overindulge on fried perfection.

Luckily, my neighbors were in search of a Sunday afternoon lunch spot that was casual, easy on the wallet and baby friendly. I knew *just* the place. A quick jaunt later and we were at Uncle Bud's. What I hadn't considered: the post-church crowd. A morning of stern looks [redacted] or raucous praise [redacted] works up an appetite and these saints were hungry! I pushed past the multitudes to put in our parties' name and then came outside to start the diabeetus™. Just as I remembered, Uncle Bud's provides SWEET tea by the gallon (literally) to impact your pancreas as you wait. Our 20-minute wait time extended to thirty but who's counting when you are playing Russian roulette with sugar? Seriously, I kept a death grip on my cup despite 'complaining' of the sugar levels. Once we sat (with my cup of sugar tea), we were greeted by the kindly Brittany who brought up fixins (beans, slaw and hush puppies; can I get an 'amen' for those hush puppies??) and took our drink orders. My friends opted for water. Me? Another sweet tea, please!*

Sundays are ALL YOU CAN EAT fried chicken days. Said fried chicken comes with never ending gravy, fries and biscuit. Despite coming here for catfish could I really compare never ending fried chicken with one piece of fish? No. No, I couldn't -- and neither can you. With every bite, I knew I was making a mistake but I couldn't push away from the table. My sexy fed. My blood got thicker. My organs screamed for relief... yet onward I pushed. My neighbors were a bit frightened but are much too kind to say anything. They simply mentioned 'getting dessert' as a way to make my savory onslaught stop. The dessert options of the day were banana pudding and peach cobbler. The pudding came topped with whipped cream and the cobbler came topped with ice cream. We got both (to share between 3 people). To my shock, I enjoyed the pudding better. I *don't* like banana pudding and this tasted fresh. It was ice box cold, had chunky bananas and the vanilla wafers were hard and crisp, not wilty and mealy like I remember from my afterschool programs. The cobbler tasted a bit off to me. As fresh as the pudding tasted, the cobbler tasted like it was made with canned peaches. I didn't care for it. But with as much as my big ass ate, I needed a reason to push back from the table. 

Uncle Bud's should only be a biannual - tops - excursion (if you want to live) but if you come here, do it up and do it right. Now, if you'll excuse me, I'll be splitting my time between the gym and standing in front of a mirror, shirtless, asking myself why I ate this way. Why is delicious deadly?

*I do it to myself. I do.

Who would have thought there would be such a legit Japanese restaurant smack dab in the heart of Downtown Nashville? Well, don't think too hard about it because Ichiban is here and fantastically real. The warm wood, full bar and expansive menu offers many experiences far past maki, I have found this restaurant to be one of the Music City's finest offerings when it comes to rolls.

The only real issue is getting here. Ichiban doesn't have a parking lot and its location on 2nd Ave means that parking is an adventure in frustration. I can count on one hand the number of times I've been able to score street parking anywhere near the joint. So, when planning an evening here, think about transportation well in advance. Otherwise, you're setting yourself up for a bad time. Once you've figured out parking, however, everything else is aces.

Whether dining in or eating out, make sure you take advantage of the marvelous maki that awaits at Ichiban. Being that I don't enjoy cream cheese or mayo or any sort on my rolls (come on, Americans; we can do better than that), my taste in rolls falls pretty squarely in the sushi chef's wheelhouse. I've been impressed by the Ichiban roll, spider roll, holly roll, rainbow roll, and caterpillar roll. All five have fantastic flavor, good balance, a nice amount of pieces for the prices, and none of the devil's condiments on raw fish. When feeling particularly hungry, you might even find me ordering a crab salad. 

While not the trendiest or most fab (location-wise) of sushi establishments in Nashville, Ichiban offers up really good product again and over again. Those 2nd Ave rents aren't cheap, y'all. Ichiban has to be doing something right to be staying in business for so long. If you haven't discovered what that is as of yet... change that. Soon.

3.5

Considering I can barely read the notes I made on the place AND I fell asleep here, I suppose The Rusty Nail did exactly what it was supposed to do. When I first moved to New Orleans, I looked in to buying a place in the Warehouse District. I was talked out of it by my mentor (he gave me life-changing advice on waiting to buy a house/vehicle; life-changing) and I wound up renting in the Lower Garden District. It's pretty fantastic to see how the Warehouse District has grown and taken over. I suppose if the me from many moons ago had bought that condo, I may have become a regular at The Rusty Nail.

The frozen Pimms Cup was enough to make me sit up and notice -- or, you know, slump over and pass out. Potato, Potatoe. This is, certainly, a place for groups. Despite hordes of people descending on the bar at the same time, I didn't have to wait for a drink nor did the bartenders seem fazed by the madness. It must have something to do with all the ample room. When I first walked in, I thought the front bar was all there was to the place. Then, I stepped outside and got a load of the courtyard. It goes on for miles and miles (or, feet and feet). The large square footage and ample seating lulls you in to extended conversation, more drinks and bad decisions. I enjoyed the chill vibe of the place (again, despite the madness all around). I don't really understand the name but, on the other hand, I don't think I want to run afoul of a rusty nail, so it's all good gravy. 

When in the neighborhood, check it out -- and go straight for the frozen Pimms Cups. No one does frozen drinks like New Orleans. Just try and stay awake.

I finally made it out to King Market. It's been on my radar for years but laziness and inertia kept me from coming here. I told myself that I couldn't abide the I24 traffic to come eat at a restaurant. Surely, I had just as good options within Nashville. No need to travel... right?

Maybe. As far as I know, most (all?) Lao offerings are going to be found southeast of the city's boundaries so if you want it, you need to travel for it. I had an outstanding lunch date with a business partner so when he asked if I had time to meet up for lunch, I asked how he felt about heading to Antioch. It was now -- as the kids say -- on. First off, the drive to Antioch (given the right time and day) wasn't bad at all. After I arrived at King Market, I wondered why I had built up the travel time in my head.* The turn in to the parking lot is sharp so be prepared for it. I had to engage in some Nashville driving™ and I wasn't too proud of that. Know, too, that the restaurant is in the rear of the grocery store. It's clearly marked but be aware and respectful. There are folks in the joint who just want to get some kitchen items and get out. Don't clog up their day with foolishness. Wait to be seated, grab a seat and start looking over the menu. As with similar restaurants I've frequented, the wait staff isn't here to be your friend. They have a job to do and you need to do your part by being ready when they are. 

I'd done my research; I was ready: an oolong tea and dry sukiyaki, please. Done. Like a boss. The tea came cold and in a very large glass. It was slightly sweet and very drinkable. Before I went all in, however, I knew to hold my horses. Ain't no free refills in this house (I see you; game recognizes game) so I was going to have to slowly sip on this brown goodness. Before too long, my meal came out. My friend got the same thing yet our plates looked a bit different. I avoided the urge to go ham and, instead, concentrated on the awesome smell beneath my nose. As soon as I started in (with chopsticks; no forks), I knew I had chosen wisely. Sticky noodles, medium spice, large, flavorful shrimp, delicious beef, crunchy vegetables, and light sauce (more binder than soup) made for very happy times in my mouth and belly. At $9 it's the priciest noodle option, but it's very filling and satisfying. Plus, it's less than $10 for a meal that will fill you up and keep you happy.

But I wasn't done.

I mean, I was done eating but I fell into the trap. When ever I visit an 'ethnic' grocer**, I can't resist finding and buying all sorts of beverages I can't find at Publix. When I saw the electric green Fanta with hard-to-identify fruit on the label, it was on a poppin'. I grabbed a cart and just started taking all sort of drinks with jellies, hard-to-find fruits and bright colors. I drew a line at 'white fungus.' That actually snapped me out of my reverie. I try not to yuck other people's yums, especially when it comes to me being outside my lane but... no. No white fungus. But bird's nest soda aside, I bought 9 drinks and they're chilling (literally) in my refrigerator for consumption when I have guests. No, I won't share them. I will show them off. That's how I host.

*Driving back in to town and seeing the traffic leaving Nashville heading southeast reminded me why I24 is evil and I do my level best to stay away from it.
**Yuck. I hate that term.

I don't know what took me so long to come here. Well... actually, I do. I'd read terrible things about the service. My former assistant was treated dreadfully by the staff here. And now that I am eating gluten-free, I don't want to tempt myself with plate after plate of pastas and pizzas. So, I guess I had some good reasons for not coming here. 

But it came to pass that an old friend was coming in town and No Reservations had gotten City House on his mind. Nothing I could say was going to dissuade him of his choice. So, off to Germantown I went. I took a deep breath and walked in and... a very pleasant hostess let me know my friend was at the bar. She told me that as soon as he settled up* at the bar, we could have a seat. He was one step ahead of both of us so we were able to sit immediately. As we started to catch up in the downstairs kitchen space, our server came by. I braced myself for attitude and he couldn't have been more pleasant. I ordered a Juno and asked for some time to go over the menu. My cocktail was very appropriate for summer. Staying on trend with gin, I was helped to a healthy mix of Carpano Bianco vermouth, Prosecco and grapefruit. I might have to try my hand at making this at home.

Because we were catching up, we hadn't had much chance to pour over the menu when our waiter returned. He understood and gave us more time. Before he took off, though, I asked him about gluten-free options... and braced myself for an eyeroll. I would have given one myself: who comes to an Italian eatery and complains about gluten? Rather than nastiness, he smiled and was very patient in going over my options. He mentioned a few dishes I was already looking at but raised an eyebrow when he suggested I try the rigatoni. Um, what? After I clarified that said pasta was made with flour, he apologized for the suggestion and I made a note to self to just go ahead and order what looked safe. We ended up sharing three dishes: the scrapple (served with 100% gluten-free (read corn) cornbread crumbs), the octopus and the chicken sugo. The scrapple was a bit neater than I'd imagined. It was served as a crispy, hot 'loaf' (for lack of a better word) and it was a savory, salty gem. What a fantastic way to begin the meal. I'd requested a glass of rose to accompany the larger plates and found the wine to pair well with both my seafood and poultry. The octopus was a generous portion of mollusk, white beans, corn, and parsley. It sounds simple. It tasted incredible. As good, though, as the scrapple and octopus were, my hands down favorite was the chicken sugo. Smoked chicken, tomato and grits served under a block of ricotta cheese. With every bite, I understood more and more why Chef Tandy received his Beard Award. I was very pleased with my meal.

Despite sitting in the kitchen area, I didn't notice the acoustics issues others mention. I heard everything clearly that night -- even the two top next to us complaining about the noise. I didn't quite understand how 'southern food' and Italian intersected but after dining here, I have a much better idea. My City House experience was a positive one and I am a bit rueful that it took me so long to come here.

*This rule drives me crazy. I get it. It's ubiquitous. But I also thinks it lacks grace. We're committing to eating at your restaurant. Transfer the tab to the table and let's do without the slight criminal accusation that is a part of making one pay a bill (before one pays another bill) ten feet away from where one is dining.

I mean... I knew it would be good but... damn! This spot is fan-freaking-tastic. In a city that's really resting on its culinary laurels, Peninsula throws down the gauntlet and offers an experience that is unlike any other in town. If you're tired of paying premium prices for yet another 'elevated Southern dish,' make your way over to Greenwood and prepare to take a vacation in your mouth.

Peninsula makes an immediate impression. From the moment you turn on to Eastland and wonder where these condos came from, you'll forget all about it once you take a gander at the large windows that make up the walls of the dining room. The high ceilings lead your eye to rounded archways, hanging plants and chandeliers that recall the Iberian Peninsula (oh... right). Listen and you'll fall in love with a soundtrack that's as comfortable as it is entertaining. The music won't distract from your meal but it fills in the empty moments where/when you're too busy eating to talk. The space isn't huge (35 seats) but it offers a variety of 2-,4- and larger tops, plus bar seating. That said, you'll want to make reservations... just to be on the safe side.

Since Craig Schoen is large and in charge, you know the drink program is going to be phenomenal. Craig is the reason why Inglewood Lounge and Rudy's got off to such strong starts. The man knows drinks and can come up with concoctions that had to have come from a spell book, they're so good. Peninsula is more of the same. Bucking the easy out of focusing on whiskey, Peninsula, instead, offers a gin & tonic menu. It's adventurous, daring and different. No one else is doing this. Not being one for gin, I was a little hesitant to try but a.) when in Spain/Portugal, drink gin and b.) Craig. So, after a quick tutorial from Jillian (more on her in a bit), I decided on the #4: gin malfy (think 'limoncello'), lemon, orange, and tonic. The result is a mild, extremely drinkable citrus take on a gin & tonic. My buddy's #1 (with fermented blackberries and fennel) had much more of the traditional juniper/herbal taste of a gin & tonic. With eight varieties, you're bound to find something you like. My second cocktail of the evening was The Life Aquatic. How could it not have been? This rum, berry and citrus cocktail was deep, round and just the seafaring potent potable you'd want for day/night drinking. I want to come back and try my hand at the wine offerings. I have full faith in what Craig tells me to drink.

I also have faith in the food set in front of me. Peninsula offers small, shareable plates (because Spain) and while the flavor combos may seem tricky, they're all delicious. Jillian suggested (between two people) to get 4-5 plates. I would opt for 5 because the food is so good you're going to want to try as much of it as you can. Because my belly has betrayed me, I needed to eat gluten-free. No worries. There's an abundance of gluten-free options on the menu. No matter your dietary hang up, you're going to eat well. Plates come out as they're ready and the menu ranges from smaller to larger so have fun and eat up. We tried the rock shrimp (the presentation reminded me of ceviche; the protein was plentiful and delectable; paired with horseradish and radicchio, the texture components blended as well as you might think), the serrano ham (unreal; not at all salty, sliced razor thin and served with tomato butter and a grilled bread I couldn't eat but looked and smelled like heaven; I had it on good authority that the bread was magnificent) and the rabbit. Whatever else you get, get the rabbit. If you order nothing else, order the rabbit. This was the best rabbit I've ever had and I used to live in New Orleans (where it's on a LOT of menus). Braised and served in a garlic broth you'll want to drink, this rabbit was wonderfully tender and seasoned with the garlic, French pepper and aromatics of the broth. For those who can eat bread, I was told that the croutons that came with the meal were divine. I would bottle the broth as I could. It might have been the best thing I've eaten in a very long time.

Lastly, a quick word about the people. From Craig to Jillian to Yuriko, everyone with whom I interacted was warm, informative, funny, and incredibly passionate about this project. Their energy was impressive and it means a lot when a staff is all in to what they're doing and makes the customer feel welcomed and important. Their good vibes added to an already incredible evening.

Peninsula offers innovation, whimsy and diversity to Nashville's dining scene. It's a needed shot in the arm in the complacency that's come over recent local food culture. Craig Schoen and co. are the future of good eats in Nashville and I am here for it. Without a doubt, Peninsula is the next restaurant experience you need to have. Without.a.doubt.

I really wished I'd had a better food experience. Most everything else about Milk and Honey was enjoyable. Perhaps I bear some of the blame for coming here for dinner rather than breakfast/brunch? Maybe I should have began my relationship with M&H by focusing on its strengths? I dunno.

Despite all the fanfare around the opening, I hadn't been in a rush to come to M&H. I'm not the sort to automatically discount chains but I do like to give the local counterparts my initial attention. Add to this the fact that I don't get to The Gulch that often* and M&H fell further and further down my list. But after a night of wondering around the neighborhood, my buddy got hungry and suggested we check it out. He'd been to M&H before and was a fan. So, off we went.

First thing I noticed was the build out. It's impressive. A deft use of indoor/outdoor space, the color black and good lighting makes one want to spend time here. The next thing I noticed: the employees were all really kind. From the gent who showed us to our table, to our waitress, to the manager, to the food runner... everyone was authentically engaging and not nice for nice's sake. It was almost shocking. A sad commentary, I know. Things were headed in a good direction. I pumped the brakes on the vibes by telling my waitress about my tricky gut and gluten issues. I told her it wasn't a huge deal and I would get a salad if a plate of food wasn't an option. She asked the kitchen and came back to tell me about my options. It worked in my favor because my eye was on the Cali Grilled Chicken and it was safe for me to eat!

When the plate arrived at the table... I was disappointed. To my mind, the description didn't live up to the execution. The first disappointment was the presentation. For a plate that reads 'Grilled chicken breast, avocado, sweet potato, brown rice, black sesame, beet, pickled red onion, garlic, kale, feta, white bean purée, carrot, buttermilk cucumber sauce, and chili', I was a bit shocked at how pedestrian everything looked. 'Hospital cafeteria' came to mind. But, the aroma was nice and food is to be eaten, not Instagrammed so I pressed on. I took a bite and... okay. It was okay. Honestly, I found the plate a bit boring and under seasoned. For so many bold flavors (on the page), I didn't understand how 'meh' it tasted in my mouth. Not finding success with the dry components, I mixed everything together and topped the plate with the three accompanying sauces (coconut-chili, another chili and, I think, a lime juice). By then the plate looked *really* unappealing but it tasted better.

Maybe breakfast/brunch is the better call?

*Although lately I have been there a lot!

Once I moved back to Nashville, I was intent on getting out of the city and understanding the nearby 'burbs. Franklin was tops on my list. And, when in Franklin, how can you not not visit the Boat House?

It's pretty tremendous that such an establishment exists. Tennessee is, firmly, landlocked. Yet, at the Boat House, you're guaranteed fresh seafood flown in daily. For all those who think they've done the Puckett's thing because they've had dinner Downtown (Nashville), think again. The Boat House is doing its own thing and it's fantastic. First off, there's ample parking. I get it: apples & oranges but not having to figure out a parking or valet situation is always a welcome experience. Secondly, there are three different businesses going on here: there's the oyster bar, there's the main dining room and there's the wine bar. Depending on the type of experience you're going after, you'll choose the room/menu best suited for you. I've been here twice for lunch: once in the wine bar and once in the main dining room. Both experiences were well worth the drive from Nashville.

Come here expecting low country cuisine. There's bbq... but there's, likely, some kind of sea creature attached to it. The shrimp & grits are a must. Try them either straight up... or in hush puppy form. Yep. I wrote 'hush puppy.' This ain't your city's Puckett's. The po' boys are filling and the hot fish sandwich is something you need to try. If you're attempting to have a lighter lunch, I found the side house salad and bowl of gumbo filled me and satisfied my taste buds but didn't stuff me. For the teetotalers, you can't go wrong with the Arnold Palmer. For those who enjoy grown-up juice, take advantage of the well-curated wine menu and fancy up your eats. But, whatever you do, save room for dessert. The Key Lime Pie sent me in to fits of pure bliss -- and I first had it only weeks after moving from south Florida. It, like everything else on the menu, is the real deal.

No matter which part of the property you park your bottom, you're sure to have great service (never have I encountered a sour puss) and a good vibe. The oyster house is good for sports lovers. The main dining room offers live music. The wine bar spills out onto a patio that overlooks the river (creek? ha!). In cooler months, it even boasts a fire pit. What more do I need to write to convince to come on down? Actually, strike that. After reading what I wrote, you shouldn't need a hard sell. 

Park in back.

Having been stricken with this gluten-problematic belly has taken some getting used to. The hardest adjustment, however, has been curbing my addiction to baked goods. While the result has been good for my waistline (oh, *there* are my feet; good to see y'all again), the parts of my brain that lit up when eating chocolate chip cookies have been sad for a while now. So, when I read there was a new bakery in town that had gluten-free treats, I had to get over and try it out!

There's a lot to like, folks. First off, there's parking. This stretch of 8th in Edgehill has gone from, largely, vacant to surprisingly busy within the past few months so having dedicated parking is a big deal. Secondly, like most things 'new bakery', the goods are very Instagrammable so come prepared to show off your eats to the world. Thirdly, the people are nice. This is essential for bakeries. Good juju when it comes to this sort of business is part and parcel of what you're paying for. Bakeries with bad attitudes are no bueno. Haven't you read/seen Like Water For Chocolate? That isht gets in the food. When eating sweet treats, you have to have good energy behind the making. Got it? Good. Now, let's get to the eating.

When I was there, there were three gluten-free options: pb & oat bar, a cherry blondie and a chocolate tarte. I ordered all 3. Seriously. And a cup of dark roast (Frothy Monkey) coffee. My eyes were bigger than my stomach but I got the tarte to go, so there's that. I am a coffee cup nerd. I collect them. I love them. Baked on 8th serves coffee in a wide assortment of cups. That scores major points with me. It's the little things. My pb bar was delicious. I inhaled it. I tried to concentrate on what I was eating... but no. Paired with the coffee, there was no slowing me down. I took my time (necessity; I was getting full) with the blondie. The cherries added a nice (different) flavor and texture to what could have been a predictable dessert. The blondie was very generously sized so you get your money's worth. Plus, there were plenty of corner pieces (for the bar as well) to choose from.* I'm saving the tarte for dessert tonight but if the first two items were any indication, I'm sure to enjoy it.

In a town like Nashville, gluten-free (vegan, etc.) items at bakeries are expected but not always delivered. Finding a place that serves said items is still rare enough to be a treat. Finding a place that serves them *well* is a place to visit over and over again.**

*I am team corner piece.
**For all you who have no gluten issue, my friend devoured her cinnamon roll and banana bread and took her iced lemon cookie to go. While there, I saw people go crazy for cake slices, as well. There's a LOT to choose from. Enjoy!

Let's get it out of the way: Sky Blue Cafe is a hipster nightmare. If you're averse to a certain segment of the city, you may be a wee bit uncomfortable here. Walking in, prepare to see plastic glasses of various thickness and color, facial hair of various lengths, jeans tighter than men should ever want to wear, and various other accoutrements of the hipster battle armor.
