It's true. But if you can get past all of that, you'll discover one of the better breakfasts and lunches in the metro area. For food this good, you can put up with uncombed hair. You can.

I say all this and recognize that my opening moments at the Cafe were rough. I was meeting a friend for lunch and to talk shop and things were unnecessarily tense from the beginning. Because we were there for a late(r) lunch on a Friday, there was no wait and, surprisingly, there were multiple available seating arrangements. Despite this, we were seated in the doorway. It was a particularly cold early spring day and the constant 'whoosh' of frigid air wasn't doing it for me, so I asked if we could move to the center/communal table or to a four top (the ones in the corner were being used by parties of 2).

"I can't move you."

"Oh? But there's open seating."

"We have a party coming in that's going to sit there."

(internally) "Where's 'there'? The communal table? The four top?" (externally) "Oh, so you accept reservations now?"

"No, but a large party is coming in."

... "So, it's not first come, first served... ?"

"Ugh. Let me ask."

I was ready to leave. This entire exchange was an example of doing entirely too much. A new waitress came to greet us and sat us at the communal table. Whereas the former was curt and dagger eyes, this one was smiles and warmth. It made all the difference. I could understand if the dining room was at capacity but there was no need for any of the drama we went through to change seats. In case it wasn't obvious, we were there to spend money. Asking to be comfortable whilst doing so in a room that wasn't full shouldn't have been too much to ask.

Ahem. Had to get that out.

Once we changed seats and waitresses, the dining experience couldn't have been more pleasant. Despite planning on eating breakfast, I was seduced by the promise of the Beastwich. The name is not misleading. This is a massive beast of a sandwich. Come hungry. Come very hungry. Between two pieces of thick bread lay blackened chicken breast, bacon, carmelized onions, spinach, tomato, colby cheese, and hummus. This was a two-hand, take breaks, set it down for a little while sandwich... and I loved every bite. The sandwich came with a choice of side and since I was already clogging my arteries for the day, I decided on the chili cheese tots. Yep. It's true. I'm not embarrassed. In an effort to balance my gluttony, I made my own smoothie with banana, blueberry and strawberry. It came in a large glass and was filled to the top. It, like my sandwich and side, was very satisfying.

Coming to SBC on a weekend in search of food is a f00ls errand. Perhaps even coming here in the morning in the warmer months isn't the smartest of tasks. Definitely don't plan on coming here with a large group. All of the above paths lead to frustration and ruin. But if you can come by yourself or one other (tops) on an off-time, you'll be rewarded with kitsch comfort that will stick to your bones and live in your memory for quite a while. Even in light of the bumpy start, I'd gladly return for more of what the kitchen's putting out and recommend others do so as well. Just know what you're getting into.

3.5

I wasn't expecting The Jam to be as quirky as it is. This isn't a bad thing. I don't spend a great deal of time in Edgehill so as I was navigating my way to the coffee shop, I missed the strip mall lot and wound up parking a block away on a residential street. Just so's you're prepared, the turn comes up quick once you pass 12th on Wedgewood. Be in the right lane and be prepared to turn in to the lot. Once I entered, I noticed the mismatched furniture and ample negative space. Mismatched furniture isn't unusual for coffee shops but theirs while paired with the empty space reminded me of an unfurnished apartment more than a homey, kitschy coffee space. YMMV.

The folks working behind the counter are all very polite and engaging and that's a plus. There's no coffee shop snobbery to be found here. I wished that I'd spent a little more time going over the menu. For as casual as the energy is here, the menu is pretty impressive and takes a little time to go over. Not wanting to hold up the line, I decided on breakfast tacos and a tea (I figured a tea would be less sugary than any coffee concoction I came up with).

My friend and I rounded the corner and set up shop at the communal table in the second room. Before too long, another couple joined us. As we were just catching up and not discussing anything too confidential, I didn't mind. Plus, I felt badly for sitting at a large table with just two people. Shortly thereafter, my tea was ready. I ordered the Kauai Cocktail. It was a non-milk tea so that caught my eye. I didn't think to ask if almond milk could be subbed for cow's milk. My tea smelled wonderful. It was a blend of hibiscus and currant in a rooibos base. Promising to fill me up with vitamin C, the tea was just sweet enough thanks to the stevia add-in. I ordered the tea hot and as it cooled, I enjoyed it even more. My breakfast tacos were run-of-the-mill but tasty. The two corn tortilla tacos came in a paper box and were filled with egg, cheese, avocado, and a hot sauce of some sort. I wasn't wowed but I wasn't offended either. The tacos were just as advertised.

Due to their early operation hours and distance from my home, The Jam was one of the few Nashville coffee shops I hadn't visited. The vibe & food didn't do much for me, but I was impressed with the service and tea. When I have more time, I'd like to explore the coffee menu more but I don't think I'll be rushing back to do so. The Jam is an inoffensive coffee shop that appeals to the early bird. If that's you and you live/work in/around Edgehill, see what you think. If none of the above apply to you, there's no rush.

In the time that passed from my first visit to The Row to my latest experience, the restaurant changed chefs and that made all the difference. Plus, I had some new dining experiences. Dinner/lunch is a nice new treat... but it's all about brunch. Wow! In the competitive world of weekend early-ish eating in Nashville, The Row is a destination you need to put into rotation. It's keep-a-smile-on-your-face good.

Now, I know most people rave about the Bloody Mary bar. And, it is quite a sight. Thing is, I don't enjoy Bloody Marys. So the genius of the bar is lost on me (although I am usually a fan of make-your-own food bars). But, the upside is that while everyone is fighting over vegetables and hot sauce, I can luxuriate in my chair was a goblet-sized mimosa. The Grand Mimosa is a delicious mix of Grand Marnier and pineapple juice to the usual champagne and orange juice combo. I approve. I approve over and over. But, one can't live on booze alone (I've tried). The brunch food items are just as fantastic as the drinks. While pancakes & fruit are a standard and hot chicken is, well, hot chicken, change it up a bit and go south. The fried chicken & biscuits served with country gravy is just the way you want to country up your first meal. As a Kentuckian, I have to admit that the breading, seasoning, temperature, and juiciness of the chicken was spot on. The biscuits were thick and buttery (not dry) and the gravy was dangerously-good. Why is southern food so bad for you? Ugh. #sucks Add a side of fried apples and cheese grits and you are good to go with a perfect Saturday brunch. If you can, eat in the bar area or out on the patio. Even when it gets cooler, the chiminea keeps things warm. Just mind your timing. The word is out and the crowds are legit. But, the thrown elbows are worth the goodness you're about to put in your belly.

Well done, The Row!

More than anything, I really like the feel of this place. Brewery/taproom/bar/live music venue, TBW has pretty much everything you need for a beer-fueled good time. I hadn't heard of this brewery before coming to Nashville but I'm mighty glad that it's on my radar now.

To begin with, as you approach the venue, you're impressed. Rather than go for an industrial 'gritty' feel, TBW welcomes you with patio seating, gorgeous wood and plenty of open air (is that a rooftop?). TBW is a celebration of one of the key elements of beer drinking: doing so with a group of friends. Yes, the craft beer movement is a serious one but it should also be fun. The fellas over at TBW remembers that. Step inside and, again, you have ample seating, a second floor/balcony access and plenty of posters letting you know of upcoming shows. A cold craft beer and live music sounds like a pretty excellent night in Nashville. And, what of the beer? I'm glad you asked. Expect inventive flavors that, if you come here during a tour, are expertly explained and generously sampled. I am not much of a basil fan (read somewhere once that it's a carcinogen and whether or not it's true, it's stayed with me for all of these years) but it was an unexpectedly tasty treat. A saison with fruit notes, the spice from the herb elevates the beer in to something I'd never tasted before (and I drink a lot of beer). The Country Roots sweet potato stout was also a fun drink. It respects the region while offering a twist on the usual stout (coffee and chocolate notes). Since the beers (while I was there) hovered around the hoppy and bitter (not my flavor profile), the last beer I tried was the Southern Wit. This is a white ale with conspicuous sweet fruit notes (orange, honey and pear). It went down very easily and would be a perfect spring/summer beer. Are you sensing a pattern? The brewers at TBW take this stuff seriously but have fun with their creations. You should as well.

If there was any doubt that Nashville is a beer town, venture into Craft Brewed and set the record straight. Yes, parking is a wee bit inconvenient, but the effort is worth it to walk into a wonderland of brews. Better yet, CB understands that there's more to offer in beer-land than hop bombs. What? WHAT?? Yes!! Beer lovers, look no more. You're home.

Making a choice easier than the options Morpheus gave Neo, choose to enter either the left or right door. The left door offers taps a'plenty but these taps are for growlers. Yes, growlers. Come here for your big boy/girl brew and get a lot of it. If you don't have a growler, you can buy one here OR (pro-tip) check-in on your Yelp app and receive a free one. That's right. Free. While you're trying to decide which beer to take home in your moonshine jug, look around: there's a lot more than beer here. What? WHAT?? Yes!! Besides a crazy awesome beer menu, the left side of the store offers a wine selection that puts other proprietors to shame, spirits of all sorts and high gravity beer. I came in looking for mix of American Bondes and Red Ales and the manager/owner/beer angel guided me throughout the selection as I got more and more of the vapors. And, better yet, you can make your own six packs on this side of the business. This. I was looking for this. When I inquired about some other choices, he replied, "Oh. That's on the other side."

Other.Side? Vas is?

Yep, if you venture through the right-hand side door, you'll enter a world of cold beer, lower ABV beer, ciders, a TAP (yes, you can sit and drink up; either by the pint or choose a sampler) with a giant chalkboard of selections (20 or so), a home brew section, incredibly nice staff, darts, beer garden, and outside patio. What? WHAT?? Yess!! How is there so much awesome captured under one roof. If there is any beer need one would have from choice, to hanging out, to growlers, to glasses, to home brews, to education, to spots in/at which to chill... Craft Brewed has you covered. If they had food, beds and showers, I don't think I'd have much reason to leave. Oh, wi-fi. I'd need wi-fi. Work on that, CB (in case you don't already have it covered).

There's a comfort to Three Brothers that helps to make it a destination for your coffee shop-going needs. It's also very close to Vandy so... there's a high likelihood that it will be packed to the gills. I don't know when a good time to visit is. I was here on a Tuesday afternoon and seating was scarce (but more on that in a bit). So, the upside is that the space is comfortable. The downside is seating may come only after a Hunger Games-ish battle.

Let's get the negatives out of the way, only one of which TB can help... and that's only sort of. Parking is not fun. Parking around West End is never an entertaining option. Honestly, when going to any business around here that doesn't have a massive lot of their own, I, typically, opt for a ride-share. But if you have to park, TB has an oddly-shaped lot in the back that it shares with Cumberland. Be mindful of which spots are which because not all of the asphalt is TB property. Don't get ticketed/towed. The other downer has little to do with TB and everything to do with... I dunno. This generation? Students? Transplants to the city (because southern mamas know better than to raise kids like this)? I've said it before at coffee shops and I'll say it again: if you are riding solo, don't take up a four top. It's pretty simple. Think about other people. Be considerate. I nearly lost my mind at all the splaying and taking up as much space as possible I witnessed at TB. My work party nearly had to talk via IM because it was difficult to find seating together. Asking singletons to make some room? No go. Huffing and puffing? Doesn't work? Practicing Scarlet Witch-level sorcery to get these [redacted] to move? Has potential. After some Stevie Nicksing, people made way and I didn't have to get crazier... but... c'mon. Is it so hard to realize that you're in public and not at home? 

Now that that's out of the way... the space is lovely. The front of the shop gets wonderful light and the native vibe (absent the splayers) is wonderful. The wifi is strong and fast -- especially considering how many people use it at the same time. The baristas are chatty and smiley (a plus not always seen at coffee shops). And the drinks are interesting. I'll drink coffee but I don't gravitate to it. Given a choice between the bean and the leaf, I'll choose the latter most of the time. That said, when given the option of trying the award-winning, spring seasonal Firewater, I took it. I'm a sucker for limited time offers. My Firewater was an orange blossom/rose candy latte. What? Right?? I had to try it. It was unusual and I doubted I'd find the concoction elsewhere. As adventurous as it sounds, the taste wasn't off-putting or trying too hard. It was, in fact, quite enjoyable and a wonderful spring drink. If the powers that be at TB, routinely, come up with such interesting recipes, sign me up to discover what else they can do.

Just be aware of seating yourself appropriately.*

*And don't come hungry. Food runs out quickly.

The Loft Restaurant is found on the grounds (in combination with?) Traders Point Creamery. So, you can come here for a field trip, rich dairy products and/or literal farm-to-table eating. Don't be fooled by the wood and barn, though. The execution of the product is as fine and fancy as you'd find in the middle of any city. I enjoyed my evening but it changed me a bit.

Being a creamery, it's no surprise that cheese was the beginning portion of the family-style meal I shared. Despite the fact that I don't consume much dairy these days, cheese (especially fresh cheese) is a weakness. As you might imagine there wasn't a bad pick in the lot. From stinky to hard to soft to citrusy, there was a cheese for every taste. Making my gluttony all the more easy, the folks at The Loft had plenty of gluten-free vehicles by which I could eat my mold to my heart's content. While I ate, I happily sipped on a seasonal Old Fashioned. This would be followed up by red wine with my meal. No, I wasn't driving.* Speaking of the meal, it was every bit the farm classic: roasted pork loin in a maitake sauce and plates of root vegetables. Dessert (made just for me) was a gluten-free apple galette. Everything tasted wonderful. So... the change?

The restaurant may have been a little 'too' farm-to-table for me. Over the years, I have been changing my diet away from dairy and meat to more plant-based.** I'm not all the way there but I'm not as meat-ravenous as I used to be.*** During an interlude in the dinner, we were able to go to the barn and watch the cows get milked. I'm from Kentucky. This isn't my first time at the rodeo. But for some reason this time was different. Being that close to the animal... as an adult... looking into her eyes... it was different. I was very thankful that beef wasn't on the menu but that pork I'd just raved about? Yeah, it was making me feel incredibly guilty and uneasy. People *should* know where their food comes from and getting it in such a local way is always the way to go. For me, though, it made me think more about what I eat and why/how I eat it. That's not a bad thing. It's just different. 

*The barn/farm/restaurant is a bit out of town so bring the DD if you're going to partake.
**My vegetarian colleague ate very well at The Loft.
***Mostly avoiding eating mammals.

Sad Trombone. I missed out. Evidently, everyone and their mama is smitten with Merchants. I didn't get it. 

The location is cool. 4th and Broadway is as perfect a location for out-of-towners as it gets in Nashville, so that wasn't it. 

The building is cool. After walking through a downstairs that looks diner-y (not an insult), you're whisked upstairs by elevator (or you can hoof it) and, suddenly, you're surrounded by brick walls, recessed flooring, long tables and pretty views. So, that wasn't it.

The cocktails were cool. I introduced my colleague to the wonder of The Dark & Stormy and I hovered around brown liquors for the rest of the night. I wasn't out of my mind, but I was feeling pretty good. That wasn't it.

The service was a little off. We were a large group and, like little Mike Brady, I get it: not everyone is going to reap the same attention as the others. It just kept happening. My appetizer was forgotten. And, then, oops, my drink order went somewhere else. 'Did you need some more silverware? I'll be right back... in ten or so minutes.' I didn't make a big deal of anything, but it didn't make me feel great that I had to persuade my dining companions to eat their food as I waited for mine. Twice. That may have been it.

The food was... satisfactory. I came in expecting to be awed and I was 'alrighted.' Again, I am wondering if it was me because my companions seemed to be loving their experience. I was bored by mine. I am not a big beef person so, perhaps if I were, I would have a different opinion. Then again, maybe not. I dined with a vegan who seemed most content with her food. The gnocchi was fine, if not a tad bit mushy. I skipped the salad but had a bite or two of the arugula (I liked it the most). My pork tenderloin was filling but not entirely satisfying. Even for a fatty such as myself, dessert was ho-hum. From the bread pudding to a toast and jelly concoction, my tastebuds weren't tickled. They were poked. Truthfully, I was bored by much of what I ate. I kept waiting for the 'moment' and it never came. I think that I ordered poorly. The overall star rating and positive experience my companions had can't be wrong. So, the food... maybe that was it. That could have been it. That was probably it.

I'm the 50th review! Awesome and not awesome. 'Awesome' in that I like silly milestones like that. 'Not awesome' in that so many more more people should be reviewing this place. Is it the location? It's gotta be the location. Forget the address: TailGate is well worth the drive from the city. Not only is the beer fun (imagine that, fun beer! Drinking can be fun? Huh?), the vibe is exactly what you want from a brewery: laid back and beer-focused. I'm mad at myself that it took me so long to come out.

From the beginning, TB stands out. The A-frame lodge is distinct and tells customers that the brewery doesn't take itself too seriously but it respects what was here before it. The powers that be could have leveled the building. They didn't. That means something. Secondly, the space is fairly large (and this is not counting the outdoor area). There's the main tap room, private rooms, TVs, video games, etc. You're more than able to bring a large group of folks here for carousing, eating and wifi-ing. Yep, there's free wifi. I didn't see that coming. What I *did* see coming was all the beer drinking. There are THIRTY taps of TailGate Beer to try. Being Nashville, there's an over abundance of IPAs (this trend has to end) but there's also so interesting depth to the perma-taps and the seasonal varieties are impressive as well. Seeing as I was there in mid-spring, the Watermelon Wheat was a timely - and tasty - choice to make. I was impressed with the balance, nose and expertise in putting together this beer. It could have gone very wrong but I was psyched with the order. I was even happier with the fact that M-F from 3-6, pints are $4. Yes, please!

I never experienced the old menu so I'm not going to get involved with the moaning and wailing. The pizza smelled (and looked) delicious and my garlic knots were exactly as advertised and filled my belly quite nicely. As I enjoyed my beer and bites, I noticed the soundtrack was all '70s -- unexpected but very welcome. Also (sadly) unexpected: such nice, chill workers. Unfortunately, Nashville's still at a stage of craft beer life that pretension and standoffishness (is that a word?) can trump the camaraderie that should come from brewing, discussing and drinking beer. The TailGate crew missed the memo that they have to be jerks. I'm glad to say that everyone with whom I interacted was nice, loose, fun, and all about having a good time. 

Many thanks to TailGate for adding some fun, skill and depth to Nashville's beer scene. If you haven't been and you fancy yourself a beer drinker, you need to fix that. Just come ready for a good time.

When I walked in to Bacchanal, my first thought was, "Hmm, this looks familiar." When I spied the cheese coolers and affordable wine selections I thought, "How do I know this place? Have I been here before?" It wasn't until I checked out the outside portion that it hit me: Lagniappe! One of the few places in Miami that spoke to a cool outside the city.... Lagniappe. That's what this reminded me of. I mentioned it and was told, "Yeah. That guy completely ripped us off."

I.should.have.known.* Dammit, Miami. You lie about everything! I knew that such an authentically New Orleans experience couldn't have been dreamed up in the 305! Ugh. The hits keep on coming from that place.

Sorry. PTSD. This review is about the awesomeness of Bacchanal, not the sneakiness of Lagniappe. The cool pours in from every crevice of the building. The employees are cool. The wine is awesome. The cheese selections pair well with just about anything you want to drink. But... it's the place, man. It's the place. New Orleans already has its own vibrational hum that lures you in and speaks to your soul. Certain places in the city add a few chords to that hum and really do a thing on you. Bacchanal is one of those places. Whether you wind up outside or upstairs (with tables and chairs that are far more comfortable than they appear), you're here. You're drinking wine. You're carousing with friends. You're experiencing life. Music is alive. Wood is alive. Wine is alive. New Orleans (with spirits roaming the streets as freely as people do) is alive. Bacchanal is able to harness all of this life and channel it through the wine bottle. It's a beautiful thing. It's a wonderful thing. It's a memorable thing. It's an authentic thing. It's wine in the 9th Ward, post-Katrina. It's a New Orleans thing.

*I should update my Lagniappe review.

I finally made it over to the famous Star Bagel. I am not often on the west side of town but since I had a reason to be close, I wanted to take full advantage of it. I can't believe that I have slept on Sylvan Park for so long. I really enjoy the neighborhood. And, it seems, that everyone else in town does as well. The west side is the new best side, huh? I digress. Star Bagel lived up to its billing and I look forward to my next opportunity to spend some time here.

First thing first, parking in the lot is a bit tricky. The lot is a weird shape, it's not very large and Star Bagel is really popular. All these elements combine to a bit of a parking nightmare. There are timed parking places across the street and the business is close enough to side streets that on a pretty day a park and walk situation isn't the end of the world but just be prepared. I came here at an off time and still had to drive around and get lucky with my timing.

Once I parked, it was clear sailing. Grad a menu from the middle column and step to the side as you decide what you want. There are a LOT of choices so, unless you're a regular, you're going to need some time. Breakfast is available all day so there's that plus. I decided to combine breakfast and lunch by getting a lunch sandwich with a smoothie. Sandwiches are available on gluten-free bread and for the celiacs out there the staff knows how to prepare/serve the food so as to avoid cross contamination. Step up, order, pay, sit, and wait for your number to be called. Before too long, my order was up and I was chowing down. Know this: the gluten-free bread is a bit smaller than other bread choices here. If you are a big eater, choose wisely (if going gluten-free is more fad than necessity). My tuna melt was fantastic. The bread was fresh and able to stand up to the sandwich fillings. The tuna was hearty and generously-portioned and NOT overly-mayo'ed (kudos; I hate wet tuna/chicken salad). The sandwich didn't have a lot of components (just swiss and tomato) but it kept it simple and delicious. The sandwich was very satisfying. Sandwiches come a la carte so if you want extras, you'll have to buy them. My Blue Lagoon smoothie was a hit as well: blueberries, pineapple, coconut... yes, please. 

Whether coming for breakfast or lunch, it's apparent why Star Bagel is such a hit in the city. It feels genuine to the neighborhood but it's not at all ostracizing to those not from SP or visiting for the first time. I just have a couple of quick dings: the dining room was pretty dirty. Granted, it is up to the patrons to eat - and not throw - their food but the tables, chairs and floors hadn't been bussed or cleaned. Additionally, my colleague and I couldn't find/connect to the wifi (if there was a network). We used our own but I don't know that I would come back for a working lunch. I would, however, come back.

The music made me curious. I am not much (well, not at all) of a dive bar kind of guy. Eating at said dive bar? Forget it. But, the strains of melodic chords will pique my interest almost every time. Add to that musical curiosity, the siren's smell of smoke? Forget it. There were only so many times I could pass by Drifters without walking in.

So it came to pass on a late summer Thursday where I couldn't take any more and had to have some of what I was smelling/hearing. The dining room wasn't too crowded and football played silently on the tv for the few who were watching. I sat down and discovered that Drifters was in the middle of a drink special. Yes, please. Tonight's special was a 2 for 1 sweet tea vodka concoction. 2 boozy drinks for $5? I can do that. I came in thinking about an American Blonde and soon was fist-deep in plastic cups and cheap booze. This was starting well. 

Because I decided to go all in, I started off with a basket of fried pickles. They came to the table screaming hot and with copious amounts of ranch dressing. No, this was not a meal I could sustain on a weekly basis but as a treat... pass the grease. For my meal, I decided on the BBQ pulled chicken sandwich with a side of fries... and another side o' sauces. On every table are a basket of sauces -- 7 in all -- that will make the trip to Drifters worth your while. SEVEN! I love sauce almost as much as I love juice and strange-colored soda. This was gonna be fun. I tasted the meat on its own first to make sure there was good flavor going on. There was. If I'd had two sandwiches, I would have eaten one plain. That's how good the smoke was. Now, it was time for the sauces. I would try each I was sure of with a bite of meat and dip my fries in the ones I wasn't so sure about. My favorite (to the shock of none) was the sweet & smokey. With a molasses base, it was a forgone conclusion. The Texas & Drifters had the tangy vinegar kick that I look for, but I prefer that flavor profile with more of a texture basis (ie slaw) than meat & bun provide. Georgia had a nice, subtle heat by way of the mustard/pepper base and New Mexico kicked it up with the unabashed pepper profile. I only dabbed Sweet Fire and stayed the h#ll away from Atomic Buffalo. My colon thanked me for the wise move. And guess what happened to make this mess o' BBQ eatin' even the mo' betta: an entire set of '90s hip-hop started to play over the speaker system AND my waitress came up to my table, rapping.

Why don't I come here more often?

I just can't do it anymore.* Despite my love of juice, frozen ethnic meals, cookies, popcorn, and (finally) cheap wine, I can't do it anymore. The parking lot. The oversized cars (unless you live in the country and tow isht on the regular, you don't need a truck; you don't. And if you don't know how to park the s.o.b. in one spot, you certainly don't need one). The unruly children (a marketing campaign for Lord of the Flies, perhaps? Control your bad a$$ kids, people!!). The congestion. The lack of stock. The overall rudeness and lack of common courtesy (you're in a grocery store in a wealthy first-world city; your life can't be that bad. It can't be). Getting my heels banged with carts as patrons race for free samples.

I can't. Not anymore. I'm convinced whoever scouted this location hates people. This has to be a social experiment. Has to be.

*My undying love for TJ juice keeps this review at 3 stars. I know. I'm weak.

Just Love is such a solid brand. Consistency can be an issue when you have multiple locations. Not so for Just Love. And, what a location this is. I have written before that I am a big fan of this particular Brentwood development so when I found myself attending a meeting here, I was all in. Brentwood, I like you. I've liked you for a while.

Parking is plentiful and I was able to score some directly in front of the shop. I took this as a sign I was meant to be here. This location is located in a storefront development, so there's not a ton of space inside (although there's enough to walk around and/or sit for a spell). I just didn't want to mischaracterize the shop, given the suburban location. Okay? Okay.

The menu is so the same savory wonder you can find at other Just Love's. Unfortunately for me, the food menu isn't very gluten-free friendly, which is a good and bad thing. It's good for my waistline -- as I'd eat everything offered. It's bad because I torture myself wanting any number of waffles. As I am want to do, then, I ordered a chai latte with almond milk. Fantastic. Made quickly and with care, my drink was hot, spiced, just sweet enough, and dairy free. 

The Just Love brand always does right by me and this location is no different. That's not always the case with (local) chains so take note. When in the area, I'll (likely) be back.

When people tell you Headquarters is small, believe them. In fact, go one step smaller in your head. It's tiny. Very narrow. Itsy bitsy. This is not the place you come to set up shop, listen to your music and 'work' all day long (in fact, there might even be a sign that says as much in the store). But, despite the small stature, this is definitely a business you want to patronize. Headquarters has quite a bit of charm packed in to its small size.

As Charlotte becomes the new 'it' stretch of transplant land, look for more and more businesses to head west to get a piece of the pie. As you do so, though, take some time and patronize the businesses that were a part of the neighborhood long before the 'east side got full.' As nerve-wracking as it is to find parking on Charlotte, there are plenty of side streets close by Headquarters (and a park across the street... jus' sayin') to rest your vehicle. Once you walk in, you'll notice two things: 1.) no one is exaggerating about the size of the shop and 2.) the brick work and high ceilings demand your attention. Once you've taken it all in, step up to the counter and check out the menu. There's a nice mix of sweet treats and savory eats so take a little time to peruse if you're here around eating times. I was here in that post-lunch, pre-dinner no man's land, so I settled on a beverage. My dirty chai was a delicious, spicy mug of creamy joy. And, speaking of 'mugs,' Headquarters is blessed with some of the most interesting custom mugware I've seen of late in a coffee shop. The mugs are real conversation pieces, in addition to being nicely sized. They add a homey element to a shop that has a lot of urban appeal. 

I was here with an associate so I took advantage of their wifi to get a spot of work done. I felt a bit uneasy about doing so (footprint and all) but given the time of day and the traffic in the shop, I was able to let my apprehension go. I definitely wouldn't have pulled that stunt at anytime before 4 pm. As we worked and tickety-tacketied, I took note of the awesome music that served as our soundtrack. I also did something that I hadn't done in quite a while: I struck up conversations with strangers. I don't know whether it was the close proximity but I had 3 separate conversations with patrons in the store. Coffee shops were borne with community as much of a component as coffee. It was nice to experience that aspect of coffee shop culture.

Headquarters is very much a destination coffee shop. You might not stay for a long time depending on the time you come (because, tiny) but you'll want to come check it out and take in some of the good energy. In a city where some things can seem painfully familiar, Headquarters stands out. That's a good thing.

I haven't eaten here but as a fun place to grab a drink and impress an out of town visitor, The Treehouse has just what you need. I'd been meaning to check it out for months but the parking situation on Clearview depressed and overwhelmed me so I always talked myself out of it. And then someone would mention the patio/treehouse and I'd get riled up about going over again.

So, it came to pass on a surprisingly warm fall evening (thanks, climate change!) that I had a friend in town and a need to impress with a good place for cocktails in a fun setting. It was finally Treehouse time. I knew it was meant to be as we found parking on Clearview. It was my time. We walked past the friendly hostess and headed straight to the crown jewel in the back. It didn't disappoint. Although I am from Kentucky, I didn't start drinking as a child. Had i done so, though, I imagine that my backyard bar would have looked similar to this. The setting dictates the energy and puts you in a good mood. This is a brilliant business move for a bar. Seeing that I was in a playful frame of mind, I had my first kalimotxo. I don't know who thought to mix red wine and coke but sir/madam, I salute you. I doesn't sound like it makes sense but it does. It really truly does. It might have made too good of sense, as I found myself drinking them in lieu of water. Oh well. red wine's good for you, right? The weather is teasing a return of spring time temps. It's safe to come out of hibernation and return to outdoor drinking at The Treehouse. An added bonus: the restaurant has a new chef. I think, upon my next visit, I'll add a food element to my daily dose of drinking. But, yeah: that backyard is everything you've heard of. It sounds odd that a place could successfully blend memories of childhood and drinking but it does, it can and it works. Spring's here. Do your drinking in a treehouse.

It's only been about a month but the word is out. My last visit to Rudy's was a crush of humanity. Even though my side-eye sorcery was in full effect, I was happy for the band and owners that so many people were in the house. I just hope that the patrons can respect that this is a jazz room and not a stop on the woo hoo express. This ain't that kind of party.

I am still making my way down the cocktail menu. I have yet to find a dud. The Maiden Voyage was surprisingly drinkable (and more tiki in appearance than I was expecting). The Vieux Carre was sippable New Orleans in a couple glass but the real surprise was the Tijuana Moods. I wasn't expecting a minty pink summer cocktail but that's just what I got. It's also the drink that threw me overboard. Watch out for Charles Mingus. He'll get you every time.

3.5

I think the reviews of this spot are a bit harsh. Tenn Sixteen is a perfectly serviceable neighborhood restaurant. While one might not drive from, say, Sylvan Park to come here, denizens from Edgefield, Maxwell Park, East End, Lockeland Springs, and the like would/should surely come here for some beer, bites and a relaxed environment.

I don't know if this is an everyday thing or just a Sunday thing, but I was mighty pleased to discover a two for one deal going on. I helped myself to two Jackalopes (poured in the proper glass). Had i been there to watch the game (or, TV in general; there wasn't much discrimination when it came to what was on the tube), I would have been more than satisfied to sit at the bar, drink some beer and TV/people watch. But, I'm a fatty... and fatties eat.

Yes, the NOLA things is a bit confusing... but go with it. How many NOLA-inspired eateries are in this part of town? In any case, I think the menu is more Southern-inspired with NOLA accents than straight up etouffee, po' boys and the like (which you can order here). I started with a cup of gumbo and, immediately, wished I'd ordered a bowl. The roux was thick, the spices were humming and the ingredients with thick, chunky and plentiful. It paired very nicely with my beer. I couldn't decide on what I wanted for my main course. I don't think I chose as strongly as I could have... but I, nevertheless, enjoyed what I got. I ordered the bbq chicken (see? Southern) with the gouda mac & cheese and red cabbage slaw. As I am want to do, I mixed everything together. The bbq sauce added a nice sweet and subtly spicy kick to the meat -- which was a big hunk of white meat. This was anemic piece of chicken. I ate the fowl atop the cabbage which was a good idea. Not only did the slaw add texture but chicken, bbq sauce and slaw (especially being so close to Memphis) is always a good idea. The mac & cheese was ok; I wanted it to be better. I have a slab of smoked gouda in my refrigerator right now. I'm pretty mad about the stuff. The pasta dish could have had much deeper flavor and thicker consistency. As it was, the cheese was a bit bland and runny which is too bad considering the potential. My service was attentive, if not over the top, but on a Sunday evening, that suited me just fine.

Perfectly respectable.

What an awesome blast from the past. For almost the entire duration of my stay in New Orleans, my Saturdays included some combination of the following: a trip on the streetcar, a visit to the comic shop, a walk around Audubon Park, and a visit to Plum Street Snoball. I was a master of favor combos and it only took a few visits to learn that I didn't need a large pail, as much as I thought I did. Of course, there are other stands in NOLA but none came close to the sheer joy that Plum Street brought.

I'm pleased to note that you CAN go home again. Despite dealing with rush hour traffic and hungry kids/moms, my group managed to make it to Plum Street, bolt out of the car (in your FACE, little kid!), stand in line, and think of all the great combos to be had. As I stood on the sidewalk and considered how to make snoball flavor history again, I realized one of the things that makes Plum Street so good is the quality of the 'sno.' It's fine, silky and shaved just right. You never get a hard clump or icy mess. It's the perfect vehicle for the metric ton of sugary sweet syrup that awaits. That's another thing: if you don't have a go-to favorite, use your line waiting time properly and figure out what you want. The line is lone, New Orleans is hot and no one's got time for you gumming up the works. 

I contemplated getting one of my old standby combos (and that's another thing -- combine flavors; don't settle for just one) but I thought better of it and used my patented system for figuring out the best combos. I came up with lemon + candy apple in a medium pail. Once I got my half bright red, half clear concoction, I raced back to the car to dig in. It's a good thing I was sitting down. The lemon was sweet & tart. The candy apple was a bit cloying on its own but when paired with the lemon produced a flavor profile so holy, so right... angels sang. Yep, I still had it... and so does Plum Street. Neveh change.

I've found the angriest woman in Nashville. She is a barback at RWW, has the strength of 40 men and if you're from Boston, live in Cincinnati and have a few days beard growth she.will.kick.your.ass. Just putting out some fair warning.

Why is she so angry? She works in one of the coolest spots in Nashville. RWW has a big ol' neon sign that out-neon's other signs on Broadway. It's true! Look at the pictures and you believe me. Visit it and you'll know. The walls are adorned with genuine Nashville memorabilia from a time when it, likely, wasn't populated with hipsters, yankees or folks who look a lot like me. But, things have changed and RWW embraces the new NashVegas while keeping one cowboy boot based in the past for authenticity. It works.

You come to Nashville for live music. Even if honky tonk isn't my go-to (I always hear Richard Pryor in my head when I say the term), I can appreciate the art form. The musicians at RWW are the real deal. There's something cool about a string bass and fiddle. The patrons know it too, as the small dance floor in front was filled with couples getting a little two step (country NOT hip hop*; although that would be the most incredible thing ever) action in. The downstairs bar got a little busy -- even though a local nightlife photographer recognized what was up and took a picture of my crew to publish in the local 'zine. Reck-a-niiize my beauty and justify my love. Thx. -- so we took refuge upstairs. Were I to come back, I would make a b-line to go upstairs. You can hear the music, people watch, but you can also snag some cool seating and maintain a conversation at an appropriate decibel level.

And, just who did I spy from my second floor perch? Ladies and gentlemen, your American Idol winner from Season 5, Taylor Hicks (canoodling, not performing)!! My Nashville experience was now complete.

*Please tell me I am not the only black person to have had reviewed this place. I am a little afraid that I might be.

First off: Graze has managed to create a completely different vibe/menu from The Wild Cow despite the same ownership and despite being less than 50 feet away from the other restaurant. Whereas The Cow has a more boho vibe and menu that accommodates lunch or the quick, casual dinner, Graze is the more refined sister, better suited for a dinner with wine and prolonged conversation. It's a real education to this non-vegan to learn to appreciate vegan food in such different situations. So, kudos to the powers that be for cultivating two very different experiences in what could have been a redundant landscape.

My friend and I came here at night after an event I produced. Cognizant of the time and not wanting to be a burden to the kitchen, we decided on small plates so as to be less intrusive -- even though our very kind server assured us that we weren't a problem. Perhaps buoyed by her words, rather than the savory, we made sure to take advantage of Graze's drink program (another difference from The Wild Cow) and kept room for dessert. Each prong of the menu was very satisfying.

Savory: not being one for spice all of the time (if you have a good tolerance, try some of the hot/peppery dishes), I kept my plate offerings to the cashew dip and the special: quinoa cake with peach chutney. The dip was incredible. It came in the form of two dips: a red and a green. Both had a wonderful creamy texture and addictive taste. Had I not known I was at a vegan restaurant, I would have sworn that I was gorging on cheese. The dips came with crostinis, watermelon radish (which I always want to taste like watermelon) and a cranberry relish that you'll want to eat on its own. The quinoa cake had flavor on its own (sometimes a challenge for quinoa) and IT DIDN'T BREAK. It held its shape. It sounds like a small thing but if you fool with these sort of things often enough, you'll know what a big deal it is. The cakes came with a peach chutney that was sweet & cool -- perfect to take the edge off the spice component of the cake/plate.

Drinks: Thar be booze at Graze. Points! I like to start meals with cocktails and switch to wine/beer later so I did just that. The Peach Sidecar was just what you imagine it to be, with peach substituting for the orange elements of the classic version. Even though we came in early summer, peach was a star of the menu. I wasn't going to argue with that and I didn't argue with the drink. It was refreshing, not bitter (as opposed to 'sweet') and had enough of a kick to remind you that you weren't drinking juice. As my meal progressed, I switched to rose because summer.

Dessert: get it. Do it. I'd been plotting to get my paws on the chocolate lava cake since I first read about it. It really satisfied. If you're not a vegan, you'll notice a slightly different texture than you're expecting; nothing that's off-putting. Just remember that you're eating a vegan cake. The small texture difference is the only difference you'll notice. Trust me. The cake is a decadent chocolate and peanut butter bomb. And I have to give props to the ice cream. The coconut ice cream (I'm assuming made from coconut milk) was everything that I wanted. This is my second time having coconut milk ice cream and I am a big fan. It tastes as good as the 'real' thing and doesn't come with any of the moral/physical unease. It's not for those on a diet (the fat content is real) but when splurging on dessert, go all in.

Places like Graze get me incredibly excited about the future of dining in Nashville. It'll get you excited, too. Promise. Well done, folks.

Magic. This place is magic. Literally. All along the walls are ingredients for potions and what not. But we'll get to that in a bit. If you read nothing else in this review, know that High Garden has the good stuff for what ails you. Leaving, I was in much better spirits than when I came in.

To start, High Garden has parking. This is a welcome relief. Even though I live within walking distance, sometimes a fella has errands to run before and after a cup of tea and needs to be in a vehicle. There's a couple of spots in front and a lot in back. The lot shares spaces with other businesses and some of the spots are dedicated so be careful when you park. Parking is the most stressful part of the stay at HG. Once it's over, soak into your relaxation.

As soon as you walk in, you feel as though you've been transported to Middle Earth. The entirety of the front room is adorned with jars of herbs, teas and other wondrous items. Each jar lists the ingredients and what it affects. Cholesterol. Anxiety. Blood pressure. Inflammation. I wouldn't be surprised if there are love potions and luck bombs in the shop. You can either request to make your own blend, bag and weigh your personal favorites, get kombucha in the back room (and tea cocktails - non-alcoholic - which looked incredible), or order off the menu. I went with the menu because I was completely and utterly overwhelmed. You could, easily, spend an hour going over the choices and coming up with a blend. As I an wont to do, I went with a seasonal option. Get it while you can and all that. I believe my selection was the Angry (I think, although I could be wrong; anger doesn't go with the vibe HG crafted) Orchard. It was a hibiscus-berry blend. The fragrance instantly captivated me. I decided on a small pot because who just wants ONE cup of tea?

My friend and I ordered and walked to the rear of the shop to find seating. Despite having a good number of seating options (all woodland and faerie-like), it was a bit of an odyssey to find a place to sit. HG is popular and people like to stay a while. Why? Well, 1.) it's magic. 2.) good tea sort of demands one relax and slow down and 3.) there's a no laptop rule. Horror of horrors, if you come here you have to either talk to another human being or read a book! Gasp! Wheeze! *faint* Conversation, like writing, is a lost/dying form. I love love love that High Garden pushes people into normal human interactions. So, yeah. The place is popular. Folks want to unplug. My friend and I sat at a small communal table and before too long, our pots were ready. Each pot was glass, allowing us to watch the tea steep. We were given hourglass timers to make sure we didn't oversteep. We were also given a variety of sweeteners. I contemplated using the natural sugar and/or honey, but my tea was flavorful enough without the added sweetness. Another cool touch of the set up was that we were given a beaker-looking pitcher set atop an open flame for hot water in case we wanted to try and get one last cup from our tea bags. The whole set up is just so d@mn charming. I don't know that I am doing it justice. Just know that you *want* to come here. And I didn't even touch upon the genuine kindness of the owners and workers. They've created a space that's unique in this city (and this time) and I am so here for it. Well, I am... as well as the rest of the city. Did I mention that HG gets really crowded?

This place is magic.

4.5

Like most other reviewers on here, I'm so psyched to have Merengue Cafe in Nashville. I've heard whispers and rumors of Dominican food in LaVergne but I haven't explored enough to check it out. Luckily for the wear & tear on my car, I won't have to drive that far to get some of the grub. Come here for all the hits: mangu, sancocho and Country Clo! It's not just Dominican fare on the menu, Puerto Rico and Cuba are represented with items like mofongo and ropa vieja. Basically, if you need a taste of the the Spanish Caribbean, you'll find it here.

But don't get ahead of yourself. First timers, should keep it 'simple' and go with a plate. If you're good on that, graduate to a specific dish (that will take time to make; homemade food always does). The good news is that the plates are large and delicious. You'll begin with your choice of rice. Then, you'll pick a type of bean. From there, it's on to 4-6 types of different stewed/grilled/barbequed meats. Finally, pick a salad (to be healthy). There are other items to choose from (maduros) but this is the basic plate options. The beautiful thing about the options is that they change daily. So you can come here a few times a week, get a plate and have a completely different meal each time. Since I try to live by the words I speak, I ordered yellow rice, red beans, stewed chicken (pollo guisado), and lettuce/tomato/cucumber (ensalada rusa). I couldn't resist a side of maduros, either. I was going to get a red Country Clo, but the woman behind the register (owner?) convinced me to go with a merengue. If this is your first time with this type of food know this: the pronounced spice is garlic/sofrito. This is not hot/spicy food. This isn't that type of party. But since heat is never misplaced with beans and rice, there are plenty of bottles of Cholula to keep you happy.*

My food was every bit as delicious as I thought it would be. After paying for my food, I chose a small table in the large dining room. Even on a rainy Wednesday after the lunch rush, the dining room decently busy and I didn't want to take up more space than I needed. I was so pleased to see that people were showing MC so much love. Talking with one of the employees, she confirmed that traffic has been constant and busy. It just goes to show that there have been food vacuums in this city and when people fill it with expertly-done food, there's money to be made. And before I end, I just have to give a shout out to the folks behind the curtain. Both of the ladies with whom I interacted were nice, funny, helpful, and chatty. They're proud of MC -- and rightfully so. It's nice to see good people succeed and I'm excited to see how MC grows. Look around at the reviews, there's a reason why people are showing MC so much love. Don't miss out and don't be late. Next time:

*Though you should opt for spicy green sauce if you need a kick of heat.

3.5

There are some fantastic qualities to Old Glory but there, too, are some nagging holdovers that keep it from the vast potential it is.

First off: the space is exhilarating. What an incredible way to repurpose an old space. With all the new construction popping out throughout the metro, Old Glory gets it right. You can create a stunning space without destroying history and depending on making something cookie cutter. A distinctive space to whet one's whistle is nearly as important as the libation program. The soaring ceiling, exposed brick, laid-to-bare boiler elements, and unusual seating/landing space (think Escher... or the Mall at Green Hills) all combine to make Old Glory one of the more unique places to grab a cocktail in Nashville. If you're able to belly up to the bar, take the space in (stools, bar, flooring); it's stunning.

And what of the cocktail program? Fantastic. Obviously, the folks behind the concept and execution know what's up wrt making inventive and delicious cocktails. Rather than cashing in on a trend, these beverages are made with skill, time, care, and consideration. The price point adequately reflects the end product and said end product isn't a flurry of ice and/or glassware tricks. My colada swizzle was a fun romp of rum, colors, fruit, and sweetness. This the Kids In The Hall Girl Drink Drunk™ taken to 11. I decided to man up for my next cocktail. The Spring Gingham was a surprising win of bourbon and grapefruit (doesn't get manlier than either of these two ingredients). When it comes to cocktails, Old Glory doesn't have many peers in town.

So... 3.5? Unfortunately, yes. Read everything I described up top: the beautiful bar, stunning space, soaring ceiling, and captivating menu... and add to it a joylessness that evokes 1980s North Korea. I don't understand. It's booze in a pretty place. Why the sighs? Why the shrugs? I dared to belly up to the bar (before realizing that there's roaming servers to help expedite drinks) and came away depressed. Not only were the folks behind the bar incredibly dismissive to me, I witnessed them be outright rude to others. While it made me feel good (that's not the right word) for a second that the contempt wasn't necessarily personal, I swung back to being annoyed when I realized that the very people making it possible for the OG ptb to pay their rent were treated with such contempt. If serving the public makes for a loathsome experience, sling bars out of your house for your friends and call it a day. It's booze. It's not medical research. Smile. Relax. 

Another ding: the atmosphere is... odd. As beautiful as the layout is, I couldn't figure out the crowd. While I pondered, my formerly-of-Los-Angeles-but-native-Tennesseean friend laid it out for me: this crowd belongs in LA (and 'crowd' is the right word; the space was uncomfortably full). This is not a slam in and of itself. LA is a cool place. It has a lot to offer wrt music, fashion, food, drink, and the like. That said, Nashville is not Los Angeles. Nashville is Nashville and that vibe is completely missing from OG. Whether that's by design or accident, I found it off-putting. I've lived in nine different American cities. I chose to move to Nashville for a reason: I liked Nashville. If I wanted to experience another city, I'd move elsewhere. Again, perhaps not the fault of OG but the vibe of my Friday night there was a bit... desperate? Inorganic? Out of sync? I dunno. For as many wonderful qualities as the bar has (and there are several; I think the 3.5/4 is accurate and fair), I felt decidedly out of place and unwelcome. 

That's too bad.

Wait. So this *didn't* replace Tequila Cowboy? I assumed it did what with the space being the same but I'm seeing reviews about TC. Is TC the bottom of the rebranded Jason Aldean space? I need answers, people!! Because I was not a fan at all of TC (wouldn't even walk in the joint) but I was very pleasantly surprised by the rebrand.

First off, it's extremely apparent that this is owned by the same folks behind FGL House. The layouts are similar (music on first floor, dining on second, gift shop on third, roof up top) and I was a little surprised to see how packed the place already is. Granted, it has a marquee position on Broadway, but it was ass to elbows on a blazing hot Saturday, already has over 70 reviews and has only been open for a little over a month. That bodes really well. As with most things Broadway, out of town friends brought me here. They wanted to eat and get a glimpse of the Broadway scene. I recalled that the building had an impressive rooftop so I pitched it. They were all in and we were on our way.

When I arrived I was gobsmacked. How were there already this many people milling about a new bar? My friends texted their location and I made my way to the third floor. Evidently, table seating is very hard to come by but you can seat yourself at the bar. AND there's a bar-specific menu. AND there are labelled gluten-free options on said menu. I know!! I was not expecting this and the revelation turned me all the way around. FGL House has a deceptively-good menu so I should have expected the food at Jason Aldean's Kitchen to be tasty as well. It was. I got the Southern Nachos. It may be listed as a starter. It is not. This was a mound of nachos. I'm a big eater and I needed help to get through it. Rather than tortilla chips, the base of the dish is larger-than-usual kettle chips. On top of that is a crazy amount of pulled pork, bacon, chives, queso sauce, cheddar cheese, and bbq sauce. It's decadent, delicious and not at all diet. Since I was going all in, I paired that with the Party Punch. It's a rum-based fruit punch so I expected sweet and boozy. The drink was a let down. Again, I don't know if it wasn't made right or if the recipe is off but it didn't match my expectations. I would skip it.

Our bartender was nice enough. She wasn't particularly attentive to me but she was nice to my friends. The difference was noted but in the spirit of keeping things namaste, I kept it moving. We couldn't come here without experiencing both namesakes so we made our way to the roof. It's very large and has, about, three distinct areas. Given the popularity and location, it's going to be packed at all times. I wouldn't come to the roof for privacy. But for top-notch people watching (with a different view from other Bway bars), it's a 'must' for tourists and a 'probably should' for locals. The kitchen & bar falls into the same schism. Tourists will love it but the locals will probably enjoy it as well -- every once and a while.

Truth in advertising. This place is small, y'all. In the warmer months, not a big deal. If you decide to come here when things get cool, be advised to take your food and hit the road. Luckily for me, I came here on a nice, sunny Sunday late morning/early afternoon. There were plenty of people milling about but the lines weren't too crazy. Part of my excitement in coming here was the adventure of driving to the location. I am hardly ever in this part of town and places like RG make me happy to further explore my city. Once you arrive, you'll notice a shack, a shed and not much else. You're here.

If you come early-ish, plan better than I did. I missed breakfast by a half hour. Considering I was planning on getting a stuffed biscuit with sausage & cheese, topped with a fried egg, perhaps it's divine intervention that I arrived late. So, I went the opposite direction and went with a veggie burger... but I topped it with blue cheese. And, I ordered fries. And, a Mexican Coke... but Mexican Coke is healthier than the high fructose corn syrup we get in the States, right? The fellas behind the counter were affable and patient with my questions. I imagine they get a lot of them and the space is pretty compact. I applaud them for their good dispositions. In a not-so-long amount of time, my food was ready and my friend & I dashed to the shed/gazebo for some seats. Outside of that covered seating, there are some random chairs/benches out there in the elements. No sir. My boy scout days are far in the past. We high-fived our seat bounty and dug in to the good stuff.

Wow! If more veggie burgers tasted like this, more people would eat them. This was a substantial, hand-made patty chock-full of vegetables and seasoning and it tasted fantastic. It also held together. Another complaint I have about homemade veggie burgers is that they disintegrate upon picking them up. This one didn't. Kudos. The fries are every bit as wonderful as you've heard. If you have nothing else when you come to RG (but why wouldn't you?), get the fries. Oh man. I could eat a sack-load of those things. My Mexican Coke (in the bottle) was a crisp, delicious and satisfying as burning acid can be. With good company, good food and a crisp blue sky overhead, I marveled at my morning and took stock of how fortunate I was just to be. Deep thoughts brought to you by good food. Try it for yourself.

Urban Grub is another one of the Nashville restaurants that helped put the city on the map it's currently enjoying. Odds are (recent transplants) before you moved here or soon after, you heard about UG. There's a reason for that. The restaurant fits the vibe of the neighborhood and reflects the energy of the city. If you're curious about what makes Nashville tick these days, UG might not be a bad place to start looking.

First off, the space is gorgeous -- and much bigger than you might imagine. From private seating to a boisterous main dining room, Urban Grub offers just the experience you're looking for. In my opinion, however, when the weather allows you have to opt for eating outside. Well, sort of outside. Y'see, the covered patio is perfect for group dining. In fact, it's so well designed that my group stayed dry even as the heavens above opened up and let out a few clouds of whoop ass on the ground below. That's some good design.

But more than marvel at the design sense of the venue, you're here to eat. You're in the right place. Rather than speak on the dinner options (if you're a fan of cured meats, come here for dinner), I want to focus on brunch. Some key points of a good brunch: booze, comfy seating and breakfast food that can morph to lunch options. UG has all three elements in spades. I began my meal with sangria. I was pleased with the goblet of wine I received and the presentation was quite pretty. The booziness of the cocktail, however, was a bit weak. It was like drinking juice -- delicious juice, but juice nevertheless. I came up big on my next selection. The margarita was a thing of beauty, size and potency. Not only could I have spent hour after hour downing the tequila goodness, the libation was quite potent. It more than made up for the sangria. The seating was as comfy as the overall design is inviting. But for needing to go about my day, I could have lazed about for a while, sipping on margaritas and taking naps. The food. Yes, there are some excellent food choices to make for all your brunchy desires. If you're on a boss level, go for the cold bar: oysters, shrimp, cured meats, cheeses... they're all there and they look fantastic. I couldn't man up that particular Saturday but I have plans to return and put it all in my belly. Instead, I started with the bread basket that came with a nice assortment of jellies and butter. Try them all -- breads and spreads. For my meal, I settled on the sausage strada (spelled that way; not strata) with a side of hasbrowns. The dish is all about the gravy. I mean, bacon & sausage at breakfast/brunch time is never wrong. And the biscuit and cheddar added to the rightness... but that gravy. Oh man. It's all about the gravy. This is why southerners are fat. The hashbrowns came in a crispy, carmelized casserole that had just the right amount of crunch and salt. All this (before tip) came to $27. Given the location and venue, not bad at all.

Urban Grub has more than earned its reputation amongst Nashville's food pantheon. Whether you check it out for dinner or brunch, at some point in your (new to) Nashville life, you just need to check it out. And check it off your list... before returning to try something else from the menu.

I have to keep up on local openings as part of my job. So, when I read that Subculture was opening its doors, I made a note to check it out. From what I'd seen, this was the most 'Miami' restaurant in Middle Tennessee and this former Miamian wanted to see what the fuss what about.

Verdict: definitely fuss-worthy.

Making the familiar trek down Nolensville, it dawned on me exactly where Subculture was -- right by the T-Mobile store I frequent.* Okay. This is familiar. Walking in, the first thing I noticed was that the place is small. If you plan on coming here, come at an off-peak time. I came on a Tuesday afternoon at 12:30 and very shortly after I sat down, there were no more seats -- even accounting for the shared table in the window. Given that the space isn't very big and there's not that much room between the door and the counter, I didn't want to spend a lot of time gumming up the works. Thanks to my research, I knew what I wanted but, in hindsight, I should have taken some more time to explore my options. This isn't because I didn't like what I got. It's because there might have been something else I liked even more.

My buddy and I ordered and took our seats. Along with my food, I ordered a Black Abbey Crossroads (I was in the mood for a Trippel or Quad but that wasn't on the menu). I was served a slightly-rancid Potus 44 (seriously, the tap couldn't have been clean). I went back to the counter to verify my beer and I was able to get my correct beer without too much of a problem. It was odd but I didn't think much about it. Given the small size of the restaurant, it's nice to know that your food gets brought out to you (rather than having to get it yourself). I ordered the churrasco with chimichurri, fried egg, avocado, and tomato. I don't eat much beef. I would run back here to eat this. Whatever they marinate the meat in is from the heavens. The seasoned, tender beef paired perfectly with the toppings but what really elevated the sandwich was the bread. I believe the bread is made in house. Wow. Wow. Making bread that stands out on its own (and isn't just a place holder) is tough work. The Subculture powers that be nailed it. The sandwich came with seasoned fries that were a nice accompaniment. The only odd thing during our meal is that (one of) the owner(s) kept coming up to my buddy and me. She would ask if I was enjoying the meal, if i was finished, if I needed anything else... It was odd. I felt like I was being rushed along and out. I understand checking on a patron once to see if everything's alright, anything else that can be done, etc. More than that and the interactions feel more like interruptions. I'm going to presume it came from excitement and general interest rather than anything untoward. It was a bit unsettling, however. It won't put me off from returning, though.

*Or, at least, used to. I think the crew I used to see there has moved on to greener pastures. #bummer

3.5

The bones are there. S&H is still new and, like most new places, they need to work out the kinks. But, they have made an undeniable positive impression on the neighborhood so good on 'em for setting up shop and showing folks that the Nashville metro area is full of neighborhoods ripe for real (local) growth.

If you come here, be prepared to wait. The word is (already) out. The demand is high. For the hour I was here, there was a line out of the door waiting to get pizza. I came on a Thursday afternoon. I wasn't here at a peak time. I wasn't here on a weekend. On a random Thursday afternoon, the place was slammed. What does that tell you? It tells me that there are significant portions of Nashville society who are underserved and overlooked and for business owners willing (and smart enough) to cater to them, there's a ridiculous amount of money to be made. So, again, good on 'em. S&H's is a neighborhood joint that is getting mad amounts of love from the neighborhood.

It will also get mad amounts of love from me... one day... I think. For now, in '90s hip-hop parlance: it's a'ight. It's a little better than a'ight but there are some things to work on. I hit up the drink line because no way I was waiting for a pizza. Plus, you know, avoiding gluten. The woman serving the drink line (also the same person cashing out food orders) was... brusque to be kind... a bit rude to be honest. She was probably overwhelmed but as a face of the business, besides working the register, her job is to be on... not to cut eyes. During the wait, another fellow got behind a register and I thought he was jumping on board to help her out. No. He just got on his phone to laugh with people. Again, wrong. If you see the line is in the weeds, jump in and help out. Make the experience positive for the customer.

Reading online about the slushies, I went to order one. Stop sign. I was told (complete with an eye roll) that they weren't available. So, be advised that the website might not reflect what's on premise. A bit disappointed, I selected a cider with which to drown my sorrow. They were out. We're not looking real good here, S&H. I let my buddy go ahead and order because everything left was a gluten bomb. Well, everything at $6 a pour. The only boozey option I had was a can of pinot noir... for $13.50 before tip (and you *will* be tipping; just trust me on this one). To be fair, the can = 2 restaurant pours of wine so it balances out. Just be advised that you might not get what you want. We took our drinks to the patio and listened to Tribe, etc. while we talked. My buddy cut himself on the wood counter, so be advised of that. With some stool seating, the patio (which overlooks the parking lot; more functional than scenic) could be prime real estate. Also: watch out for the low seating inside. It's hard, wooden and set at knee level. If you aren't paying attention or trying to navigate a traffic jam... you might be in for a world of hurt.

3.5 rounded up because I see the potential but they only get one shot to make me talk up something I didn't experience for myself. I'm giving you the benefit of the doubt, S&H. Don't make me look stupid.

I'm a couple of years too late in coming to/reviewing this spot. Although it was my first time at H&C, I am past the point of my life where I drink beer. So... why go to a beer bar? Because it's a fairly popular drinking hole in the city and I'd never been. Plus, the menu boasts cider, hard root beer and kombucha. So, I thought, all would be well even if I wasn't having a cold wheat beer on a mid-spring evening.

I thought.

Don't get me wrong: the place was/is fine but it didn't knock my socks off. To start, the online menu and the menu at the location don't match up. There's no boozy kombucha. There's no Gnarley Grove cider. My buddy didn't find the lagers he came to drink. This wasn't starting well. It's a bummer to head to a place expecting one thing and not delivering on much of any of it. Left without my a or b selection, I went with the hard root beer. In other reviews I'd read complaints about a dirty line. I can't speak to how H&C keep their taproom but I have to admit that I hadn't had a hard root beer that had such an unusual mouthfeel and aftertaste... and I've had that hard root beer before.

The taproom is fairly small and we're finally heading into patio weather so my friend and I took our drinks outside. The table hadn't been cleaned in a long time. It was visibly grimy, gritty to the touch and reeked of the discarded cigarette butts that adorned the table top. Yeah, it was as appealing as it sounds. I powered through and concentrated on the conversation rather than everything else but I was embarrassed to have suggested this place. As it was, we left our drinks unfinished and went to another establishment. H&C could have been a *lot* better. My experience was nothing I'd rush to recreate. As far as the service goes... it was fine. Our bartender wasn't rude but she didn't jump at the chance to be our new best friend... which is fine. She served us drinks and left things at that.

It's fantastic to see another new(er) addition to Downtown (especially 2nd Ave) that has something to offer locals rather than a business that caters to tourists. My only complaint about The Stillery is that I can't seem to come here when there's a perfect storm of upstairs access, full food menu and all the drinks I want to try. I'm guessing there might be some user error involved so, for now, check out this half review of The Stillery.

Luckily for me, you and everyone else, even half is worthy of your time. I first came here after a day of carousing and I didn't want the party to end. My buddy asked me where to go and I mentioned that I'd wanted to check out the new spot on 2nd. So, we ambled over to find a nicely remodeled (if not as big as I would have imagined) Downtown spot that focused on a lot of what's making Nashville so desirable these days: good drinks, fun food, nice people, and live music. Since I had a wild hair to check out the second floor and it was a Saturday night, we forwent a downstairs booth in order to belly up to the bar.

Why we didn't get something to eat, I don't know. This would have disastrous consequences later in the evening. But, for now, all was well and I was determined to find out what this cocktail program was all about. For a place that does well by locals, I think The Stillery can lose the mason jar kitsch. BUT mason jars with Sonic™ ice... well, that's another thing. Mason jars with Sonic™ ice filled with cocktaily things for $8... well, that's an awesome thing. After a brief stint of hemming and hawing, I settled on the Blueberry Smash. The first thing I noticed was how big it was. You definitely get your money's worth at TS. That's reason alone to patronize it over a LOT of Downtown establishments. After noticing the size, I realized that it was a well-made drink. Rather than being one note or cloying, my blueberry vodka (I will NOT be judged), simple syrup, smashed blueberries, lime, and soda concoction was a refreshing and boozy way to spend an early summer night. I kept 'em coming. They were enough to make me ear blind to the fact that the musicians on stage were being drowned out by some woo-hoo bachelorettes. The the band had the brilliant idea of incorporating the gaggle into the act -- and proceeded to drown them out as collaborators rather than interlopers. Brilliant. Oh, and I got one of their numbers. What? I mentioned that there were disastrous consequences to come. AND I mentioned that I wouldn't be judged. Come here. Drink good drinks. Listen to good music (rumor has it the space becomes a club on the weekends) and try some of the food that everyone talks about. That's next on my list!

It's Frothy Monkey. It's a Nashville staple. If you've lived here for more than a week, you know the drill by now and have, probably, been to a FM location. But know this: this location is ground zero. It's peak FM and 12 South. Come here only when willing to go directly into the belly of the beast.

I don't spend a lot of time in 12 South. I'd like to explore the residential parts of the neighborhood but the actual 12 Avenue South strip makes me a wee bit crazy. It's congested. It's packed with bachelorettes taking the same picture over and over. If on the sidewalk, you will get knocked over by a dog or a double-wide or both. It's a lot. But, a work reason brought me to the neighborhood and when that reason was over, I decided to stay and grab some breakfast. Honestly, I'd scored a rockstar parking place and I wanted to revel in it for as long as possible. 

I made the short walk to FM (at 1030 am) and... ugh. Seriously? Packed. The place was packed. How is it that, during a school day, there are so many people loitering around? What is happening?? Get off my lawn! I took a deep breath and made my way inside. The longish line gave me an opportunity to decide what I wanted so I wasn't gumming up the works with ums and ahs when I made it to the counter. Before too too long, it was my turn to order: 'a gluten-free Julie and raspberry matcha tea, please.' Done. I grabbed a number, gave it to my friend to source out a seat and I stayed up front to pay and grab the drinks. 

Since it was so crowded, we had to make our way to the side room (abutting the deck). I didn't mind but it is galley-like. If you have claustrophobia, be advised. But any anxiousness on my part was washed away with one sip of the seasonal tea concoction. A pint glass full of dark green (color) tea, with a base of raspberry syrup and a floater of sparkling water will always put me in a good mood. Seriously. If this is on the menu, order it. FM seasonal drinks are always a win. My Julie came out soon after. Made on gluten-free bread rather than a bagel, this was a very satisfying breakfast sandwich: eggs, feta, basil, and tomato. Simple ingredients but very filling & very tasty.

Hunger abated, I was ready to face the world again. I still maintain that this location is entirely too busy (good for them; bananas for me) for me to be a regular but when in the neighborhood and in need of something quick and substantial, I can see myself returning. There's a reason the brand does so well and populates new areas on the regular. If you don't know, find out.

Nashville, I can't keep up with you. Who knew that a Pleasantville-like community popped up behind The Mall at Green Hills. Businesses. Condos. A HOTEL? And Deb Paquette's new venture, etc. Immediately, I think that the universe did her a solid by complicating matters in Sylvan Park and forcing a relocation to Green Hills. This restaurant works so much better in this neighborhood. The area locals will be able to keep it packed (as it was on a Thursday night) and the vibe/POV of the place goes far better in Green Hills than I would imagine it would in Sylvan Park. #thingsworkout

etc. is my first Paquette restaurant. I missed the Zola train and I have yet to eat at Etch (many many long stories). Due to the end of the month bringing a hole to our Yelp Nashville team, I thought a celebratory/good-bye dinner at a new Paquette restaurant was just what we needed. I was right. First off, make reservations. As you might imagine, the interest in eating here is high. Valet parking is the name of the game but there was some limited street parking available at night. I can't imagine, though, that it's easy to come by. Valet is complimentary with an expected tip for the porter.
